    Extension · The hypergraph family 1/8

    The arity of a relation: why pairs are sometimes not enough

    A hypergraph is not the only way to record who is connected to whom, and it is not always the right one. This section places it among its relatives — directed graphs, bipartite graphs, multigraphs — explains the two equivalent ways of defining a hypergraph, and then spends three cards on the question the literature argues about most: where the hyperedges actually come from. That last question is the one Chapter 7 puts to this paper.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThe arity of a relation is the number of objects it involves simultaneously. A binary (pairwise) relation has arity 2; an -ary relation involves objects at once. An ordinary graph can only record relations of arity 2, whereas a hypergraph places no restriction on arity.How many things does one relationship involve at the same time? Two — that is what a normal graph can hold. Some relationships genuinely involve five, or nine hundred.

    Where pairwise edges break down. Take co-authorship. A paper by four people is one event involving four people at once. Write it as pairs and you get six edges: . Three separate problems follow, and they are worth stating separately because they are the reason this family of models exists.

    • The count explodes. A relation over 982 objects needs up to 481,671 pairs. DBLP-Conf has 20 such relations — the pairwise version would be millions of edges carrying less information than the original 20.
    • Provenance is lost. From the six edges you cannot tell whether the four people wrote one paper together or whether Alice–Bob, Bob–Carol and so on were three unrelated collaborations that happened to share names.
    • The pairs are not independent. The six edges all co-occur: if one exists, the others are implied. Any model that treats them as six separate observations has mistaken one event for six.

    The point is not that graphs are wrong. It is that arity is a property of the data, and a model that fixes it at 2 makes a choice on the data's behalf. This paper's ten datasets split cleanly along that line: four are genuinely pairwise (citations, follows), and six involve relations of higher arity. Chapter 6's Table I marks the two groups, and the paper's results lean on the distinction.

    Keep the phrase higher-arity relation in mind. It is the accurate name for what a hyperedge represents, and it is the term used in the literature this paper's Related Work section surveys.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — arity three, by hand. Three friends split a restaurant bill together: Ana, Bo and Cai. The relationship "shared this meal" involves all three at once, so its arity is 3.

    RepresentationEncodingWhat is preserved
    Hyperedge — 1 relationthe meal as one event; arity 3
    Pairwise graphAna–Bo, Bo–Cai, Ana–Cai — 3 edgeswho sat together, but not that it was one meal

    Both encodings contain the same three names. Only the first can answer "how many group meals were there?" — because only the first stores a group as a thing.

    Now scale it: suppose 900 people attended a single conference. The hypergraph records one relation.
    This is DBLP-Conf's situation exactly: 4,057 authors gathered by 20 hyperedges, each embracing about a thousand of them.
    The pairwise version needs edges for that one conference.
    The combinatorial cost is quadratic. It is the first thing to estimate when deciding whether a hypergraph is worth it.
    And even after paying it, none of those 404,550 edges records that the people were at the same conference rather than in 404,550 separate pairs.
    This is the deeper cost: the expansion is not merely expensive, it is lossy in the direction that matters. Reason enough that the field built models for the unexpanded object instead.
    Not every multi-party event should become a hyperedge. A phone call among three people is awkward to model either way, and a group chat with a thousand members is closer to a broadcast than to a relation. The test is whether the group itself is a meaningful unit — "bought on the same receipt", "published in the same venue", "enrolled in the same course". If the group is not the unit, pairwise edges are honest and a hyperedge is decoration.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDA paper has 5 authors. How many pairwise edges does the co-authorship relation require, and how many hyperedges?

    APPLYA department has 12 people who jointly wrote one report. How many pairwise edges would the full expansion require? edges

    TRANSFERWhich of these is not a good reason to prefer a hypergraph over a pairwise graph?

    Where this is going: arity is one axis along which a model can specialise. Card 2 lays out the others — and shows that the hypergraph is one point in a family of choices, not a single answer.
    Extension · The hypergraph family 2/8

    The family of relational structures, and which choice each one makes

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA relational structure is fixed by independent modelling choices: the maximum arity of a relation (2, or unbounded); whether relations are directed; whether two objects may be related more than once, and with what weight; and whether the objects fall into distinct kinds that may only relate across kinds. A structure is named by which of these it relaxes.There is more than one way to record who is related to whom, and each way makes a different compromise. Picking the right one is a modelling decision, not a notation preference.
    StructureWhat it relaxesCanonical example
    Ordinary graph— (arity 2, undirected, single edges)friendship between people
    Directed graphdirectionwho follows whom; who cites whom
    Weighted graphsingle edges → weightsnumber of e-mails exchanged
    Multigraphsingle edges → parallel edgesseveral distinct flights between two cities
    Bipartite graphobjects split into two kindsusers and the films they rated
    Hypergrapharityauthors and the papers they co-wrote

    These choices are independent, which is why the family is a grid rather than a ladder: you can have a weighted directed hypergraph, and the literature contains such things. A hypergraph is not a more advanced graph; it is a graph that has given up the arity restriction. It makes no claim about direction, weights or kinds.

    This paper treats several genuinely directed relations — citations in Cora, follows in Github — as undirected. That is a deliberate simplification inherited from the datasets' standard usage, and it is not the same decision as using a hypergraph. When Chapter 7 asks what the paper does not address, direction is one of the items worth remembering.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — one dataset, five structures. Take a music streaming service with users and songs, where each user has several listening sessions, and each session is a list of songs played in order.

    • Bipartite graph — users on one side, songs on the other, a link for each play. Good for "who listens to what"; it treats users and songs as different kinds of thing.
    • Ordinary graph on songs — link two songs if one user played them back to back. Every link is a pair, so a 30-song session becomes 29 links and the session is gone.
    • Directed graph on songs — the same links with an arrow. Preserves order, still loses the session.
    • Weighted graph on songs — weight each link by how often that transition happens. Preserves frequency, still loses the session.
    • Hypergraph on songs — one hyperedge per session, containing every song played in it. Preserves the session as a unit; loses the order within the session.
    Notice that no structure wins outright: the hypergraph preserves the group but discards the ordering, and a directed graph does the reverse. The right question is never "which structure is better" but "which property of my data do I refuse to lose" — and then checking that the method you pick does not quietly require the property you sacrificed.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich restriction does a hypergraph relax, relative to an ordinary graph?

    APPLYA dataset has 40 listening sessions, with 15 songs in each on average. How many hyperedges does the session-based hypergraph have? hyperedges

    TRANSFERA dataset records that Alice follows Bob, but Bob does not follow Alice. Which structure records this without loss?

    Where this is going: having chosen the hypergraph, there are still two equivalent ways to write one down. Card 3 gives both, and shows why the matrix version is the one that ends up in the paper's equations.
    Extension · The hypergraph family 3/8

    Two equivalent definitions of a hypergraph

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA hypergraph may be defined set-theoretically as a pair where is a finite set and is a collection of non-empty subsets of ; or matrix-theoretically as a 0/1 matrix with rows and columns, where exactly when . The two definitions carry exactly the same information: the columns of the matrix are the elements of , and reconstructing one from the other is mechanical.A hypergraph is either "a set of vertices plus a list of groups", or "a table of 0s and 1s". They are the same object written two ways.

    Why the matrix definition is the one that matters here. A set-theoretic object cannot be added, multiplied or differentiated. Every learning method needs arithmetic, so at some point the group structure has to become numbers — and the incidence matrix is that translation. The paper's Equation (3) sums a row of it; Equation (1) multiplies by it and by its transpose. Once the object is a matrix, "which groups does this vertex belong to" becomes "what is this row's sum".

    And the translation is lossless, with one caveat worth naming. The matrix records the memberships faithfully, but it records them in a chosen order of rows and columns. Reorder the columns and you have the same hypergraph written differently — which is why the paper's invariance lemma is stated about exchanging columns rather than about permuting vertices. Both are relabellings of the same object.

    A pair of terms you will meet in the literature: a hypergraph is uniform if all hyperedges have the same size, and simple if no hyperedge is contained in another. Neither is required here. This paper's datasets are neither uniform (edge degrees run from 2 to 982) nor generally simple.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the dorm, both ways. Vertices ; one relation, "lives in dorm 302".

    Set-theoreticMatrix
    The whole object
    "Who is in the group?"look inside the one element of read column 1
    "How many groups is Zhang in?"count elements of containing sum row 1
    Take the matrix of the four-person graph used in the graph-theory section: 4 rows, 3 columns, sixteen 1s and 0s in total.
    Start from the matrix and recover the sets — the direction you need when reading a paper that only shows you the matrix.
    Read column 2 top to bottom: entries , , , .
    The 1s sit in rows 2 and 3, so the hyperedge is — a pair. You have just turned a column of a matrix back into a set of vertices.
    Now do the same for column 1: 1s in rows 1 and 2, so . And column 3: 1s in rows 2 and 4, so .
    All three columns turned out to hold exactly two 1s, which is the signature of a plain graph. Had one column held three, the object would have been a genuine hypergraph — and that is a check you can run on any incidence matrix in a paper.
    Here is a shortcut worth carrying: count the ones in each column. All 2 → a plain graph. Some larger → a hypergraph, and the largest column tells you the largest group the data contains. For DBLP-Conf that largest column holds about a thousand authors, which is the fact that makes the dataset interesting.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDIn the matrix definition, what does a column with four 1s represent?

    APPLYAn incidence matrix has 25 rows, 8 columns and 60 entries equal to 1. What is the average vertex degree? degree

    TRANSFERWhy does a paper state its invariance result as "columns may be exchanged" rather than "vertices may be relabelled"?

    Where this is going: knowing that a hyperedge is a set leaves the hard question untouched — namely, where the sets come from. Cards 4 and 5 are about the two very different answers, and the choice between them changes what the model can learn.
    Extension · The hypergraph family 4/8

    Where hyperedges come from (1): when the data already has groups

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA hypergraph is called native when each hyperedge corresponds to an event or container that exists in the data independently of any modelling choice — a publication, a purchase, a session, an enrolment. In that case the hyperedge is read off the record rather than invented, and the incidence matrix is filled in directly.Sometimes the groups are simply there in the data. A paper has authors; a receipt has items; a class has students. You read the group off the record — you do not have to invent it.

    This is the case where a hypergraph is unambiguously the right structure, because forcing the data into pairs would destroy a unit that the data itself treats as a unit. The modelling questions do not disappear entirely — you still have to decide what counts as an event (is one paper an event, or a whole journal issue?) — but the hyperedges are not fabricated out of similarity.

    DataVertexHyperedgeWhere the group comes from
    Co-authorshipauthorone publicationthe author list on the paper
    Market basketsproductone receiptthe items on that transaction
    Course enrolmentstudentone coursethe class roster
    Co-citationpaperpapers cited togetherthe reference list of a citing paper
    Browsing sessionspageone sessionthe sessionised click stream
    Conference listsauthorone conferenceeveryone who published there
    Even in the native case, one decision is unavoidable: how large a group is allowed to be. A conference with 982 authors produces a hyperedge that is essentially a broadcast — it says "these people are all in this field" and nothing more specific. Truncating, weighting or splitting such groups is a judgement call, and it is a call the dataset does not make for you.
    EXAMPLE
    Take DBLP-Conf: 4,057 authors and 20 hyperedges with an average size of 982.2. The paper says these hyperedges are formed from shared authorship, shared terms or a shared venue — so they are read off the data rather than invented.
    This dataset is native — the conference is the event, and the membership is the author list.
    Read one column of the incidence matrix: 982 rows carry a 1, the remaining 3,075 carry a 0.
    One relation, almost a quarter of the dataset as its members. This is what "higher arity" looks like at full scale — and it is why the paper needs a normalisation that damps large relations.
    Now ask what such a hyperedge can express. Any two authors at that conference become neighbours of each other through it.
    The relation is real but coarse. It says "could have met" rather than "worked together". Contrast the same dataset's other use: co-authorship hyperedges would have size 2–10 and carry far more specific information. Same domain, two different native groupings, two very different graphs.
    That last step is the important one for reading papers critically. "DBLP-Conf" does not name a dataset; it names a decision about what the groups are. When Chapter 7 asks whether the authors' choice of hyperedges was justified, this is the kind of choice being questioned.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhat distinguishes a native hypergraph from a constructed one?

    APPLYA bookshop records 500 receipts, each with 6 books on average. How many memberships does the resulting hypergraph contain? memberships

    TRANSFERFor a co-authorship dataset, which choice is not settled by the data itself?

    Where this is going: most datasets do not arrive with groups. Card 5 covers the other answer — inventing hyperedges from features — which is what this paper does for several of its ten datasets.
    Extension · The hypergraph family 5/8

    Where hyperedges come from (2): inventing them from the data

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA hypergraph is called constructed when the data supplies no groups and the hyperedges are produced by a stated procedure — most commonly by joining each vertex to its nearest neighbours under some similarity, or by expanding an existing graph. In that case the hypergraph is an artefact of the procedure and its parameters, not a record of the data.Sometimes there are no groups in the data at all — just a table of numbers. Then you have to manufacture the groups yourself, and how you manufacture them decides what the model sees.

    Why anyone would do this. Many datasets are tables: a patient with a set of clinical measurements, a point cloud with coordinates, a credit application. There is no relation recorded anywhere. But the rows still resemble each other, and similarity is enough to build structure — join every row to the rows most like it, and call each neighbourhood a hyperedge.

    ProcedureHow the hyperedge is formedCharacteristic weakness
    -nearest neighbourseach vertex plus its most similar verticesevery group has the same size; similarity is forced even where none exists
    Clique expansionevery pair inside a dense region becomes an edgequadratic blow-up; the group ceases to be a unit
    Star expansionadd an auxiliary vertex per group and connect itthe auxiliary vertex carries no meaning of its own
    Threshold / attributeall vertices of one category, or above a similarity cutgroup sizes swing wildly; the threshold is another hidden parameter

    The consequence to hold onto: the hypergraph is now a hyperparameter. Two datasets of the same underlying data, processed with and , are different hypergraphs — different edge degrees, different vertex degrees, different numbers of relations. Every reported number describes one point in that space, and none of the differences came from the data.

    This is the sharpest critical question you can put to a paper that constructs its hyperedges: the choice of construction is a free parameter, so what happens at other settings? Hold that question; Chapter 7 returns to it with this paper's own numbers.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a point cloud becomes a hypergraph. ModelNet40 is a collection of 3D shapes; each shape is a cloud of points with coordinates. Nothing in it is a relation. This paper turns it into a hypergraph in three steps.

    Convert each point cloud into a table: one row per shape, columns for geometric features.
    Nothing relational has happened yet. This is an ordinary feature matrix, the kind a decision tree would eat directly.
    Measure similarity between rows — here, distance in feature space.
    Similarity is the raw material a constructed hypergraph is made of. It exists whether or not the data intends it: two shapes will always be nearer or farther.
    For each row, take its nearest neighbours and declare that set of rows one hyperedge.
    The hypergraph now exists. Note precisely what decided its shape: a distance function and a number , neither of which came from ModelNet40 itself. Change and every column of Table I's ModelNet40 row changes.

    Example 2 — how much a single number moves. With rows and , each vertex belongs to 6 hyperedges only if neighbourhoods are perfectly symmetric; in general the count varies. Push to 50 and every hyperedge grows tenfold while the number of vertices does not move at all.

    The honest reading of a constructed hypergraph is therefore: "this is what the data looks like under the procedure and parameter I chose." That is not a criticism — it is what any feature engineering is. It only becomes a problem when the paper reports the hypergraph as though it were a property of the dataset. Both Heloc (credit data) and ModelNet40 in this paper's Table I are of this kind.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDIn a -nearest-neighbour construction, what determines the size of a hyperedge?

    APPLYA dataset of 800 rows is turned into a hypergraph with . How many members does each hyperedge hold? members

    TRANSFERA paper constructs hyperedges by -NN with chosen from a small range and reports no experiments at other values. What is the precise nature of the concern?

    Where this is going: whenever a constructed hypergraph is used, the model it feeds is being evaluated on an artefact of a parameter choice. Card 6 turns to the last question in this section: given a hypergraph, why would anyone convert it back into a plain graph?
    Extension · The hypergraph family 6/8

    Converting back: three ways to turn a hypergraph into a graph

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONAn expansion converts a hypergraph into a graph so that graph-based methods can be applied to it. The clique expansion replaces each hyperedge by all pairs of its members. The star expansion introduces one auxiliary vertex per hyperedge and connects it to every member. The line (or dual) expansion swaps the roles, making each hyperedge a vertex and joining two hyperedges when they share a member.If you already have a tool that works on pairs and you do not want to write a new one for groups, you can rewrite the groups as pairs — three standard ways, each throwing away something different.

    Why this is a live option rather than a historical curiosity. The graph-learning toolbox is vast and mature; the hypergraph toolbox is small. Expansion lets a hypergraph problem be solved with an off-the-shelf graph network, which is exactly what several of this paper's baselines do. The paper's own approach is the opposite bet: keep the hypergraph intact and handle it directly.

    ExpansionWhat is addedWhat is lostCost for a hyperedge of size
    Clique pairwise edgesthe group as a unit; all pairs look independent — quadratic
    Star edges plus 1 auxiliary vertexauxiliary vertices are meaningless objects — linear
    Line / dualone vertex per hyperedgethe distinction between members and relationsroles swap, not expand
    Keeping itnothingnothing1 relation, unchanged
    The row that matters is the last one. Every expansion trades structure for compatibility, and the trade is irreversible: once a 982-member hyperedge is expanded, no downstream method can recover the fact that those 481,671 pairs were one event. This is the precise sense in which this paper's "keep the hypergraph" stance is a real choice and not a stylistic one.
    EXAMPLE
    Take a hyperedge of size 10 — a ten-author paper, say.
    Small enough to enumerate. The pattern is what matters.
    Clique expansion: all pairs of the 10 authors, which is edges.
    The relation's arity has been paid for quadratically — 45 edges for 1 event. And all 45 are now indistinguishable from 45 independent collaborations.
    Star expansion: introduce one auxiliary vertex (the paper itself) and connect all 10 authors to it — 10 edges, plus 1 new vertex.
    Linear instead of quadratic, and it preserves the grouping: everyone connected to the same auxiliary vertex was on the same paper. The price is a graph in which 10 of the 11 vertices are people and one is an artefact.
    Line expansion: make the paper a vertex and the authors into... nothing, since an author with several papers would need to be a hyperedge itself.
    This is the dual view the bipartite formulation already gives you. It is the right move when the relations are the objects of interest — for instance when classifying venues rather than authors.

    Example 2 — why the choice shows up in the results. Apply clique expansion to DBLP-Conf and one 982-member hyperedge becomes 481,671 edges. Run a graph network on that and the structure is dominated by a handful of enormous conferences; run it on the star expansion and the auxiliary vertices are 20 out of 4,077. The same dataset, two graphs, two different sets of numbers — which is why a results table is only interpretable alongside the construction it used.

    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich expansion introduces new vertices that were not in the original data?

    APPLYClique expansion is applied to a hyperedge of size 8. How many pairwise edges does it produce? edges

    TRANSFERWhy would a research group choose to keep the hypergraph rather than expand it, given the maturity of graph-learning tooling?

    Where this is going: having seen where hyperedges come from and how they can be converted away, card 7 assembles the section and states the rule this all implies for reading a results table.
    Extension · The hypergraph family 7/8

    The hypergraph is a modelling decision, not a property of the dataset

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONTwo hypergraphs over the same underlying records are equivalent as datasets but not as objects if they differ in arity structure, in edge construction, in weighting, or in which records were treated as groups. Every downstream quantity — edge degrees, vertex degrees, what a network can learn — is a property of the hypergraph, not of the records it was built from.The same data can honestly produce several different hypergraphs. Which one you get depends on decisions someone made, and every number in the paper describes the one that was chosen.
    • Are the groups native or constructed? Native groups are read off records (conferences, receipts); constructed ones are manufactured from similarity, and their parameters are free.
    • What counts as a group? One paper, or one research lab, or one year at one venue — each is defensible and each gives different edge sizes.
    • Is the object kept or expanded? Keeping it preserves groups; clique expansion publishes 481,671 edges where the group used to be.
    • Do you normalise? Without degree normalisation, one 982-member relation dominates its 982 members' every result.

    This paper's own position, stated plainly. It keeps the hypergraph and handles it directly; it does not expand. Six of its ten datasets arrive as hypergraphs; the other four are plain graphs whose hyperedges it must construct. For those four it uses -nearest neighbours, with in a small range chosen by judgement. Those are the paper's choices, and they are the terms on which its numbers should be read.

    The habit to carry away: whenever a results table comes from a dataset that had to be built, ask what the building parameters were and whether they were varied. A number produced under one untested parameter setting is a description, not a claim about the method. Chapter 7 puts exactly this question to this paper.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the same ten datasets, read as a column about provenance. Table I's Type column marks four datasets as graphs and six as hypergraphs. That marking is about what the data arrived as, not about what the method consumes — after preprocessing, all ten are hypergraphs.

    For DBLP-Conf, CA-Cora and CC-Cora the relations are native: the paper reads groups off the data (co-authorship, co-citation, a shared venue) rather than inventing them from similarity.
    Nothing needed to be invented, so there is no to interrogate — but there is still the question of scope: a whole-conference hyperedge of 982 members is a very coarse relation.
    For ModelNet40 and Heloc the relations are constructed from feature similarity, and here directly sets every hyperedge's size.
    This is the case where the artefact argument bites hardest. The hypergraph is what these rows of Table I are under one setting of one parameter.
    For Cora, Github and the two Amazon datasets — marked as graphs — hyperedges must also be constructed before the paper's method can run.
    So the four "graph" rows are not a control group free of construction. Every one of the ten rows passed through some preprocessing that the results inherit. Notice that this is not a criticism of the paper; it is what reading an experimental table honestly requires.
    You now have what you need to read Table I the way its authors read it. When Chapter 6 walks that table, the Type column will not be a label to memorise but a statement about where each dataset's relations came from — and Chapter 7's critique of the untested will not be a surprise but a conclusion you reached yourself.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDTable I labels four datasets as graphs. After preprocessing, what does the method actually consume?

    APPLYFor a dataset whose hyperedges are built by -NN with , how many members does each hyperedge initially hold? members

    TRANSFERYou are reviewing a paper that builds hyperedges with a fixed and reports results at that setting only. What is the most useful question to ask?

    Pre-knowledge · in this paper

    Hypergraphs in this paper: the object every equation runs on

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThis paper writes a hypergraph as with vertices and hyperedges, and represents it throughout by its incidence matrix . Every dataset in the paper is expressed in this form before anything is learned, and Equation (3) sums a row of to obtain each vertex's structural knowledge.In this paper the hypergraph is not the setting — it is the thing being processed. The paper writes it as a 0/1 table and every later equation is arithmetic on that table.

    What the paper commits to, in two decisions. The general section left open four questions: are the groups native or constructed, is the object kept or expanded, is it normalised, and what counts as a group. This paper answers three of them explicitly and leaves the fourth — the construction parameter — open, which is exactly what Chapter 7 will press on.

    DecisionThis paper's answerConsequence
    Keep or expand?Keep. No clique or star expansion anywhere.Relations of arity 982 stay intact — Equation (1) is written on the incidence matrix, not on a graph
    Normalise?Yes, on both the vertex and the hyperedge sideOne 982-member hyperedge cannot swamp its 982 members' every result
    Native or constructed?Both. Six datasets arrive as hypergraphs; four are built from plain graphsThe four graph rows of Table I are not construction-free
    What counts as a group? (constructed case)-nearest neighbours in feature space, chosen by judgementEvery hyperedge of those datasets is an artefact of one untested parameter — see Chapter 7
    The notation carries one trap worth fixing now. The paper uses for the hypergraph and for its incidence matrix; both appear in the same equations. It also uses for the hyperedge set and for experimental settings in Chapter 6's tables. Read each symbol by what it is doing in its line, not by its letter.

    Where the object enters the method. Equation (3) computes each vertex's structural knowledge by summing one row of — the vertex degree, which the graph-theory section showed you how to count. Equation (1) multiplies by and then by , which is the vertex → hyperedge → vertex round trip. Both operations were already carried out by hand in the two extension sections; nothing new is required here.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — read the paper's own extreme case. Table I's DBLP-Conf row: authors, hyperedges, average edge degree 982.2, average vertex degree 4.8.

    Write the incidence matrix: rows and columns, so entries in total.
    Shapes first, always. Comparing that against an adjacency matrix's entries shows why the incidence form is the compact one for this data.
    Only 19,644 of those entries are 1, because — about a quarter of the table.
    Compare the size of the two encodings rather than their density: the adjacency form of this dataset would need entries, roughly two hundred times as many as the here. Sparsity is what makes the incidence form usable at this scale, and it is why implementations store edge lists rather than the matrix itself.
    Sum a row and you get a vertex degree; average them and you get 4.84, which rounds to the 4.8 the table prints.
    The identity from the graph-theory section, now on the paper's own numbers. You have reproduced a column of Table I from the other two columns — which is precisely the kind of check Chapter 6 will ask you to perform on every table.

    Walk 2 — what the paper does to the four graph datasets. Cora, Github and the two Amazon datasets arrive as plain graphs: pairwise citations, follows and co-purchases. The method needs relations of the hypergraph form, so hyperedges are constructed for them.

    • The construction is -nearest neighbours in feature space: each vertex plus its most similar vertices becomes one hyperedge.
    • So all ten datasets are hypergraphs by the time the method runs. Table I's Type column records what each dataset arrived as, not what the network consumes.
    • The consequence is that the four 'graph' rows are not a control group free of preprocessing. Whatever governed the construction of their hyperedges is inherited by every score in those rows.
    This is the single most important thing to carry from this card into Chapter 6. When you read Table I's Type column, you are reading a statement about provenance — and when Chapter 7 asks whether the untested undermines the results, the question applies to all ten rows, not only to the six labelled as hypergraphs.

    Extension · Decision trees 1/8

    What a decision tree is

    Gradient-boosted decision trees are the model the paper trains, and a boosted model is nothing but many small trees added together. This section builds the single tree from zero: how it asks questions, how it chooses which question to ask (entropy, gain ratio, Gini), why it memorises its training set, and the four ways it fails. Nothing here assumes you have seen a tree before, and everything here is assumed by the boosting section that follows.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA decision tree is a predictor that routes an input through a fixed sequence of tests to exactly one region. Each internal node holds one test on one feature: for a numeric feature a threshold comparison against a constant ; for a categorical feature a membership question against a chosen subset of that feature's categories. Each leaf holds a prediction — the majority class of the training rows that reached it, if the target is a class; their mean, if the target is a number. To predict for an input you start at the root, follow the branch each test selects, and read off the leaf you arrive at. The tree therefore partitions the feature space into one region per leaf, and the prediction is constant on each region.A decision tree is a flowchart of questions about the features; you answer each question in turn, follow the branch, and the leaf you land on holds the answer.

    The whole model is a readable list of rules. Every path from the root to a leaf is a conjunction — the tests along that path, joined by AND. Reading all the paths off a tree gives you an if-then rule list that a domain expert can inspect, argue with, and overrule. Almost no other model of comparable accuracy offers this, and it is the reason trees are still the default first attempt on structured business data.

    Why tabular data in particular. A tree makes no assumption that the features are comparable to each other, no assumption that the rows have an intrinsic distance, and no assumption that the prediction varies smoothly as a feature moves. It uses each feature only through the question or . This matters because real tables are mixtures: an age in years next to a country code next to a price in yuan. A tree consumes all three without any preprocessing, and it does not care whether you measured the age in days or in decades — multiplying a feature by a positive constant merely renames every threshold to , and the same partition results.

    One tree is readable; the model in the paper is not. A boosted model is a sum of hundreds of small trees, and the sum of hundreds of readable rules is not itself readable. Keep the scale of the claim straight: the tree is the unit you have to understand in order to understand the ensemble, not a description of what the ensemble outputs.

    What this section does. Card 2 explains how a tree decides which question to ask, and names the three classical measures of a good question. Cards 3, 4 and 5 work each measure through on real numbers and introduce the three algorithms that use them — ID3, C4.5 and CART. Card 6 covers pruning, card 7 gives the four concrete ways a tree fails, and card 8 is the skip check.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — one tree, walked by hand. The task is to decide whether to play outside, from two features: temperature in degrees, and wind, which is either Weak or Strong. The tree has two internal nodes and three leaves:

    • Root test: is temperature ? If yes, go left to Leaf A.
    • If no, go right and ask a second question: is wind = Strong? If yes, go to Leaf B; if no, go to Leaf C.
    • Leaf A holds the prediction No. Leaf B holds No. Leaf C holds Yes.
    Predict for the input temperature , wind Strong. The root asks: is ? Yes. Go left.
    The test is evaluated, not discussed. There is no arithmetic on the second feature at all, because this branch never asks about wind.
    The left branch is Leaf A, which holds No. The prediction is No.
    A leaf terminates the route. Every input stops at exactly one leaf, and the leaf's stored value is the prediction.
    Predict for temperature , wind Weak. Is ? No. Go right. Is wind Strong? No, it is Weak. Go right again to Leaf C.
    This input takes a longer path, so it is answered by a narrower rule — it had to satisfy both tests rather than one. That is where the conjunctions in the rule list come from.
    Leaf C holds Yes, so the prediction is Yes. For contrast, temperature with wind Strong also goes right at the root, then takes the left branch at the second node and lands in Leaf B, predicting No.
    Two inputs that agree on temperature and differ only in wind receive different predictions whenever the temperature is above 20 — which is exactly what the second test is for.

    Example 2 — the same tree as a rule list and as a partition. Walking every root-to-leaf path and joining the tests along it with AND gives the entire model in three lines:

    1. IF temperature THEN No.
    2. IF temperature AND wind Strong THEN No.
    3. IF temperature AND wind Weak THEN Yes.

    Equivalently, the tree carves the plane of (temperature, wind) into three regions, one per leaf:

    RegionCondition that defines itPrediction
    1temperature No
    2temperature and wind StrongNo
    3temperature and wind WeakYes

    Two structural facts are worth reading off this table. First, the regions are nested, not overlapping: region 2 and region 3 both live inside the half-plane temperature , and between them they leave no gap, so every possible input lands in exactly one region. Second, the boundary between regions 2 and 3 is a vertical line in the wind direction and runs the whole length of the temperature range above 20 — a tree's boundaries are always perpendicular to one feature axis, never diagonal.

    What this example does not show. It is a classification tree, so its leaves hold class labels; a regression tree's leaves hold numbers instead, and card 5 works one out. It also never asks about a feature twice on the same path, and it has only two levels of tests. Both gaps are filled later: re-asking a feature is legal (card 7 uses it to explain instability), and depth is what cards 6 and 7 are about.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDIn a decision tree, what exactly does a leaf hold?

    APPLYA binary decision tree in which every internal node has exactly two children, and in which every root-to-leaf path contains exactly 3 tests, is grown until no further tests are allowed. At most how many leaves can it have? leaves

    TRANSFERThe paper's model is a gradient-boosted ensemble of several hundred trees. Which statement about reading it off as rules is correct?

    TRANSFERMultiplying a numeric feature by 100 (so a temperature in degrees becomes a temperature in hundredths of a degree) is applied to a table, and the tree is then rebuilt from scratch on the rescaled table. What happens?

    Where this is going: a tree is defined, but nothing yet says how it chooses its tests. The next card supplies the criterion — a numerical score for "which question separates the labels best" — and names the three classical versions of it.
    Extension · Decision trees 2/8

    How a tree chooses which question to ask

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONAt a node holding a set of training rows, a candidate split is the partition of produced by one test on one feature. A splitting criterion is a function that scores each candidate split by how thoroughly it separates the class labels within the parts, and the tree is grown by taking the candidate with the best score (highest, for the gain-based criteria below). The score is always written as the impurity of the node before the split minus the impurity of the parts after it, where the impurity of a set of rows is a fixed function of the proportions of the classes in it.A splitting criterion is a score for a candidate question: it is the mixed-upness of the current pile of rows, minus the mixed-upness of the piles the question would create. The tree asks whichever question lowers mixed-upness the most.

    Impurity, informally. A node is the set of training rows that have survived the tests above it. Those rows carry class labels, and the node is impure to the extent that its labels disagree with each other. If every row in the node has the same label, the node is pure and there is nothing left to ask. If the labels are evenly split, the node is as mixed as it can be. A criterion is simply a way of turning that picture into a number.

    Two properties are wanted, and both entropy and Gini have them. An impurity measure should be zero at purity — so that splitting a pure node is never scored as an improvement — and it should be maximal when the classes are equally represented, so that the measure is largest exactly where the node is least informative. Both conditions also make the measure independent of which class is which: swapping the names of the classes does not change the number, which is what you want, since the labels are arbitrary names.

    This is why the quantity used is a smooth function of the proportions rather than the misclassification error of the node. Take the node with 3 rows of class A and 1 of class B, whose majority-class error is 0.25, and split it into a child holding 2 A and 0 B (error 0) and a child holding 1 A and 1 B (error 0.5). Weighting the children by size gives — identical to the parent, so the error criterion reports this split as worthless. The Gini criterion reports a gain of 0.125 for exactly the same split. The cause is that misclassification error is not strictly concave: it stays flat as long as the identity of the majority class does not change, so any split that purifies a node without making the other class the majority is invisible to it. A criterion has to detect those changes, because they are the ones that let the next level of the tree finish the job.

    The three families of algorithm differ only in which smooth function they use and how they divide one node's impurity drop by something. Here they are by name; cards 3, 4 and 5 work each through.

    Entropy, the measure used by ID3. The score for a candidate is the information gain: how much entropy the split destroys.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the entropy of the node — its mixed-up-ness, in bits. exactly when the node is pure.
    the number of distinct classes present in the node. For the two-class problems in this section, .
    the proportion of rows in whose label is class ; the proportions sum to 1. The intuition is that is the probability that a row drawn at random from the node is of class .
    how surprising getting a class- row is, measured as the length in bits of the shortest code for an event of probability . Rare classes give a large negative logarithm.
    the leading minus sign exists only because is negative (a probability is at most 1), and an impurity must be non-negative. The minus sign converts the surprise into a quantity that decreases as the node gets purer.
    Information gain for the test on feature : the node's entropy, minus the average entropy of the parts the test creates. The average is weighted by part size, so a large unusually mixed part counts for more than a small one.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the feature being tested — the question whose value is being scored
    the subset of rows in that the test sends to branch (for a numeric feature, is the side of the threshold; for a categorical feature, runs over the categories, or over the two sides of a subset test)
    the fraction of the node's rows that land in branch ; this is the weight of branch in the average. Large branches weigh more, which is what stops a split from looking good merely by isolating one row.
    summed over every branch of the test, so the second term is the weighted average child entropy
    the entropy destroyed, in bits. means the test told you nothing about the label; means the parts came out perfectly pure.
    Gain ratio, used by C4.5. is the entropy of the branch assignment itself — it measures how finely the test cuts the node, ignoring the labels entirely. Dividing by it charges a split for the number and balance of the pieces it makes. Card 4 shows the bias this repairs and the new one it introduces.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the entropy of the partition the test induces, computed from branch sizes with no reference to the labels at all
    information gain per unit of splitting — the same kind of normalisation as measuring fuel per passenger rather than fuel per trip
    again the logarithm of a size, with the same meaning as before: the information content of the branch chosen
    Gini impurity, used by CART. Read it as a probability that reveals what it measures: the sum is the probability that two rows drawn independently from the node have the same label, so Gini impurity is the probability that they disagree.
    SymbolWhat it means
    is the chance a random pair of rows agrees; one minus that is the chance they disagree, which is exactly the mixed-up-ness wanted
    the chance that both members of the pair are of class , since the two draws are independent
    the CART impurity. It has the same two anchor points as entropy: 0 at purity, and its largest value when all classes are equally frequent.
    The criterion is greedy, not optimal. At each node the tree takes the single best-scoring test available locally, with no lookahead, because choosing the smallest tree that fits the data exactly is computationally intractable: the value of a split cannot be judged without knowing which splits follow it, so the search does not decompose into independent subproblems. Every algorithm in this section is greedy, and card 6 shows the concrete price of that: a test that scores zero can be the necessary first step of a perfect tree.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — what impurity looks like at the two extremes and between them. Two-class nodes, characterised by the proportion of the larger class. Zero means pure; 0.5 means perfectly balanced. Both measures anchor at the same two points and rise between them:

    Proportion of the larger class, pEntropy H (bits)Gini impurity
    1.00 (pure node)0.00000.0000
    0.900.46900.1800
    0.750.81130.3750
    0.50 (most mixed)1.00000.5000

    Two readings of the table. The endpoints are the ones the criterion needs: a pure node scores zero under both measures, so no test can be credited with improving an already-pure node, and the perfectly balanced node is the maximum under both. The scales differ — entropy reaches 1, Gini only 0.5, so the two numbers are never compared with each other. What matters is that the ordering of splits is almost always the same, which is why ID3 and CART usually agree on which question to ask while disagreeing about numbers.

    Example 2 — one split, scored end to end. A node contains 6 training rows with labels Yes, Yes, No, No, No, No. That is 2 of one class and 4 of the other. A candidate test would send 3 of these rows one way and 3 the other way.

    Parent proportions: and . Entropy: . Numerically and , so bits.
    Gini of the same node: . Different number, same conclusion: the node is mixed, and neither measure says how it should be split.

    This is the division of labour in the whole section. The formula produces one number per candidate split; the algorithm compares the numbers and takes the largest. Everything that follows is the arithmetic of producing those numbers correctly, and the three-card sequence 3, 4, 5 is nothing more than three different choices of the formula.

    What this example does not show. It scores a node but does not perform a split, so it never exhibits the weighted-average term that is the actual heart of information gain. Card 3 computes that term in full, twice, on a six-row dataset.

    Extension · Decision trees 3/8

    ID3: information gain on a worked dataset

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONID3 grows a tree top-down by, at each node, computing the information gain of every remaining feature and splitting on the one with the highest gain. It recurses on each resulting child, using only the rows that reached that child and only the features not already used on the path above it, and stops a branch when its rows all share one label, when no feature remains, or when a pre-set stopping condition holds. The gain of a candidate feature at a node is : the entropy of the node before the split, minus the size-weighted average entropy of the parts afterwards.ID3 asks, at every node, which of the remaining features reduces the mixed-up-ness of the labels the most, splits on that feature, and repeats inside each resulting group.

    Why entropy measures mixed-up-ness. Take a node and draw one row at random from it. Before you look at the label, there is uncertainty about what you will see; if the node is pure, there is none. The term is the number of yes/no questions needed to pin down an outcome of probability , and averages it over the classes. So is the average number of bits you still need to transmit a row's label after being told only which node the row is in. A split that makes the labels easier to transmit has destroyed bits, and the count of bits destroyed is the information gain.

    Two arithmetic conventions are needed, and both are forced rather than chosen. A class that is absent from a node has , so its term is ; this is taken to be 0, because a class that does not occur carries no uncertainty and must not contribute. A class that is the only one present has and , so a pure node scores exactly 0 with no special case at all. Between them these make the measure continuous as a node approaches purity, which is what allows a split that produces a nearly pure child to be credited with nearly all of the node's entropy.

    A gain is a comparison at one node, not a property of a feature. The number depends on the node as well as on , and gains computed at different nodes are on different scales, because the parent entropies differ. A feature with a gain of 0.45 at one node and a feature with a gain of 0.30 at another are not ranked by those numbers relative to each other — each was compared only with its rivals at its own node. Reporting "the most important feature" by totalling gains across a whole tree, as if they were commensurable, is a common and unjustified summary.
    EXAMPLE

    The dataset. Six rows of a play-outside decision. Two features, Outlook and Wind, and the label Play.

    RowOutlookWindPlay
    1SunnyWeakNo
    2SunnyWeakNo
    3SunnyStrongNo
    4SunnyStrongYes
    5RainWeakYes
    6RainStrongYes

    The label column has 3 Yes and 3 No, so the root node is perfectly balanced. Everything below is arithmetic on this table.

    Step 1 — the root's entropy. With and : . Since , this is bit.
    A perfectly balanced two-class node is the maximum of entropy, so 1 bit is the whole budget available. Any gain below is a fraction of this 1, which makes the numbers easy to judge by eye.
    Step 2 — entropy of the Sunny branch. Outlook Sunny selects rows 1, 2, 3, 4, whose labels are No, No, No, Yes: 3 No to 1 Yes. So , , and . With and : the first term is and the second is , giving bit.
    Three quarters of the rows agree, so most of the surprise is gone: 0.8113 bits remain out of the original 1. The dominant part of what remains is the single Yes row, whose surprise is 0.5 bits on its own.
    Step 3 — entropy of the Rain branch. Outlook Rain selects rows 5 and 6, both Yes. So and bit.
    A pure node costs nothing. This is the case that needs no special handling: makes the formula report zero by itself.
    Step 4 — weight the two branch entropies by their sizes and subtract. Sunny holds 4 of the 6 rows and Rain holds 2 of 6, so the weighted average is bit. The gain is bit.
    The weighting is the part people drop. Without it, a test that isolates a single row into a pure leaf would look as good as a test that purifies half the data, because the unweighted average of 0 and 0 is 0 either way.
    Step 5 — repeat for Wind. Wind Weak selects rows 1, 2, 5: No, No, Yes, so , , and bit. Wind Strong selects rows 3, 4, 6: No, Yes, Yes, which is the mirror image with bit as well.
    Two branches with identical entropy is not a coincidence here: both are 2-to-1 splits in opposite directions, and entropy depends only on the proportions, never on which class is in the majority.
    Step 6 — Wind's gain. Both branches hold 3 of the 6 rows, so the weighted average is bit, and the gain is bit.
    Wind barely separates anything: each of its groups is still two-to-one mixed, so it has destroyed only 0.08 of the 1 bit available. Outlook destroyed 0.46. The comparison is decisive and the root test is Outlook.
    Step 7 — recurse on the Sunny branch. The Rain branch is pure and becomes a leaf labelled Yes. Inside Sunny the four rows No, No, No, Yes have entropy 0.8113 bit, and Outlook is now excluded because it was used on the path above. Wind splits those four into Weak (rows 1 and 2, both No, ) and Strong (rows 3 and 4, No and Yes, ). Weighted: . Gain: bit.
    The gain is smaller than the root gain only because the node itself was already less mixed; the two numbers are not comparable, which is exactly the warning in the callout above.
    Step 8 — stop, and look honestly at the result. The final tree tests Outlook at the root and Wind below the Sunny branch. Its leaves are: Rain gives Yes; Sunny and Weak gives No; Sunny and Strong holds rows 3 and 4, which are one No and one Yes. That leaf is a tie and no feature is left to break it, so the tree stops with a 50/50 leaf and assigns it a label by an arbitrary tie-break.
    The dataset is simply not separable by these two features: rows 3 and 4 agree on both Outlook and Wind and disagree on Play. No tree on these two features can reach purity, and an honest algorithm reports the tie rather than hiding it. Adding a third feature is what would resolve this, and it is also the first symptom of why trees are grown until resource limits and then pruned back — see card 6.
    Reading the result as a sentence. The tree says: rain means play, and sun means play only when the wind is strong. That single sentence is the entire fitted model, and the arithmetic above is the entire reason the algorithm preferred that sentence to the alternative of asking about wind first.

    Extension · Decision trees 4/8

    C4.5: gain ratio, thresholds and pruning

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONC4.5 is ID3 with four changes. First, the score of a candidate split is the gain ratio , where is the entropy of the branch sizes alone. Second, a numeric feature is always tested with a two-sided threshold , and the candidate thresholds are the midpoints between consecutive distinct observed values. Third, branches are pruned after growing, by estimating the error of each subtree on a held-out portion and replacing it by a leaf whenever the estimate is no worse. Fourth, a row whose value for the tested feature is missing is not discarded: it is sent down every branch with a weight equal to that branch's share of the known rows, so its contribution is split in proportion.C4.5 is ID3 with the split score divided by a penalty for cutting the data into many pieces, with numeric features handled by a two-sided threshold, with missing values distributed down all branches, and with a pruning pass at the end.

    The bias that information gain has. Add a column to the six-row dataset that is the row number: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Every value is distinct, so testing this column splits the node into six branches of one row each. Every child is pure, so its entropy is 0, so the weighted average child entropy is 0, so the information gain is exactly 1.0000 bit — the maximum achievable. By the rule "take the largest gain" this useless column beats Outlook's 0.4591 and the tree's root test becomes the row identifier.

    The failure is not arithmetic; it is that a gain computed on the training rows cannot tell the difference between a test that explains the label and a test that indexes the rows. A column with distinct values can always partition rows into pure singletons, whatever the labels are, and it will do the same on any other dataset — which is to say it carries no information that generalises. The quantity that distinguishes the two cases is not the purity of the children but the number and balance of the pieces the test creates, and that quantity is measurable without any reference to the labels.

    is the entropy of the partition itself: feed it the branch sizes as if they were class proportions and it returns how finely the node was carved up. Dividing the gain by it converts the score from bits destroyed into bits destroyed per bit of splitting.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the share of the node's rows sent to branch ; the whole measure depends only on these shares, never on the labels
    0 when a test sends every row down one branch (no split at all); larger the more branches a test makes and the more evenly the rows are spread across them. For a balanced -way split it equals .
    gain per unit of splitting. Dividing by a size-dependent quantity is the same idea as normalising any count by its opportunity: a test that is allowed to make six pieces has six chances to look good, so its gain is charged six ways.
    Gain ratio has a defect of its own, and C4.5 patches it. When a test puts almost every row in one branch and a handful in another, is close to zero, and a tiny numerator over a tiny denominator can produce a very large ratio from a split that is obviously useless. The patch: at each node, first discard every candidate whose information gain is below the average information gain of all candidates at that node, and only then rank the survivors by gain ratio. The gain filter removes the degenerate uneven splits; the ratio then ranks what is left. Real implementations of C4.5 do exactly this two-stage selection, and skipping the first stage is a common way to get an inexplicably bad tree.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the same three candidates, scored three ways. This is the six-row dataset of card 3, plus the row-identifier column. The information gains were computed there in full; the new column is the penalty each test pays.

    Candidate featureInformation gainSplitInfo of the testGain ratio
    Outlook (2 branches, 4 and 2 rows)0.45910.91830.5000
    Wind (2 branches, 3 and 3 rows)0.08171.00000.0817
    Row number (6 branches of 1 row)1.00002.58500.3869
    for Outlook: the branch shares are and , so it is , exactly the entropy of a 2-to-1 split. Then .
    for Wind: two equal branches, so it is the entropy of a 50/50 split, . Then — dividing changed nothing, because the penalty is already 1.
    for the row number: six equal branches, so it is . Then .

    Reading the table honestly. The correction works, and it works only partly. Under information gain the order was row number 1.0000, Outlook 0.4591, Wind 0.0817 — the useless column came first and would have been chosen. Under gain ratio the order is Outlook 0.5000, row number 0.3869, Wind 0.0817 — the useless column has been demoted from first to second, and the tree now starts with Outlook, which is correct. But it is still ahead of Wind, and it still carries no generalisable information. Gain ratio is a repair, not a solution: the underlying problem is that any criterion evaluated on the training rows alone can be gamed by a sufficiently flexible feature, and the durable answer is to judge a tree on data it was not fitted to.

    Example 2 — a numeric feature, scanned threshold by threshold. Four rows, with a numeric Temperature and the label Play: 12 gives No, 18 gives Yes, 22 gives Yes, 27 gives No. Sorted, the distinct values are 12, 18, 22, 27, so there are 3 candidate thresholds, at the midpoints 15, 20 and 24.5. A threshold other than a midpoint would give exactly the same partition as the nearest midpoint, which is why only these need to be tried.

    Threshold tLeft branchRight branchChild entropiesWeightedGain
    1512 (No)18, 22, 27 = 2 Yes, 1 No0 and 0.91830.68870.3113
    2012, 18 = 1 No, 1 Yes22, 27 = 1 Yes, 1 No1 and 11.00000.0000
    24.512, 18, 22 = 1 No, 2 Yes27 (No)0.9183 and 00.68870.3113
    The parent holds 2 Yes and 2 No, so its entropy is 1.0000 bit. For : the left branch is one row, pure, entropy 0; the right branch holds 3 rows with proportions and , entropy 0.9183. Weighting by branch sizes, and : . Gain bit.

    Two things to take from the scan. The middle threshold, , has gain exactly zero, and this is not a coincidence: it cuts the rows into two halves that each contain one of each label, so it recreates the parent's mix on both sides. A threshold search that reports zero for the middle of an alternating dataset is behaving correctly. And the best thresholds, and , tie at 0.3113 because the data is symmetric about its centre; a tie is broken by a fixed rule, such as taking the first found, and the resulting trees differ only in which of the two outer rows is isolated.

    Two of C4.5's four changes are dealt with elsewhere. Pruning is card 6 — what matters here is that C4.5 grows the full tree first and cuts it back afterwards, rather than stopping early. And the missing-value rule is worth stating once plainly: a row with no recorded Temperature does not get dropped and does not get a guessed value; it travels down both sides of the threshold carrying a fractional weight, and its contribution to each side's entropy and to the gain is scaled by that weight. Dropping such rows silently biases the feature's score towards whatever the missingness correlates with.

    TRANSFERA dataset of 5000 rows includes a column that is a unique customer identifier, plus a column that is the customer's country, with 40 possible values. Which statement best describes what gain ratio does for these two columns?

    Extension · Decision trees 5/8

    CART: Gini impurity, binary splits, and regression

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONCART (classification and regression trees) is a family of trees with three defining restrictions. Every split is binary: a numeric feature is tested as , and a categorical feature with levels is tested as for a chosen subset of those levels, so a -level feature is handled by search over groupings rather than by one branch per level. The impurity of a classification node is the Gini impurity , where is the proportion of class in the node. For a regression node, the impurity is instead the sum of squared errors around the node's mean , and the best split is the one that minimises the total of that quantity over the two children — equivalently, that maximises the reduction in squared error. CART then prunes the grown tree by cost-complexity pruning.CART always splits a node into exactly two parts, measures how mixed a classification node is with the Gini impurity, measures how spread out a regression node is with its squared error, and cuts the finished tree back.

    Reading Gini as a probability. Draw two rows independently from the node. The probability that both are of class is , so the probability that the pair matches is , and the probability that the pair disagrees is one minus that. Gini impurity is therefore exactly the chance that two randomly drawn rows carry different labels, which is the most literal possible reading of "mixed up". It needs no logarithm, and that absence is why CART is the faster of the two families to fit: the Gini of a candidate split is computed with additions and multiplications only.

    The classification criterion. It has the same shape as information gain — impurity before, weighted impurity after, difference is the score — with a different impurity function. Its maximum over equally frequent classes is , so 0.5 for the two-class problems here.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the proportion of class in the node; the proportions sum to 1
    the probability that two independently drawn rows are both of class
    the probability that two independently drawn rows disagree — the mixed-up-ness
    the same size weighting as in information gain: larger children count for more, which prevents a split from scoring well by isolating a single row
    The regression criterion. A regression node's impurity is how far its targets are spread around their own mean, and the score of a split is . The prediction at a regression leaf is of the rows that reached it.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the numeric target of row
    the mean of the targets in the node — which is also the constant a regression tree predicts inside that node
    the residual of row against the node's own mean; its square is the error the node would incur on that row
    summed over the rows of the node. This is the total squared error of predicting the single best constant for this set of rows.
    Binary-only is a real cost, not a stylistic preference. A categorical feature with levels has distinct ways to be split into two subsets, and finding the best one exactly is expensive. For binary targets there is an efficient ordering trick that reduces the search, but for multi-class targets and unordered categories CART must search groupings heuristically. This is why the same table can be a comfortable fit for C4.5 and an awkward one for CART. The compensation is that a binary tree has leaves that are simple two-way comparisons, which is what makes the regression version and the boosting machinery clean.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the six-row dataset, scored by Gini. The same data as card 3: 3 rows labelled Yes and 3 labelled No at the root, Outlook and Wind as candidates.

    Parent node: , so . This is the maximum for two classes.
    Outlook branches. Sunny holds rows 1 to 4, labels No, No, No, Yes: proportions and , so . Rain holds rows 5 and 6, both Yes: . Weighted: . Gini gain .
    Wind branches. Weak holds rows 1, 2, 5, labels No, No, Yes: proportions and , so . Strong holds rows 3, 4, 6, labels No, Yes, Yes, which is the mirror image and gives as well. Weighted: . Gini gain .

    Outlook wins, 0.2500 against 0.0556 — the same conclusion ID3 reached by a different route with different numbers. The absolute values are not comparable across the two criteria (gain 0.4591 bits against Gini gain 0.2500), but the ordering is identical, and on this dataset it always will be. The two measures disagree on the winner only on data where two candidate splits are extremely close in quality, which is a known and practically small effect.

    Step 1 — a regression parent. Four rows with numeric targets . The parent mean is . Its squared error: .
    This 404 is the total error of the best constant prediction for these four rows. Prediction error is what the split is trying to reduce, so this number is the budget available, exactly as the parent entropy of 1 bit was the budget in card 3.
    Step 2 — split between 12 and 30. Left child holds 10, 12 with mean 11 and squared error . Right child holds 30, 32 with mean 31 and squared error .
    Each child now predicts its own mean, so the residual of every row is halved in magnitude. That is the mechanism: a regression tree reduces error by giving different regions different constants.
    Step 3 — total the children and take the difference. Total child error is , so the reduction is .
    A reduction of 400 out of 404 means the split explains almost all the variation, which is correct here: the data is two tight clusters 20 apart, and the split is exactly the boundary between them.
    Step 4 — compare with a bad split. The alternative split between 12 and 30 is not the only one; consider putting 10, 12, 30 on the left and 32 on the right. The left mean is , with squared error . The right child is a single row and costs 0. The reduction is .
    161.3 is far below 400, so the first split is strongly preferred — and the reason is visible in the arithmetic: the bad split leaves 10 and 30 in the same child, and their 20-unit gap contributes 160 of the residual error on its own. A criterion that separated the two clusters cleanly had to win.
    ID3C4.5CART
    Split criterionInformation gainGain ratio, on candidates whose gain is above averageGini impurity gain (classification); squared-error reduction (regression)
    Impurity functionEntropy, with a logarithmEntropy, with a logarithmGini for classes, squared error for numbers; no logarithm
    Feature typesCategorical by default; numeric handling is an extensionCategorical and numeric; numeric handled by thresholdCategorical and numeric natively; both handled by two-way splits
    Split shapeOne branch per value of the featureOne branch per value for categorical; two-way for numericAlways two branches, for every feature type
    PruningNone built in; stopping rules onlyPruning after growing, by estimated errorCost-complexity pruning after growing, with a parameter to search
    Typical useThe historical origin; teaching and simple categorical problemsMixed tables with both categorical and numeric columns, small to medium sizeThe modern default, and the base learner inside every boosted tree ensemble
    Why the paper's model sits on CART. Gradient boosting adds trees one at a time, each fitted to the residuals of the model so far. That construction needs each new tree's output to be a number it can be multiplied by a learning rate and added — which forces regression trees, and forces the squared-error criterion of this card's second formula. It also needs the split search to be cheap, because it happens hundreds of times per fit; Gini and squared error cost no logarithms. Both requirements point at CART rather than at ID3 or C4.5, which is why essentially every modern boosting library implements CART.
