    Where this is going: every tree in this section has been grown to the limit of its stopping rule, and a tree grown to the limit memorises its training rows. Card 6 is about cutting it back.
    Extension · Decision trees 6/8

    Pruning: why the tree has to be cut back

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONPruning is any procedure that removes nodes from a grown tree in order to improve its accuracy on data it was not fitted to. Pre-pruning (also called early stopping) halts the growth of a branch before it reaches purity, according to a condition checked during fitting — a minimum information gain, a minimum number of rows in a node, or a maximum depth. Post-pruning grows the tree to a stopping rule first and then replaces selected subtrees by single leaves, using an estimate of error computed on data held back from the split decisions. Cost-complexity pruning does the second of these with a specific objective: it chooses the subtree minimising , where is the total misclassification count of the tree's leaves, is the number of leaves, and is a penalty per leaf.Pruning is removing the parts of a tree that fit the training rows but not the pattern. You either stop growing early, or you grow fully and then cut branches off.

    Why an unpruned tree memorises. Keep splitting any node that still contains two labels. Each split reduces the node's impurity, and since impurity is 0 exactly at purity, the process terminates only when every leaf is pure. A leaf containing a single training row is pure by definition, so a tree grown without restraint can always reach a state where every training row is correctly classified — training error exactly zero, no exceptions and no matter how noisy the labels are. The mechanism is worth naming precisely: work through the Sunny branch of the dataset in card 3, split until the tie between rows 3 and 4 is broken by some incidental third feature that happens to differ between them, and the tie disappears. The tree has not learned that the two rows are genuinely alike; it has learned an accident of the table.

    Why zero training error is not automatically bad. The argument above does not say every perfectly fitted tree is useless. If the labels really are a deterministic function of the features, a tree that fits every row has found the function, and cutting it back would only hurt. The problem is that in real tables the labels are usually noisy: two rows with the same feature values can carry different labels, and no model can resolve them. Zero training error then guarantees that the tree has fitted the noise as well as the signal, because the last few splits were forced to isolate individual rows. The remedy is to decide the amount of cutting from data the tree did not see, which is what both pruning families do — the first by an early-stopping rule tuned by validation, the second by direct measurement.

    Pre-pruning (early stopping)Post-pruning (grow, then cut)
    When the decision is madeDuring growth, at each node, before any descendants existAfter the full tree exists, on complete subtrees
    What it can seeOnly local evidence at the node being consideredThe whole subtree's performance, including its descendants
    Principal defectMyopic: it can stop a split that is useless alone but necessary as a first step, and then the useful deeper structure is never builtIt must fit the full tree first, so it costs one extra fit; and its estimate of error must be built from held-back data
    Typical settingsMinimum rows per leaf, maximum depth, minimum gain thresholdCost-complexity pruning with chosen by cross-validation
    The cost-complexity objective. The first term wants accuracy; the second charges for every leaf. Increasing is like raising a tax on complexity, and the minimising tree shrinks as the tax rises — first losing a leaf or two, then collapsing whole subtrees, and finally becoming the single root leaf.
    SymbolWhat it means
    a candidate subtree, regarded as a set of leaves
    the number of leaves in that subtree — the complexity measure being charged for
    total misclassification: sum over leaves of the number of training rows in the leaf that disagree with the leaf's prediction
    the price per leaf, in units of misclassified rows. At only accuracy matters; as grows, correctness stops being worth the extra leaves.
    EXAMPLE
    Step 1 — the two candidates. A node holds 12 rows: 8 labelled A and 4 labelled B. Candidate 1 is to stop here and make it a leaf. Its prediction is the majority label A, so it misclassifies the 4 B rows: , and with one leaf .
    The single leaf is the smallest possible tree, and it is not a strawman: it is what the pruning procedure will collapse the whole subtree into if the subtree does not earn its keep.
    Step 2 — the subtree. Candidate 2 splits those 12 rows into three leaves: one with 6 rows all A (0 errors), one with 4 rows of which 2 are A and 2 are B (2 errors, since it predicts A), and one with 2 rows all B (0 errors). So , with 3 leaves, giving .
    The subtree is more accurate — 2 errors against 4 — and it pays for that with two extra leaves. The whole question of pruning is whether the accuracy is worth the complexity, and is the exchange rate.
    Step 3 — solve for the break-even penalty. Set the costs equal: . Subtracting 2 and from both sides gives , so .
    At exactly the two candidates tie, and by convention the smaller tree is preferred when the costs are equal. So the break-even penalty is 1 misclassified row per leaf.
    Step 4 — check the answer on both sides. At : the leaf costs and the subtree costs , so the subtree wins. At : the leaf costs and the subtree costs , so the leaf wins.
    The direction reverses exactly at and not before, which confirms the algebra. The economic reading: when each leaf is cheap, three leaves are a good buy for two fewer errors; once each leaf costs two errors, three leaves cost six and the accuracy no longer pays for them.

    The myopia of pre-pruning, made concrete. The classic failing case is the exclusive-or pattern. Four training rows with two binary features A and B, and the label set to 1 exactly when the two features differ.

    RowABLabel
    1000
    2011
    3101
    4110
    Two of the four labels are 1 and two are 0, so the root entropy is bit. Split the root on A: the branch A holds rows 1 and 2 with labels 0 and 1, one of each, so its entropy is 1.0000 bit; the branch A holds rows 3 and 4 with labels 1 and 0, also one of each, entropy 1.0000 bit. Weighted child entropy is , so the information gain of A is exactly 0. By symmetry the gain of B is also exactly 0.

    A pre-pruning rule that refuses to split when the gain is 0 therefore stops at the root and outputs a single leaf with one label, which is correct on 2 of the 4 rows — 50 percent. Yet a tree that splits on A and then on B has four leaves of one row each and is perfect. The first split looked worthless in isolation and was indispensable as a first step. Pre-pruning cannot see this, because when it evaluates the root it has no descendants to look at; post-pruning cannot fall into it, because the subtree it evaluates exists in full when the decision is made.

    How this connects to the paper. A boosted ensemble never wants a deep, accurate tree anyway: the boosting loop adds a weak learner repeatedly, and the standard way to make each learner weak is to cap its depth — a single split, or a depth of a few levels. That is pre-pruning by another name, and it is why the myopia argument above does not sink gradient boosting: the ensemble's total depth is built across hundreds of trees rather than inside one, so a single tree being unable to express the interaction between A and B is not fatal — a later tree in the sequence is fitted precisely to what the earlier ones got wrong. The single tree's failure modes in card 7 are survivable in an ensemble for the same structural reason.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDA tree grown without any stopping rule classifies 100 percent of its training rows correctly. What does this establish?

    APPLYA subtree has 2 leaves and misclassifies 3 rows. Collapsing it to a single leaf would misclassify 7 rows. At what value of do the two candidates have exactly equal cost? alpha

    APPLYA tree has 5 leaves and misclassifies 6 of the 40 training rows. Collapsing it to a single root leaf would misclassify 20 rows. With , what is the cost of the 5-leaf tree? R-alpha

    TRANSFERA practitioner wants to pre-prune and picks the rule "never split a node whose best information gain is below 0.05". On a dataset built from an exclusive-or pattern of two binary features, what happens?

    Where this is going: pruning treats one symptom — fitting the noise. Card 7 collects the structural limits that pruning cannot treat at all, because they follow from the shape of a tree rather than from how far it was grown.
    Extension · Decision trees 7/8

    When decision trees fail

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA decision tree is a piecewise-constant, axis-parallel model. Piecewise-constant: the feature space is divided into one region per leaf, and the prediction is the same number throughout each region, so a tree can never express a smooth or gradual change inside a leaf. Axis-parallel: every test compares a single feature with a threshold, so every boundary between two regions is a hyperplane perpendicular to one feature axis, and a boundary that runs diagonally relative to the axes can only be approximated, in steps. Every limitation in this card follows from one of those two words.A tree slices the feature space into boxes with cuts that are always parallel to the feature axes, and it gives the same answer everywhere inside each box. Anything that is not box-shaped has to be imitated with many boxes.

    1. Overfitting. Covered in card 6, and repeated here for completeness: a tree grown until every leaf is pure reaches zero training error regardless of how noisy the labels are, because a leaf holding one row is pure. The symptom is a large gap between training and validation accuracy, and the treatment is pruning, a depth limit, or averaging many shallow trees.

    2. Axis-parallel splits cannot express a diagonal boundary cheaply. Take the grid of integer points with coordinates from 1 to 4, and label a point positive exactly when its first coordinate exceeds its second. The positive points form a staircase: at there is one, at there are two, at there are three. To reproduce this boundary exactly, every leaf region must be a rectangle whose sides are parallel to the axes — a product of an interval of values with an interval of values. The staircase needs three such rectangles: across from 2 to 4; across from 3 to 4; and the single point . Two rectangles are impossible: whichever rectangle contains cannot also contain , and any rectangle spanning both would have to include the off-staircase point .

    The point generalises. A staircase whose step heights are 1, 2, 3, ..., needs rectangles, so the number of leaves grows linearly with the resolution demanded of the boundary. A linear model with two coefficients represents the same diagonal exactly, with one boundary. So on any problem whose true boundary is oblique, a tree pays in leaves for what a linear model gets for free — and it pays again in the variance of having many leaves. This is one of the reasons boosted trees and linear models are often blended rather than chosen between, and it is why a single oblique boundary is a case where a tree is the wrong tool.

    3. No extrapolation beyond the training range. A regression leaf predicts the mean of the targets that reached it. The mean of a set of numbers always lies between the smallest and the largest of them, so a regression tree can never predict a value larger than the largest training target in its leaf, nor smaller than the smallest. And because the leaf is a region, the prediction does not change as a test point moves further and further outside the training data: it stays at that mean forever.

    4. Instability. The chosen splits depend on comparisons between criteria that are often close, and a close comparison can be reversed by a small change in the data. In the six-row dataset of card 3, Outlook wins the root decisively: information gain 0.4591 against Wind's 0.0817. Change the label of row 5 from Yes to No — one label out of six — and the parent becomes 2 Yes and 4 No, after which Outlook's gain collapses to 0.0441 while Wind's rises to 0.4591. The root test changes from Outlook to Wind. A single relabelled row out of six has rewritten the tree's first question.

    5. Sensitivity to feature scaling: there is none, and that is a strength. A test on a numeric feature is . Replace by for any positive constant and the test routes exactly the same rows, so every candidate score is unchanged and the fitted tree is identical. This holds for any strictly increasing transformation: taking logarithms, or ranks, or monotone rescaling to a fixed interval, all leave the set of achievable partitions untouched. Trees therefore need no feature standardisation, unlike distance-based models and gradient-descent models. One boundary case is worth stating, because the invariance is often overstated: a non-monotone transformation breaks it. Squaring a feature that takes negative values reorders the rows along that feature, and the tree changes. The invariance is with respect to monotone transformations only.

    PropertyConsequenceWhat can be done
    Grown to purity, leaves hit single rowsZero training error regardless of label noise; a large train-validation gapPrune (card 6), cap the depth, or average many shallow trees
    Axis-parallel boundariesA diagonal or oblique boundary costs a staircase of leaves; shallow trees cannot fit it at allFeed a linear combination of the features as an extra column, blend with a linear model, or accept many leaves
    Prediction constant on each leafNo extrapolation: the output is capped by the training target range, and forecasts go flat outside itRemove a trend or rescale the target before fitting; do not use a tree to forecast a growing series
    Split choice decided by close comparisonsSmall data changes can rewrite the split structure — instabilityAverage over many trees, which is exactly what a random forest or a boosted ensemble does
    No dependence on feature scaleNo standardisation needed, and results are unchanged by monotone transforms of any featureNothing to fix — but do not rely on it for non-monotone transforms such as squaring a signed feature
    The fourth and fifth rows are the reason ensembles exist. Instability is the one failure mode on this list that is not a limitation of the model class but an opportunity: if the tree structure changes when the data changes slightly, then averaging the trees fitted to many slightly different versions of the data cancels much of the change. That is the entire justification for random forests and, with a different correction mechanism, for the boosted ensemble in this paper. Extrapolation and axis-parallel boundaries, by contrast, do not go away in an ensemble — a sum of trees is still piecewise constant and still cannot predict outside the range its trees saw.
    EXAMPLE
    Step 1 — build a regression leaf. Suppose the training targets that reach a particular leaf are 20, 24 and 31. The leaf's prediction is their mean: .
    The mean is the constant that minimises squared error over those three rows, which is why the criterion of card 5 and the leaf's prediction are the same quantity. A regression tree is a collection of conditional means.
    Step 2 — query it far outside the training range. A test row whose numeric feature value is far beyond anything in the training set still routes through the same sequence of tests if each threshold comparison points the same way, and lands in the same leaf. Its prediction is 25, the same as a training row's.
    Nothing in the model depends on the distance from the training data. The leaf region extends to infinity in whichever directions the thresholds allow, and the prediction is constant on the whole of it.
    Step 3 — see why this kills trend forecasting. If the feature is time, the last leaf's region is the unbounded interval from the final threshold onwards, and every future time point lands in it and receives that leaf's mean. A series that grew throughout the training window is forecast to hold exactly still at the average level of the last window, forever.
    This is a structural cap, not a tuning problem. No amount of depth or boosting changes it, because every tree in the ensemble is subject to the same argument, and a sum of numbers each bounded above by its own training maximum is bounded above by their sum. Growing a trend-based series without removing the trend first will always produce a forecast that is flat and too low, and the standard remedies are to difference or detrend the target before fitting, or to fit the trend with a model that can extrapolate it.
    Step 4 — the oblique boundary, counted. Return to the 4-by-4 staircase. A single leaf cannot do it: one rectangle containing all six positive points also contains the negative points , . Two cannot do it, by the argument in the paragraph above. Three can, so the minimum leaf count is 3 — against one boundary for the linear rule .
    The comparison is the useful part. The tree has not failed at an impossible task; it has paid three leaves where a linear model paid two coefficients. That price is the honest measure of how badly a tree suits an oblique boundary, and it is why the answer is often to give the tree the linear combination as an input column rather than to abandon trees.
    What this example does not show. The instability demonstration is entirely absent from these steps: it needs a comparison of two root candidates, which the paragraph on instability above carries out with its numbers. Neither part of the example shows overfitting, which requires a training and a validation set to measure.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDA regression tree trained on a series with targets between 10 and 60 is asked for a prediction at a feature value far beyond the largest one it saw. What is the guarantee?

    APPLYThe training targets reaching a particular regression leaf are 40, 44 and 60. A test row lands in that leaf. What does the tree predict? predicted value

    TRANSFERA team standardises every feature of a table to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1 before fitting a decision tree, then a colleague re-runs the pipeline without the standardisation and gets a slightly different tree. Which is the correct reading?

    TRANSFERA dataset has a single continuous feature and a binary label separated by the diagonal rule "positive when the feature is above a straight line that is not parallel to either axis". A decision tree, a linear classifier, and a boosted ensemble of 200 depth-3 trees are all fitted. Which statement is best supported?

    Where this is going: the section ends with the skip check. Card 8 collects the definitions and the criteria in one list and asks whether you can leave without them.
    Extension · Decision trees 8/8

    Skip check: can you leave this section?

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONRecap of the object the whole section builds. A decision tree routes an input through tests of the form (numeric) or (categorical), one test per internal node, and returns the prediction stored at the leaf reached — the majority class for a classification leaf, the mean of the training targets for a regression leaf. It is grown by greedily choosing, at each node, the candidate split that most reduces the node's impurity: entropy for ID3, the gain ratio for C4.5, and Gini impurity with the squared-error criterion for CART. It is then cut back by pruning, because a tree grown to purity has zero training error on any dataset.A tree is a flowchart of threshold tests ending in leaves that hold answers, built by repeatedly taking the question that separates the labels best, and then trimmed so it stops fitting the noise.

    This section taught eight things. If you can do all of them unaided, skip ahead — the boosting section assumes this material and does not repeat it.

    • State what a decision tree is, and extract the if-then rule list and the feature-space partition from a drawn tree.
    • Say what impurity means, and name the three classical measures with their formulas: entropy and information gain for ID3, gain ratio for C4.5, Gini impurity for CART.
    • Compute the entropy of a node from its class counts, and compute the information gain of a candidate split, including the size weighting of the children.
    • Explain why information gain is biased towards features with many distinct values, and how dividing by SplitInfo repairs it — and how it fails to repair it completely.
    • Explain what a numeric feature's threshold candidates are, and why there are one fewer of them than there are distinct values.
    • Compute a CART split: Gini impurity and its gain for classification, squared-error reduction for regression.
    • Explain why an unpruned tree reaches zero training error, and compare pre-pruning with post-pruning, including what cost-complexity pruning minimises.
    • Name the four limits of a tree — overfitting, axis-parallel boundaries, no extrapolation, instability — and say which of them an ensemble does and does not remove.
    The questions below are the check. Two of the four correct is not the bar — the bar is that you did not have to think hard about any of them. If you hesitated on the split arithmetic, stay: the boosting section fits each new tree to the errors the previous trees left behind, and it assumes you can already evaluate a criterion and read a leaf.
    EXAMPLE

    One recap, end to end. Four rows, two features, and the whole procedure from entropy to a decision. This is the shortest complete run of the machinery in this section.

    RowSizeColourLabel
    1BigRedYes
    2BigBlueYes
    3SmallRedNo
    4SmallRedYes
    Parent: 3 rows labelled Yes and 1 labelled No, so the proportions are and . Entropy bits. Gini .
    Candidate Size. Big holds rows 1 and 2, both Yes: entropy 0, weight . Small holds rows 3 and 4, one No and one Yes: entropy 1.0000, weight . Weighted , so the gain is bits. By Gini: Big gives ; Small gives ; weighted ; Gini gain .
    Candidate Colour. Red holds rows 1, 3, 4, labels Yes, No, Yes: proportions and , entropy , weight . Blue holds row 2 only, Yes: entropy 0, weight . Weighted , so the gain is bits. By Gini: Red gives ; Blue gives 0; weighted ; Gini gain .

    Both criteria prefer Size, and both prefer it by a comfortable margin: 0.3113 against 0.1226 by entropy, 0.1250 against 0.0417 by Gini. The tree's root test is Size. Note that the two criteria report different numbers for the same split and agree on the ranking, which is the expected behaviour and the reason either can be used; note also that the Colour split sends only one row to its Blue branch, which is the structural signature of a feature that will not generalise and the kind of case gain ratio was built to notice.

    Reading the whole section off this one example. The parent entropy is the budget; the weighted child entropy is the cost; the difference is the score; the largest score picks the question. Everything in cards 2 to 5 is a variation on those four lines, and everything in cards 6 and 7 is about what happens to the tree after it has been grown this way.

    Pre-knowledge · in this paper

    Decision trees in this paper: read as a list of questions, never as a predictor

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONIn this paper a decision tree appears only through its inner nodes: the set of nodes, each carrying a predicate on a single feature, is enumerated and each member becomes one coordinate of a vertex's rule embedding. The tree's leaves, its predictions, and its structure as a graph play no role in any equation.The paper takes a trained tree, ignores what it predicts, and keeps only the questions. Every question becomes one slot in a vector.

    Why this is worth stating as its own point. The general section on decision trees covered what a tree is, how it chooses its splits, and when it fails. All of that matters here, but for one purpose only: to make the questions intelligible. The paper's usage is unusual enough that a reader who assumes "the paper uses a decision tree to make predictions" will misread every equation that follows.

    Aspect of a decision treeDoes this paper use it?
    Its predictionsNo. The ensemble's output is computed during pre-training and then discarded
    Its inner nodes (the questions)Yes — one coordinate per inner node
    Its depth structureYes, but only as a single number per node: the node's depth, used as an importance weight
    Its leavesNo. Figure 2 draws them with class colours only to show what was trained
    Its impurity or split criteriaNo. The tree is used after training; how it chose its splits never appears
    Its axis-parallel cut structureIndirectly — it is why each question involves one feature and a threshold
    This is a general pattern worth naming: a trained model can be used as a source of structure rather than as a function. A tree is a flowchart built to predict, but the flowchart is also a learned description of the feature space, and that description can be repurposed. The paper's contribution is essentially an opinion about what to keep from a tree — the questions and their depths — and what to throw away.

    One consequence to hold on to. Because only inner nodes are used, the size of the rule embedding is determined by how many questions the ensemble asks, not by how many leaves it has or how accurate it is. A larger, more accurate ensemble produces a longer embedding — so the feature dimension and the model's capacity are coupled to a hyperparameter that was chosen to suit a different purpose.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — the two trees of the paper's own Figure 2, read the paper's way. Tree asks and then ; tree asks , then and .

    • Kept: five questions, in the order the trees present them — , , , , . Each is one slot.
    • Kept: each question's depth — 0, 1, 0, 1, 1 respectively — converted to an importance weight by Equation (6).
    • Discarded: the leaves' class labels. The figure colours them orange, green and blue so you can see that the ensemble was trained to classify, but no equation refers to them.
    • Discarded: which leaf a vertex reaches. Equation (5) tests every question against the vertex independently, so the leaf reached is never computed.
    Note what the four kept-details have in common: they are all local to a node. The paper never needs to know how a vertex flows through a tree, only which questions its features happen to satisfy. That is what makes the encoding computable in parallel over all vertices and all nodes at once — and it is also why the encoding can describe a vertex using questions from branches it would never reach.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich part of a trained decision tree does this paper encode?

    APPLYAn ensemble contains 4 trees with 3, 5, 2 and 4 inner nodes. How many coordinates does a vertex's rule embedding have? coordinates

    TRANSFERThe paper evaluates each question against a vertex even when the vertex could never reach that node during a normal traversal. What does this make the encoding?

    Next in this chapter: the ensemble those trees came from. The paper's trees are not standalone — they are members of a gradient-boosted team, which is why depth carries information about importance at all.
    Extension · Boosting and ensembles 1/6

    Why combine models at all

    The paper's model is a gradient-boosted forest of decision trees. This section places that model inside ensemble learning: how averaging many diverse models reduces variance, the two ways to manufacture that diversity (resampling and sequential error correction), how gradient boosting turns the second route into an algorithm, what XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost each added, and when a tree ensemble is the wrong tool entirely.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONAn ensemble is a collection of models whose outputs are combined into one prediction, most often by averaging for regression, , or by majority vote for classification. The individual models are called base learners; when each one is only slightly better than a trivial guess, it is called a weak learner.Instead of trusting one model, you train several and combine their answers. The combined answer is usually better than any single member of the team.

    The problem a single model cannot escape. Every model family has a fixed capacity — a ceiling on how complicated a function it can represent, and a matching floor on how much it must simplify. A decision stump, a tree that makes exactly one split, can only output one of two values. It cannot say "low, then medium, then high"; it can only say "below the line" or "above the line". Give one stump a curved target and it fails in a fixed, predictable way. Give it a very deep tree instead and it can draw any staircase it likes — including a staircase that traces the noise in your particular training set rather than the pattern underneath. One model, one impossible trade-off.

    The escape is not a cleverer single model. It is to train many mediocre models and combine them. The reason this works is error cancellation, and the arithmetic is worth seeing because it explains everything that follows.

    Errors that are independent cancel. Suppose each of models produces the true value plus a random error, and each error has variance . When you average the predictions, the errors are averaged too. Variances of independent quantities add, and averaging divides by twice over, which leaves one factor of :

    Averaging models with independent errors divides the error variance by . The spread of the team is the spread of one member divided by — with that is a tenth of the noise.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the number of models in the ensemble
    the prediction of the -th model
    the error variance of a single model — how far one model's answer typically lands from the truth
    variance — the average squared distance of a quantity from its mean; a measure of spread, so smaller is better

    Diversity is the whole game. The formula above assumed the errors are independent — that whenever one model is too high, another is too low. Real models trained on the same problem rarely agree to disagree so conveniently. If every model makes the same mistake, averaging does nothing: the common error survives untouched. The degree to which errors move together is measured by the correlation (rho), a number between and where means independent and means perfectly in lockstep. With correlation the variance of the average becomes

    Only the second term shrinks as you add models. The first term, , is nailed down: however many models you stack, the variance can never fall below . Diversity is what makes an ensemble worth building, and correlation is what limits it.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the correlation between two models' errors — means independent mistakes, means identical mistakes
    the irreducible floor on ensemble variance; no amount of averaging can push below it
    the reducible part — the portion of error that averaging can cancel

    Two ways to manufacture diversity. Since diversity is the whole game, the next question is where to get it. There are exactly two families, and the rest of this section is their contrast. The first trains each model on a different sample of the data, so that each sees a slightly different world; the models are independent and can be built at the same time. This is bagging, and its most famous member is the random forest. The second trains models in sequence, each one fitted to the mistakes the ensemble is still making; the models are deliberately coupled, because each one exists to repair the last. This is boosting, and its most widely used member is gradient boosting — the family the paper's model belongs to.

    Common misconception. "More models is always better." It is not. Adding a model whose errors are identical to the ones you already have () changes nothing — the floor is already the whole variance. Fifty copies of the same tree are one tree; fifty trees that disagree are an ensemble.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — four independent models. Take models, each with error variance . Because the errors are independent, , and the correlated formula collapses to the first one. The variance of the averaged prediction is , so the typical error — the standard deviation — is . The team is half as noisy as one member.

    Write the variance: .
    Start from the general formula. Setting is the assumption "the models err independently", which is exactly what we are testing the value of.
    The floor term is ; the reducible term is . So .
    With independent errors there is no floor at all — every bit of error is reducible. This is the best case, and it never quite happens in practice.
    The standard deviation is , against for a single model: a factor-of-two reduction from four models.
    The growth is the reason ensembles give diminishing returns. Going from 1 to 4 models halves the noise; going from 4 to 16 (four times the models) halves it again.

    Example 2 — four models that agree too much. Now suppose the four models share a common weakness, so their errors are correlated with . The formula of Example 1 gives . The team is worse than four independent models would be ( against ), and most of the error is now irreducible: however far grows, the first term stays put, so the variance can never drop below — twice the independent case's final value of , which was itself only reached because the independent case has no floor.

    Side by side, at : independent () gives ; mildly correlated () gives . Push to independent models and the variance falls to , but push the correlated ones to and it only reaches — barely below the correlated case at . The correlation, not the count, is what caps the gain. Every trick in the next two cards — bootstrap resampling and per-split feature randomisation — exists to push down.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhat single quantity decides whether adding models to an ensemble will actually help?

    APPLYSix models each have error variance and their errors are independent. What is the variance of their averaged prediction? variance

    TRANSFERYou have two options: double the number of trees from 50 to 100, or change the training procedure so the trees' errors become less correlated. Which offers the larger gain?

    Where this is going: the two routes to diversity named here — resample the data, or correct the mistakes — become bagging and boosting in the next two cards, and the correlation floor becomes the reason random forests randomise features.
    Extension · Boosting and ensembles 2/6

    Bagging and random forests: diversity by resampling

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONBagging (bootstrap aggregating) draws bootstrap samples from the training set — each is the full dataset of rows sampled with replacement, so some rows appear several times and others not at all — fits one base learner per sample, and averages the predictions. A random forest is bagging with decision trees as the base learners, plus one extra ingredient: at each split of each tree, only a random subset of of the features is considered as candidates, rather than all .Train each tree on its own random sample of the data (drawn with replacement), and also let each split look at only a random handful of the features. Then average the trees. The random sampling and the random feature choice make the trees different from one another, which is what makes the averaging pay off.

    Why "with replacement" matters. Drawing with replacement means you pick a row, note it, and put it back before the next pick, so the same row can be chosen twice or not at all. If you drew without replacement every sample would be a reshuffle of the same data and every tree would see essentially the same information. With replacement, each sample is a genuinely different dataset.

    How much of the data does one sample miss? A specific row is left out of a given draw with probability ; across all independent draws it is left out with probability . As grows this approaches , so roughly of the rows are missing from any one bootstrap sample and about are present (some of them more than once). The missing rows are called out-of-bag rows.

    For the sample sizes used in practice the limit is already tight: at the probability is , at it is , and at it is — each within a hair of .
    SymbolWhat it means
    the number of rows in the training set, and also the number of draws in one bootstrap sample
    the chance a specific row is not picked on a single draw
    the limit of the expression, — the fraction of rows a bootstrap sample leaves out

    The extra ingredient in a random forest: feature randomisation. Bagging alone gives each tree a different sample, but on a dataset with a few dominant features the trees will still lean on the same split again and again, and their errors stay correlated. A random forest breaks that by restricting each split: instead of searching all features for the best cut, it searches a random subset of of them. A commonly used default is for classification and for regression. With features, a classification forest considers about at each split rather than .

    Why that decorrelates the trees. A split that would be chosen by nearly every tree is often unavailable now, so different trees are forced to build on different features and to make different mistakes. On the variance formula of card 1, this is a direct attack on : it lowers the floor that averaging alone can never get under. The cost is that each individual tree becomes slightly weaker — restricting the candidate features can only reduce the quality of any single split — but the drop in correlation more than pays for it, and the average comes out better.

    Parallel, not sequential. The bootstrap samples are drawn independently and the trees are fitted independently, so the whole forest can be built in parallel across cores. No tree ever sees another tree's output or its mistakes. This is the sharpest point of contrast with boosting, where every model depends on the one before it — the subject of the next card.

    Two common misconceptions. First, "a random forest's trees are trained one after another, each fixing the last" — they are not; they are trained independently and in parallel. Second, "each tree uses the full dataset" — each tree uses one bootstrap sample, which contains only about of the distinct rows and repeats others.
    EXAMPLE

    Extension · Boosting and ensembles 3/6

    Boosting: diversity by correction

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONBoosting builds an ensemble one model at a time. Model is fitted to the errors that the ensemble of the first models is still making, and the final prediction is a weighted sum of the base learners with fitted weights . Each is deliberately a weak learner — barely better than a trivial guess on its own.Train one small model. Look at where it is wrong. Train the next small model to fix exactly those mistakes. Repeat, and add up the models with weights. Each model exists to repair the last one, so the models are built in sequence, not side by side.

    The motivating picture. A single decision stump — one split, two outputs — is close to useless on a curved target. But imagine many stumps, each allowed to see how the running ensemble is doing and nudged to correct its worst region. The first stump gets the broad shape roughly right, the second fixes the biggest remaining error, the third fixes the biggest error after that, and so on. No individual stump is impressive; the accumulated sum can be. This is the opposite logic to bagging: bagging relies on models failing differently and independently, boosting relies on each model depending on the last.

    A concrete way to do the correction: AdaBoost. The oldest boosting algorithm reweights the training points rather than fitting residuals. After each round it increases the weight of the points the current ensemble misclassifies and decreases the weight of the points it gets right; the next weak learner is trained to focus on the now-heavier hard points. Each round also assigns the learner a weight that measures how much the ensemble should trust it: a learner with a low weighted error rate earns a large weight, a coin-flip learner earns almost none.

    Here is the weighted error rate of the round's weak learner. When the learner is accurate ( small) the ratio is large and is large; at the learner is no better than a coin and , so it is given no say at all.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the weighted error rate of the weak learner on the current data weights — the fraction of weight it gets wrong
    the weight the ensemble gives this learner when summing predictions
    the natural logarithm; here it converts a ratio of errors into the scale on which weights are added

    Which kind of error does each family fix? A model's error splits into bias — being systematically wrong because the model is too rigid to capture the pattern — and variance — being unreliably jumpy because the model is fitting the particular sample rather than the signal. Averaging many independent models cancels their independent jumps, so bagging and random forests attack variance; they barely change a systematic bias that all the trees share. Boosting works differently: each added model reduces the ensemble's systematic error on the points it is still getting wrong, so boosting attacks bias. This one distinction explains almost every practical difference between the two families, including the table below.

    Bagging / random forestBoosting
    How models are trainedIn parallel, independently of one anotherSequentially, each depending on the one before
    What each model is fitted toA bootstrap resample of the dataThe current ensemble's remaining errors
    Error component mainly reducedVarianceBias
    Where diversity comes fromDifferent row samples plus random feature subsetsEach model specialising in the mistakes the ensemble still makes
    Base-learner sizeDeep, fully grown treesVery shallow trees — a stump at the extreme
    Behaviour on noisy labelsRobust: the noise is spread over many independent samples and averaged awayFragile: the sequence keeps re-chasing the few hard, wrongly-labelled points
    Risk as you add modelsError falls, then flattens; adding more is safeError can start to rise; needs a learning rate and early stopping
    Common misconception. "Boosting is just bagging with more trees." The two are opposite in mechanism: bagging's members are independent and could be trained in any order, while boosting's members are a chain in which removing one invalidates the rest. A second misconception is "boosting never overfits because each model is weak" — with noisy labels a long boosting run will happily memorise the mislabelled points, which is why a learning rate and early stopping are standard parts of every boosting implementation.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — weighting a weak learner. Suppose a round's stump has weighted error rate : it gets of the weight wrong. Its weight is .

    Compute the ratio: .
    The ratio compares the weight of the correct answers to the weight of the errors. Greater than means the learner is right more than wrong, so its vote should count positively.
    Take the logarithm: .
    The log turns the comparison into a signed quantity: ratios above give positive logarithms (trust the learner), ratios below give negative ones (distrust it).
    Halve it: .
    The factor of normalises the weight so that a learner at the coin-flip boundary gets exactly — the next two rows show that.
    Check the boundaries: at , ; at , ; at , .
    A confident learner ( error) earns a weight of , more than five times the of a weak learner, and the useless learner earns nothing. That is the whole point of the formula: accuracy is converted into influence.

    Example 2 — why noisy labels hurt a boosting chain. Take one training row that is labelled but truly belongs to the class. A bagged forest shows it to roughly of the trees and it is averaged among all their predictions, so its influence is diluted and mostly washed out by the correctly-labelled majority. A boosting run, by contrast, sees the ensemble keep getting this row wrong, keeps raising its weight, and eventually trains later weak learners almost exclusively to satisfy it. The ensemble's error on the clean rows can rise while its error on this single row falls to zero: the sequence has been captured by an outlier.

    Reading the contrast table, row by row. Row 1 (parallel vs sequential): bagging's trees are independent, so they can be built on separate cores at the same time; boosting's trees form a chain and must be built in order. Row 3 (variance vs bias): averaging independent trees cancels their independent jumps, lowering variance; the sum of error-correcting trees lowers the systematic error, i.e. bias. Row 6 (noise): these two mechanisms give opposite noise behaviour — dilution for bagging, capture for boosting — which is why random forests tolerate dirtier labels than boosting does. Every row in the table traces back to the one structural fact that bagging is parallel and boosting is sequential.

    Extension · Boosting and ensembles 4/6

    Gradient boosting: fitting the negative gradient

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONGradient boosting builds the ensemble by initialising a constant prediction , then repeating for : compute the pseudo-residual for every training row, fit a small regression tree to the pairs , and update the ensemble with a learning rate (also called the shrinkage factor). The negative gradient is the direction in which the current prediction must move to reduce the loss fastest.Start with a constant guess. At each round, ask each training row 'which way, and by how much, should my prediction move to make the loss smaller?' — that answer is the negative gradient. Train a small tree to predict those moves, add it to the running prediction, and repeat. For the squared-error loss the answer turns out to be the gap between the target and the current prediction, i.e. the residual.

    Why a gradient, and not just the error? Boosting's job in card 3 was "make the next model fix what the ensemble gets wrong". To make that precise you need a definition of wrong — a loss function — and a way to ask which change to the predictions reduces it fastest. Calculus answers that: the gradient of the loss with respect to the prediction points in the direction of increasing loss, so moving against it decreases loss. Fitting a tree to that negative gradient is the machine-learning version of gradient descent, one whole tree per step instead of one coordinate per step.

    The squared-error case collapses to residuals. Let the loss for one row be the squared error, halved so its derivative is clean: . Differentiating with respect to the prediction gives . Negating to get the negative gradient gives — the residual, plain and simple. So for squared error, "fit each tree to the negative gradient" and "fit each tree to the residual" are the same sentence. That equivalence is what makes the worked example below hand-checkable; for other losses (logistic, Poisson, ranking) the negative gradient is a different quantity but the procedure is unchanged.

    The first expression defines what the next tree is fitted to. The second adds that tree, scaled by , to the running prediction. With squared-error loss the first becomes , the residual.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the loss function — the number you are trying to make small; it measures how wrong a prediction is
    the ensemble's prediction for row before round
    the pseudo-residual — the target the next tree is fitted to; equals the ordinary residual for squared error
    the small regression tree fitted to the pseudo-residuals in round
    the learning rate, a small positive number (often –) that shrinks each tree's contribution

    Why the learning rate is there. Fitting the residual and adding the tree in full is a greedy, large step that follows the training data very closely and overfits fast. Scaling each tree by makes every round take a smaller step in the same direction, so the ensemble reaches a similar fit only after many more, gentler rounds — the same idea as a small step size in gradient descent. A smaller usually needs more trees; the pair is traded off against each other.

    Common misconception. "Gradient boosting fits each tree to the target ." It does not — it fits each tree to the negative gradient, which for squared error is the residual , the part of the ensemble has not explained yet. Fitting every tree to would make the rounds nearly identical instead of mutually correcting.
    EXAMPLE

For the row with , the gradient is and the negative gradient is , again exactly the residual. A finite-difference check of the derivative agrees to four decimal places. The tree in each round is therefore being trained on residuals.

    Extension · Boosting and ensembles 5/6

    The modern implementations: XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONXGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are three software implementations of the same gradient-boosting algorithm of card 4. They differ not in what the algorithm computes but in three engineering choices layered on top: how the tree is regularised and scored (XGBoost), how features are discretised and how the tree is grown (LightGBM), and how categorical features are encoded without leaking the target (CatBoost).These are not three different kinds of model. They are three optimised builds of the same boosted-tree idea, each adding one or two tricks that make it faster, more accurate, or easier to use on awkward data. Knowing which trick belongs to which library is enough to read a methods section that cites one of them.

    XGBoost: a regularised objective and second-order splits. XGBoost rewrites the loss as a sum of a per-row gradient and a per-row curvature (the second derivative), plus an explicit penalty on the trees themselves, , where is the number of leaves and the value of leaf . The penalty is what its name denotes: charges a price for every extra leaf, and shrinks leaf values toward zero, taming trees that would otherwise fit noise. With the curvature term available, XGBoost chooses splits by a gain that no longer needs the residual to be the whole story:

    The three fractions compare a candidate split's left leaf, right leaf, and unsplit parent: the gain is how much loss the split removes, minus the charge for the leaf it creates. A split is taken only when this is positive. The leaf value itself is .
    SymbolWhat it means
    sums of the per-row gradients in the left and right child
    sums of the per-row curvatures in the left and right child
    the L2 penalty on leaf values — larger means more shrinkage
    the penalty added for each extra leaf — larger means fewer, coarser splits

    XGBoost also handles missing values with a sparsity-aware split: when it evaluates a candidate split it assigns missing entries to whichever side gives the larger gain, learning a default direction per split rather than imputing the gaps. A commonly used default configuration is a learning rate of and a maximum depth of .

    LightGBM: histogram binning and leaf-wise growth. Its central speed trick is to bin every feature into a small number of buckets — the default is at most — before any tree is built. Splitting then only ever compares bin boundaries, so the cost of finding the best split falls from the number of distinct feature values to a few hundred. On a feature with a million distinct values that is a reduction of roughly a factor of in the work per candidate split. The second trick is to grow the tree leaf-wise rather than level-wise: level-wise growth expands every leaf on the current level and a tree of depth always ends with exactly leaves, whereas leaf-wise growth always expands whichever leaf would reduce the loss the most and stops at a fixed leaf budget, which is by default. Leaf-wise growth reaches a given loss with fewer leaves, at the cost of bushy, deeper trees that overfit more easily on small data.

    CatBoost: ordered target statistics. Plain target encoding replaces a category by the average target of its rows — which leaks the row's own target back into its own feature and inflates its apparent usefulness, a failure called prediction shift. CatBoost's fix is to compute each row's category statistic from only the rows that precede it in a random permutation of the data, so a row never sees itself. The estimate for a category is a smoothed average : is a prior such as the global mean, and the smoothing weight pulls small categories back toward that prior so that a category seen twice is not trusted as much as one seen a thousand times.

    LibraryWhat it added to the boosting loopEffect
    XGBoostRegularised objective; second-order (gradient and curvature) split gain; sparsity-aware default directionsPenalises complex trees; uses curvature to score splits; handles missing values natively
    LightGBMHistogram binning of features (at most 255 bins); leaf-wise growthFinds splits far faster; reaches a target loss with fewer leaves
    CatBoostOrdered target statistics for categorical featuresEncodes high-cardinality categoricals without leaking the target
    Common misconception. "XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are three different algorithms, so which one is used changes the model family." They are one family — gradient-boosted decision trees — with different regularisation and engineering. A paper that reports GBDT results with any of the three is reporting the same class of model; what differs is the training cost, the default hyperparameters and the handling of categorical or missing data.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a leaf value and a split gain by hand. Take a candidate split with gradient sums , , curvature sums , , penalty , and leaf charge .

    Numerator is the squared gradient sum, denominator the curvature sum plus the leaf penalty. A large gradient caught by a low-curvature leaf scores high — that is a leaf doing useful work.
    Right leaf term: .
    The square removes the sign, so a leaf with a large negative gradient sum is just as valuable as one with a large positive sum.
    Parent term: .
    This is the score before splitting, when both groups share one leaf. Subtracting it turns the three terms into the improvement a split actually buys.
    Gain . Positive, so the split is worth taking.
    A positive gain means the split removes more loss than the charge costs. Had been, say, , the gain would be and XGBoost would refuse the split — the regularisation doing its job.

    Example 2 — a leaf value, a bin ratio, and a CatBoost statistic. Three one-line computations that show the scale of each library's trick.

    • LightGBM binning: one million distinct values compressed into bins is a ratio of — every split search now examines at most candidate cut points instead of up to a million. LightGBM's default leaf budget of leaves sits just under the leaves a level-wise tree would have at depth .
    • CatBoost ordered statistic: a category appearing times whose targets sum to , with prior and smoothing , gets the value . Without smoothing it would be — close, because this category is well-populated; raise the smoothing to and the value moves to , visibly pulled toward the prior.     Extension · Boosting and ensembles 6/6

    When not to use trees, and the skip check

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA decision tree predicts by routing an input down a chain of axis-parallel tests ("is feature below this threshold?") until it reaches a leaf, then outputting the value stored in that leaf. Two structural consequences follow from this definition: every prediction is one of the values stored in the leaves, so it always lies within the range of the training targets in those leaves, and the prediction is a piecewise-constant function that is flat inside each leaf and jumps at each boundary.A tree answers a fixed set of yes/no questions and then reads off whatever number was stored at the end. It never calculates — it only looks up. So it can never predict a number it did not essentially see during training, and its answer changes in jumps rather than smoothly.

    These two properties are the whole strength and the whole weakness. Look-up structure is why trees fit interactions and non-linearities so easily, handle mixed feature types, and resist outliers in the features. The same look-up structure is why a tree is the wrong tool whenever the truth is that (i) a trend continues beyond the data, (ii) the relationship is genuinely smooth, or (iii) the meaningful structure of the input is not "does this individual coordinate exceed a threshold". Each failure below is a direct consequence of the definition, not a tuning problem.

    • Extrapolation is impossible. A prediction is always one of the stored leaf values, so it can never leave the interval spanned by the training targets. A test point far outside the feature range simply routes to an existing leaf and returns a value seen in training.
    • High-dimensional, sparse data. When rows are sparse (a handful of non-zero features among tens of thousands), a single feature value rarely carries signal and the useful pattern is a dense weighted sum. Linear models and neural networks capture that sum directly; axis-parallel splits on individual sparse coordinates fragment the data and generalise poorly.
    • A genuinely smooth target. A tree approximates a smooth curve with a staircase: flat inside each leaf, jumping at each boundary. Matching a slope costs many leaves, and the fit stays discontinuous — a tiny change in an input across a leaf boundary produces a jump in the prediction, whereas a linear or smooth model captures the slope with a handful of parameters.
    • Images, text and audio. Here neighbouring pixels, tokens or samples are related by position, and the meaningful pattern is spatial or sequential. Comparing one raw pixel or one token against a threshold is close to meaningless; convolutional, recurrent and transformer architectures encode that structure directly, and axis-parallel trees cannot.
    • Rotated linear boundaries. A tree draws only horizontal and vertical cuts, so separating two classes along a diagonal requires a staircase of many axis-parallel splits, and the number of splits needed grows with the number of features. A linear model needs one hyperplane.
    The misconception to retire. "A strong model is strong everywhere." A gradient-boosted forest can be state of the art on tabular data and simultaneously hopeless on the same relationships when the test points sit outside the training range. The choice of model family is a statement about the structure of the target, not about which model won a competition.

    Skip check. This section taught five things. If you can do all five without thinking hard, you may move on — nothing later depends on a definition you already hold. The bar is fluency, not half-remembrance: if any item below leaves you reaching for the card it came from, stay and re-read that card.

    • Explain why averaging decorrelated models reduces variance, and state what limits the reduction (the correlation floor ).
    • Describe bootstrap sampling: draw with replacement, and that roughly of distinct rows appear while the rest are out-of-bag.
    • Say why a random forest also randomises the features considered at each split, and that its trees are trained in parallel.
    • Describe boosting's sequential error correction and contrast the two families: parallel vs sequential, variance vs bias, robust vs fragile on noisy labels, deep vs shallow base learners.
    • Explain gradient boosting's negative-gradient fit, note that it equals the residual for squared error, and name what XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost each added.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the same three points, two models, one impossible extrapolation. Take the three pairs , , , which lie exactly on the line .

    1. A linear model fits intercept and slope exactly. Asked for it answers , continuing the trend.
    2. A tree can only return leaf values drawn from the targets it saw, so its predictions are confined to the interval . Asked for , it follows the same test it would give any large and returns at most .
    3. Nothing about the tree is broken; the definition makes extrapolation structurally impossible. If your data has a trend that continues past the observed range, a tree ensemble must be replaced by, or combined with, a model that can carry a slope.

    Example 2 — a tree with few leaves cannot even represent a slope inside the range. Fit the same line with a single depth-1 tree (one split, two leaves). The split at gives leaf values and ; the split at gives and . Both leave the same total squared error of , i.e. a mean squared error of over the three points, and no other single split does better. The prediction is two flat steps trying to describe a line.

    Give the tree enough leaves and it can fit those three points exactly — splits at and isolate each point and drive the error to . That is the trap: a tree can fit any finite sample perfectly, yet between the sample points it is still flat, and outside the range it is still flat. A depth- tree has at most leaves and a depth- tree at most , so the staircase can be made very fine — but a staircase it remains, and the ground beyond its last step never rises.

    Pre-knowledge · in this paper

    Gradient boosting in this paper: a question generator, and the cost of that choice

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONIn this paper a gradient-boosted ensemble is trained once on a predefined task to produce a frozen set of trees, and thereafter serves purely as a source of predicates. Equation (2) is the ensemble's construction rule, quoted from the standard literature and used unchanged; nothing in the paper modifies how boosting works.Train a boosted team of trees on some task, freeze it, and then mine its questions. The paper never changes how boosting works — it only changes what the result is used for.

    Why a boosted ensemble rather than one big tree. The paper's Equation (6) weights each question by its depth, and the justification it gives is specific to boosting: because the ensemble adds trees sequentially, each correcting the last, features selected earlier carry more of the task's signal. A single deep tree would not license that assumption — its questions would all be chosen in one pass, and depth would mean only specificity, not importance. The depth weighting is an argument about the training procedure, and it holds only for the procedure actually used.

    Property of the ensembleWhere it shows up in the paperWhat depends on it
    Number of trees Table IV reports a tree count per datasetThe length of the rule embedding, since every tree contributes its own block
    Depth of each treeTable IV reports a depth per datasetThe range of the depth weights , and hence how sharply importance decays
    Questions per treeNot reported directlyThe embedding length — is the total inner-node count, which the paper never states
    The pre-training taskDescribed only as "predefined"Everything — the questions are the only channel by which task information enters the model, and the task is not named
    The last row is the one to keep. The rule encoder's entire content is the questions a boosted ensemble learned, so the model inherits whatever those questions encode. The paper says the ensemble is trained "on predefined tasks" without specifying what they are or how they relate to the final classification. That leaves a question a reviewer has to ask — and Chapter 7 asks it — namely whether the pre-training ever saw labels that the final evaluation also uses. An explicit sentence ("pre-training uses training-split labels only") would settle it; the paper does not contain one.

    The added cost, stated plainly. A pure hypergraph network trains one model on one dataset. This method additionally trains a boosted ensemble per dataset, before the network begins, and carries an extra preprocessing dependency into inference: at test time the frozen ensemble must be run on each new vertex's features to produce its rule embedding. Neither the training time nor the inference overhead is reported anywhere in the paper.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — read Table IV's two columns as embedding parameters. The paper reports a tree count and a depth for each dataset. Take an illustrative pair — say 100 trees at depth 3 — and work out what that implies for the embedding's width.

    A binary tree of depth 3 has at most inner nodes.
    Powers of two: depth 1 has 1 inner node, depth 2 has up to 3, depth 3 up to 7. This is the maximum, and boosted trees are usually grown to the full depth requested.
    Across 100 trees that is at most questions, so can approach 700.
    This is the number of coordinates each vertex carries before any fusion. The paper never reports it, which is why a reader has to reconstruct it from Table IV — and why the fusion's concern about dimension disparity is a real concern rather than a rhetorical one.
    After fusion, has entries — approaching 1,400 per vertex in this illustration.
    The doubling is the concatenation. At 37,700 vertices (Github) that is a feature matrix of order fifty million entries, before the network's own parameters. The cost is not prohibitive, but it is substantial and it is unstated.
    What this walk is for. It turns two unremarkable columns of a hyperparameter table into a concrete statement about the model's size, and it shows where the paper is silent. The illustrative numbers here are mine, not the paper's — the method is what matters: read a hyperparameter table as a description of the model it produces.

    Extension · Deep learning basics 1/7

    From a line to a curve: why one nonlinearity changes everything

    The paper's model is a stack of matrix operations trained by gradient descent, and it never stops to explain any of that. This section supplies the whole assumed toolkit: the neuron and the layer, the nonlinearity that makes depth mean anything, the loss that turns a task into a single number, gradient descent, backpropagation, and the train/validation split that decides when to stop. Read it and the paper's equations stop being notation and start being a network.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA linear model predicts a target from an input by a weighted sum plus a constant: with one input, ; with inputs, . The weight sets the slope and the bias sets the height. Its signature is that the output is a flat function of the input — a straight line in one dimension, a flat plane in two, a hyperplane in more.A linear model draws a single straight line through the data and reads its answers off that line. It owns exactly two knobs — how steep the line is, and how high it sits — and a straight line is all two knobs can buy.

    The problem with one line. Suppose you measure something that first rises and then falls: the height of a thrown ball against time, or the accuracy of a model as you add layers, which climbs and then falls again. Plot the measurements and the points bend. A line cannot bend. Whatever slope and height you choose, the shape is fixed — straight. You can tilt the line and lift it, and there is no third knob. On a bending dataset the best line is a compromise that is wrong everywhere at once, and collecting more data does not conjure the knob the line lacks.

    The fix: bend the computation, then bend it again. Instead of one line, build several, evaluate them all, and pass each result through a nonlinearity — a fixed function that bends its input, such as the ramp , which is zero for negative inputs and equal to the input for positive ones. A weighted sum of these bent pieces can trace a curve. Repeat the operation — form linear combinations, bend, combine the results — and each round adds another input location at which the composite function may change direction. That is the whole idea of a neural network: many simple bends, summed and re-bent, until the total shape can follow the data.

    The nonlinearity is not decoration. Remove it and a composition of linear maps is still a linear map — card 2 proves this in one line of matrix algebra — so a thousand-layer network with no nonlinearities is exactly one linear model wearing a thousand coats.
    A two-layer network written out. The inner piece is a stack of linear models; bends each of their outputs; the outer weights and bias combine the bent pieces into the final answer. The bend is what the next layer gets to work with, and it is why the second layer is not redundant with the first.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the input vector — the raw measurements for one example
    the first layer's weights and bias: a stack of linear models applied to
    the fixed nonlinearity applied independently to every output of the inner sum
    the second layer, combining the bent inner outputs into the final prediction

    What universal approximation promises — and what it does not. A theorem says that a network with a single hidden layer and enough units can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region to any accuracy you name. Read it precisely, because it promises less than it sounds. It says some such network exists: it says nothing about how wide that network must be, and the required width can be astronomically large. It does not say that gradient descent (card 5) will find that network from data, nor that a finite dataset determines it. And it says nothing about generalisation — a wide-enough network can fit every training point and still be useless on new ones (card 7). Universal approximation is a claim about what is representable, not about what is learnable.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — where one line fails. Three measurements. At the target is ; at it is ; at it is again.

    Fit the best straight line by least squares. The three values average to and the three values to . The covariance numerator is .
    A zero numerator means the best slope is . The fit has given up on the shape and is reporting a single average — the straight line with the smallest possible total error here is flat.
    With slope , the intercept is the mean, . So the best line predicts at every input.
    Predictions at are all , against targets . The line is too low at both ends and too low in the middle.
    Residuals: , , . Squared and averaged, .
    That is the best a line can do, and the error is concentrated at the middle point, which the line cannot reach. A single linear model has no way to be high in the middle and low at both ends — that shape needs a bend.

    Example 2 — the same three points, fitted exactly by a sum of bends. Build a small network whose hidden layer holds three ReLU pieces and whose output is a weighted sum of them:

    Three ReLU pieces added with weights . The first rises from ; the second, subtracted twice, bends the sum down after ; the third flattens it out after . The weights were chosen by hand to make the shape obvious — finding them automatically is card 5's job — but the bend is the point.

The line needed a bend it did not have; the ReLU sum supplies bends, and with enough of them any piecewise-linear shape can be built. That is the practical content of universal approximation: bends are the raw material, and adding them is the strategy.

    The neuron and the layer: a matrix multiply, a bias, and a bend

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA layer maps an input vector to an output vector by three steps: multiply by a weight matrix , add a bias vector , and apply a fixed nonlinearity to each coordinate: . Each of the rows of is the weight vector of one neuron, so one layer is neurons evaluating in parallel on the same input.A layer is a bank of neurons that all read the same input. Each neuron is a weighted sum plus a constant, and then the same bend is applied to every neuron's result. The whole bank is one matrix times the input, plus one bias vector, plus one bend.

    Read the shapes and the layer explains itself. If the input has numbers and the layer produces , then has rows and columns, and has entries. Row of dotted with gives the -th neuron's weighted sum; adding offsets it; bends it. The matrix is not a mathematical convenience bolted on afterwards — it is the statement apply separate weighted sums at once, and the rows are the neurons.

    Why the nonlinearity is load-bearing. Drop and a layer becomes a purely linear map. Now suppose you stack two of them: the second layer receives and outputs . Expand the brackets: . The product is a single matrix and a single vector, so the two layers together equal one linear layer with weight matrix . The argument repeats for any number of layers. Without a bend between them, depth changes the parameterisation and nothing else.

    The layer, in one line. is weighted sums of the input; shifts each; bends each — and because is applied entry by entry, it cannot be absorbed into the matrix, which is exactly why the stack escapes being a single linear map.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the input vector, with entries
    the weight matrix, rows by columns; row is neuron 's weights
    the bias vector, one entry per neuron — the constant added to each weighted sum
    the elementwise nonlinearity; applied to every coordinate independently (card 3 lists the common choices)
    the layer's output — the feature vector handed to the next layer, with entries
    A common misreading: that each neuron 'sees' only part of the input. It does not. Every neuron in a layer reads the whole input vector; what differs between neurons is the weights they apply. Conversely, applying one neuron to every input in a dataset is again just a matrix multiply — the matrix rows are the examples.
    EXAMPLE

    First neuron: .
    Row 1 of dotted with . A dot product is a weighted sum — the neuron's raw opinion before the bias and the bend.
    Second neuron: . So .
    Row 2 is a different weighted summary of the same input. Both neurons read every entry of ; they differ only in their weights.
    Add the bias: .
    The bias shifts each neuron's output independently — here it lifts the first neuron off zero. Without a bias a neuron whose weighted sum happened to be zero could never be switched on.
    Apply ReLU entry by entry: , , so .
    Here both entries were positive so ReLU did nothing. Had the first entry been negative the bias would have been the only thing keeping it alive. The bend acts on each coordinate separately.

    Example 2 — two layers that collapse into one. Let and , and ignore biases for clarity. Feed the input through both, in order.

    • Through the first layer alone: .

Insert any nonlinearity between the layers and the fourth line breaks: is not a matrix, so cannot be written as a single matrix times . The bend is the only thing standing between a deep network and an expensive copy of a shallow one.
