    Activation functions: the bend, and why ReLU won

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONAn activation function is a fixed, non-linear, scalar function applied independently to every entry of a layer's pre-activation , so that the layer's output is . It is chosen once by the designer and is never updated by learning. The four in common use are the step function, the sigmoid, the hyperbolic tangent, and the rectified linear unit (ReLU).An activation function is the bend applied at each neuron. It is a fixed rule — same rule for every neuron in the layer, and the same rule every time you run the network — that turns a straight-line computation into a curved one. It has no parameters to learn.

    Why a non-constant, non-linear function is required. Card 2 showed that a stack of purely linear maps is one linear map. So the activation must be non-linear; if it were linear, it would fold into the weight matrix like any other matrix and add nothing. It must also be non-constant — a function that output a fixed number for every input would discard the input entirely. Within those two requirements there is a large menu, and the four standard entries trade off differently against one thing above all: what the derivative looks like, because the derivative is what gradient descent uses to train the network (card 6).

    The sigmoid and its saturation problem. The sigmoid squashes any real number into the interval , which is why it suits probabilities: extremely negative inputs map near , extremely positive inputs near , and maps to . Its difficulty is exactly this squashing. Once its input is large in magnitude — say below or above — the output is pinned near or and the slope is nearly zero. A nearly zero slope means the gradient flowing back through that neuron is nearly zero, so the weights feeding it barely change. The neuron is said to be saturated, and in a deep network saturation at many layers compounds: multiplying many near-zero derivatives together produces a gradient of essentially zero, and the early layers stop learning.

    ActivationFormulaRangeDerivativeMain problem
    Step if , else Zero almost everywhere, undefined at Derivative is zero — gradient descent cannot train it
    SigmoidSaturates: slope near zero for large , so gradients vanish
    TanhAlso saturates, though its range is centred on zero
    ReLU if , else Dead units: a neuron stuck at has zero gradient

    Why ReLU became the default. Look at the derivative column. For any positive input, ReLU's slope is exactly — no narrowing, no compounding loss of signal however deep the stack. Its arithmetic is a comparison rather than an exponential, which is far cheaper. And because it outputs exactly for negative inputs, a typical layer leaves some fraction of its units switched off, which makes the activations sparse and the effective computation lighter. Tanh, by contrast, centres its output on zero instead of on (helpful for the layers that follow) but still saturates. The trade ReLU accepts is its own failure mode: a unit whose input is negative for every training example receives zero gradient forever and is permanently dead — a real and common problem that the tanh and sigmoid families do not have.

    Do not read the table's 'problem' column as ruling a function out. Sigmoid is still the standard final activation for a binary classifier, because its range is what a probability needs. The choice is per-layer: a hidden layer usually wants a cheap non-saturating bend (ReLU or tanh), and the output layer wants whatever shape the target demands.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the sigmoid at a spread of inputs. The sigmoid is . Compute it at a few points and watch the curve flatten at the ends.

    At : , so .
    Zero is the centre — the sigmoid maps it to the midpoint of its range. Any input above zero gives a value above half.
    At : , so .
    An input of 2 already pushes the output to 0.88. The function is steep near zero, so small inputs move the output a lot.
    At : , so .
    By symmetry, : negative inputs give values below half, mirroring the positive side.
    At : , so .
    An input of 4 buys only where 2 bought . The gain per extra unit of input is shrinking fast — the curve is flattening towards its ceiling of 1.
    Input Sigmoid Slope
    0.0179860.017663
    0.1192030.104994
    0.5000000.250000
    0.8807970.104994
    0.9820140.017663

    The third column is the saturation problem made numeric. At the slope is , the maximum the sigmoid ever attains. By the slope has fallen to , roughly fourteen times smaller. Stack ten sigmoid layers and a gradient passing through them is multiplied by numbers of this size at each step: raised to the tenth power is smaller than , and the effective gradient reaching the first layer is, for practical purposes, zero. The early layers receive no information about how to improve.

    ReLU does not have this particular failure. Its slope is exactly for every positive input, so a gradient passing through a chain of active ReLU units is unchanged in magnitude by the activations themselves. That single property — a derivative that neither shrinks nor explodes over the active region — is the reason ReLU displaced the sigmoid in hidden layers and made genuinely deep networks trainable.

    Extension · Deep learning basics 4/7

    Loss functions: turning a task into a number to minimise

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA loss function maps a model's prediction and the true target to a single non-negative real number measuring how wrong the prediction is, and the training loss is the average of this over all training examples. Training means choosing the parameters to make the training loss as small as possible. For regression the standard choice is the mean squared error; for classification over classes it is the cross-entropy.A loss is one number summarising how bad the model's answers are across the data. Learning is just making that number small — so the loss has to be built so that a smaller number really does mean a better model.

    Why the number has to be a single scalar. The model has many parameters written as a vector, and a prediction error is naturally a vector too — one error per example. But gradient descent (card 5) works by asking 'if I nudge this parameter, which way does the loss move?' That question only has an answer if the loss is one number. A vector cannot be minimised: making one component smaller generally makes another larger, and there is no single direction that improves everything. Collapsing the error to a scalar — by squaring and averaging, or by averaging negative log-probabilities — creates the one quantity whose direction of decrease can be followed.

    Mean squared error, the regression default. Each prediction's error is squared (so negative and positive misses both count as bad, and large misses count disproportionately) and the results are averaged over the examples. Squaring is what makes the loss a smooth function of the parameters, which is what lets the gradient exist and point somewhere useful.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the number of examples averaged over
    the model's predicted value for example
    the true target for example
    the squared error for example — zero when perfect, growing quadratically with distance
    Cross-entropy, the classification default. For each example the model outputs a probability for every class; is the probability it assigned to the true class of example , and the loss is the average negative log of that number. If the model is confident and right, the probability is near 1, its log near 0, and the loss near 0; if it is confident and wrong, the probability is near 0, its log is a large negative number, and the minus sign makes the loss large. The negative logarithm's steep drop near zero is what punishes confident mistakes.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the probability the model gave to the correct class of example
    the natural logarithm — here it measures unlikelihood: the closer a probability is to 0, the more negative its log
    the leading minus sign flips log-probabilities (which are negative) into non-negative losses that we want to drive to zero

    What each loss is for, and where each fails. Mean squared error belongs to regression, where the target is a real number and distance is the natural notion of error. Applying it to a classifier is a known mistake: combine the squared error with a sigmoid output and the gradient at a confidently wrong prediction becomes nearly zero, so the model learns slowest exactly where it is most wrong. Cross-entropy fixes this — its penalty grows without bound as the assigned probability of the true class approaches zero, so a confident mistake produces a large gradient and is corrected fast. Its own failure mode is the mirror image: because it never stops penalising, a single mislabelled example can contribute a very large loss and pull the model towards fitting an error, and its logarithm means a predicted probability of exactly zero yields an infinite loss, so probabilities are always clamped away from the extremes in practice.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — mean squared error, three predictions. A regression model predicts ; the true targets are . Compute the mean squared error.

    Errors: , , .
    The sign records the direction of the miss, but MSE will discard it — over-prediction and under-prediction should be penalised equally.
    Squares: , , .
    Squaring removes the signs and weights the misses by size. The third example's error of 2 contributes 4, four times as much as the first example's error of 1, which contributes 1.
    Sum: . Mean over three examples: .
    So the model's mean squared error is . In the same units squared, the error is moderate: the worst single example is off by 2.

    Example 2 — cross-entropy on three probability vectors. A three-class classifier outputs a probability vector for each example. Take three examples whose true class is the first class in every case, so the only thing changing is how the model distributes its probability. The three predicted vectors are , , and .

    Predicted vectorProbability of true classCross-entropy
    Row 1: , because . Row 2: — the familiar value that makes the 'one bit' of uncertainty. Row 3: . Mean over the three: .
    Compare rows 1 and 3. The model that was right about the true class, giving it 0.90, pays ; the model that was wrong, giving the true class only 0.05, pays — about twenty-eight times as much for a prediction that was confidently wrong in the other direction. The logarithm is doing precisely the work the classification task needs: a confident error is expensive, and the loss cannot be reduced by hedging on the wrong class. Confident and correct is cheap, which is the behaviour you want.

    Extension · Deep learning basics 5/7

    Gradient descent: walking downhill on the loss

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONGradient descent updates each parameter by subtracting a small multiple of the loss's derivative with respect to that parameter: , where is the learning rate and is the gradient — the rate at which the loss changes as changes, holding the other parameters fixed. The subtraction is there because the gradient points in the direction of increasing loss; moving against it decreases the loss. Repeating this update over many steps is the whole of training.Gradient descent is walking downhill on a hilly loss landscape. The gradient tells you which way is uphill, so you step the other way. The learning rate is your stride length: it decides how far you move on each step.

    The loss surface. Plot the loss against every parameter and you get a surface: high where the parameters are wrong, low in the valleys where they are right. Training is a search over this surface for a low point. The gradient is the local slope — a vector holding, for each parameter, the direction and steepness of the loss's increase at the current point. The gradient does not tell you where the global valley is; it tells you which way is down right here, and descent follows that local signal in steps, re-evaluating the slope after each one. For a loss that is a smooth function of the parameters — which is why card 4 chose squaring and logarithms — this slope exists everywhere and can be computed by the chain rule (card 6).

    The update rule for a single parameter, applied simultaneously to every parameter at each step. The gradient carries the units of 'loss per unit of ', so multiplying it by the learning rate converts it into an actual change in . The minus sign is the descent: the gradient points uphill, so we go the other way.
    SymbolWhat it means
    one parameter being adjusted — a weight or bias
    the learning rate, a small positive number chosen in advance, not learned
    the gradient: how fast the loss changes per unit of , at the current values
    the arrow means assign: the new value replaces the old, and the process repeats

    What the learning rate does. The update is a balance between two quantities: the slope tells you how much a step should matter, and the learning rate bounds how far you actually go. Three regimes, all visible in the worked example below. If is too small, each step barely moves the parameters; the descent is correct but so slow that training may take an impractical number of steps, and near a flat region the tiny gradient makes progress stall entirely. If is just right, the steps shrink as the slope flattens near the bottom and the parameters settle towards a minimum. If is too large, a step taken against a steep slope overshoots the valley and lands on the opposite wall, higher than before; repeated overshoots make the loss oscillate or grow without bound — divergence.

    The learning rate is not learned by gradient descent — you cannot differentiate the update rule with respect to it — so it is set by hand and is called a hyperparameter. In practice it is the single most consequential setting: a network with a good architecture and a bad learning rate will not train, while the same architecture with a good one will. Practitioners often reduce it over training, so that early steps move fast and later steps refine the position.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — descent on a parabola, three learning rates. Take the toy loss , a parabola with its minimum at . Its derivative is , so the update is . Start every run from and follow the first few steps.

    Learning rate . At the slope is , so . Next: slope , . Then , then , then , climbing towards .
    A small rate: every step moves in the correct direction and the steps shrink as the slope flattens, but after five steps is still only — a long way from in relative terms. Correct but slow.
    Learning rate . From : , then , then , then , then .
    A larger rate that still converges: the same sequence of updates but with much bigger strides, reaching in five steps what the slow rate took dozens to approach. This is the 'just right' regime for this loss.
    Learning rate . From : , then , then , then .
    The step exactly overshoots the minimum to the symmetric point on the other wall, then back. The loss never decreases — the parameters bounce between and forever.
    Learning rate . From : , then , then , then , then .
    Each bounce is larger than the last: the parameters fly off to ever-greater magnitudes and the loss grows without bound. This is divergence, and it is what a too-large learning rate looks like on the loss curve — a number that climbs instead of falls.
    The four runs used one loss and one starting point; only the learning rate changed, and it alone decided whether the model converged slowly, converged quickly, oscillated, or exploded. The value converges here, and note why it can: the slope near a curvature-2 parabola is at most about , and a step of is smaller than the remaining distance, so the step lands short of the far wall rather than past it. Scaling the rate to the curvature is what keeps descent stable, which is why practitioners tune it against the specific loss at hand.

    Where this is going: gradient descent needs the gradient for every parameter, and a network can have millions of them. Card 6 shows how the chain rule computes them all efficiently — the algorithm called backpropagation.
    Extension · Deep learning basics 6/7

    Backpropagation: the chain rule, run backwards

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONBackpropagation is the systematic application of the chain rule to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter of a layered network. Because the network is a composition of functions, the derivative of the loss with respect to an early parameter is the product of the derivatives of every function between that parameter and the loss: for a two-layer chain. Backpropagation evaluates these products from the output backwards to the input, so that each intermediate derivative is computed once and reused.Backpropagation is bookkeeping for the chain rule. To learn how much a weight near the input contributed to the final error, you multiply together the local effects of everything that came after it. You compute those local effects starting from the output and working backwards, so each one is used exactly once.

    The chain rule, restated for networks. If affects , and affects , and affects the loss , then the rate at which changes with is the product of the three individual rates: how responds to , how responds to , how responds to . Each factor is a local derivative — it only involves one operation in the network — and the chain rule assembles them into the global one. A network is many such links in a chain, so for any weight is the product of the local derivatives along the path from that weight to the loss.

    Why the computation runs backwards. The derivative of the loss with respect to the output, , is a factor in the gradient of every weight upstream of . Compute it once at the output and pass it back. Then the derivative with respect to the last hidden layer's pre-activation, in turn, is a factor in the gradient of every weight upstream of that. Working backwards means each layer's gradient is built from the layer-after-it's gradient, already computed, times a cheap local derivative — the same accumulation for every layer, reusing work rather than repeating it. Done forwards, each weight's gradient would require its own separate traversal of the whole network; done backwards, all of them fall out of one sweep. That factorisation is the difference between a network that trains in seconds and one that never trains at all.

    The backward pass implies something with consequences for deep models: each layer's gradient is a product of the derivatives of all the layers after it. Multiply together many factors larger than 1 and the gradient explodes; multiply many smaller than 1 and it vanishes. This is the same compounding that made sigmoid saturation dangerous in card 3, now stated in general — depth is a chain of multiplications in the gradient, and the health of a deep network depends on those products staying moderate.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a two-layer chain rule, evaluated numerically. Take the smallest interesting network: one input , one hidden unit with weight , one output with weight , no bias and no nonlinearity (so the chain is as transparent as possible), and squared-error loss against the target . The forward computation is , then .

    Forward pass. . Then . The loss is .
    Two multiplications and a subtraction. This is everything the network does on one example; the backward pass now asks how each weight contributed to that loss of 4.
    Gradient at the output. .
    The outermost local derivative, and the one every upstream factor starts from. It is positive because the prediction overshot the target, so the loss increases with .
    Gradient of the output weight. , so .
    Only one link stands between and the loss: . The chain rule gives . The factor is large, so this weight is implicated strongly.
    Gradient of the hidden weight. and , so .
    Two links now: . The gradient is the product of three local derivatives. It is larger than because feeds the blow-up at .
    One gradient step with : and .
    Both gradients were positive, so both weights are reduced. This is the correction — the network was over-predicting, so it shrinks the weights.
    Recompute the loss with the new weights. , , .
    The loss fell from to about after a single step, confirming the gradients pointed the right way. The target of 4 is still not reached — the step was deliberately small, and training is the repetition of this over many examples and many steps.
    Note the structure of the backward pass: the factor was computed once, and then reused for both weights. needed it times one more factor; needed it times two. In a network of a million parameters, that single output derivative is reused a million times — which is exactly why backpropagation makes training tractable rather than merely possible.

    Where this is going: backpropagation and gradient descent together are the training loop the paper's model uses. Card 7 covers the last piece of the standard toolkit — the obstacle that training tends to run into — and then offers a check that you can leave this section.
    Extension · Deep learning basics 7/7

    Overfitting, regularisation, and the skip check

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONOverfitting is when a model fits the training data more closely than it fits the pattern that generated it, so that its error on new data is worse than its error on data it has seen. It is detected with a validation set — data held out of training and never used to update the parameters — and shows up as a gap: the training loss keeps falling while the validation loss stops falling and begins to rise. Regularisation is any technique that penalises model complexity to keep that gap small.Overfitting is memorising the training examples instead of learning the pattern behind them. You catch it by testing on examples the model never trained on: if its error there is much worse, and getting worse while the training error keeps dropping, it has memorised.

    Why you cannot judge a model on the data it trained on. Gradient descent is designed to reduce the training loss, and a sufficiently large network can drive it to nearly zero by memorising each example — including its noise. The training loss therefore tells you how hard the model worked to fit, not whether it captured anything transferable. To measure the latter you need examples the parameters never saw. The standard split is to hold out a fraction of the data — commonly 20 percent — as a validation set. With 10,000 examples that is 8,000 for training and 2,000 for validation. The validation set is used to make decisions (when to stop, how strong the regularisation should be); a further test set, held out even from those decisions, is reserved for the final reported number. Reusing the validation set to make too many decisions gradually contaminates it, which is why a separate test set exists.

    The four standard remedies. All of them reduce the model's effective freedom to memorise. More data is the most reliable — more examples leave less room to fit noise — but it is often unavailable. Weight decay (also called L2 regularisation) adds a penalty proportional to the squared size of the weights to the loss, discouraging large weights, which are what let a network fit sharply and noisily. Dropout randomly switches off a fraction of units during each training step, so no unit can rely on the presence of any other and co-adapted memorising circuits cannot form. Early stopping stops training at the point where the validation loss is lowest, before it starts rising — the simplest remedy, and it needs no change to the model at all.

    Weight decay in one line. The ordinary loss is augmented by a term proportional to the sum of squared weights, with strength controlled by the hyperparameter . Gradient descent then has to reduce both the error and the weight magnitudes, so it prefers small weights unless a large weight earns its size by reducing the error substantially. Large weights are what let a network bend sharply to touch every training point; shrinking them smooths the learned function.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the original loss — mean squared error or cross-entropy, from card 4
    the sum of the squares of all the weights — a single number measuring how large the model's weights are
    the regularisation strength, a hyperparameter: disables the penalty, large pushes weights hard towards zero

    The trade-off, and where each remedy fails. Regularisation deliberately makes the training loss worse — it forbids the model from fitting some of the training data — in exchange for a better validation loss. Push it too far and the opposite failure appears, underfitting: the weights are crushed towards zero, the model can no longer bend enough, and both training and validation loss stay high. Overfitting and underfitting are the two ends of one dial, and the validation set is how you find the middle. Weight decay cannot tell a genuinely large, useful weight from an oversized noisy one, only that large weights are penalised; dropout adds noise that can slow convergence; early stopping requires a validation set to monitor, and its result depends on how often you check.

    • Explain why a linear model cannot fit a curve, and what a nonlinearity between layers adds (card 1).
    • Write a layer as and give the shapes of and for a given input and output size (card 2).
    • Say why removing the nonlinearity collapses any stack of layers to a single linear map (card 2).
    • Name the four common activations and state the saturation problem of the sigmoid and why ReLU avoids it (card 3).
    • Write cross-entropy for a classification prediction and explain why it punishes confident errors heavily (card 4).
    • Apply one gradient-descent update , and say what an over-large learning rate does (card 5).
    • Explain why backpropagation runs backwards, and why an early layer's gradient is a product of the derivatives after it (card 6).
    The questions below are the check for the whole section. The bar is not 'two out of four' — it is that you did not have to stop and reconstruct anything. If any line of that list made you hesitate, the relevant card is short and worth the re-read: card 4's cross-entropy and card 6's chain rule are the two the paper leans on most heavily.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — reading an overfitting curve. The table is an illustrative training run (numbers chosen to show the shape of the phenomenon, not measured from any specific dataset): the training loss and the validation loss, at several points in training.

    EpochTraining lossValidation lossGap
    12.102.200.10
    21.401.500.10
    31.051.180.13
    50.720.950.23
    100.400.980.58
    200.151.251.10
    500.031.801.77
    Early on, both losses fall together: by epoch 3 the training loss is 1.05 and the validation loss 1.18, a gap of 0.13.
    The model is learning a pattern that transfers — the validation loss, measured on unseen data, improves alongside the training loss. This is healthy.
    The validation loss reaches its lowest value, 0.95, at epoch 5. After that it stops falling while the training loss keeps dropping.
    Epoch 5 is the point to stop. The model is no longer improving on new data; further training only tightens its grip on the training set.
    By epoch 50 the training loss is 0.03 and the validation loss has risen to 1.80 — a gap of .
    The widening gap is the signature of overfitting. The training loss of 0.03 looks excellent in isolation and is misleading: on data the model has not seen, it is far worse than it was at epoch 5.
    Early stopping on this run would have halted at epoch 5 and kept the model with validation loss 0.95 — better on unseen data than the epoch-50 model by a factor of nearly two, despite the epoch-50 model's training loss being thirty times smaller. The training loss is not the number to report. Any claim of quality has to come from data the model never trained on.

    Example 2 — what weight decay adds. Take a model whose weights are and set the strength . The penalty is . This is added to the ordinary loss: if the data loss were , the value actually minimised becomes . Weight decay thereby makes the model pay for large weights, and the gradient of the penalty ( per weight) nudges each weight towards zero by an amount proportional to its own size.

    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDA model's training loss is 0.03 and its validation loss is 1.80. What does this combination indicate?

    APPLYA model has weights and weight decay strength . What penalty does the regularisation term add to the loss?

    TRANSFERA validation set is held out of training. Why is it not also used, step by step, to update the weights?

    TRANSFERA colleague removes the nonlinearity from every hidden layer of a deep network and adds more layers to compensate. Why does this not increase the model's expressive power?

When the paper's Equation (1) introduces its hypergraph convolution, read it as a layer: a matrix-like operation, a bias, and a ReLU — trained exactly the way this section described.
    Extension · Supervised learning 1/5

    The supervised setup: labelled examples, a hypothesis class, and the gap between fitting and generalising

    The part of an experimental paper most readers skip and most reviewers read first. This section builds the supervised setup from scratch — labelled examples, features and targets, the hypothesis class, and the gap between fitting the data you have and generalising to data you do not. It then takes apart the three-way split, cross-validation, the parameter/hyperparameter distinction, and the contract every results table is supposed to honour. By the end you can tell a real number from a manufactured one.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA supervised learning problem is a triple. First, a set of labelled examples for , where is a feature vector — a list of measurements describing one case — and is its target, the answer we want to predict. Second, a hypothesis class : a fixed family of candidate functions, each mapping a feature vector to a predicted target. Third, a loss function that scores how far a prediction is from the true . Learning means searching for the that fits the training examples best.You show the program a pile of labelled examples. It picks one rule out of a family of rules you supplied. The rule that fits the examples you showed it is the one it keeps. But the number that matters is how that rule behaves on cases it has never been shown.

    Why the machinery is the topic, not the model. A paper's headline claim is rarely "our network is clever." It is "our network scored 73.4 on these five datasets." That sentence is a claim about a procedure: how the data was cut, what was fixed before learning began, and what was finally measured. A reader who skips this part cannot tell a strong result from a lucky one — and reviewing a paper consists almost entirely of trying to tell exactly that.

    Features and targets. Every example is a pair. The feature vector gathers everything you are permitted to know before the answer appears: a node's neighbourhood, a molecule's atom types, a patient's lab values. The target is the answer: a category, or a number. A dataset is labelled when each example arrives with its . The word supervised names the role of — it supervises the search, because it is the signal the learner is told to reproduce.

    The hypothesis class. The learner is not free to return an arbitrary program. You hand it a family and let it pick one member. The family "lines of the form " is indexed by two numbers; "a neural network with this fixed architecture" is a family indexed by all of its weights. The family decides what can be expressed at all: no quantity of data will teach a straight line to bend. Choosing the family is the modeller's decision, taken before any learning happens, and it cannot be corrected by the training set.

    Fitting is a means, not the goal. During training the learner reduces error on the examples it was given. That is a proxy. The quantity that matters is error on examples it has never seen — which nobody can compute exactly, only estimate from held-out data. When a model does well on the first and badly on the second, it has memorised rather than learned. This is why "accuracy on the data you trained on" is not a result: it is guaranteed to look good, because the training procedure was explicitly instructed to make it good.

    The trap, stated plainly. A model with enough capacity can reach 100% training accuracy on almost anything, including data whose targets were assigned by a coin flip, by drawing a boundary that threads through every point. Perfect training accuracy is therefore evidence of nothing — not of a good model, not of an informative dataset, not of a good idea. The only number that carries information is one computed on examples that had no influence on training.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — two rules fit equally well and disagree anyway. Four students, one feature each: hours studied. The target is the outcome, pass or fail.

    hours studiedoutcome
    1fail
    2fail
    4pass
    5pass

    The hypothesis class is every rule of the form "pass if hours ," with a whole number from 1 to 5 — five candidate rules. We try each on the four examples and count how many it gets right.

    Rule : predict pass when hours . Hours 1 and 2 give fail (correct); hours 4 and 5 give pass (correct). Training accuracy .
    Every training example is matched. This is the only quantity the training procedure can see, so it is the only quantity it can optimise.
    Rule : predict pass when hours . Hours 1, 2 and 3 give fail; hours 4 and 5 give pass. Training accuracy again .
    A different rule with the identical training score. The training data expresses no preference between the two.
    Now a fifth student, 3 hours studied, whose true outcome is fail. Rule predicts pass — wrong. Rule predicts fail — right.
    The two rules were indistinguishable on the training set and disagree precisely where it matters. Training accuracy cannot separate them; only data they did not learn from can. That is the concrete sense in which it is not a result.
    The training set contains no example at 3 hours, so the two rules differ only on inputs it never mentions. This is the normal situation, not a contrived one: a finite training set under-determines the model unless it happens to pin down the answer everywhere. Generalisation is the study of what the model does in those gaps.

    Example 2 — a trained model with a large gap. A model is fitted to 100 labelled examples. On those it scores . On 100 fresh examples drawn from the same source it scores .

    Training accuracy . Test accuracy . Gap . With two classes, guessing would score , so the model is five percentage points above chance on new data.
    Notice which number the word result attaches to. "100% accuracy," quoted without any mention of a held-out set, describes how hard the model worked, not how well it works. Example 2 is not a failure of the model; it is what the two different measurements mean.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDIn the supervised setup, what is the target of an example?

    APPLYA model scores 47 correct out of 50 on its training set and 31 correct out of 50 on a held-out set. What is the gap between training accuracy and held-out accuracy, as a fraction? fraction

    UNDERSTANDWhy is training accuracy guaranteed to look good?

    TRANSFERIn Example 1, rules and both scored 1.00 on the training set. What does that tell you about the training set itself?

    Where this is going: the gap in Example 1 is the reason data must be divided. The next card takes the single held-out set and runs it through its three distinct jobs — training, choosing, and reporting — and shows what happens when they are confused.
    Extension · Supervised learning 2/5

    The three-way split: training, validation, test — and how tuning on the test set manufactures a result

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA three-way split partitions the labelled data into three disjoint sets. The training set is used to fit the model's parameters. The validation set is used to choose everything that is fixed before or during fitting — hyperparameters, when to stop, which model to keep — and its scores may be looked at repeatedly. The test set is used exactly once, at the end, to report performance; no decision may depend on it. A number is a result only if it comes from the test set and the test set influenced no choice.Three buckets. One to learn from, one to make decisions with, and one you open a single time at the end. If a decision was informed by a bucket, that bucket has stopped being a test set.

    Why one held-out set is not enough. Card 1 established that a model must be judged on data it did not learn from. But a real experiment makes many decisions beyond fitting: how many layers, what learning rate, how long to train. If those decisions are made while looking at the same held-out set used to report, then that set has been used for learning too — and the reported number inherits the optimism of everything that was tuned on it. The fix is to give the two jobs two different sets.

    The three jobs. Training decides the parameters. Validation decides the choices the experimenter controls: it is the set you are allowed to score your model on dozens of times, comparing settings, and it is expected to be used and abused. Test is the untouched set you consult once, after every choice is frozen, to ask the single question "how well does the finished procedure do?" Because it was never consulted while choices were being made, its score carries no optimism from the search.

    Leakage, and the specific leak of tuning on the test set. Leakage is any flow of information from the data used for evaluation into the model or the choices behind it. It is subtle because it need not be intentional: if you compute a feature's mean over the whole dataset and then split, or if you try twenty settings and keep whichever has the best test score, information from the test set has entered the model. In the second case the test score is no longer an estimate of how the procedure would behave on fresh data — it is the maximum of many scores you searched over, which is systematically higher than any of them is on average.

    The rule in one line: a set can either guide decisions or report on them, never both. Looking at the test set once and then adjusting anything — a hyperparameter, a feature, a threshold — converts it into a validation set permanently. There is no way to undo this later; the honest response is to obtain fresh test data.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the three buckets on a real-sized dataset. Take 10,000 labelled examples. A conventional split is 60 / 20 / 20: 6,000 for training, 2,000 for validation, 2,000 for test.

    setsize heredecideshow often you may look
    training6,000the model's parameters (weights)continuously, during fitting
    validation2,000hyperparameters, stopping point, model selectionas often as you like
    test2,000nothing — it reportsonce, at the very end

    The split does not have to be equal. When data is scarce, the conventional ratios shift towards training, and validation and test shrink — which is exactly the situation card 3's cross-validation is designed for. What never changes is the rule attached to the test row: nothing is allowed to depend on it.

    Example 2 — how much of an apparent gain is noise? This is the quantitative heart of the leak, and it is worth doing honestly rather than by assertion. Suppose you try 20 hyperparameter settings. In truth all 20 are identical: the same expected test accuracy , with no real difference between them. You score each on a test set of 200 examples and keep the winner. How much better than will the winner appear?

    Each setting's test score is an estimate, not the truth. For a held-out set of examples and true accuracy , the standard deviation of that estimate is , about 3.2 percentage points.
    A test score is an average of correct-or-wrong outcomes over a finite sample, so it wobbles around the truth exactly as any sample mean does. This is the size of one setting's wobble.
    The score you keep is the maximum of 20 such noisy numbers. For 20 independent standard-normal draws, the expected maximum sits about standard deviations above the mean. This number comes from numerical integration of the maximum's distribution, not from a textbook constant.
    Taking the best of several noisy estimates systematically overshoots the truth, and the overshoot grows with how many settings you try. This is why a search can look productive while changing nothing real.
    Convert back to percentage points: . So the winning setting would appear to be about 6 points better than the truth, on average, even though all 20 settings are identical.
    Nothing improved. The apparent improvement was manufactured entirely out of sampling noise, by the act of choosing the largest number in a noisy list.
    Two honest caveats, because overstating this would itself be a form of the error it describes. First, the 20 scores are not independent — they share one test set, so their errors move together, which shrinks the effect below 6 points; the figure is an upper guide, and the direction is what matters. Second, this is not an argument against trying many settings. It is an argument against doing so on the test set. Search on validation, where choosing is legitimate, and the test set stays clean.

    The size of the illusion depends on the test set. On a 1,000-example test set the same calculation gives a wobble of , about 1.4 points, and a 20-way search would look about points better than it is. On 5,000 examples the wobble is , about 0.65 points, and the inflation falls to roughly points. A larger test set shrinks the illusion; it never removes it, because the maximum of any finite set of noisy estimates still exceeds their average.

    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich split is intended to be looked at repeatedly, while choosing hyperparameters?

    APPLYYou try 20 identical hyperparameter settings and keep the best by test score. Each score has a standard deviation of 5 percentage points. Using the factor 1.87 from the card, by roughly how many percentage points will the winner appear to beat the truth? percentage points

    TRANSFERA paper states: "We tuned the learning rate, depth and dropout, and report the best test accuracy over all configurations." What is wrong with the reported number?

    UNDERSTANDWhy does using the test set to tune cause a problem, even if the tuning is honest and unintentional?

    Where this is going: a single split wastes data — the validation and test portions inform no fitting at all. When data is scarce, that waste is unaffordable, and the standard remedy is cross-validation, the subject of the next card.
    Extension · Supervised learning 3/5

    Cross-validation: estimating generalisation when data is scarce

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONIn -fold cross-validation the data is partitioned into folds of roughly equal size. Training is run times: on round , fold is held out for scoring and the other folds are used for training. The reported score is the average of the held-out scores. Every example is held out exactly once, so all of the data is used both for training (in rounds) and for evaluation (in one round).Cut the data into parts. Train times, each time hiding one part and scoring on it. Average the held-out scores. Nothing is wasted, because every example gets a turn as test data.

    Why it exists. A single split spends most of its data on fitting and keeps a slice aside that never helps fit anything. When the dataset is small — 25 examples, or 200 labelled nodes — that slice is a large fraction of everything you have, and giving it up both weakens the model and leaves you with a noisy estimate computed on very little. Cross-validation recycles the held-out portion.

    What the average estimates. The held-out scores estimate how a model trained on folds behaves on the remaining fold. Their average is an estimate of the procedure's generalisation performance, and because it averages numbers it is less variable than any single holdout score. It is not the performance of one particular trained model — it is the performance of the training procedure itself, retrained times. For reporting what a method does, that is usually the more honest target.

    The cost. Cross-validation multiplies training time by , and leaves you with fitted models instead of one. In the end you still have to choose: either train a final model on all the data and accept that its score is not the cross-validated one, or average the models' predictions. For expensive models the multiplier is the whole decision — on a model that takes a day to train is a ten-day experiment.

    schemedata used for trainingtraining runsvariance of the estimate
    single holdoutone fixed fraction, say 80%1high — the score depends on which examples landed in the holdout
    5-fold80% per round, 100% overall5moderate — averaged over 5 held-out scores
    10-fold90% per round, 100% overall10lower, with diminishing returns past about 10
    leave-one-out per round, 100% overalllow bias, but high variance and very expensive

    When it fails. Two failure modes are common. First, leakage inside the folds: any preprocessing learned from the data — a mean and standard deviation for scaling, a choice of which features to keep — must be fitted on the training folds only and applied to the held-out fold. Fitting it on everything first lets information from the held-out fold reach the model, and the cross-validated score is then as optimistic as a plain training score. Second, dependence between examples: if the data contains groups (several nodes from one graph, several images of one patient), folds must be split along those groups. A random split will place near-duplicates in both training and held-out folds and score the model on data it has effectively already seen.

    Cross-validation gives you a better estimate. It does not give you a test set. If cross-validation is used to compare hyperparameter settings, the scores it produces are validation scores and are subject to the same optimism as card 2's tuning leak. To both tune and report honestly you nest the two: an inner cross-validation chooses settings, an outer one produces the reported number.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a 5-fold split of 25 items, done by hand. Twenty-five labelled items, split into folds. Since , each fold holds exactly 5 items.

    Fold sizes: five folds of 5 items each. On each round one fold of 5 is held out and the other four folds, items, are used for training.
    Every item is held out exactly once across the five rounds, and appears in the training portion in the other four. That is the recycling that a single holdout cannot do.
    Suppose the held-out scores come back as , , , , . The reported score is the average: .
    The average is over five numbers, so it moves less than any one of them. The single fold that scored 0.4 has weight one-fifth, not all of it.
    Each fold score is a count out of 5: 4, 3, 5, 2, 4 correct. Sum them: . As a pooled fraction over all 25 items, — the same number.
    With folds of equal size, averaging the fold accuracies equals the overall accuracy over the pooled held-out predictions. That identity is a useful check: if your reported average disagrees with the pooled count, a fold size or a weights error has crept in.
    The cost is visible in the same example. Five folds means five training runs on 20 items each, not one run on 25. The benefit is that all 25 items contribute a held-out prediction, and the estimate is an average over five numbers instead of one.

    Example 2 — scaling up, and leave-one-out as the limit. With 250 items and , each fold holds items and each model trains on . Push the scheme to its extreme, , and each round trains on 24 items and scores 1 — leave-one-out. It uses the most training data per round and produces the least biased single-fold estimate, but it requires training runs, and its held-out scores are now highly correlated with one another because the 25 training sets differ by a single item. The average of many nearly identical scores barely reduces variance, so leave-one-out often has higher variance than 10-fold despite costing far more. This is why 5-fold and 10-fold are the defaults and leave-one-out is reserved for very small datasets.

    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDIn -fold cross-validation, what does the reported number estimate?

    APPLYA 5-fold cross-validation on 60 items gives held-out scores of 0.9, 0.8, 0.7 and 0.6 on the first four folds. What must the fifth fold score for the reported average to equal 0.75? accuracy

    TRANSFERA dataset has 200 images from 40 patients, 5 images each. Why does ordinary random 5-fold cross-validation over the 200 images give a number that is too optimistic?

    UNDERSTANDYou want to both choose hyperparameters and report an honest score using cross-validation. What is the standard arrangement?

    Where this is going: cross-validation multiplies training runs because it retrains under many settings. Deciding which settings to try belongs to a separate category of choices — the hyperparameters — and the next card draws the line between what the model learns and what the experimenter decides.
    Extension · Supervised learning 4/5

    Parameters and hyperparameters: what the model learns versus what you decide

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONParameters are the quantities a learning algorithm adjusts by optimisation in order to fit the training data — the weights and biases inside the model. They are the output of training and are meaningless before it. Hyperparameters are the quantities fixed before optimisation begins, chosen by the experimenter, that control the learning process itself: the learning rate, the model's depth and width, the strength of regularisation, the batch size. They are not fitted by the training loop; they are inputs to it.Parameters are what the model learns from the data. Hyperparameters are what you, the experimenter, decide before learning starts. One is produced by training; the other steers it.

    Parameters, concretely. For a small fully connected network taking 100 input features, with one hidden layer of 32 units and 2 output classes, the first layer holds weights plus 32 biases, and the second holds weights plus 2 biases: parameters in total. Every one of those 3,298 numbers is set by the training loop, by repeatedly nudging them to reduce the loss. You never write any of them down.

    Hyperparameters, concretely. The same network has a hidden size (32) that you did write down, before training. It also has a learning rate, a batch size, a number of training epochs, and a weight-decay strength. None of these is adjusted by the training loop. The hidden size is not learned; a network with 32 units and a network with 64 units are different hypothesis classes, and choosing between them is a decision outside learning.

    Why the distinction carries weight. It marks the boundary between the part of the experiment that is legitimately automatic and the part that is the experimenter's judgement. That judgement is a research degree of freedom, and every degree of freedom must be documented and must be exercised on data that is not the test set. It also explains a habit of careful papers: they report hyperparameters in a table or an appendix, because a result without them is not reproducible. The parameters need not be reported; they can be retrained. The hyperparameters cannot be inferred from the result and must be stated.

    The protocol. Search hyperparameters on the validation set (or a nested cross-validation), select the combination that performs best there, then retrain once on training plus validation and report on the test set. The order matters: the test set is consulted only after every hyperparameter is frozen. Reporting a hyperparameter because it scored well on test is card 2's leak wearing a different hat.

    • Model shape: number of layers, hidden dimension, number of attention heads or message-passing steps.
    • Optimisation: learning rate, weight decay, batch size, number of epochs, early-stopping patience, learning-rate schedule.
    • Regularisation: dropout rate, feature dropout, label smoothing.
    • Architecture-specific choices: the aggregation function or the type of graph layer, the readout or pooling function, the number of samples per estimate.
    • Evaluation: which metric, the fold count, and the number of random seeds to average over.
    • A typical graph-network paper must fix at least ten such choices, and each is a degree of freedom a reviewer is entitled to see stated.
    The misconception to kill. It is tempting to think that hyperparameters are also "learned from data," since they are picked using validation data. They are not learned by the model — they are chosen by a search you run, and that search can be inspected, stopped, and reported. The distinction is not "magic versus method"; it is "produced by optimisation inside the model" versus "fixed outside it, by choice."
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — sorting one model's numbers into the two boxes. Take the 100-to-32-to-2 network.

    quantityvalueparameter or hyperparameterwhy
    first-layer weights and biases3200 + 32 = 3232parameterset by the training loop
    second-layer weights and biases64 + 2 = 66parameterset by the training loop
    hidden size32hyperparameterfixed before training; it defines the architecture
    learning ratee.g. 0.01hyperparametercontrols each update step; not fitted
    training epochse.g. 200hyperparameterdecides how long the loop runs

    The 3,298 parameters are the model's contents. The four listed hyperparameters are the experimenter's settings. If someone deleted the saved weights, the model could be retrained from the hyperparameters; if someone deleted the hyperparameters, the weights would not tell you how the model was made.

    Example 2 — what a search actually costs. A grid search considers every combination in a list. Suppose a paper tries 4 learning rates, 3 hidden sizes, and 3 layer counts.

    Count the combinations: distinct hyperparameter settings.
    A grid tries the Cartesian product, so the count multiplies rather than adds. Adding one more learning rate to the list costs 9 new settings, not 1.
    Evaluate each setting by 5-fold cross-validation: each setting requires 5 training runs, so training runs in total.
    This is the search multiplied by the resampling. It explains why cross-validation and grid search together dominate the compute of a small paper — neither multiplier is large, but they compound.
    Choose the setting with the best cross-validated score, then retrain once on the full training set and report on test.
    The 180 runs produced a choice, not a result. The reported number comes from the single frozen configuration evaluated once on data that took no part in the 180 runs.
    Notice that a random search over the same budget would usually beat the grid. If only 3 of the 36 combinations turn out to matter, a grid spends most of its runs varying settings that do nothing, whereas sampling the space at random gives each important setting many distinct values to try. This is the standard reason large searches are randomised rather than gridded.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich of these is a hyperparameter rather than a parameter?

    APPLYA search tries 5 learning rates, 4 dropout rates, and 3 layer counts, evaluating every combination with 10-fold cross-validation. How many training runs does the search require? training runs

    TRANSFERA reader tries to reproduce a paper and cannot match its number. The paper reports the architecture and the number of layers but no learning rate, batch size, or dropout. What has been left out, and why does it matter?

    UNDERSTANDWhere should hyperparameters be chosen, and where should the reported number come from?

    Where this is going: once the protocol is fixed, the question becomes what the results table is obliged to disclose — which metric, which split, which hyperparameters, and over how many seeds. That contract, and a check that you can leave this section, is the last card.
    Extension · Supervised learning 5/5

    The reporting contract — and a skip check for this section

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONAn experimental result is a claim of the form: on dataset , model configured with hyperparameters , achieved metric on the test or cross-validated split, averaged over random seeds, with spread . A number missing any of these parts cannot be compared with another number, because the comparison would be between differently-measured quantities.A result is a full sentence: which metric, on which data, on which split, with which settings, averaged over how many runs, and how much it wobbled. A bare number is not a result.

    What a results table owes the reader. Five items, each of which changes the meaning of the number if omitted. The metric — accuracy, F1, mean reciprocal rank, area under a curve — because two papers quoting "90%" may be measuring different things. The split — a test score, a cross-validated average, a validation score — because these are not interchangeable and only the first two are reportable. The hyperparameters, at least those that materially change the score, because without them the experiment is not reproducible. Whose numbers are whose, because a comparison table mixes the authors' results with values copied from other papers. The number of seeds, because a single run cannot distinguish a real improvement from run-to-run noise.

    The seed count is the quiet one. Training is stochastic: weight initialisation, data order, and dropout all draw random numbers. Run the same code twice with different seeds and the score moves. A method reported as 73.4 on a single run, next to a baseline at 73.2 on a single run, has demonstrated nothing — the gap is well inside the wobble. Reporting the mean and spread over several seeds is what turns a single observation into a claim. Five seeds and a standard deviation is the common minimum, and reviewers increasingly ask for it.

    Whose numbers are whose. Many tables compare a new method against published baselines. It is standard and legitimate to quote another paper's reported number, but the row then carries a different provenance: it may have used a different split, a different metric convention, or a different number of seeds. Marking which rows were reproduced by the authors and which were copied is the difference between a fair comparison and an accidental one. Where the split or metric differs, the two numbers are not on the same scale at all.

    • State the supervised setup: features, targets, and the hypothesis class under test.
    • Keep training, validation and test apart, and let the test set guide nothing.
    • Recognise that a score is a noisy estimate, and that choosing the best of many settings inflates it.
    • Use cross-validation when data is scarce, and keep all preprocessing inside the training folds.
    • Separate parameters from hyperparameters, and report the hyperparameters.
    • Reading a results table: identify the metric, the split, the hyperparameters, the provenance of each row, and the seed count before believing the gap.
    The questions below are the check. The bar is not a passing score — it is that you answered each one without hesitating. If the seed-count item gave you pause, stay: the worked example computes exactly how a mean and spread are obtained from a list of runs.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — from five runs to one reported number. A method is trained five times with different seeds. The test accuracies are , , , and .

    Mean: , and .
    The mean is the reported point estimate. Averaging over seeds is what removes the luck of any single run from the centre of the claim.
    Deviations from the mean: , , , , . Their squares: , , , , , summing to .
    Squaring makes every deviation count positively, so a run below the mean and a run above it both contribute — that is what measures spread rather than direction.
    The sample standard deviation divides the sum of squares by : variance , standard deviation . Reporting the population version, dividing by , gives and .
    The two differ because the sample version corrects for the fact that the spread was measured around an estimated mean rather than the true one. The convention must be stated, since quoting and for the same five runs confuses readers who assume the other divisor.
    The reported result is therefore over 5 seeds. Any comparison must be read against that spread: a baseline reported at 72.5 is inside it, and a baseline at 70.0 is outside.
    This is the whole point of the seed count. The spread converts "our method scored higher" into "our method scored higher by more than run-to-run noise," which is a claim a reader can test.
    Note what is not recovered here: the hyperparameters, the split, and the metric. Five seeds give you a spread, not a comparison. A table row is only interpretable when all five contract items are present together — the example supplies one of them.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTAND"Our method reaches 91.2%." What single missing item most directly decides whether this is a result at all?

    APPLYA method is run with three seeds, giving test accuracies 70, 76 and 82. What is the sample standard deviation, dividing by ? accuracy points

    APPLYWhich of the following must accompany a reported test accuracy for the number to be comparable with another paper's? Select all that apply. (select all that apply)

    TRANSFERA comparison table shows the authors' method at 73.4 and a baseline at 73.2, with a note that the baseline was copied from its original paper. Both are single runs. What is the fairest reading?

    You are ready for the paper's experimental section. Every results table you meet now resolves into the same five questions — metric, split, hyperparameters, provenance, seeds — and every claim about "our method does better" becomes a claim you can check rather than accept.
    Extension · Graph neural networks 1/7

    A graph has no grid, so a layer cannot read its neighbours in order

    A hypergraph network is a graph network with the pairwise assumption relaxed, so the family tree comes first. This section builds the message-passing recipe that nearly every graph network instantiates, then walks the four that define the lineage — GCN's normalised aggregation, GAT's learned attention, GraphSAGE's inductive sampling, and GIN's expressiveness question — and closes on what changes when a single relation has many members rather than two.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA symmetric (or permutation-invariant) function of a collection of vectors is a function whose output does not change when those vectors are listed in a different order. A graph layer is a function that produces each vertex's new feature from that vertex's own feature together with the features of its neighbours, and it is required to be symmetric in the neighbour collection, because a graph supplies no canonical ordering of a vertex's neighbours.A graph layer computes each vertex's new numbers from the vertex plus its neighbours. It must give the same answer whatever order the neighbours are listed in, because there is no 'correct' order to list them in.

    The obstacle, in one paragraph. An image sits on a grid, and a grid hands a convolution two gifts. The first is translation: a rule that sends pixel to pixel , so a filter can slide. The second is a canonical order among the neighbours of a position — the eight neighbours of a pixel are always north, north-east, east, and so on, so a weight can mean "the neighbour directly above" and mean it every time. A graph hands you neither gift. Its vertices carry no coordinates to translate along, and a vertex's neighbours are an unordered set — vertex 2's neighbours might be written or with identical meaning. There is no "first neighbour". You met this in the graph-theory section; the reason to restate it is that everything below is a response to it.

    What a layer must therefore do. Take a vertex . It has its own feature vector, and each neighbour has one. The layer has to turn this bag of vectors into a single new vector for . The only tools available are operations that do not care about order — because order is not part of the data. Adding vectors does not care about order; so does taking their average; so does taking their componentwise maximum. Each of these reads a bag of vectors and returns one vector, and each returns the same vector for every listing of the bag. That is the entire design constraint, and it is the seed from which the whole family of graph neural networks grows.

    • What breaks if you ignore the constraint. A layer that assigns weight to "the -th neighbour" is assigning weights to a position that does not exist in the data. Two readers who happened to store the same graph with different neighbour orderings would compute different answers for the same vertex.
    • What does not break. A layer that weighs every neighbour by a number that depends on the neighbour itself — its feature, or its degree — rather than on the neighbour's position in some list. This is still order-independent, because each neighbour carries its own weight along with it.
    • What this note is the source of. Every architecture in this section is a different answer to one question: how should the bag of neighbour vectors be summarised?
    The mistake to avoid: assuming that because the vertices are numbered , the numbering somehow orders each vertex's neighbours. It does not. The numbers are bookkeeping that identifies vertices, and they are arbitrary — relabel the graph and the same connections reappear with different numbers. If a layer reads neighbour features in the order the numbers happen to appear, then relabelling the graph changes the layer's output while the graph itself has not changed at all. Section 1 made this point about matrices; here it becomes an operational requirement on the layer.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — watching a positional weight fail. Suppose a vertex has three neighbours with scalar features , and , and a would-be layer that (wrongly) attaches fixed weights to the neighbour positions. Run it once with the neighbours listed in the order :

    Now relabel so the same three neighbours are listed as . Nothing about the graph changed; only the order in which the layer happens to read the bag changed. The same formula gives:

    Two different outputs, and , for one graph. Notice which weights did the damage: and landed on different neighbours in the two runs. The layer treated "position in the list" as if it were information, and it is not.

    Example 2 — the same bag, read symmetrically. Keep the same neighbour features and give the layer order-independent aggregations instead. Sum: . Average: . Maximum: . List the neighbours in any order at all — , , anything — and each of these three numbers comes out the same, because each is built from operations that commute. The information that position used to (falsely) carry is gone, and in exchange the layer's answer is now a property of the graph rather than of the file that stored it.

    The three aggregations are not interchangeable, and Example 2 hides the reason: on this bag they happen to give three different values, but on another bag they can agree or disagree in ways that matter. Card 5 makes that precise with a pair of bags a sum separates and a mean does not.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhy must a graph layer be symmetric in a vertex's neighbour collection?

    APPLYA vertex has neighbours with feature values , and . What number does an order-independent sum aggregator return for this vertex? aggregate

    TRANSFERA layer attaches the weight to every neighbour but the weight is applied after multiplying by that neighbour's own degree. Is this layer symmetric?

    Where this is going: the fix — summarise the neighbour bag with a symmetric operation — is the whole content of card 2, where it becomes the message-passing recipe every network in this section specialises.
    Extension · Graph neural networks 2/7

    Message passing: the recipe almost every graph network instantiates

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONMessage passing is the update rule in which each vertex replaces its feature vector by a learned function of two things: its own current feature, and a symmetric aggregation of its neighbours' current features. Written for a single vertex and a single layer,For every vertex, gather the numbers from its neighbours, squash that bag of numbers into one summary with an operation that ignores order, combine that summary with the vertex's own numbers, push the result through a small learned function, and apply a nonlinearity. That is one layer.
    Read it left to right as four moves: aggregate the neighbours symmetrically, transform the result with a learned matrix, add the vertex's own transformed feature (a self-connection), then apply a nonlinearity . Network architectures differ in which choices they make for and how they set the weights — but they are all this shape.
    SymbolWhat it means
    vertex 's feature vector before this layer. is the layer index; is the raw input feature.
    the feature vector of a neighbour of , at the same stage
    the set of 's neighbours — a set, with no order, which is why the next symbol must be symmetric
    a symmetric operation applied to the bag of neighbour vectors: a sum, a mean, or a componentwise maximum. Any one of these returns the same vector for every ordering of the bag.
    learned matrices. is applied to the aggregated neighbour summary; to the vertex's own feature. Both are trained by gradient descent like any weight.
    a nonlinearity applied entry by entry (a ReLU is the common choice). Without it, stacked layers collapse into one linear map and depth buys nothing.
    the vertex's new feature vector, which the next layer will read exactly as this layer read

    Why each piece is there. The aggregation is symmetric because of card 1: it is the only way to consume an unordered bag. The self-connection exists because a vertex's own state would otherwise be overwritten by its neighbourhood every layer, and a vertex in a dense region would lose all trace of itself. The learned matrices exist because the shape of a useful summary is not known in advance — the layer learns which directions in feature space matter. The nonlinearity exists because a composition of linear maps is a linear map: with no , a hundred layers would be algebraically a single matrix, and depth would be a cosmetic change of notation.

    The self-connection has two spellings. One is the explicit term above. The other is to add a self-loop to the graph — to declare every vertex its own neighbour — and then let the single aggregation include itself. These are the same idea written differently, and the choice of spelling is a convention of the paper rather than a different model. It is worth knowing both, because the GCN of card 3 uses the self-loop spelling and the formula above uses the explicit term.

    The claim to take away: GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE and GIN are not four unrelated inventions. Each is this one template with a different answer to "what is , and what weights does it use?" — GCN fixes the weights by degree, GAT learns them per edge, GraphSAGE samples the bag before aggregating, and GIN asks which choice of is most discriminating. When you read a new graph architecture, find these four slots and you have read the method.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — one layer by hand. A vertex has self-feature and two neighbours with features and . Take to be the sum, set for this example so the self term enters through the aggregation instead, use a scalar weight , and let be the ReLU .

    Aggregate the neighbours. Sum: .

    Add the self-connection. Instead of use the self-loop spelling: include in its own bag, so the bag becomes and the sum is .

    Transform. .

    Example 2 — the same layer with the three aggregations side by side. A vertex has self-feature and three neighbours with features , and . Keep , keep the self-loop spelling so the bag is , and apply the ReLU at the end.

    Extension · Graph neural networks 3/7

    GCN: a degree-normalised sum, and two reasons it is the right one

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA graph convolutional network (GCN) layer, as introduced by Kipf and Welling (2017), is the message-passing update in which the aggregation is a sum over the neighbours of the self-loop-augmented graph, each neighbour's contribution scaled by , and the result transformed by a learned matrix. In matrix form, with and the degree matrix of ,Take each vertex's neighbours, and also the vertex itself. Add up their feature vectors, but give each one a weight of so that being connected to a hub counts for less. Then multiply by a learned matrix and pass through a nonlinearity.
    The middle three factors are the entire novelty: a fixed, non-learned matrix that says how much a vertex listens to each of its neighbours. Everything learnable sits in . The two factors are what make the listening weights depend on degrees.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the adjacency matrix of the graph — 1 where two vertices are joined
    the identity matrix. Adding it gives every vertex an edge to itself, the self-loop: the self-connection of card 2, written into the graph instead of into the formula.
    the augmented adjacency. Its row sums are the ordinary degrees plus one.
    the diagonal matrix of those augmented degrees — in position , zeros elsewhere
    the diagonal matrix holding . It is the degree normalisation, applied on both sides.
    the matrix of all vertices' current features, one row per vertex
    the learned weight matrix for this layer — the only trained object in the formula
    the nonlinearity, applied entry by entry

    Reading one — the spectral argument. Graph convolution is defined by analogy with the Fourier transform. On the graph, the role of frequencies is played by the eigenvectors of the Laplacian, and a filter is a function of the Laplacian's eigenvalues. The trouble is that a general such function costs a full eigendecomposition, which is too expensive for graphs of the sizes papers care about. The fix is to approximate the filter by a low-order polynomial in the Laplacian, whose terms can be evaluated by repeated multiplication with the adjacency structure and no eigendecomposition at all. Kipf and Welling's layer is what that approximation looks like when it is truncated at the first order and the largest eigenvalue is rescaled to : the polynomial collapses to , and the factors appear as the renormalisation that keeps the numbers from growing as layers stack. Read this way, the odd-looking is not invented for the layer — it is inherited from a spectral construction that the layer has been engineered to approximate cheaply.

    Reading two — a weighted average of neighbours. Ignore eigenvalues entirely and look at what one row of the operator does. Row holds in each neighbour's column. Applied to the feature matrix, it forms a weighted sum of the neighbours' features (plus 's own, through the self-loop), where the weight on neighbour is inversely related to 's degree: if is a hub with many connections, each of the vertices it talks to hears it faintly; if is sparsely connected, its contribution is heard more strongly. The vertex's own in the denominator is a second, global scaling: hubs sum over many terms, so each term is damped to keep the total in a comparable range. A useful sanity check on the alternative: with the plain random-walk normalisation (no square roots, no self-loops) each row sums to exactly , so the operation is literally a weighted average. The symmetric normalisation used here does not make rows sum to — for this section's four-vertex graph the hub's row sums to about — because symmetry, not row-stochasticity, is the property that makes the operator behave well when it is applied repeatedly. That last sentence is the thread card 6 picks up.

    Why the self-loop is not optional: without it, a vertex's own feature is thrown away at every layer and a vertex's new state depends only on its neighbourhood. Adding before normalising is the smallest possible fix, and it changes the degrees that the normalisation then reflects — a detail worth checking, since is and not .
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the degrees and the augmented degrees. Take the four-vertex graph used throughout the graph-theory section: edges , , . Vertex 2 is the hub. Ordinary degrees are , , , . Adding the self-loop raises each by one: . The augmentation is not decoration — it changes every normalising factor. The hub, already the busiest vertex, becomes more damped still.

    Example 2 — one full layer, by hand. Give the vertices the scalar features , take to be the identity for the moment so the arithmetic is visible, and to be the ReLU. The normalised operator is

    Vertex 1's new value: .
