    Extension · Graph neural networks 4/7

    GAT: letting a vertex learn how much to listen to each neighbour

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA graph attention network (GAT) layer, introduced by Veličković et al. (2018), replaces GCN's fixed degree-based weights with attention coefficients: for each ordered pair with a neighbour of , the layer computes a score from the two vertices' transformed features, normalises those scores across 's neighbourhood with a softmax, and forms 's new feature as the resulting weighted sum. Because the weight on depends on 's features rather than on 's position in a list, the aggregation remains symmetric in the sense card 1 required.Instead of weighting every neighbour by its degree, the layer learns, from the neighbours' own features, how much each one should matter to this vertex — and then normalises those weights so they sum to one.
    The second line computes a raw score for the pair; the first line turns all of 's scores into weights that are positive and sum to one. The vertex's new feature is then .
    SymbolWhat it means
    the current feature vectors of the vertex and of one of its neighbours
    a learned matrix applied to both vertices. It reshapes features before they are compared, so the comparison happens in a learned space rather than the raw one.
    concatenation: the vertex's transformed feature and the neighbour's, joined into one longer vector
    a learned vector. Its dot product with the concatenated pair reduces that pair to a single number — the score. This vector is the entire mechanism of attention, and it is small: one number per output dimension per head.
    a nonlinearity that lets small negative scores through with a gentle slope instead of flattening them to zero, so pairs can be actively unattractive, not merely uninteresting
    the raw attention score for the pair — an unnormalised "how much should care about "
    the attention coefficient: after a softmax over all of 's neighbours. These are non-negative and sum to across the neighbourhood.
    the neighbour set of , again unordered — the softmax is a sum over this set, so it is order-independent

    Why a softmax, and why that keeps the layer legal. The softmax does two jobs. It forces the coefficients to be positive, so no neighbour is subtracted from 's state. And it normalises them to sum to one, so a vertex with three neighbours and a vertex with thirty produce outputs on a comparable scale — a vertex does not shout louder merely by being popular. Legality is preserved for a different reason: is a function of the features of and . Swap two neighbours in the list and each weight travels with its own neighbour, so the weighted sum is unchanged. This is exactly the move card 1 identified as valid: a weight carried by the neighbour's identity rather than by its position.

    What it costs — three concrete bills. The first is parameters: besides , every head carries an attention vector . With input features, output features, is numbers; the attention vector is more, a increase for a single head. Using the usual eight heads to stabilise training, the count becomes for the same layer that GCN does with . The second is compute: every edge gets scored, then every vertex's incoming scores are softmaxed, then the weighted sum is taken — so the aggregation touches the edge list more times per layer than GCN's single sparse product. The third is interpretability, and it is the one most often oversold. The coefficients sum to one locally and look like importances, but they are the output of one layer of one head, trained only to serve the final loss. Nothing in the training objective asks them to correspond to anything a human would call importance, and they are not invariant to how the features are scaled. Reading them as an explanation of the model's behaviour is an assumption, not a measurement.

    The misconception worth naming: "softmax weights are probabilities, so they tell you why the prediction was made." A softmax over a neighbourhood gives numbers in that sum to ; that is all it implies. A high weight means the score for that pair was high relative to the other neighbours of that vertex in that layer, which is a much weaker statement than "this neighbour caused the prediction".
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — turning scores into weights. Vertex has three neighbours. Suppose the layer's scoring has produced the raw scores , , for them. Apply the softmax:

    , , , total
    , ,

    The three coefficients are positive and sum to . The scoring already carried most of the weight to the third neighbour: a score gap of (from to ) was amplified into a weight ratio of about to . That amplification is the exponential's doing, and it is the reason small score differences can produce sharply peaked attention.

    Example 2 — what the weighting does to the output. Keep the same three coefficients, and give the neighbours scalar transformed features of , and . The layer's output for is the weighted sum:

    Compare that with what a fixed weighting would give. The plain mean of the three neighbour features is . Attention has moved the answer from to about , towards the highest-scoring neighbour, because that neighbour received the largest coefficient. Two checks that pin the behaviour down. If the three scores are equal, the softmax returns each and the output is the plain mean, — attention reduces to uniform aggregation when there is nothing to distinguish. And the softmax is unchanged if the same constant is added to every score: shifting to gives the identical coefficients , so only score differences matter, never their absolute level.

    Notice how little interpretability Example 2 supports. The coefficient tells you the third neighbour scored highest, in this layer, for this vertex. It does not tell you that the third neighbour is important to the task, and with eight heads there would be eight such coefficient vectors per layer, none of them reconciled with one another.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhat does GAT's attention mechanism replace, relative to GCN?

    APPLYA vertex has three neighbours whose raw attention scores are , and . What attention coefficient does the third neighbour receive? (Give three decimal places.) attention coefficient

    TRANSFERA paper reports average attention coefficients as evidence for "the model attends to meaningful neighbours". What is the strongest reason to treat that claim cautiously?

    Where this is going: GCN and GAT both assume every vertex is present at training time and every neighbour can be read. Card 5 removes both assumptions — GraphSAGE samples neighbours so the model generalises to vertices it has never seen, and GIN asks which aggregation is the most discriminating.
    Extension · Graph neural networks 5/7

    GraphSAGE and GIN: learning on unseen vertices, and which aggregation is sharpest

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONGraphSAGE (Hamilton, Ying and Leskovec, 2017) is a message-passing architecture that, instead of reading every neighbour of a vertex, samples a fixed number of neighbours and aggregates only those. This makes the layer a reusable function of features rather than a lookup over a fixed vertex set, so it produces features for vertices that were not present during training. GIN, the graph isomorphism network (Xu, Hu, Leskovec and Jegelka, 2019), is the study of which choice of aggregation gives the most discriminating layer, and its conclusion is that a sum aggregation combined with a sufficiently expressive transform is strictly more powerful than mean or max.GraphSAGE fixes a sample size so that a vertex's update depends on a bounded, randomly chosen handful of its neighbours; because the rule is about features rather than about specific vertices, it also works on vertices the model has never seen. GIN is the question of how much two different neighbourhoods can be told apart by a layer at all, answered: a sum can tell apart more than a mean or a max.

    The first problem: vertices that were not there during training. GCN and GAT, as originally posed, are transductive: the graph — including the vertices you will later be asked to predict on — is present while the weights are trained, and the layer's output is an embedding of that particular, fixed vertex set. Introduce a genuinely new vertex afterwards and the weights do not tell you what to do, because the new vertex was never part of the sum. GraphSAGE answers this with two changes. It samples a fixed fan-out — say two neighbours per vertex per layer — from each vertex's neighbourhood, so the computation graph for a minibatch has a size you chose in advance rather than a size the data dictates. And it defines the update as a function of the self feature and the aggregated sample, so the same function can be applied to any vertex, seen or unseen. The trained object stops being a table of embeddings and becomes a rule for producing embeddings.

    Why sampling is doing real work, not only saving time. Consider a vertex of degree , two hops out, in a graph where each neighbour also has degree . Updating that one vertex by reading every neighbour touches vertices. Sample two neighbours per vertex instead and a two-hop update touches vertices — a fixed budget that does not grow with degree. The saving is the point: without it, a minibatch's memory footprint is set by the densest vertex in the graph. GraphSAGE's paper pairs this with several aggregator choices — a mean, a pooling/max variant, and an LSTM — to show the recipe is not tied to one summary. One cost to name: the aggregation now depends on which neighbours were drawn, so its output is a random quantity, and the model's training has to tolerate that noise.

    The second problem: how much can a layer tell apart at all? Suppose two vertices have neighbourhoods whose feature bags differ, but in a way the aggregator cannot see. Then a layer using that aggregator produces identical vectors for them, and no later layer can recover the difference, because later layers only ever see the vectors. This is why the choice of is not a cosmetic detail. GIN analyses the comparison against the Weisfeiler–Lehman test, a classical procedure for deciding whether two graphs are isomorphic: it proves that a sum aggregation followed by a learned transform can be as discriminating as that test, and that mean and max aggregations are strictly less discriminating than a sum, so there are neighbourhoods they provably cannot separate. The next section gives the concrete case.

    AggregatorValue on bag Value on bag Can it separate them?
    sumyes — different values
    meanno — identical values
    maxno — identical values
    State this precisely, because it is easy to overclaim. GIN's result is about the aggregator's ability to distinguish bags, under the assumption that features come from a bounded set. It does not say a sum-network is better on every task — mean aggregation discards degree, which can be a benefit when degree is noise, and sum aggregation makes features grow with degree, which needs care when degrees vary wildly. The claim is about representational power, not about which will score higher.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the two neighbourhoods a mean cannot separate. Fix a vertex and suppose every feature is the scalar value . In graph , has three neighbours. In graph , has one neighbour. Nothing else about the two situations differs in what the aggregator is shown.

    • Mean aggregator. In graph the bag is and the mean is . In graph the bag is and the mean is . The aggregator returns the same vector for in both graphs, so any downstream layer receives identical inputs and must give identical outputs.
    • Sum aggregator. In graph the sum is ; in graph it is . The two are different, so the aggregator has separated the cases, and the rest of the network has the opportunity to use the difference.
    • Max aggregator. Both bags have maximum , so like the mean, the max cannot separate them.
    Be careful about what this example does and does not show. The two graphs differ in size, and any reader comparing the graphs as wholes notices that immediately. The point is narrower and it is the point that matters: the aggregation at maps both neighbourhoods to one vector under a mean, so the layer at has lost the distinction before any later layer can help. Discriminative power has to be present at the first aggregation, because nothing downstream can add back information that was never carried. A parallel failure for max: bags and both have maximum , so a max aggregator cannot separate them either.

    Example 2 — the sampling budget, in numbers. A vertex sits in a graph where it and its neighbours all have degree . Compare a two-hop update that reads the whole neighbourhood with one that samples a fan-out of two at each step.

    Full neighbourhood, one hop: the vertex plus its neighbours is vertices to read.
    One hop already means touching every neighbour. This is the minimum for a method that reads the complete neighbourhood.
    Full neighbourhood, two hops: vertices.
    Each of the first-hop neighbours brings its own neighbours. The growth is multiplicative, which is why depth and degree are jointly explosive for full-neighbourhood methods.
    Sampled fan-out of , two hops: vertices.
    The count is now a function of the fan-out you chose, not of the graph's degree. The same two-hop model costs the same seven vertices whether the graph is sparse or a hundred-deep. That fixed budget is what makes minibatch training on very large graphs possible, and it is what GraphSAGE's sampling contributes.

    What the two examples together establish. Example 2 shows sampling's practical role: bound the computation so the method reaches vertices and graphs that a full-neighbourhood method cannot, at the price of a stochastic aggregate. Example 1 shows the expressiveness role the choice of aggregator plays: mean and max lose neighbourhood cardinality, sum preserves it, and GIN turns this observation into a theorem relating the sum-based layer to the Weisfeiler–Lehman test. Neither example demonstrates the training behaviour — GIN's theorem is about what can be represented, not about what gradient descent will find.

    Extension · Graph neural networks 6/7

    Depth, and why stacking layers hurts

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONOver-smoothing is the degradation of a graph network's vertex features under repeated neighbour-aggregation: as layers are stacked, each layer replaces a vertex's feature with a blend of itself and its neighbours, so features of neighbouring vertices become increasingly alike, vertex-to-vertex differences shrink, and beyond a few layers the representations can no longer be told apart well enough to classify.Each layer averages a vertex with its neighbours. Do that often enough and every vertex ends up carrying approximately the same vector, so there is nothing left to distinguish them and accuracy falls.

    Why anyone would want depth. Every layer moves information one hop. Stack layers and a vertex's final feature can depend on anything within hops of it. If the quantity you are predicting depends on something far away — a label set by a distant part of the graph — you need enough layers for that information to arrive. Short paths need few layers; long paths need more. This is the genuine motivation for depth, and it is not wrong.

    Why depth nevertheless backfires. The same aggregation that carries information also destroys it, and it does both things at once. A layer is a local averaging, and averaging pulls values towards each other: a vertex above its neighbours is lowered, a vertex below is raised. Apply it once and differences soften but survive; apply it repeatedly and they are driven towards zero. The signal that spread is the signal that got flattened. There is a second, subtler limitation too, called over-squashing: when information from many hops away is funnelled through one vertex's fixed-size feature vector, the number of sources grows exponentially while the vector's capacity does not, so long-range information is compressed into a bottleneck. Over-smoothing and over-squashing are distinct failures, and both make depth a liability. This card covers over-smoothing; the paper discusses both in more depth elsewhere.

    How the paper measures it. This paper's own Table VIII reports a baseline hypergraph network with eight layers dropping from to — a collapse, not a gentle decline, and it is what motivates the paper's attention to layer count and its residual design. The drop is the phenomenon in a single pair of numbers: the same architecture, the same data, differing only in depth, losing more than forty points of accuracy.

    • Use fewer layers. Most graph networks are best at two or three layers. If the task's dependencies are short, depth was never needed; the cost of the third layer is already often net negative.
    • Residual connections. Add a vertex's input feature back to its output, , so a layer is free to learn a small correction rather than being forced to rewrite the feature entirely. This gives the network a route by which the original, un-smoothed information survives to the last layer.
    • Jumping knowledge. Concatenate or aggregate the outputs of all layers, not only the last, so the read-out can use the sharper early-layer features alongside the smoothed later ones. The network decides how much depth it actually wants per vertex.
    • Watch the normalisation. A degree-weighted average smooths hubs differently from leaves, so the normalisation interacts with how fast smoothing proceeds — one reason the symmetric normalisation of card 3 behaves differently from a plain row-stochastic mean.
    The misconception to discard: that a graph network is like a deep feedforward network, where adding layers adds expressiveness and you should make it as deep as compute allows. On graphs the reverse is often true. Adding a layer adds a smoothing operation, and smoothing is destructive at scale. Depth is a resource you spend to reach distant neighbours, not a resource whose quantity is a proxy for power.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — watching a signal flatten. Take the path and put the values on it. At each round, every vertex replaces its value with the mean of itself and its neighbours (so each vertex includes itself, the self-loop of card 2). Compute by hand for a few rounds and watch the range — the largest value minus the smallest — shrink.

    Round 1. Vertex 1 keeps ; vertex 2 becomes ; vertex 3 becomes ; vertex 4 keeps . The values are now and the range is still .
    The two ends have nothing new to learn yet, so the range holds. The interior has already moved towards the middle. This is information propagating, and it is the useful part of depth.
    Round 2. Vertex 1 becomes ; vertex 2 becomes ; vertex 3 becomes ; vertex 4 becomes . Values , range .
    The ends have now moved inwards. The range has fallen from to — the signal is spreading and shrinking at the same time.
    Round 3. Values become , range . Round 4: , range about . Round 5: range about .
    Each round shrinks the spread by roughly the same factor. The sequence of ranges is the collapse in slow motion. The limit is the global mean, — all four vertices converge to , and every distinction the input carried is gone.

    Example 2 — depth is set by how far the signal must travel. Consider a path on six vertices, . To predict something about vertex that genuinely depends on vertex , information has to travel the five edges between them. Since each message-passing layer moves data exactly one hop, you need at least five layers for that information to arrive. But Example 1 says that by five layers the features have largely flattened. This is the central tension of graph depth compressed into one graph: the quantity that tells you how many layers you need (the distance) is the same quantity that makes those layers harmful.

    A precise caveat about Example 1. That averaging used the row-stochastic mean, which converges to a single constant. The symmetric normalised operator of card 3 does not converge to one constant: applied repeatedly to the four-vertex hub graph with features it settles towards values proportional to , so the hub keeps a larger magnitude than the leaves. Over-smoothing still occurs — vertices of equal degree converge to the same value and become indistinguishable — but "everything becomes one number" is a property of the averaging normalisation, not of every graph operator.

    Extension · Graph neural networks 7/7

    The hypergraph turn, and can you leave this section?

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA hypergraph generalises a graph by dropping the pairwise restriction: each hyperedge is a non-empty subset of of any size, so one relation may join two vertices or fifty. A hyperedge is the collection of vertices that take part in one relation. When every hyperedge has size the object is an ordinary graph; hypergraphs are what remain when that restriction is lifted.In a hypergraph, one relation is allowed to contain any number of things at once — a whole group, not a pair. Everything in this section so far has quietly assumed relations come in pairs, and this card is where that assumption is removed.

    Why the pairwise assumption had to be doing something, and what breaks. Every operator in this section fed a vertex a bag of neighbours — vertices directly attached to it. That is exactly what a pairwise relation guarantees: if edge exists, is a neighbour of . A hyperedge of five members does not give you a bag of four neighbours in the same sense. Do vertex and vertex count as neighbours because they share a hyperedge, or only because they share a hyperedge with each other specifically? The pairwise vocabulary does not answer this, and the two naive ways of forcing it back into the vocabulary each pay a price.

    Naive option one — clique expansion. Replace each hyperedge of members with all pairwise edges among its members. This makes the data graph-shaped and lets any graph network run unchanged. Two costs. The size blows up combinatorially: a hyperedge of members becomes edges, and a relation with members becomes . And, more damaging than the size, the group disappears: after expansion all the network sees is a dense tangle of pairs, and it cannot recover that they came from a single event, nor distinguish a vertex that belongs to two groups with the same membership from one that belongs to only one.

    Naive option two — star (bipartite) expansion. Give each hyperedge its own new vertex, and connect it to each of its members. A hyperedge of members becomes a star of edges, so the count grows linearly rather than quadratically, and the memberships are all still there. This removes the blow-up but not the conceptual problem: the result is a bipartite graph, and a graph network running on it treats hyperedge-vertices and ordinary vertices as the same kind of object, with the same message-passing rules. The two-hop path vertex → hyperedge → vertex can represent 'two things in the same group', but a standard graph layer has no built-in notion that the middle object is a relation rather than a thing, and the vertex set has been inflated by one new vertex per relation.

    Why a dedicated operator was wanted. Both expansions trade the object away: one destroys the group, the other disguises it as a vertex. A hypergraph layer instead keeps the incidence matrix of the graph-theory section — rows for vertices, columns for hyperedges — and aggregates in two explicit stages: vertices to hyperedges, then hyperedges back to vertices. The hypergraph neural network of Feng et al. (2019) is this idea written as an operator, and it is the direct generalisation of the GCN of card 3, with the incidence matrix playing the role the adjacency matrix played.

    Read the sandwich in the middle as two passes. sends each vertex's feature to the hyperedges that contain it; averages within each hyperedge; sends the hyperedge summaries back to their members; the two factors normalise by how many relations each vertex belongs to. This is GCN's operator with 'edge' replaced by 'relation of any size', and with every hyperedge of size two it collapses back to a graph operator of the GCN family, up to a constant and the self-loop convention.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the incidence matrix — rows are vertices, columns are hyperedges, entry 1 when a vertex belongs to a hyperedge
    its transpose — the pass in the opposite direction, hyperedges back to vertices
    diagonal matrix of vertex degrees — how many hyperedges each vertex belongs to (the row sums of )
    diagonal matrix of edge degrees — how many vertices each hyperedge contains (the column sums of ). divides by the hyperedge's size, which is the step that makes a large relation not drown its members.
    a diagonal matrix of hyperedge weights, letting one relation count more than another. It is often set to the identity.
    the learned weight matrix — the only trained object here, exactly as was in GCN
    the nonlinearity, applied entry by entry

    Skip check. This section taught six things beyond this card. If you can do all of them without hesitating, you have what the paper's own layer assumes.

    • State why a graph layer's aggregation must be symmetric in the neighbour set (card 1).
    • Write the message-passing update and name its four moves — aggregate, transform, self-connection, nonlinearity (card 2).
    • Explain GCN's normalisation, and give at least one of the two readings of why it is there (card 3).
    • Say what GAT learns that GCN fixes, and one cost of doing so (card 4).
    • Explain inductive versus transductive learning, and give a pair of neighbourhood bags that a sum separates and a mean does not (card 5).
    • Define over-smoothing and name one mitigation (card 6).
    • Say what changes when a relation has more than two members, and why clique expansion is not a free fix (this card).
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the blow-up, counted. A hyperedge with members becomes pairwise edges under clique expansion. The counts rise fast:

    Members in one relationClique-expansion edgesStar-expansion edges
    Read the last row: one real-world relation — a conference with authors, say — becomes edges under clique expansion, while star expansion spends . The quadratic-versus-linear gap is the reason star expansion is the more common practical compromise among the naive options.

    Example 2 — the information clique expansion discards. Take a hypergraph with two hyperedges over the same three vertices: and . These are two distinct relations that happen to have identical membership.

    Expand to a graph. Each hyperedge is the same triangle, so the union of the two triangles is that one triangle: edges , , . Three edges, and no trace of there having been two relations.
    Clique expansion maps edge sets to edge sets and forgets multiplicity. Two relations with the same members produce a graph identical to the one a single relation produces.
    Look at the incidence matrix instead. It has rows and columns, and every entry is . Row sums to .
    That row sum is vertex 's degree — it takes part in relations. The count that clique expansion erased is exactly what the incidence matrix keeps, and it is the object the dedicated operator computes with.
    Keep the two examples in view together. Example 1 prices the naive options in edges; Example 2 shows what even the cheaper option can lose. The dedicated operator's case is the combination: no combinatorial blow-up, and the group and its membership counts survive intact into the arithmetic.

    What this card does not do. It does not develop the hypergraph operator's properties — its derivation, its relationship to spectral hypergraph theory, or its behaviour under stacking. Those belong to the paper's own treatment. This card closes the family tree: the operator above is what the paper's network generalises further.

    Extension · Message passing 1/3

    The recipe: message passing in four moves

    This section writes down the message-passing template — collect the neighbours, aggregate them symmetrically, transform with a learned matrix, mix in the vertex's own feature, apply a nonlinearity — that nearly every graph and hypergraph network instantiates. It then shows why the aggregation must ignore ordering, and what over-smoothing does to a deep network. The paper leans on both: its own layer is a message-passing rule, and the first failure mode its introduction cites is over-smoothing.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONMessage passing is the update rule shared by almost every graph network. Each vertex replaces its feature vector by a learned function of two things: the vertex's own current feature vector, and a symmetric aggregation of its neighbours' current feature vectors. "Symmetric" means the aggregation returns the same value for every ordering of the neighbours; a vertex's neighbours carry no order, so only symmetric operations can consume them. One application of the rule is one layer.For every vertex: collect its neighbours' feature vectors, squash that unordered bag into one summary, transform the summary with a learned matrix, mix in the vertex's own feature vector, and apply a nonlinearity. That is one layer of message passing.

    Why one recipe covers a whole field. A graph network has to turn a vertex together with its neighbourhood into a new feature vector for that vertex, and you would expect many unrelated ways to do so. Almost all published architectures are instead the same four moves with different choices inside them. Written out, the moves are:

    1. Collect. Read the feature vector of every neighbour of . The neighbours form the set — a set, so there is no first element and no last.
    2. Aggregate. Combine that bag of vectors into one vector with a symmetric function: the same output for every ordering of the bag.
    3. Transform. Multiply the aggregated vector by a learned matrix , and the vertex's own feature vector by a second learned matrix . "Learned" means the entries are trained by gradient descent, as any weight in a neural network is.
    4. Combine and squash. Add the two transformed vectors and push the sum through a nonlinearity — a function applied entry by entry, with the ReLU the common choice.

    Why move 2 must be symmetric. A vertex's neighbours come with no canonical order. The dataset stores an edge list, and the order in which the neighbours of happen to appear in that list is an artefact of how the file was written — relabel the vertices and the order changes while the graph does not. If the aggregation read the neighbours positionally ("the first neighbour", "the second neighbour"), two copies of the same graph written differently would produce different answers, and a trained model would be fitting the file format rather than the graph. Card 2 makes this failure concrete with numbers.

    Why the other moves are there. The self-feature term exists because without it a vertex's own state is overwritten by its neighbourhood at every layer, and a vertex in a dense region would lose all trace of itself. The learned matrices exist because the shape of a useful summary is not known in advance; the layer learns which directions in feature space matter. The nonlinearity exists because a composition of linear maps is itself a linear map: drop and a hundred layers collapse algebraically into a single matrix, so depth would buy nothing.

    Read it from the inside out: collects and squashes the neighbours, transforms that summary, adds the vertex's own feature, and squashes the result. Every architecture differs only in which function fills and how the two matrices are built.
    SymbolWhat it means
    vertex 's feature vector before this layer. The superscript is the layer index; is the raw input feature.
    the feature vector of a neighbour of , at the same stage of the computation
    the set of 's neighbours — a set, with no order, which is why the next symbol must be symmetric
    a symmetric operation applied to the bag of neighbour vectors: a sum, a mean, or a componentwise maximum. Each of these returns the same vector for every ordering of the bag.
    the learned matrix applied to the aggregated neighbour summary. One such matrix, shared by every vertex in the graph.
    the learned matrix applied to the vertex's own feature — the self-connection. It keeps the vertex's state from being washed out by its neighbourhood.
    a nonlinearity applied entry by entry (a ReLU is the common choice). Without it, stacked layers collapse into one linear map and depth buys nothing.
    the vertex's new feature vector, which the next layer will read exactly as this layer read
    A common misreading. It is tempting to hear as a weight per neighbour, so that each neighbour receives its own learned number. It is not. There is one matrix , shared by every vertex in the graph, and the formula applies it to the aggregated summary. The same shared matrix could be applied to each neighbour before aggregation without breaking symmetry, because it is the same matrix for all of them; giving different neighbours different weights by position cannot, and that broken variant is exactly card 2's failure.
    The claim to take away. GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE and GIN are not four unrelated inventions. Each is this one template with a different answer to "what is , and what weights does it use?" Read a new graph or hypergraph architecture by finding those four slots.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — one vertex, three legitimate aggregations. Vertex has self-feature and three neighbours with features , and . Take , , and the ReLU . The neighbours form the bag , and the aggregator is the only part that changes between the three runs.

    Collect the bag and sum it: .
    Sum is symmetric. Write the same bag as and the sum is still — the order in which the file lists the neighbours never enters the computation.
    Keep the same bag and change only the aggregator. Mean: . Max: .
    All three aggregators are symmetric, and they differ in what they keep. The sum grows with the number of neighbours, so it carries the neighbourhood size. The mean divides by that count and forgets it. The max keeps the single largest contribution and drops the other two.
    Push each through the rest of the recipe: multiply by , add the self term , then apply ReLU.
    Only the aggregation changed, yet three different outputs emerge. The self term and the ReLU are identical in all three runs, so the whole difference comes from move 2.
    AggregationBag summary (self term)Output after ReLU

    mean
    max
    All three are legitimate. None of sum, mean and max is the correct aggregation; they are three modelling choices, and each of the three is a valid message-passing layer. The choice decides what the layer can notice. The sum can notice that a vertex has many neighbours of a given feature; the mean and the max cannot. Card 2 puts a number on that difference.

    Example 2 — every vertex of a small graph. The path graph carries initial features , , . Use sum aggregation over each vertex's neighbours, , , and ReLU. Both matrices are shared across all three vertices, which is what makes the layer one layer rather than three.

    Vertex 1. Its only neighbour is vertex 2, so the bag is and the sum is . Then from the neighbours, plus from the vertex itself, giving .
    An endpoint has degree 1, so its aggregated term is one neighbour's feature. The self term still contributes, so the output is not purely the neighbour's value.
    Vertex 2. Its neighbours are 1 and 3, so the bag is and the sum is . Then plus , giving .
    Degree 2, so the sum collects two contributions and the aggregated term is larger than for vertex 1. A higher-degree vertex reads more of the graph into its summary.

    Extension · Message passing 2/3

    Why the aggregation must ignore order

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA function of several arguments is symmetric if every rearrangement of its arguments leaves its value unchanged: for three arguments, , and so on for all six orderings. A function that fails to be invariant under some rearrangement is not symmetric. Symmetry is also called order-independence, or permutation-invariance.A symmetric function gives the same answer whatever order you list its inputs in. Sum, mean and max are symmetric; "the first input" is not.

    Why the aggregation has to be one of these. A vertex's neighbours are consumed as an unordered collection, which for numbers means a multiset: a collection in which repeats count separately and order is meaningless. The bag is a three-element multiset — the repeated is two members, and writing it as describes the same bag. The aggregation reads the whole bag, so its output may not depend on any ordering of it. The reason the ordering is arbitrary is card 1's point restated: the neighbours are stored in a file, and the file's order is an artefact of how it was written, not a fact about the graph.

    What breaks without symmetry. Suppose the aggregation is a positional weighted sum: the neighbour in position 1 is multiplied by a learned weight , the neighbour in position 2 by , and so on. The weights are learned and the arithmetic is well defined, so the layer trains without complaint. But the output now depends on the order in which the neighbours were listed, and that order changes under a relabelling of the vertices — without a single connection changing. Two labelings of one graph then give two different feature vectors, and part of what the model fits is the file format rather than the graph.

    Function of the bagSymmetric?What it does
    sumyesadds every element; its value grows with the number of elements
    mean (average)yesthe sum divided by the count; forgets the count
    maxyeskeeps the largest element and drops the rest
    minyeskeeps the smallest element and drops the rest
    productyesmultiplies every element together
    "the first element listed"nodepends entirely on how the bag was written down
    positional weighted sum noreordering permutes the values past fixed weights, so the total changes

    Sum against mean and max. A symmetric aggregator can still be a poor one, because symmetry is necessary but not sufficient: it says nothing about what the aggregator can tell apart. The sum is the most informative of the simple choices, because its value grows with the number of elements, so a bag of three equal values and a bag of one of that value give different sums ( against ). The mean divides by the count and the max keeps only the largest element, so both map those two bags to the same value ( for the mean, for the max). A layer using mean or max therefore cannot tell a vertex with many identical-featured neighbours from one with a single such neighbour.

    Symmetry does not make the sum infallible either: the bags and both sum to . The standard fix is to apply a learned elementwise transform before summing, which can separate the two. This is the content of the widely used result that a sum aggregator with a sufficiently expressive inner function can distinguish any two unequal multisets, while mean and max cannot.

    A common misreading. Because max, min and mean are symmetric, it is tempting to conclude that any symmetric aggregator is as good as any other. It is not. Symmetry only makes the aggregator legal; what it can represent is a separate question, and example 3 below gives two pairs of bags that different symmetric aggregators fail to separate.
    What to take away. Symmetry is a hard constraint: break it and the model reads the file rather than the graph. Expressiveness is a soft choice: among symmetric aggregators the sum keeps the most information and the mean and max the least, and the trade-off is whether the size of the neighbourhood should influence the answer.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — positional weights on two neighbours. Vertex has two neighbours with features and , listed in the file in the order . Suppose the aggregation assigns weight to the first-listed neighbour and to the second, and sums: .

    As the file lists them, : the aggregation gives .
    The first value meets weight , and the second value meets weight .
    Relabel so the file now lists : the aggregation gives .
    The same two neighbour features, the same two weights, the same graph — only the order of the list changed.
    The outputs differ: against . For comparison, the symmetric sum gives under either ordering.
    Nothing about the graph changed, so the difference between and is entirely an artefact of ordering. This is what a symmetric aggregation rules out.

    Example 2 — three neighbours, six orderings. Vertex has neighbours with features , and , and the positional weights are , , . The table compares the illegal positional sum against the legal symmetric sum on the same bag.

    Order in the filePositional sum Symmetric sum
    The positional column takes six different values, from to — a spread of across six orderings that all describe the same three neighbours. The symmetric sum is in every row. A trained layer using the positional version would have to fit one graph through a keyhole shaped like a file format, and which keyhole it gets depends on how the data happened to be written.

    Example 3 — where symmetric aggregators disagree. Symmetry rules out the failure above, but it does not make all symmetric aggregators equally informative. Two pairs of bags show the split.

    Two bagssummeanmaxWhich aggregator tells them apart
    and and and and sum only

    The first row is the size distinction of card 1: only the sum sees that three neighbours differ from one. The second row shows the sum is not universal — two bags of different shapes share the total , and only the max separates them. Expressiveness is therefore a modelling choice rather than a settled fact, and the sum's advantage over the others is normally realised together with a learned elementwise transform, not on raw values.

    Where this is going: a symmetric aggregation is legal, but every layer you stack applies it once more, and enough repetitions drive all vertices to the same value. Card 3 shows that collapse happening on a path graph, and names the checks that catch it.
    Extension · Message passing 3/3

    Over-smoothing, and the skip check

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONOver-smoothing is the failure of a deep message-passing network in which repeated neighbour aggregation makes the feature vectors of distinct vertices converge to nearly the same value, so the network can no longer separate them and its accuracy collapses. It is not caused by a bug and it is not overfitting; it is what the aggregation operation does when it is applied enough times.Run the neighbour-averaging long enough and every vertex ends up holding roughly the same numbers. There is then nothing left for the classifier to tell apart.

    Why it happens. One message-passing layer replaces each vertex's value with a blend of its neighbours' values. A blend cannot increase the spread of the values, so each layer shrinks the differences between vertices a little. After layers a vertex's value depends on its whole -hop neighbourhood — every vertex reachable within edges. Once is comparable to the graph's diameter (the longest shortest path between any two vertices), every vertex's -hop neighbourhood is the entire graph, so every vertex is averaging over the same thing and all the values drift to one number. The features have been smoothed away rather than propagated. The example below works this out on a path graph.

    The mitigations. Depth is useful — some tasks need information from distant vertices — so the goal is to gain reach without collapsing the features. Three standard responses:

    MitigationWhat it does
    Keep depth small (two or three layers)keeps the receptive field smaller than the graph diameter, so different vertices still average over different neighbourhoods
    Residual (skip) connectionsadd each layer's input back to its output, , so a vertex keeps a copy of its earlier, more distinctive state alongside the smoothed one
    Jumping knowledgekeep every layer's output and let the final classifier read all of them, so the shallow, still-distinctive layers stay available even when the deep one has collapsed
    A common misreading. Over-smoothing is not the same as overfitting. Overfitting is a model that has memorised the training set and does worse on unseen data; the cure is regularisation or more data. Over-smoothing is a model that has become too weak to separate even its own training vertices, and more data does not help. If both training and test accuracy fall as layers are added, the cause is over-smoothing, not overfitting.

    What this section established.

    • Write the message-passing update: aggregate the neighbours symmetrically, transform the summary and the vertex's own feature with learned matrices, add the two, and apply a nonlinearity.
    • Explain why the aggregation must be symmetric — a vertex's neighbours have no canonical order, and only a symmetric function can consume an unordered bag.
    • Give a concrete failure of positional weighting: two orderings of the same bag produce two different outputs.
    • Name the symmetric aggregators — sum, mean, max, min, product — and say what the sum preserves that the mean and max discard: the size of the neighbourhood.
    • Explain over-smoothing: repeated averaging drives all vertices to the same value, and the mitigations are fewer layers, residual connections and jumping knowledge.
    The questions below are the check. The bar is not a score — it is that none of them made you think hard. If the over-smoothing walkthrough in the example still needs reading, the paper's own depth tables will read as arbitrary numbers rather than as consequences.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — one round, four vertices. A path graph is four vertices in a line, , carrying the values . The averaging rule here is: replace each vertex's value by the average of its neighbours' values. The two endpoints have one neighbour each and copy it; the two interior vertices have two neighbours and average them.

    Vertex 1 (endpoint): its only neighbour is vertex 2, so its new value is .
    With a single neighbour the average is that neighbour's value. This is the degree-1 case.
    Vertex 2 (interior): neighbours 1 and 3, so the average is .
    Two neighbours, both read and averaged. The vertex's own value does not enter this rule.
    Vertex 3 (interior): neighbours 2 and 4, so the average is . Vertex 4 (endpoint) copies vertex 3, giving .
    The right half of the line still holds the larger values, so it stays high for this round.
    The new values are . The range — the largest value minus the smallest — has fallen from to in one step.
    Averaging pulls every value towards its neighbours, so the extremes move inwards. The range is the quantity that over-smoothing ultimately destroys.

    Example 2 — the same rule run for many rounds. Now five vertices in a line, , with values . The rule is unchanged: each vertex becomes the average of its neighbours. The first round, vertex by vertex, is: vertex 1 copies vertex 2, giving ; vertex 2 averages and , giving ; vertex 3 averages and , giving ; vertex 4 averages and , giving ; vertex 5 copies vertex 4, giving . Round by round, from there:

    RoundValues at vertices 1, 2, 3, 4, 5Range (max − min)
    0 (start)1, 2, 3, 4, 54
    12, 2, 3, 4, 42
    22, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 42

    52.75, 2.75, 3, 3.25, 3.250.5

The limit is , which is exactly the average of the starting values (, and ). The centre vertex never moved, because it began at the average and every average leaves it there. Every other vertex was pulled in.
    This rule uses no learned weights and no self term — it is the purest form of the operation. A trained layer is a weighted version of the same averaging and inherits the same pull towards a common value; the weights change which common value is approached and how fast, not whether the spread collapses.

    Extension · Two roads to a graph convolution 1/4

    The Laplacian's eigenvectors are the graph's Fourier basis

    Convolution cannot be lifted from a grid onto a graph unchanged, so the field built it twice. One road reads the Laplacian's eigenvectors as the graph's Fourier basis and defines convolution there; the other writes the aggregation directly on vertices and relations. This section walks the spectral road — the eigenbasis, the convolution, the two problems that stalled it, and the polynomial approximation that rescued it — and then places the paper's own incidence-matrix layer on the spatial road.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONFor a symmetric matrix , the spectral eigendecomposition is the factorisation in which the columns of are mutually perpendicular unit vectors and is diagonal with real entries , chosen so that . (A general square matrix need not admit this form — its eigenvalues can be complex and its eigenvectors need not be perpendicular; symmetry is exactly what guarantees the tidy version.) The are the eigenvectors, the the eigenvalues, and because the columns are orthonormal we have . The graph Laplacian is symmetric, so this decomposition exists for it; it is also positive semi-definite in the graph case (meaning for every real vector ; the quadratic form equals , a sum of squares, which is what forces every ). Its eigenvectors are the graph Fourier basis — the objects playing the role sines and cosines play on a line.The Laplacian has its own set of special directions: vectors it stretches but never rotates. Those directions are the graph's pure oscillation patterns, and how much each one is stretched measures how fast that pattern alternates from vertex to vertex.

    You have already met the Laplacian (with the diagonal matrix of vertex degrees and the adjacency matrix), its zero row sums (), and the fact that a graph has no translation operator with which to slide a convolution window. This card builds the substitute that the spectral road offers: a graph's own notion of frequency.

    Why anyone reaches for eigenvectors. On a line, Fourier analysis writes any signal as a sum of sines and cosines, and the sines have a privileged status: differentiating one twice gives back the same sine scaled by a constant — by a negative constant, which is why the operator usually taken for the analogy is the negative second derivative, whose eigenvalue on is the positive number . That property — an operator returning a scaled copy of its own input — is the definition of an eigenvector. The Laplacian is the graph-shaped version of that operator: at each vertex it sums the differences between the vertex's own value and its neighbours', , so its eigenvectors inherit the sines' role. One warning about the word 'frequency': on a graph there is no time axis, so a frequency is not a rate in cycles per second. It is how often a pattern changes sign as you cross the graph's edges.

    The Laplacian's eigenvectors are the graph's Fourier modes. Each eigenvector is a pattern over the vertices that the Laplacian leaves unchanged in shape; its eigenvalue says how rapidly that pattern alternates across the graph's edges. Together they form the basis in which a signal on the graph can be described frequency by frequency — the graph's substitute for the sines and cosines of the line.

    Two structural facts carry the whole analogy. First, is symmetric, so its eigenvectors can be chosen mutually perpendicular and of length one, giving . This makes the transform free to invert: is the inverse of , so moving a signal into the basis and back loses nothing. For an arbitrary matrix you would need to compute a separate inverse; here the transpose already is one. Second, is positive semi-definite, so every eigenvalue is . This is the fact that lets a graph eigenvalue be read as a squared frequency: a squared quantity cannot be negative, and the smallest allowed value, , sits at the flattest possible pattern.

    Read the equation as a description of what does: change coordinates into the eigenbasis (), stretch each coordinate independently by its eigenvalue (), and return to the original coordinates ().
    SymbolWhat it means
    the graph Laplacian — the graph's version of a second derivative
    the matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors — the Fourier modes. Because they are orthonormal, is its inverse.
    the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues — all real and all . These are the squared frequencies.
    the transpose, equal to . Multiplying by it is the graph Fourier transform; multiplying by is the inverse transform.

    A first misconception, and a second. The most common first reading takes an eigenvalue to be a frequency. It is the squared frequency: in the two-vertex graph below the non-constant eigenvalue is , corresponding to frequency , not . On a line the negative second derivative of is , so there the eigenvalue is exactly — the pattern is the same here, but the numbers need not be. A second common misreading assumes the eigenvalues run evenly like along a frequency axis. They do not: their actual spacing is a property of the graph, and some may repeat. What survives is only the order — larger eigenvalue means faster oscillation.

    When the analogy breaks — three ways. (i) On a disconnected graph there is not one constant mode but one per connected component, so the number of zero eigenvalues equals the number of components; the zero-frequency component is then not a single vector. (ii) Eigenvalues can repeat, and a filter that is a function of cannot tell two modes sharing one eigenvalue apart. (iii) The entire basis belongs to this graph: change the graph and every frequency changes, so there is no graph-independent notion of frequency. That third point becomes the second problem of the next card.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — small enough to do by hand. Two vertices joined by a single edge. Then and , so

    Every row sums to zero, as it must.
    Find the eigenvalues without solving the characteristic equation from scratch. The trace is , and the eigenvalues of a matrix sum to the trace, so . The determinant is , and the eigenvalues multiply to the determinant, so .
    The trace and determinant give two equations in the two unknown eigenvalues, which is quicker than expanding a determinant and is a useful habit for small cases.
    The only pair satisfying both is and .
    One of the two eigenvalues is forced to by the determinant; the other is then fixed by the trace. The is the general row-sum fact showing up in a two-vertex case.
    The mode: reads , so — the constant pattern , normalised to . This is the zero-frequency (DC, or constant) mode; it is flat because the two vertices agree across their one edge.
    Constant means it never changes sign across any edge, which is the definition of frequency zero.
    The mode: reads , i.e. — the alternating pattern , normalised to .
    The two entries have opposite signs, so across the single edge this graph owns, the pattern disagrees as much as it possibly can. That is the highest frequency a two-vertex graph can carry.
    Verify the two facts that make it a Fourier basis. Orthonormality: the dot product is , so the modes are perpendicular, and each has length . Reconstruction: with and returns .
    Both properties are what the definition claimed: perpendicular unit modes () and exact reconstruction of the matrix. Checking them on a tiny case is what makes the general statement believable.

    Example 2 — a graph whose modes are no longer obvious. The four-vertex hub from the earlier section: edges , , , so vertex is the hub. Its Laplacian is

    Its eigenvalues are , , and . The two extremes can be confirmed by hand.
    The mode is forced: every row sums to zero, so and the constant vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue . Normalised, each entry is .
    This reuses the row-sum identity you already hold: is always in the kernel, so is always an eigenvalue.
    Test for the large eigenvalue. Row 1: , which is , matching the first entry. Row 2: , which is , matching the second entry. Row 3: . Row 4: same, .
    Every row of applied to the candidate reproduces the candidate entry scaled by , which is precisely the statement . So is an eigenvalue and its mode.
    Interpret that mode. It is normalised by dividing by , giving . The hub carries a large negative value while the three leaves carry small positive ones, so on every edge the pattern flips sign — the fastest oscillation this graph allows.
    A mode alternating across every edge is exactly what a large eigenvalue should look like; here the hub is the vertex that can disagree with all three leaves at once.
    The remaining eigenvalue is , and it occurs twice. The three leaves play symmetric roles, and that symmetry yields a two-dimensional space of patterns all with eigenvalue . A numerical routine returns the spectrum as and the normalised mode as , matching .
    A repeated eigenvalue means two genuinely different patterns share one frequency. Any filter that depends only on gives both the same gain and cannot separate them — the concrete form of failure mode (ii) above.
    The two examples span the range. On two vertices the eigenbasis can be guessed outright; on four it already needs a symmetry argument, and the spectrum contained a surprise (a repeated eigenvalue). On the graphs a paper actually uses, guessing is hopeless and a numerical routine is the only option — and that routine is exactly what the next card identifies as a cost.

    Extension · Two roads to a graph convolution 2/4

    Spectral convolution, and its two problems

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThe graph Fourier transform of a signal on the vertices is , its coordinates in the Laplacian's eigenbasis; the inverse transform is . A spectral graph convolution chooses a filter — a function of the eigenvalue, applied to every frequency at once — and defines , where is the diagonal matrix holding . It is called a convolution because it acts diagonally in the frequency basis, scaling each frequency independently, which is the property the classical convolution theorem singles out.Send the signal into the frequency basis, scale each frequency by a chosen amount, and send it back. That scaling-in-the-frequency-basis rule is the definition of convolution on a graph.

    Where the definition comes from. On a line, convolving a signal with a small window is the same as multiplying their Fourier transforms: the transform turns convolution into an ordinary product, one factor at each frequency. Two facts are bundled in that theorem — convolution is built from shifts, and being built from shifts is why it becomes diagonal in the Fourier basis. A graph has no shift (the translation you were told it lacks), so the spectral road keeps the second fact and promotes it to the definition: choose the operator that scales each frequency independently, and call it convolution.

    A graph convolution is an operator that multiplies each frequency by its own factor in the Laplacian's eigenbasis. That single sentence is the convolution theorem with the eigenvectors standing in for sines and cosines. Diagonal in the frequency basis means no frequency is mixed with any other — each mode comes out of the operation scaled, never blended, exactly as on a line.

    Three steps left to right. transforms the signal into frequency coordinates. multiplies the -th coordinate by — one gain per frequency, and are the parameters that choose the filter. transforms back to the vertices. Because is diagonal, no two frequencies interact.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the input signal, one value per vertex
    the Fourier transform: the signal rewritten as amounts of each eigenvector
    the filter — a function of the eigenvalue. The subscript marks its learnable parameters; different give different filters.
    the diagonal matrix with in position — the gain applied to each frequency
    the inverse transform: turn frequency coefficients back into vertex values

    It is a real convolution, not a metaphor. Two things have to hold, and they do. First, the operation is diagonal in the frequency basis, so every frequency is scaled and none is mixed — precisely the structure the convolution theorem produces on the line. Second, when the graph is a cycle, the Laplacian's eigenvectors are the discrete Fourier modes, so reduces to the classical Fourier multiplier and the line's convolution is the special case. The spectral construction is therefore a strict generalisation.

    Problem one — the eigendecomposition is cubic. To use you must compute it, and computing all eigenvectors of an matrix costs operations; the matrix itself holds numbers, and even applying it once costs . For the graph sizes papers care about this is fatal, and it must be redone for every new graph. Worse, there is no fast transform to help: the intuition that Fourier transforms are cheap comes from the grid, where the FFT exploits the regular spacing. A graph's is dense and irregular, and multiplying by it is a full dense matrix-vector product.

    Problem two — the filter is tied to one graph. The gains are indexed by this graph's eigenvalues. Training learns the parameters against one particular spectrum; applied to a graph with a different spectrum, the same defines a different function of frequency. So a spectral filter does not transfer between graphs — it is transductive, tied to the graph it was fit on. A layer whose parameters act on the features instead of on the spectrum does not have this problem, and that distinction is the whole reason the field moved on.

    When this construction fails. Besides the two costs above: if eigenvalues repeat, assigns the same gain to every mode sharing that eigenvalue and cannot separate them (the four-vertex graph of the last card has with multiplicity two). And the filter gives no control over locality — a single gain per frequency can make every vertex depend on every other vertex, with no notion of 'neighbours only'. The next card's polynomial approximation repairs both the cost and, incidentally, the locality.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a filter you can compute by hand. On the two-vertex graph of the last card, (columns are the two modes), and the eigenvalues are and . Take the signal and the filter , a low-pass that keeps the smooth mode and kills the fast one.

    Transform: . So the signal holds of the constant mode and of the alternating mode.
    The first coordinate is the sum direction (the DC projection) and the second is the difference direction; the makes both coordinates comparable in size.
    Apply the gains. and . Multiply coordinatewise: .
    This is the diagonal step, and it is where the filter acts: the constant frequency passes through untouched, the alternating frequency is removed entirely.
    Invert: .
    The two coordinates of the answer are equal, so the output is constant across the graph. Note is exactly the mean of the input, .
    Read the operator. Killing the fast mode leaves the graph average — this filter is neighbour-averaging, seen from the frequency side. Swap to the high-pass , whose gains are and : the transform scales to , and inverting gives — the difference from the average, with the smooth part removed.
    Low-pass and high-pass are two ends of the same dial. Recognising that averaging is a low-pass spectral filter is what lets the spectral and spatial roads later be shown to meet.

    Example 2 — the same filter, a different graph, a different meaning. Apply that same to the three-vertex path , whose eigenvalues are , and . The gains become:

    GraphEigenvaluesGains of g(λ) = 1 − λ/2

The parameters did not change, but the meaning of the filter did, because the eigenvalue it now acts on is rather than . This is Problem two made visible: a spectral filter describes an action on a spectrum, and every graph brings its own spectrum.

    The cost, counted. The eigendecomposition is cubic in the number of vertices, so the numbers grow quickly:

    Vertices NMatrix entries (N²)Eigendecomposition (order N³)

Nor does the example show the cost in wall-clock time — only the operation counts, which are what separate a workable method from an unusable one.

    Extension · Two roads to a graph convolution 3/4

    Chebyshev truncation, and the step to GCN

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA polynomial filter is a filter — a chosen function of the eigenvalue, applied in the Laplacian's eigenbasis — that is itself a polynomial, . The consequence is that the spectral convolution (feeding the signal through the eigenbasis, scaling each frequency by the filter, and coming back) can be rewritten with no eigenvectors at all, as a polynomial in a graph shift operator . Here is either the combinatorial Laplacian (with the diagonal matrix of vertex degrees and the adjacency matrix) or, as the GCN derivation below uses, the symmetric normalised Laplacian ; is the matrix whose columns are that operator's eigenvectors and the diagonal matrix of its eigenvalues. A Chebyshev approximation is the standard way to choose such a polynomial: the filter is expanded in Chebyshev polynomials (introduced below) and truncated at degree , which approximates a general smooth filter while being numerically stable.Replace the filter by a polynomial in the Laplacian. Polynomials in the Laplacian can be applied directly to the signal by repeated sparse multiplication, and the eigenvectors cancel out of the algebra entirely.

    Why a polynomial is the escape hatch. Both problems of the last card came from needing : the cubic cost of computing it, and the filter being tied to its eigenvalues. A polynomial in defeats both at once. If is a sum of powers of , then is the same sum of powers of the diagonal matrix, and the two 's that bracket it collapse:

    The middle equality uses the fact that for powers of a diagonal matrix, . Once written this way, the operator is a polynomial in alone — no , no eigenvalues, no eigendecomposition.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the degree of the polynomial — how many powers of are kept
    the coefficient of the -th power; these are the learned parameters, replacing the function
    the -th power of the Laplacian. It is applied to a signal by successive multiplications by the sparse matrix .
    the same operator written in the spectral form; the identity says the two descriptions are one and the same operator

    A K-th order polynomial is a K-hop operator. The Laplacian connects each vertex only to its immediate neighbours, so multiplying by once mixes a vertex with its one-hop neighbourhood, twice with its two-hop neighbourhood, and times with its -hop neighbourhood. A degree- polynomial in therefore reaches every vertex within hops — no further out than that, and, when the constant term is nonzero, always the vertex itself. Two consequences follow: the operator is local, since information travels only steps per layer; and it is sparse, since each of the multiplications touches only the graph's existing edges rather than a dense matrix. A general smooth filter is approximated to any accuracy by some polynomial (this is the classical Weierstrass fact that polynomials are dense among continuous functions), so nothing is lost by restricting to polynomials — only accuracy is traded for degree .

    Why Chebyshev specifically. Among the many polynomials that could approximate a filter, the Chebyshev family is chosen because on an interval it spreads the approximation error evenly rather than concentrating it at the ends, and it is evaluated by a stable three-term recurrence, , starting from and . To use it, the eigenvalues are rescaled into by , where is the largest eigenvalue. For the symmetric normalised Laplacian — the variant whose eigenvalues lie in — this bound is exactly , so is not a crude guess but the actual ceiling.

    The GCN simplification: keep only the first two terms. Truncate at and tie the two remaining coefficients together. The chain of algebra is short, and every step is worth seeing, because it is where a spectral filter becomes a plain aggregation.

    Truncate at : . With the rescaling — legitimate because — this reads .
    Only the first two Chebyshev terms are kept, so the filter becomes a straight line in , fixed by the two coefficients and .
    Replace the eigenvalue matrix by the operator it belongs to. The truncated filter is the operator , and since , this becomes .
    This is the identity that has driven the whole card: a polynomial in is the matching polynomial in . The constant survives and is replaced by the operator .
    Tie the coefficients: set . Then .
    Two coefficients collapse into one, halving the parameters and forcing the filter to a single degree of freedom — the shape Kipf and Welling chose.
    Renormalise: replace with , where and holds its degrees. This is the layer written below.
    The replacement adds the self-loop and rescales the degrees. The reason it is needed is in the warning box that follows, and it is not something the truncation itself produced.

    From one scalar to a weight matrix. The derivation above ran on a signal with a single feature channel, where the tied coefficient is a single number. A real layer carries input channels and produces output channels, and there the scalar generalises to a matrix that mixes the channels; the fixed coupling matrix stays as it is and contributes no learned parameters. That is the layer written below.

    Everything learnable is in . The middle three factors are a fixed coupling matrix: entry is when and are joined (counting the self-loop), zero otherwise. This is the graph convolutional network's layer of Kipf and Welling (2017).
    SymbolWhat it means
    the adjacency matrix — 1 where two vertices are joined
    the identity; adding it gives each vertex an edge to itself, the self-loop
    the self-loop-augmented adjacency. Its row sums are the ordinary degrees plus one.
    the diagonal matrix of those augmented degrees
    the matrix of all vertices' current features, one row per vertex
    the learned weight matrix, mixing feature channels — the only trained object here
    the nonlinearity, applied entry by entry

    When this fails. The truncation is the source of the trade-offs. At the filter reaches only one hop: it does keep each vertex's own feature, through the constant term , but anything beyond the one-hop neighbourhood is invisible in a single layer. Reaching further means stacking layers, which brings back over-smoothing: many rounds of neighbour-averaging push every vertex towards the same value, until the differences a classifier needs are gone. (An operator built from the bare — with no constant term — would discard each vertex's own feature, but that is not what the truncation produces; the is there.) Larger approximates the filter better and sees further in one layer, at more compute and with a wider smoothing footprint. And the Chebyshev recurrence, applied without the rescaling into , can amplify rather than contract, so the rescaling is not optional.

    One honest correction to the tidy story: the self-loop and the normalisation are not forced by the truncation. The derivation as written gives the operator , whose repeated application grows without bound. Kipf and Welling replace it with the same recipe evaluated on the self-loop-augmented graph, , so that the values stay in a stable range when layers stack. The self-loop is a deliberate renormalisation, not a term that fell out of the algebra.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a polynomial filter needs no eigenvectors. On the two-vertex graph, take the polynomial . (Every degree here is , so the combinatorial and normalised Laplacians coincide, and is unambiguous.) Its eigenvalues are and , so as a function of frequency it is the same low-pass filter — it keeps the smooth modes and suppresses the fast ones — as in the last card. Apply it to directly, with no in sight.

    This is one sparse multiplication — the only kind of operation the polynomial method ever performs.

And one layer says nothing about what happens when many are stacked, which is where over-smoothing becomes the binding constraint.

    Extension · Two roads to a graph convolution 4/4

    Which road the paper's layer belongs to — and can you leave this section?

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA layer is stated on the spectral road when the operator itself is written as a function of the graph's spectrum — the Laplacian's eigenvalues , with the matrix whose columns are its eigenvectors — for instance a filter applied in the eigenbasis. It is stated on the spatial road when the operator is written directly in terms of the graph's vertices and relations — an explicit aggregation over neighbours or members, using only the adjacency or incidence matrices. The paper's Equation (1) is spatial: it is assembled from the incidence matrix, and no eigenvector or eigendecomposition appears anywhere in it.One road describes a layer by what it does to the graph's frequencies; the other by who sends what to whom along the graph's relations. The paper's layer is written entirely the second way.

    The paper's layer is spatial, and its algebra says so. Equation (1) is built from the incidence matrix — rows for vertices, columns for relations — in the sandwich . That expression names vertices and relations and nothing else. There is no eigenvector matrix , no eigenvalue matrix , no eigenvalue, and no step that would require one. Where the spectral road would begin 'take the eigendecomposition', this layer begins 'send each vertex's feature to the relations that contain it, and send the summaries back'.

    Read the middle as two passes. Because has one row per vertex and one column per relation, its transpose is what carries each vertex's feature to the relations containing it; weights each relation as a whole; averages within each relation; and then carries the relation summaries back to their members. The two factors normalise by how many relations each vertex belongs to. Nothing here consults a spectrum — which is exactly why the same expression survives when a relation has any number of members.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the incidence matrix — rows are vertices, columns are relations, entry 1 when a vertex belongs to a relation
    vertex degrees down the diagonal — how many relations each vertex belongs to (the row sums of )
    relation sizes down the diagonal — how many vertices each relation contains (the column sums of ); turns a relation's sum into a mean
    a diagonal matrix of relation weights, letting one relation count more than another. It is often set to the identity, which is what this card's example does.
    the learned weight matrix — the only trained object
    the nonlinearity, applied entry by entry

    Why the spatial form matters here. The spectral road's central object, the Laplacian, is defined for pairwise relations. A hyperedge of any size has no single pairwise Laplacian waiting for it. Writing the layer with the incidence matrix sidesteps that entirely: the same formula runs whether every relation has two members or a thousand, because the incidence matrix records membership rather than pairs. The paper's choice of the spatial road is not a stylistic preference — it is what makes relations of arbitrary size expressible in the first place.

    When the spatial form fails. Three concrete ways. (i) A vertex belonging to no relation has vertex-degree , and then divides by zero — isolated vertices break the formula unless they are handled separately. (ii) The factor equalises relation sizes: a relation with a thousand members contributes the same mean as one with two, which is usually desirable but discards any signal that lives in the size difference itself. (iii) The incidence matrix records membership only, so it cannot express ordering or intensity within a relation — a vertex is in or out, with nothing in between. And like any single-hop aggregation, it sees one hop per layer, so depth is needed to reach far, carrying the same over-smoothing risk as a graph network.

    An honest caveat about the two roads. They are not disjoint families. The polynomial filter of the previous card is the meeting point: it is derived from the spectral road, but stated as powers of it is a plain aggregation over neighbours — a spatial operator. GCN (the graph convolutional network of Kipf and Welling) is the prototype, a spatial formula with a spectral justification. So the two labels describe how an operator is written and justified, not two disjoint kinds of mathematics. What does separate them in practice is transferability: spatial parameters act on features and move between graphs, while a spectral filter is indexed by one graph's spectrum.

    Section recap. This section built the spectral road, its costs, its repair, and placed the paper on the other road. If you can do all six of the following unaided, skip ahead.

    • Say why the Laplacian's eigenvectors play the role of a graph's Fourier modes, and why its eigenvalues are squared frequencies (card 1).
    • Write the spectral convolution and explain what makes it a genuine convolution (card 2).
    • State the two blockers of the spectral road: the eigendecomposition and the filter being tied to one graph's spectrum (card 2).
    • Explain why a polynomial filter needs no eigenvectors, using , and why a degree- polynomial is a -hop operator (card 3).
    • Recognise GCN's — where adds self-loops and holds those degrees — as the , tied-parameter collapse of the spectral derivation (card 3).
    • Say why the paper's Equation (1) is spatial, and what the incidence form buys that a Laplacian cannot (this card).

    The threshold. The questions below are the check. The bar is not 'two of four correct' — it is that none of them made you stop and reconstruct something. If the polynomial identity did not come back to you cleanly, stay and reread card 3; the paper's spatial form is a deliberate departure from exactly that identity, and you will read it better knowing what is being departed from.
