    Extension · Hypergraph neural networks 1/5

    What a hypergraph network layer does

    A hypergraph is only useful to a learner once something can run a neural network on it. This section builds the standard hypergraph network layer from its incidence-matrix form, then walks the family that grew around it — HGNN, HyperGCN, DHGNN, UniGNN, AllSet and HGNN+ — and states the one limitation all of them share: structure decides how vertex features are smoothed, and nothing else enters the layer. That gap is what the paper under study answers by adding a stage in front of the layer while leaving the layer itself unchanged.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA hypergraph network layer replaces every vertex's feature vector with a new one computed from that vertex together with the vertices it shares hyperedges with, using the incidence matrix. Its standard form, the hypergraph convolution of Feng et al. (2019), is the map , where is the incidence matrix, and hold the vertex and hyperedge degrees, weights whole hyperedges, is a learned matrix, and is a nonlinearity applied entry by entry. The output is unchanged if the vertices or the hyperedges are relabelled.Each vertex takes a damped summary of the vertices that share a hyperedge with it. Large hyperedges and busy vertices are damped more, so no single group and no single hub can dominate. A learned matrix reshapes the summary, and a nonlinearity is applied.

    The two objects the layer reads, in one place. The incidence matrix has one row per vertex and one column per hyperedge, with when vertex belongs to hyperedge , and otherwise. Its row sums are the vertex degrees — how many hyperedges contain . Its column sums are the edge degrees — how many vertices contains. The layer uses the diagonals of these two lists as the matrices and .

    Why the degrees appear at all. Without them the summary would be a plain sum, and a vertex inside a 982-member hyperedge would receive a contribution hundreds of times larger than a vertex inside a 2-member one. The factors and put every vertex and every hyperedge on a comparable scale, so a large relation speaks more softly rather than more loudly. This is the same idea as the degree normalisation of a graph convolution, transplanted to relations that can have any size.

    The layer as six moves. Read the formula left to right and each multiplication is one move.

    1. Normalise the vertices — multiply by , dividing each vertex's row by the square root of its degree.
    2. Collect into hyperedges — multiply by , replacing each hyperedge by the sum of the vertex rows inside it.
    3. Average within each hyperedge — multiply by , dividing each hyperedge by its size. The optional reweights whole hyperedges at this step.
    4. Distribute back to the vertices — multiply by , giving each vertex the sum of the values of the hyperedges it belongs to.
    5. Normalise the vertices again — a second , dividing by the square root of the degree once more.
    6. Transform and activate — multiply by the learned , then apply entry by entry.
    This is the entire layer. Everything between and is fixed by the hypergraph: it is the listening pattern, not something the network trains. Only , and the optional , are learned.
    SymbolWhat it means
    one row per vertex; row is vertex 's current feature vector. The superscript is the layer index, and is the raw input feature.
    the incidence matrix; when vertex is a member of hyperedge
    diagonal matrix of vertex degrees — the row sums of
    diagonal matrix of edge degrees — the column sums of
    diagonal matrix of per-hyperedge weights; the identity when every hyperedge counts equally. Raising one diagonal entry makes that hyperedge speak more loudly.
    divides each vertex's contribution by . It appears on both sides, so an edge shared by vertices of degrees and carries weight .
    divides each hyperedge by its size — the averaging step that stops a 982-member relation from swamping a 2-member one
    the learned weight matrix; it mixes feature dimensions, and is the only trained object besides
    a nonlinearity applied entry by entry, a ReLU being the usual choice
    Hold the layer as one sentence: normalise the vertices, gather them into hyperedges, average inside each hyperedge, scatter back to the vertices, normalise again, transform, activate. Every hypergraph network in this section is a rearrangement of those moves, and the paper under study leaves all of them untouched — it changes what arrives at the layer, not the layer.
    The mistake to avoid: reading and as interchangeable. gathers vertices into hyperedges; scatters hyperedges back out to vertices. Swap them and you average along the wrong axis, producing a -rowed object where a -rowed one belongs. The test is the shape: the layer must return one row per vertex.
    When the layer fails. It is, at heart, a smoothing operator. Apply it many times and every vertex's feature drifts towards its neighbourhood's, until vertices that share hyperedges become hard to tell apart — the over-smoothing that card 2 measures. And the layer can only be as good as the hypergraph it is handed, which it takes as fixed and correct: if the hyperedges are wrong, or if the information needed lives in the structure rather than in the features, adding layers does not recover it.
    EXAMPLE

    Row sums give the vertex degrees ; column sums give the edge degrees . Both lists total , the number of ones in the matrix — every membership is counted once from each side.

    Extension · Hypergraph neural networks 2/5

    HGNN: the layer everyone else starts from

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONHGNN, the hypergraph neural network of Feng et al. (2019), is the model whose layer is the hypergraph convolution of card 1, . It is derived by writing down a hypergraph Laplacian and reading the layer as the first-order spectral filter built from it.HGNN is the first network that ran a graph-convolution-style layer directly on a hypergraph. It takes the same normalised operator a graph network uses, with the graph Laplacian replaced by the hypergraph Laplacian, so the group structure is never expanded away.

    Where the layer comes from, in two steps. A graph convolution is built from the graph Laplacian : the filter is a function of , and the cheapest useful version approximates that function by a low-order polynomial in . HGNN does the same with the hypergraph Laplacian. Define the normalised operator ; then the hypergraph Laplacian is , and reading as the hypergraph's version of the graph Laplacian makes the layer above the hypergraph counterpart of a graph convolution. One fact worth holding: when every hyperedge has size 2, HGNN's operator is the familiar degree-normalised graph operator with self-loops, up to a constant factor — card 4 checks this numerically. HGNN is therefore not a different species from the graph networks; it is their hypergraph generalisation.

    What it improved over expanding the hypergraph into a graph. Before HGNN, the only way to run a neural network on a hypergraph was to convert it first: either into all its pairs (clique expansion), or into a graph with one added vertex per hyperedge (star expansion), and then run a graph network on the result. Both conversions cost something a hypergraph network avoids. Clique expansion needs a number of edges that grows with the square of the hyperedge size, and in doing so it stops recording that the pairs came from one event. Star expansion is cheaper but adds vertices that exist only as bookkeeping. HGNN never converts: it multiplies by the incidence matrix and its transpose, so the cost is proportional to the number of memberships — the number of ones in — and the relation stays whole.

    The limitation, stated honestly, in one sentence: the layer smooths vertex features along hyperedges and that is all it does. The hypergraph is an input fixed before training; the only things a network trains are and the optional per-hyperedge weights . There is no mechanism inside the layer to invent a hyperedge, to reweight one from evidence, or to reason about the structure as data. A common over-reading is that HGNN learns the hypergraph — it does not.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the expansion HGNN avoids. Take the same four-vertex hypergraph: , , . Convert it to a graph by clique expansion and count the edges each hyperedge becomes.

    e1 (size 3) → 3·2/2 = 3 edges e2 (size 2) → 2·1/2 = 1 edge e3 (size 2) → 2·1/2 = 1 edge total = 5 edges

    So the incidence matrix's memberships become pairwise edges. In this tiny example the counts are close. Watch what happens as groups grow: a single hyperedge of size becomes pairs, so a 10-member group becomes 45 edges and a 982-member one becomes 481,671. HGNN's cost, by contrast, is the number of memberships — 10 and 982 respectively. Star expansion would instead add one auxiliary vertex per hyperedge: here new vertices, giving a graph on vertices of which are not in the data.

    Example 2 — the layer, and what repeated smoothing does. HGNN's operator is , the normalised object on the left of . On this hypergraph, applying to gives — the arithmetic of card 1, because HGNN's tensor product is exactly the layer of card 1. The spread of the values shrank from to about . Apply the layer again:

    AfterValuesSpread
    1 layer
    2 layers
    5 layers
    Each application pulls the values closer together, and after enough layers adjacent vertices become hard to tell apart. This over-smoothing is a property of the smoothing operator itself, not a bug in HGNN, and it is why these networks are kept shallow. It matters for reading the paper under study: because the backbone layer is unchanged, the same ceiling applies to it.

    Where this is going: HGNN fixes the layer, so later work attacked a different question — how to change the structure the layer reads. Card 3 covers the two sharpest answers: reduce the hypergraph to a graph, or update the hypergraph as training proceeds.
    Extension · Hypergraph neural networks 3/5

    HyperGCN and DHGNN: change the graph, not the layer

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONHyperGCN (Yadati et al., 2019) trains graph networks on hypergraphs by first reducing the hypergraph to an ordinary graph: within each hyperedge one member is chosen as the mediator, and an ordinary edge is added from the mediator to every other member. DHGNN (Jiang et al., 2019) keeps the hypergraph but treats its structure as dynamic: the hyperedges are recomputed from the current vertex features during training, so the structure the layer reads changes from layer to layer.Two different ways to dodge the problem of defining a hypergraph operator. HyperGCN turns each group into a little star of ordinary edges and runs an ordinary graph network on it. DHGNN keeps the groups but redraws them as training goes on. HyperGCN changes the graph once; DHGNN changes it repeatedly.

    HyperGCN: a mediator inside each hyperedge. A hyperedge of size becomes ordinary edges — the mediator joined to each other member. Crucially, the mediator is a member of the hyperedge, not a new vertex, so the resulting graph has exactly the original vertices. This is the difference from the star expansion of the graph-theory material, which invents one fresh vertex per hyperedge; HyperGCN reuses an existing one. For a hyperedge of size 2 the step is vacuous, since the two members are already an ordinary edge. The mediator is chosen by a stated rule, and the choice is a heuristic — the paper that proposed it selects the member that is, in a precise sense, most central to the group.

    DHGNN: redrawing the structure. DHGNN never converts the hypergraph into a fixed graph. Instead it recomputes the hyperedges from the current features at each layer — typically by joining each vertex to its nearest neighbours in the current feature space — and then applies a vertex convolution over the hyperedges a vertex currently belongs to. A vertex that drifts into a different region of feature space acquires a different set of hyperedges, so the structure tracks the features.

    MethodIdeaNew verticesCost per hyperedge of size sWhat it gainsWhat it gives up
    HyperGCNmediator inside each hyperedge, one ordinary edge to each other membernone edgesany graph network applies unchanged; linear costthe group is gone — its members connect only through the mediator, and fidelity depends on which member was chosen
    DHGNNrebuild hyperedges from current features each layernonerecomputed per layerstructure adapts to the learned featuresthe structure becomes a moving target: it can drift, costs an extra step, and is harder to reproduce and interpret
    The mistake to avoid: describing HyperGCN as adding an auxiliary vertex per hyperedge. That is the star expansion, a different construction. HyperGCN's mediator is chosen from the hyperedge, so the vertex count never changes. The distinction matters because it is exactly what the comparison table turns on: adding a vertex invents an object with no meaning, whereas reusing one makes the representation depend on a choice.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — HyperGCN on the four-vertex hypergraph. Edges , , . Choose the first-listed member of each hyperedge as its mediator.

    HyperedgeSizeMediatorEdges created
    31–, – — two edges
    21– — one edge
    22– — one edge
    HyperGCN graph: 4 edges on 4 vertices. Clique expansion of the same hypergraph: 5 edges.

    Four edges instead of five, and the vertex count is unchanged where star expansion would have pushed it to seven. But look at what the mediator cost: vertices 2 and 3 sat together in , yet the HyperGCN graph has no edge –. They are connected only through the mediator vertex 1. Had the mediator been chosen as vertex 3 instead, the edge set would read –, –, –, – — a different graph from the same hypergraph. The reduction is not unique, and the difference is not nothing.

    Example 2 — what "dynamic" changes. Suppose DHGNN builds each hyperedge as a vertex plus its nearest neighbours in the current feature space, so every hyperedge holds members. At layer 0 the neighbours are read from the input features. After one round of convolution the features have moved, and the nearest neighbours of a given vertex may be a different three vertices — so the hyperedge it sits in is rebuilt, not reused. A single training run therefore visits many different hypergraphs. This is the source of both its flexibility and its cost: nothing downstream can assume the structure it saw at layer 0 still holds at layer 5.

    What these examples do not show. The mediator example fixes a particular mediator rule for concreteness; other rules give other graphs, and none of the numbers here should be read as HyperGCN's published results. Example 2 uses a neighbourhood as an illustration of the dynamic idea, not as DHGNN's exact construction, which the original paper specifies in more detail.

    Extension · Hypergraph neural networks 4/5

    UniGNN, AllSet and HGNN+: unifying, formalising, generalising

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThree later works step back from individual models. UniGNN (Huang and Yang, 2021) is a unified framework in which graph and hypergraph networks are both written as two-stage message passing: a vertex-to-edge aggregation, then an edge-to-vertex aggregation. AllSet (Chien et al., 2022) formalises a hypergraph network as a pair of permutation-invariant multiset functions — a function of a collection whose output does not depend on the order in which the collection is listed. HGNN+ (Gao et al., 2023) generalises the HGNN layer to typed, weighted, multiway relations rather than a single kind of hyperedge.UniGNN shows that the graph networks and the hypergraph networks are the same two-step recipe, so they can be studied together. AllSet writes that recipe as two order-independent functions and proves the earlier models are special cases of it. HGNN+ widens the layer to handle several kinds of relation at once.

    UniGNN: two stages, with hyperedges as the middle. The recipe is a round trip. First, vertices send to the hyperedges that contain them and each hyperedge aggregates its members — a vertex-to-edge stage. Then each vertex aggregates the values of the hyperedges it belongs to — an edge-to-vertex stage. Written for one layer, with and the two aggregations, a hyperedge becomes and a vertex becomes . Both aggregations must be order-independent, for the reason given in the graph-network material: a hyperedge's members are an unordered set. The unification claim is that when every hyperedge has size 2, this collapses to an ordinary graph network — choose the right aggregations and it becomes GCN, GAT or a GIN-style sum aggregator.

    AllSet: the recipe as two multiset functions. AllSet notices that both stages are the same kind of object — a function of a multiset. It defines a hypergraph network as one multiset function that maps the members of a hyperedge to the hyperedge's value, and a second that maps a vertex's hyperedges to the vertex's new value, with the single requirement that both ignore order. HGNN, HyperGCN and the UniGNN family all turn out to be particular choices of these two functions. This level of abstraction is what makes a new model provably a member of the family rather than merely similar to one.

    Why AllSet is in this section rather than a footnote. Its permutation-invariant multiset formulation is a direct ancestor of the paper's own structural encoder — the module the paper places in front of the backbone layer — and the paper cites AllSet for exactly that reason. Reading AllSet first is what makes the paper's encoder legible: the encoder is a multiset function over structure, chosen to satisfy the same order-independence requirement.

    HGNN+: widening the layer. HGNN assumes one kind of vertex and one kind of hyperedge. HGNN+ allows several vertex types and several hyperedge types, with weights on the relations, and treats the single-type case as a special instance. In practice this is what lets one layer consume a dataset built from relations that are not all of the same nature — for example co-authorship and co-citation side by side — without forcing them into one undifferentiated set of hyperedges.

    What unification does not buy, and the misconception to avoid. It is tempting to read "unified" or "general" as "more capable". It is not. UniGNN and AllSet reorganise how the smoothing is expressed, but every function they admit still takes the structure as fixed input and returns a smoothed vertex feature. HGNN+ widens what may count as a relation, yet the widening is about the input's shape, not about turning structure into information the layer can read. A clearer map of the family is not a larger family — and the gap that card 5 names is left untouched by all three.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — UniGNN's two stages, by hand. Take the same four-vertex hypergraph, , , , features , and let both aggregations be sums.

    Vertex-to-edge. Each hyperedge sums its members: , , .
    A sum rather than a mean. The sum keeps the hyperedge's size in the value, so the two-member hyperedges and the three-member one are not forced to the same scale — the opposite choice from the averaging of HGNN.
    Edge-to-vertex. Each vertex sums the hyperedges it belongs to: , , , .
    Vertex 3 belongs to alone, so it inherits that hyperedge's value unchanged. Compare HGNN, which would have averaged and degree-normalised; the two-stage view keeps the steps separate and visible.
    The two-stage form is not a different computation from HGNN — it is the same round trip written as two named aggregations instead of one product of matrices. What UniGNN adds is the ability to change each stage independently and to say what the result reduces to. Replacing both sums with means would give edge values and vertex values : the same pipeline, different aggregations, a different model.

    Example 2 — the reduction, checked numerically. Take the four-vertex graph used in the graph-theory material — edges –, –, – — and read it as a hypergraph whose three hyperedges all have size 2. Because every edge degree is 2, is one half times the identity, and the operator's inner part becomes

    Here is the vertex-degree diagonal and the adjacency matrix of the graph. The diagonal of the left side counts, for each vertex, its edges divided by 2; the off-diagonal entries are wherever two vertices share an edge.
    SymbolWhat it means
    vertex degrees down the diagonal — for this graph
    the adjacency matrix: 1 where two vertices share an edge
    the factor that every size-2 hyperedge introduces

    Applying the full operator (with and the identity) to gives . The formula behind it is — a degree-normalised graph operator with an implicit self-loop, which is precisely the shape of the graph convolution. On pairwise data, the hypergraph layer is a graph layer. That is UniGNN's unification made arithmetic rather than asserted.

    What these examples do not show. Example 1 uses sums in both stages, which is only one choice among the aggregations AllSet allows; a mean or a max would give different numbers and a different special case. Example 2 covers pairwise hypergraphs only; it does not demonstrate HGNN+'s typed relations, which the original work defines in more detail than this section needs.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhat is the defining property AllSet requires of both of its functions?

    APPLYUse UniGNN's two stages with sum aggregation (no degree factors) on the four-vertex hypergraph, with vertex features . What is vertex 4's value after one round? feature value

    TRANSFERWhy does it matter that HGNN+ accepts several vertex and hyperedge types rather than a single kind?

    Where this is going: the family is now complete — a standard layer, three ways to alter the structure, and an abstract form that contains them all. Card 5 states the one limitation they share, and closes the section with a skip check.
    Extension · Hypergraph neural networks 5/5

    The shared limitation, and can you leave this section?

    WHAT

    The pattern every model in the family follows. HGNN, HyperGCN, DHGNN, UniGNN, AllSet and HGNN+ differ in how they read the structure and how they aggregate, but underneath all of them is one sentence: the structure of the hypergraph decides how vertex features are smoothed along it, and nothing else enters the layer. Features go in; a smoothing pattern fixed by the structure comes out. No model in the list looks at the structure as data to be described, questioned, weighted from evidence, or fed forward as information in its own right.

    The degrees are used, but not as features — and the distinction matters. Degree information does enter the computation: divides by the square root of each vertex's degree, and divides by each hyperedge's size. But it enters as a fixed scale factor baked into the operator, chosen when the model is written down and never learned or passed on. A degree of 4 and a degree of 1 are used to set two different scalings; they are not handed to the network as an input column it could reason about. So a hub and a leaf with identical features produce different outputs, yet the network has no way to say why — the reason lives in the operator, not in the representation.

    This is the gap the paper under study addresses. It keeps the standard layer of card 1 exactly as it is, and adds a stage in front of it whose job is to turn the structure itself into features the layer can read — a structural encoder, in the permutation-invariant multiset form that AllSet formalised. The layer did not change; what arrives at it did. Everything in this section is the ground that makes that addition meaningful: the layer is standard, its input was not.

    • What a hypergraph network layer does — six moves on the incidence matrix: normalise the vertices, gather into hyperedges, average inside each hyperedge, scatter back, normalise again, transform and activate.
    • HGNN — the standard layer, motivated by the hypergraph Laplacian; it avoids the quadratic and lossy expansion into a graph, and its limitation is that it smooths features along hyperedges and does nothing else.
    • HyperGCN and DHGNN — two ways to attack the structure instead: reduce each hyperedge to a star of ordinary edges through an existing mediator, or rebuild the hyperedges from the current features during training.
    • UniGNN, AllSet and HGNN+ — the same recipe as two-stage message passing, as a pair of permutation-invariant multiset functions, and widened to typed and weighted relations.
    • The shared limitation — structure guides smoothing; degrees act only as fixed normalising factors, never as features the network can learn from.
    The questions below are the check. The bar is not two of three correct — it is that none of them required hard thought. If the incidence-matrix form of the layer still feels like a string of symbols, or if you cannot yet say what the standard layer cannot do, stay with this section: card 1's operator is the backbone the rest of the paper is built around.
    EXAMPLE

    One concrete instance of the limitation. Take two vertices with identical feature value . One has degree 1, the other degree 4. In the normalisation step each is divided by the square root of its degree:

    degree 1: 8 / √1 = 8 / 1 = 8.0 degree 4: 8 / √4 = 8 / 2 = 4.0

    The two vertices are treated differently purely because of their degree — the model does respond to degree. But notice how: the factor and the factor are fixed by the graph before training begins, and no row of the feature matrix ever holds "this vertex has degree 4". A downstream layer therefore cannot tell the difference between this vertex is a hub and this vertex's feature was divided by two for an unrelated reason. Degree is used up inside the operator rather than made available as information.

    The mistake to avoid: concluding that the family "ignores" degree. It does not — degree is central to the normalisation. The precise claim is narrower and stronger: degree enters only as a constant scale inside the fixed operator, so it is used but never represented. Keeping that distinction straight is what makes the paper's added stage look like a genuine contribution rather than a restatement.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich of these reduces the hypergraph to an ordinary graph before any convolution runs?

    APPLYIn the layer's first normalisation, a vertex of degree 4 has its feature divided by what factor? factor

    TRANSFERWhich statement captures the shared limitation of every model in this section?

    You have what the backbone needs. The paper under study keeps this standard layer and places a structural encoder in front of it; card 4 pointed to AllSet as that encoder's ancestor, and card 1's operator is the layer as the paper writes it. If you skipped this section, you will meet the incidence-matrix layer again in the paper's own equation — come back then.
    Extension · Symmetry and permutation invariance 1/3

    Symmetry: when two descriptions name the same object

    Every graph and hypergraph in this paper arrives as numbers in an order that someone else chose, and the paper proves its structural encoder does not depend on that order — a lemma about exchanging columns of the incidence matrix. This section supplies the general idea that lemma is an instance of: what a symmetry of a function is, the difference between invariance and equivariance, which relabellings of a graph are free, and the two standard routes to invariance together with what each route costs.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA symmetry of a function is a transformation of its input under which behaves in a fixed, prescribed way. Two behaviours are distinguished. is invariant under if for every input : the output does not move. is equivariant under if for every : the output moves by the same transformation that was applied to the input. In both cases changes only the description of the input, never the object being described.A symmetry is a way of rewriting the input that either leaves the answer alone (invariant) or moves the answer in exactly the same way the input moved (equivariant). The input is renamed; the object is not.

    Why this needs a name at all. In a computer every object arrives as a list of numbers in some order, and that order is a fact about the file, not about the object. If a function's answer changes when the same items are listed in a different order, the function is not reporting on the object — it is reporting on how the file was laid out. A symmetry statement is the precise claim that a function does not do this.

    Invariance and equivariance: one idea, two prescriptions

    The two words make different promises. Invariance promises that the output is a single thing that ignores the relabelling entirely — typically one number per graph, or one fixed-length summary. Equivariance promises that the output is indexed the same way the input is, and that relabelling the input relabels the output to match, so item 1's answer travels with item 1. Neither is stronger; which one is correct is decided by what the output is supposed to mean.

    The distinction is routinely blurred — many talks use the two words interchangeably. The concrete confusion: a layer that emits one vector per vertex is expected to follow its vertex when the vertices are renamed, so it is equivariant. Only the final graph-level readout that pools all the vertices into one answer is expected to be invariant. Calling the per-vertex layer "invariant" states a different and usually wrong requirement, because it would forbid the model from knowing which vector belongs to which vertex.

    When symmetry fails, it fails visibly. A function with no symmetry contains a term tied to a position or an index — for instance a weighted sum whose weights are the positions . Such a function is neither invariant nor equivariant under reordering: it is maximally sensitive to the layout, and the third example below shows the numbers. That failure is not a curiosity; it is exactly the shape of a wrong model.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — invariance in one line of arithmetic. Take the list and reorder it to .

    sum(3, 1, 4, 1, 5) = 14 sum(5, 1, 3, 1, 4) = 14

    The sum is invariant under reordering: both orders give 14. The mean is invariant too, because it is the sum divided by a count that reordering never changes: .

    Example 2 — invariance and equivariance are different promises. Take . Two natural functions behave differently on it.

    • Sorting returns the values in increasing order: . Reorder the input to and sorting still returns . Sorting is invariant — the output list is the same either way.
    • Ranking returns, for each entry, its position in that sorted order: for the ranks are . Reorder the input to and the ranks become — the original rank list with the same swap applied to it. Ranking is equivariant: swapping two entries of the input swaps the same two entries of the output.
    A frequent slip: sorting is often called equivariant because it "rearranges things". It is not. Sorting's output values are identical for every ordering of the input, which is invariance. It is ranking — the label attached to each entry — that moves with the input, and that is equivariance. Fixing this now prevents a real misreading later, because the same slip recurs with neighbourhood aggregation.

    Example 3 — a function with neither symmetry. Weight each entry by its position and add: compute .

    w·(3, 1, 4, 1, 5) = 1(3) + 2(1) + 3(4) + 4(1) + 5(5) = 3 + 2 + 12 + 4 + 25 = 46 w·(5, 1, 3, 1, 4) = 1(5) + 2(1) + 3(3) + 4(1) + 5(4) = 5 + 2 + 9 + 4 + 20 = 40

    The two orderings give 46 and 40. Same five values, same object, a different answer. This function is neither invariant nor equivariant: it is a function of the arrangement, and the arrangement is not part of the object. Every design error this section warns about has this shape.

    Carry one sentence away. Invariance: the answer does not change. Equivariance: the answer changes exactly the way the input did. Anything else: the answer is about the layout, not the object.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich equation states that a function is equivariant under a transformation of its input?

    APPLYWith weights equal to the positions , compute for the list . weighted total

    TRANSFERA model outputs one feature vector per vertex of a graph. Under a relabelling of the vertices, what should happen to that output?

    TRANSFERIs sorting a list invariant or equivariant under a reordering of that list?

    Where this is going: graphs and hypergraphs arrive as exactly such lists, ordered by whoever wrote the file. The next card asks which reorderings of a graph are free to change, and which function types must respect them.
    Extension · Symmetry and permutation invariance 2/3

    Permutation invariance on graphs and hypergraphs

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONLet an object be indexed by labels. An incidence matrix with rows and columns carries two independent label sets: the vertices (rows) and the hyperedges (columns). A relabelling is a bijection of one label set. An operator reading the object is permutation invariant under relabelling a given label set if returns exactly the same value after that relabelling; it is permutation equivariant under it if its output is relabelled the same way. Because rows and columns are labelled independently, invariance must be asserted separately for each: a claim about rows is not a claim about columns.A graph or hypergraph is stored with a number on every vertex and every edge. A relabelling just renumbers them. An operator is permutation invariant if renumbering does not change its answer, and equivariant if its answer is renumbered along with the input. Vertices and hyperedges are renumbered separately, so there are two separate statements to make.

    Which relabellings are free to change. For a plain graph there is one label set — the vertices — and permuting it is the only relabelling. For an incidence matrix there are three: permuting rows (vertices), permuting columns (hyperedges), and both at once, which is the same as choosing a new numbering in each direction. Each corresponds to writing the identical object down differently, so none of them changes the object, and a correct operator must account for all of them.

    ConstructionUnder a vertex relabellingUnder a hyperedge relabelling
    Per-vertex embedding (one vector per vertex)equivariant — each vector moves to its vertex's new positioninvariant — the vertices are untouched
    Graph-level prediction (one fixed-size answer)invariantinvariant
    A vertex's degree (its row sum in )invariant — the degree is a property of the vertex and moves with itinvariant
    Vertex index fed in as an input featureneither — it breaks by constructioninvariant — vertex features are untouched

    Why this is not an academic point. The numbering on a graph is chosen by whoever prepared the file, not by the object. Two files can hold the same graph with its vertices numbered in two different orders; they describe one object. Any dependence on that numbering is therefore a dependence on the file rather than on the object, and it will show up as a model whose prediction changes when an unrelated preprocessing step reorders the rows. The paper's lemma is the statement that its structural encoder has no such dependence: exchanging columns of the incidence matrix leaves the encoder's output unchanged.

    A tempting mistake. Because the indices are sitting right there in the matrix, it feels harmless to feed the row number in as an extra feature. It is not. That feature carries the file's arbitrary ordering and nothing about the graph; the model can then distinguish two structurally identical vertices by their file position, and two files holding the same graph in different orders produce different predictions. The index is bookkeeping, not structure.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — start from a graph and a symmetric aggregation. Four vertices with edges , , (vertex 2 is the hub), and a measured feature on each vertex. The aggregation for a vertex is the sum of its neighbours' features — a symmetric function of the neighbour set.

    Read row by row: vertex 1 has one neighbour with value 20; vertex 2 (the hub) has neighbours , summing to 80; vertices 3 and 4 each have the single neighbour 20. The adjacency matrix encodes which neighbour values each vertex is allowed to see.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the adjacency matrix in the ordering
    the feature attached to each vertex, in that same ordering
    the sum of the features of vertex 's neighbours

    Example 2 — relabel the vertices and watch what happens. Swap the roles of vertices 1 and 2, so the new ordering is . The feature vector must be reordered along with the vertices, becoming , and the adjacency matrix is rebuilt in the new order.

    looks nothing like — the rows and columns have been shuffled. Yet is exactly the old result with the same swap applied. The output did not change value; it changed position, one entry per vertex. That is equivariance.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the same adjacency matrix after the swap, visibly different in layout
    the same features carried along with their vertices
    the aggregate result, relabelled the same way as the input

    Example 3 — where invariance and positional weighting part ways. Collapse the per-vertex result into one graph-level number by adding the entries.

    sum of the aggregate: 20 + 80 + 20 + 20 = 140 (same after the swap: 80 + 20 + 20 + 20 = 140) sum of the features: 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 = 100 (and 20 + 10 + 30 + 40 = 100) positional sum i·x: 1(10) + 2(20) + 3(30) + 4(40) = 300 (versus 1(20) + 2(10) + 3(30) + 4(40) = 290)

    The graph-level sum is invariant: 140 before and after, because the same four numbers are being added. The positional sum is not: 300 becomes 290. It reads the position of each feature instead of the feature itself, so it is answering a question about the file's ordering — exactly the failure the lemma rules out.

    The pattern to remember. Summing over a vertex's neighbours is equivariant per vertex and invariant once pooled. Weighting by position is neither. Every invariance claim in this project is one of those two first cases, stated for a specific relabelling.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDThe paper's lemma proves the structural encoder returns the same value when the columns of the incidence matrix are exchanged. Which relabelling is that?

    APPLYA star graph has one centre joined to four leaves whose features are . A sum-aggregator sets the centre's value to the sum of its neighbours' features. What is that value? aggregated value

    TRANSFERA modeller adds the vertex index as an extra input feature, reasoning that more information cannot hurt. What is the effect?

    TRANSFERA function returns a single number summarising a whole hypergraph, such as a predicted label. Which invariance should it have?

    Where this is going: knowing that invariance is required says nothing about how to obtain it. The next card gives the two standard routes and states honestly what each one costs.
    Extension · Symmetry and permutation invariance 3/3

    How invariance is achieved — and the skip check

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThere are two standard routes to permutation invariance. Symmetric aggregation: combine a collection of values with a function whose output does not depend on the order of its arguments — the symmetric functions, of which sum, mean, max and min are the common ones. Invariant statistics: compute quantities that are themselves unchanged by relabelling — degrees (the row sums of the incidence matrix), edge sizes (its column sums), the multiset of Laplacian eigenvalues, or any sorted list of per-item numbers — and use only those as inputs.Either add the values up in a way that ignores order (sum, mean, max, min), or hand the model numbers that never depended on the order in the first place (degrees, counts, eigenvalues, sorted lists).

    Route one, in detail. A symmetric function is defined so that shuffling its inputs changes nothing. This is exactly why neighbourhood aggregation can be permutation invariant: the neighbours of a vertex form a set, not a list, so any honest summary of them must be a symmetric function. Sum answers "how much in total"; mean answers "how much per neighbour"; max answers "the strongest"; min answers "the weakest". All four are legitimate, and the choice is a modelling decision about which question is being asked.

    Route two, in detail. An invariant statistic sidesteps the problem by never looking at the order at all. The degree of a vertex does not depend on how the vertices were numbered; the eigenvalue spectrum of the Laplacian does not either; a sorted list throws the order away by construction. Feed a model only quantities of this kind and invariance is automatic, with no aggregation rule to design.

    ConstructionRouteWhat it is blind to
    sum / mean / max / min over a vertex's neighbourssymmetric aggregationwhich neighbour contributed which value
    a vertex's degree (row sum of the incidence matrix)invariant statistichow a vertex's neighbours connect among themselves
    the Laplacian eigenvalue spectruminvariant statisticwhich vertex sits where — and it does not in general reconstruct the graph
    a sorted list of per-item featuresinvariant statisticthe identity of each item; every value is kept, only the order is dropped
    features concatenated in file order, or an index used as a featureneither — invariance is brokennothing: it is exactly the file order that leaks in

    The cost, stated honestly. Neither route is free. Symmetric aggregation discards order, which is harmless when the inputs genuinely are a set — the neighbours of a vertex — and harmful when they are not. If a hypergraph's columns carry information that is tied to their position, such as a year, a colour or a rank, then summing over columns deletes the pairing between each value and its label, and invariance has been bought at the price of content. Invariant statistics can be too coarse to separate different structures: the degree sequence is not a complete fingerprint of a graph, so two genuinely different graphs can share one, and a model that reads only degrees cannot tell them apart. Both routes trade the same thing — robustness to the file's layout is paid for in discriminating power.

    An overconfidence to avoid. Because a statistic is invariant, it is easy to assume it captures the object. Invariance and completeness are different properties. A quantity can be perfectly invariant and still fail to separate two distinct structures; the second example below shows a concrete pair of graphs that defeat one of the most familiar invariant statistics.

    This section in five points

    1. Define invariance and equivariance of a function, and give an example of each: a sum is invariant under reordering, while the rank of each entry is equivariant.
    2. Name the relabellings of a graph or hypergraph that are free to change: vertex renumbering (rows), hyperedge renumbering (columns), or both.
    3. Say why a per-vertex output should be equivariant while a graph-level output should be invariant.
    4. Name the two routes to permutation invariance — symmetric aggregation and invariant statistics — and give one construction for each.
    5. State the cost of each route: symmetric aggregation discards order, and invariant statistics can be too coarse.
    The four questions below are the check. The bar is not a score — it is that none of them required hard thought. If you hesitated on which relabelling the paper's lemma concerns, or on what each route gives up, go back to card 2 before continuing.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — one symmetric aggregator, four summaries. A vertex has a set of neighbour features . Each symmetric function below returns the same value whatever order the neighbours happen to be listed in.

    sum: 4 + 9 + 2 + 7 = 22 mean: 22 / 4 = 5.5 max: 9 min: 2
    The order of never entered any of the four lines. That is what makes each of them a valid aggregation over a set of neighbours: no renumbering of the graph can change any of these outputs.

    Example 2 — an invariant statistic that is too coarse. Two different graphs on five vertices, both with degree sequence and both with 4 edges.

    • Graph one is the path : degrees , which sort to .
    • Graph two is a triangle on vertices 1, 2, 3 together with a separate edge : the triangle gives three vertices of degree 2, the edge gives two of degree 1, which also sort to .

    The two graphs are not the same object — the path is connected, while the triangle-plus-edge falls into two pieces — yet their degree sequences are identical. The sum of the degree sequence is in both cases, which by the handshake identity means both have exactly edges: even the edge count agrees. Any model reading only degrees and counts is blind to the difference between them.

    The lesson in one line. Example 1 shows route one working; Example 2 shows route two reaching its limit. Invariance makes a model robust to the file's layout, and it is paid for by some loss of discriminating power — the design question is always which loss is acceptable for the task at hand.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich route to permutation invariance does taking the maximum over a vertex's neighbour features use?

    APPLYA vertex has neighbour features . A mean-aggregator replaces the vertex's value by the mean of its neighbours' features. What is that value? aggregated value

    TRANSFERTwo graphs on five vertices both have degree sequence . One is the path ; the other is a triangle together with a separate edge. What does this show?

    TRANSFERA hypergraph's columns each carry a year label, and a model sums its values over the columns. What has been lost by that choice?

    You are ready. The paper's structural encoder is an instance of route two read through route one: it aggregates over hyperedges with a symmetric function, and its lemma proves that exchanging columns — renumbering the hyperedges — leaves the result unchanged. Every position-dependent construction you might meet in the method is the failure case this section described.
    Extension · Over-smoothing and over-squashing 1/3

    Over-smoothing: why depth turns every vertex into the same vector

    The taught paper's introduction names two failures of the prior paradigm: over-smoothing, where stacking layers drives every vertex's representation to a common value, and feature compression (equated with over-squashing), where an expanding neighbourhood is crushed into a fixed-width vector. This section makes both phenomena precise and measurable — a number for the first, a counting bound for the second — because a later chapter checks the paper's evidence for them against exactly these predictions.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONOver-smoothing is the decay of the differences between vertex representations as smoothing layers are stacked. Its model is the closed-neighbourhood average: each vertex replaces its value with the mean of its own value and its neighbours'. That update is row-stochastic (every row is non-negative and sums to 1, so each new value is a weighted average of previous ones), and on a connected graph its repeated application converges to the stationary average — a single number assigned to every vertex — so the range (largest entry minus smallest) tends to zero.Average every vertex together with its neighbours, again and again, and every vertex ends up holding the same vector — the graph's average. Once that happens, no classifier can tell the vertices apart.

    Why this matters for a classifier. A node classifier reads one vertex's representation and names it. If every vertex in a connected component carries the same vector, the classifier has one input for the whole component and can emit only one label — the information it needed to separate them has been averaged away, and nothing later in the network can recover it.

    The mechanism, in one line. Each layer is a weighted average, so every new value lies between the smallest and largest values of the previous round. A sequence whose terms always lie inside the previous range can never leave that range, and the range strictly shrinks whenever the values are not already equal. Depth therefore means repeated mixing, and mixing drives the range towards zero.

    The usual misconception. Smoothing is not the bug — it is the operation that lets a graph network use neighbours at all, and one or two steps of it are exactly what a graph network is for. The failure is depth: the same operation applied many times. It is also not the case that over-smoothing means "the model forgets its training data"; it means the vertex representations have become equal, which is a statement about the forward pass, not about memory.

    When it actually hurts, and the standard fixes. The damage is real only when depth is large relative to the graph's diameter, because a small graph mixes after very few rounds. Every standard fix does one of four things: use fewer layers; add a residual (skip) connection, which adds each layer's input back to its output so the pre-averaging signal is carried around the smoothing; use jumping knowledge, which reads the representations of every layer rather than only the last, so an early, un-smoothing layer is still available at the readout; or decouple propagation, separating the learned transformation from the averaging so many averaging steps can be taken at readout without stacking a nonlinear layer between each one.

    The closed-neighbourhood average, with every symbol tied to the intuition above: the sum collects the neighbours' values, and the in the denominator is the vertex itself (written as a self-loop). The fraction is the averaging weight; it makes the weights sum to 1, which is what forces each new value inside the previous round's range.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the representation of vertex after rounds
    the degree of — how many neighbours it has
    the neighbour set of
    the averaging weight; it makes the weights sum to 1, which is what forces each new value inside the previous range
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — one round, by hand. Four vertices in a line, numbered 1–2–3–4 with edges 1–2, 2–3, 3–4. Vertices 1 and 4 each have one neighbour; vertices 2 and 3 have two. Start with a wide spread: , whose range is .

    Vertex 1: closed neighbourhood , so .
    It averages itself with its single neighbour. The result 15 sits between 10 and 20 — inside the old range, as the mechanism promised.
    Vertex 2: closed neighbourhood , so .
    A middle vertex blends both sides. It keeps the value 20 only because this particular signal happens to be symmetric around it.
    Vertex 3: closed neighbourhood , so .
    The mirror of vertex 2.
    Vertex 4: closed neighbourhood , so .
    The other end pulls in by 5, towards its only neighbour.
    After one round the signal is and the range has fallen from 30 to .
    Every value moved towards its neighbours, so the extremes pulled inward and the range contracted by a third in a single step.

    Example 2 — run it to the limit. Applying the same four calculations over and over gives:

    RoundRange
    01020304030
    11520303520
    217.521.66728.33332.515

    Here , summing to , so .

    Two qualifications, because they matter when you read the paper. First, the limit here equals the plain mean only by coincidence: the weights happen to be symmetric and the signal rises evenly. The pure averaging here isolates the contraction so you can see it; it is not the whole layer, and a trained model can delay the collapse without preventing it.

    Where this is going: over-smoothing is the first of the two failures the paper's introduction names. The second — a growing neighbourhood crushed into a fixed-width vector — is a different phenomenon with a different cause, and it is the next card.
    Extension · Over-smoothing and over-squashing 2/3

    Over-squashing: too much through too narrow a channel

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONOver-squashing is the loss of information that occurs when a vertex's receptive field — the set of vertices whose features can influence its representation after rounds of message passing, which grows with — must be summarised into a representation of fixed width . When the field carries more independent numbers than , the map from neighbourhood state to representation cannot be injective (one-to-one: distinct inputs giving distinct outputs), so different neighbourhood states are forced onto the same representation and the difference cannot be recovered by any later layer.A vertex has to crush everything its growing neighbourhood contains into one short vector. Past a certain size, the crushing loses detail, and nothing later in the network can put it back.

    Why a classifier feels it. Two vertices whose neighbourhoods differ in some task-relevant way must come out with representations a classifier can separate. If the summary map collides them — sends two different neighbourhoods to the same vector — then a distinction that mattered has been destroyed inside the network, and the resulting error is not fixable downstream.

    The mechanism. Message passing updates a vertex from itself and its neighbours, so each round extends, by one hop, the set of vertices that can influence it — its receptive field. But the layer writes its result into a vector whose width is fixed by the architecture, no matter how large that field has grown. Two quantities therefore fall out of step: the amount of input, which grows with reach, and the channel that carries it, which does not grow at all.

    Do not confuse it with over-smoothing. They are two different failures with two different causes. Over-smoothing is about depth: too many averaging rounds collapse distinct representations to a common one. Over-squashing is about width versus reach: a receptive field larger than the fixed representation width forces many distinct states onto one vector. A two-layer network can over-squash if its neighbourhoods are huge; a twenty-layer network can over-smooth on a graph with a hundred vertices. The table at the end of the examples keeps the two apart.

    The curvature view, stated honestly. A second way to describe the same failure looks at the graph rather than at counting. In this view an edge is a bottleneck when everything passing between the two sides of the graph has to squeeze through it; over-squashing is then the shrinking influence of a distant vertex on a near one, and it is worst across such bottleneck edges, which sit in negatively curved regions of the graph. This is a different lens on the same underlying fact — a bounded-width representation of an expanding neighbourhood must lose influence from far away — not a competing explanation. The counting view says that information is lost and roughly how much room there was; the curvature view says where in the graph it happens.

    Why hypergraphs make it acute. In a plain graph every relation joins two vertices, so a one-hop neighbourhood stays small unless the degree is enormous. In a hypergraph one relation can contain hundreds of vertices at once — a paper with hundreds of co-authors is a single hyperedge — so the aggregation for one relation already has to summarise a very large set into the same fixed width. A hypergraph vertex's receptive field can therefore outgrow its representation after very few hops.

    The message-passing update, with each symbol tied to the mechanism above. The width of is fixed by design, while the receptive field that feeds it grows with . The counting bound that follows is for injectivity, where is the receptive field and the per-vertex feature dimension.
    SymbolWhat it means
    vertex 's representation after rounds, of fixed width
    the message function applied to each neighbour
    the aggregation — a fixed-width summary such as a sum or a mean that combines the neighbours' messages
    the update function that produces 's new representation
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a collision you can see. Two positions in a neighbourhood carry feature vectors and . Suppose the aggregation is a sum.

    sum = (3, 1) + (1, 3) = (4, 4)

    Swap the two vectors — put first and second — and the sum is still . The aggregation is symmetric (a permutation-invariant operation: it does not depend on the order of its inputs), so it cannot report which position held which vector. With two positions there are arrangements collapsing onto one output; the summary is not injective, and the two inputs are unrecoverable from it.

    Example 2 — the counting bound, on a real shape. Take a root with children, each of which has children of its own — a 10-ary tree of depth 2. Within two hops of the root lie the root, its 10 children, and its 100 grandchildren:

    |receptive field| = 1 + 10 + 100 = 111 vertices

    Suppose each vertex carries an -dimensional feature vector. Then the receptive field holds independent numbers, and the root's representation — fixed at width — must be a function of all of them:

    888 numbers in → 8 numbers out; 888 / 8 = 111 times too little room
    A continuous one-to-one map cannot send an -dimensional input into an -dimensional output — that is a counting fact, not a training problem. So this layer must collide different neighbourhood states however it is trained. To be injective it would need width at least ; and that is only the 2-hop case, before the field widens further. The general bound is width .

    Why the bound is worse than it looks. Sum aggregation is permutation-invariant, so whenever all the feature vectors differ, permuting them among the field's positions leaves the sum unchanged. For the -vertex field that is distinct neighbourhood states sharing one output. A mean aggregator is no better: it is the same sum, rescaled. Injectivity is not merely expensive at this width — it is impossible.

    Example 3 — the paper's own scale. The largest relation in the paper's Table I is DBLP-Conf, whose hyperedges average members. If each member carries features, one relation holds numbers that must be summarised into the same fixed width a Cora relation — two members — uses:

    982.2 / 2 = 491.1 (times more information per relation than a pairwise edge)
    This is the mechanism's most testable prediction: datasets with the largest relations should be where a fixed-width summary loses most, so a remedy that adds an un-aggregated channel should help them most. A later chapter asks whether the paper's per-dataset results actually show that.
    Over-smoothingOver-squashing
    CauseToo many layers: each averages, so differences decay with depthA receptive field larger than the fixed representation width; growth comes from reach, not depth
    SymptomDifferent vertices' representations become equal (or degree-determined); accuracy rises then falls with depthInformation from distant or numerous vertices is distorted or lost; specific signals stay inaccessible however well the model trains
    RemedyFewer layers; residual (skip) connections; jumping knowledge; decoupled propagationWider representations; rewiring the graph to shorten bottlenecks; explicit relation features; an independent channel that does not pass through the aggregation
    EXERCISES

    Extension · Over-smoothing and over-squashing 3/3

    Skip check: the two failures, and how the paper answers them

    WHAT

    This section made two failures precise — over-smoothing and over-squashing — and previewed how the taught paper responds to each. Below is that response, then the recap; if you can do everything in the recap unaided, skip ahead.

    How the taught paper responds

    To over-smoothing, a structural embedding computed once. The paper's High-Order Incidence Encoder reads the incidence matrix and produces, for every vertex, a single structural number — how many relations the vertex belongs to. This is computed before the propagation and then injected as an input feature; its width is deliberately . The move does not fight the averaging; it changes what the averaging is given. The paper's sharper framing is that the layer already uses each vertex's degree inside its normalisation and then discards it, so the encoder's job is to expose that degree as a feature the network can read.

    To compression, a second channel built without aggregating neighbours. The Task-Driven Rule Encoder runs a gradient-boosted tree ensemble — many small decision trees, where a decision tree is a sequence of yes/no questions about a single vertex's features, and the trees' answers are combined into one prediction — on each vertex's own feature vector, and returns a per-vertex embedding . Every step of that construction reads one vertex at a time, so no neighbour averaging enters it anywhere. That yields a description of the vertex which is a function of the vertex alone, available to the network before the first smoothing step — exactly the kind of signal a fixed-width neighbourhood summary was destroying.

    FailureThe paper's answerWhat it addressesWhat it does not
    Over-smoothingHOI-Encoder: computed once from , injected as an input featureGives the network a structural quantity that neighbour-averaging was never going to produceDoes not alter the layer — the propagation still averages, so representations still contract with depth
    Feature compression (= over-squashing)TDR-Encoder: from a tree ensemble on each vertex's features, built with no neighbour aggregationGives the network a per-vertex channel whose construction does not depend on the size of a neighbourhoodDoes not widen the representation or shrink the receptive field, so one very large relation is still summarised into a fixed-width vector
    The honest bottom line, and the number that settles it. The paper does not stop over-smoothing; it enriches the layer's input. Its own layer-count ablation (Table VIII on CC-Cora) shows the contraction is still there. The plain HGNN falls from at 2 layers to at 8 layers — a drop of points. DD-HGNN, which carries both encoders, also falls: , a drop of points. Enriched input makes the model more robust to depth; it does not make it immune. The paper attributes the decline to overfitting — whether the smoothing contraction better explains the shape is exactly what a later chapter examines.

    Recap

    • Over-smoothing: with depth, vertex representations converge to a common value, the range shrinks to zero, and a classifier can no longer separate vertices.
    • Its mechanism: every layer is a weighted average, so no value leaves the previous round's range, and the range strictly shrinks unless the signal is already flat.
    • Over-squashing: the receptive field grows with reach while the representation width is fixed; once the field carries more numbers than the width, the summary map cannot be injective and distant detail is lost.
    • The two are different: different causes (depth versus reach-and-width), different symptoms, different remedies — which is why the paper uses two encoders rather than one.
    • The paper's answer: two encoders that compute information outside the propagation — a structural embedding from , and a rule embedding from a tree ensemble on per-vertex features — spliced into the layer's input rather than replacing the layer.
    The questions below are the check. The bar is not a score; it is that you did not have to think hard about any of them. If you hesitated on why depth and reach are different causes, stay: the chapter that checks the paper's evidence leans on exactly that distinction.
    EXAMPLE

    Walk — the arithmetic behind the bottom line. The claim that the paper's answer does not stop the contraction is a claim about numbers, and the numbers are in the paper's own ablation.

    Read the plain HGNN column at 2 layers and at 8 layers: and .
    Both are accuracies on the same 40-class task, so they are comparable. Blind guessing scores percent — the floor the deep plain model is crawling towards.
    Subtract: points lost from 2 layers to 8.
    A model that got worse as it got deeper is the signature of over-smoothing, not of a model that merely lacked capacity.
    Read the DD-HGNN column at the same two depths: and . Subtract: points.
    DD-HGNN carries both encoders, so this comparison isolates the paper's answer. It loses less than the plain HGNN, but it still loses — richer input slows the decline without reversing it.
    That contrast is the whole preview: points of decline without the encoders, with them. Smaller, not zero.

    Extension · Sigmoids and gating 1/3

    The logistic sigmoid

    The taught paper uses the logistic sigmoid twice: its structural encoder ends in a sigmoid, and its structural gate behaves like a value in (0, 1). This section builds the sigmoid from zero — its formula, its range, and the way it saturates — then shows what happens when a quantity that can only lie strictly between 0 and 1 is used as a multiplier. That single fact makes the paper's word "amplified" a relative claim among vertices rather than an absolute increase, so reading the fusion honestly depends on this section.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThe logistic sigmoid is the function defined by , where is Euler's number. It accepts any real number, however large or negative, and returns a number strictly greater than 0 and strictly less than 1. The notation means the open interval: the endpoints 0 and 1 are never produced.Hand the sigmoid any number at all; it hands back a number that behaves like a probability — always above 0, always below 1, and never exactly either one.

    Why anyone wants this. A neural network computes numbers that can be any real value: a pre-activation might be or . Sometimes the next step needs a number on a fixed scale instead — a weight, a percentage, a probability. That is the job of an activation function: a fixed, simple function applied entry by entry to turn unbounded numbers into something with a controlled range. The sigmoid is the oldest and most familiar activation, and it is the one the paper you are reading relies on.

    What the curve looks like. Plot along the bottom and up the side. The curve is an S-shaped ramp: low and nearly flat on the left, steep through the middle, high and nearly flat on the right. The two flat regions are called the saturated regions, and they are the source of every problem the sigmoid causes.

    The formula is built from three pieces, each with an intuitive job: turns any input into a positive number; adding 1 keeps the denominator above 1; dividing 1 by a number above 1 keeps the result below 1. The minus sign in the exponent is what makes the curve rise from left to right rather than fall.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the input — any real number, typically a pre-activation, meaning a weighted sum of earlier values plus a bias
    Euler's number raised to ; always strictly positive, and tiny when is large positive, huge when is large negative
    the denominator, always strictly greater than 1
    the output, always strictly between 0 and 1

    The range is an open interval. Because the denominator is always strictly larger than 1, the quotient is always strictly less than 1. Because the numerator is positive, the quotient is always strictly greater than 0. Neither endpoint is achievable: to reach 0 you would need to be infinite, and to reach 1 you would need to be exactly 0. As grows, the output creeps towards 1 without ever arriving; the same holds for 0 on the far left. This is not a pedantic detail — it is exactly why the paper's structural embedding can never contain a 0 or a 1.

    Input Reading
    0.002473deep in the left flat region
    0.017986nearly flat
    0.119203beginning to bend
    0.268941on the ramp
    0.500000the exact midpoint
    0.731059on the ramp
    0.880797past the bend
    0.982014nearly flat
    0.997527deep in the right flat region

    Notice two things. First, the table is symmetric around the midpoint: and add to exactly 1, which follows from . Second, the outputs crowd towards the ends: by the value is already 0.9975, so a further increase in changes almost nothing visible. That flattening is saturation.

    Saturation and the gradient. Training a network by gradient descent uses the derivative, which measures how strongly an output moves when the input is nudged. Differentiating by the chain rule gives ; since , the same expression rearranges into the compact identity , written in terms of the output alone. The derivative is largest at , where it equals , and it falls off quickly on both sides. This is the derivative with respect to the input; a small number here means the gradient signal travelling backwards through this unit is multiplied by something near zero.

    Input Fraction of the peak (peak )
    0.002467about 1%
    0.017663about 7%
    0.104994about 42%
    0.196612about 79%
    0.250000100%
    0.196612about 79%
    0.104994about 42%
    0.017663about 7%
    0.002467about 1%

    The consequence for gradient-based training. When a unit's pre-activation is large in magnitude, its sigmoid is saturated, its derivative is near zero, and the gradient passing through that unit is multiplied by near zero. In a deep network, hundreds of such multiplications compound, and the gradient reaching the early layers collapses towards zero. The early layers then receive almost no signal and stop improving. This is the vanishing gradient problem, and it is the price the sigmoid pays for its tidy range. It is also why modern deep networks avoid the sigmoid in hidden layers and keep it for output units and gates, where a bounded, probability-like value is what is actually wanted.

    The standard alternatives. Two other activations appear so often that they belong in the same picture. Hyperbolic tangent, written , is the sigmoid stretched and shifted: , with range instead of . Its derivative at 0 is , four times the sigmoid's peak, so its gradients are healthier — but it still saturates at both ends, so it only delays the vanishing gradient rather than removing it. ReLU, the rectified linear unit, is : it passes positive values through untouched and outputs exactly 0 for negative ones. ReLU does not saturate on the positive side at all, which is why it became the default activation for hidden layers. Its failure is different: on the negative side its derivative is exactly 0, and a unit stuck there receives no gradient and can stop updating altogether.

    ActivationFormulaRangeDerivative at 0Failure mode
    Sigmoid open0.25saturates at both ends — vanishing gradient
    Tanh open1.0saturates at both ends, but less sharply
    ReLU closed at 0not defined at 0; 1 to the right, 0 to the leftunits with negative input output 0 and can stop learning
    The most common mistake is to treat the sigmoid's output as a genuine 0 or 1. It is not: is close to 1, and is closer, but no finite input reaches 1. The paper you are reading contains a proof that depends on this exact fact. Its structural encoder — the part of the model that turns the graph's structure into a vector — ends in a sigmoid, so the vector it produces inherits the open range . An argument that treated those entries as possibly 1 or 0 would be wrong, which is why this small detail is stated here rather than assumed.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — compute two values by hand. Start with the easiest point, then one off-centre point.

    .
    Since , the midpoint falls out with no arithmetic. This is why 0 is always the symmetry centre of the curve.
    : first the exponent, .
    Compute the inner quantity before the outer division; this is the piece most easily got wrong by entering the exponent with the wrong sign.
    Then , and .
    The denominator is only slightly greater than 1, so the output is pushed well above the midpoint. Large positive inputs land here.

    Example 2 — a sigmoid applied to a real pre-activation. In a neuron the input to the sigmoid is a weighted sum. Take a single input value with weight and a bias of :

    z = 1.5 × 2 + (−0.5) = 3.0 − 0.5 = 2.5
    σ(2.5) = 1 / (1 + e^(−2.5)) = 1 / (1 + 0.082085) = 1 / 1.082085 = 0.924142

    So the neuron outputs about . If we pushed the input value from 2 up to 4, the pre-activation would rise from to , and the output would rise only from to . Doubling the input moved the output by about 0.07. That is saturation being felt in a concrete forward pass — the second half of the input's effect was nearly erased.

    Check the extremes. and . These two numbers sum to exactly 1, and neither is 1 or 0. However far you push , the output stays inside the open interval — the claim the rest of this section relies on.
    This example used a single input. That is enough to show the range and the saturation, but it does not demonstrate the derivative identity or the multi-entry behaviour a real layer has; those appear in the next card.

    Extension · Sigmoids and gating 2/3

    A number in (0, 1) is a gate

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA gate is a value used as a multiplier, entry by entry. If a vector is combined with a gate vector whose every entry lies strictly in , the gated result is the entrywise product . When every is in , the magnitude of each entry can only stay the same or shrink: , with strict decrease whenever and .A gate is a dial that sits in front of each number. Because the dial is stuck between 0 and 1, turning it can only make a number smaller in magnitude (closer to zero) — never larger in size.

    Why gates exist. Sometimes a model should be able to turn a piece of information down. It might learn that part of a feature vector is irrelevant for the current example, or that a whole channel should be suppressed. A gate in is the simplest such control: multiply by 0.1 and the entry is nearly gone, multiply by 0.9 and it is barely touched. The gate becomes learnable by being produced by a sigmoid (the S-shaped function of card 1, whose range is exactly ) — the sigmoid's range is exactly the range a gate needs.

    Attenuate, never amplify. The inequality holds for every entry, independently, and does not depend on the sign of . A negative entry stays negative and shrinks in absolute value; a positive entry stays positive and shrinks. Multiplying by a value in is a contraction: it can never increase any coordinate, and it can never change a coordinate's sign. That asymmetry is the whole content of this card, and it is what makes the taught paper's word "amplified" worth a careful look.

    The contrast with attention. The attention weights of a transformer (the model family behind large language models, built on attention as its core operation) are a different pattern that also uses numbers in . Attention assigns one weight to each token (a word or word-piece, the unit the model reads), and those weights are normalised to sum to exactly 1 across the set of tokens. The output is the weighted average of the value vectors, one vector per token — the piece of information each token contributes to the mix. So attention and a gate share the range but differ in the constraint placed on the values: gate entries are independent, while attention weights must share a fixed total of 1. That single extra constraint changes what the operation can do — explained concretely below.

    PropertyEntrywise gateAttention weights
    How many valuesone per feature entryone per token, reused across all feature entries of that token
    Range of each value
    Extra constraintnone — entries are independentthey must sum to exactly 1 across the tokens
    What the operation doesscales each entry by its own factorforms a weighted average of the value vectors
    Effect on the totaltotal magnitude shrinkstotal is redistributed, not created
    Can it make an output larger than its inputsnono — a weighted average lies between the smallest and largest inputs

    When a gate fails. Two failure modes follow directly from the definition. First, a gate cannot strengthen a signal: if a feature is being suppressed by everything upstream and the only remaining operation is multiplication by a value below 1, the feature only shrinks further. Second, a gate near 0 is also a near-zero derivative. This is the sigmoid's saturation (card 1) showing up again: a gate held at 0.001 blocks the forward value and multiplies the backward gradient by 0.001 as well, so the gate that shut a channel also stops learning to reopen it. Gates are useful precisely when they are allowed to sit away from the extremes.

    Do not read a gate in as "boosts the important part". It cannot boost anything. It can only leave a value roughly alone (gate near 1) or reduce it (gate nearer 0). Comparisons of the form "this entry is amplified relative to that one" are legitimate — the ratio between two entries can change — but "this entry became larger than it started" is not.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — gate a small vector. Three entries, gated by three values drawn from the sigmoid's range.

    v = (4, −2, 6) g = (0.9, 0.7, 0.5)
    g ⊙ v = (0.9 × 4, 0.7 × (−2), 0.5 × 6) = (3.6, −1.4, 3.0)

    Check each entry against its original: became , became , and became . Every magnitude fell, and no sign flipped. The sum of absolute values fell from to — the vector as a whole shrank by a third. That is what an entrywise gate does to a set of numbers: it removes energy, it does not move it around.

    Example 2 — attention over four tokens. Now the other pattern. Four tokens, each with a value vector we only need the first coordinate of. The attention weights are .

    Confirm the weights sum to one: .
    This is the constraint that separates attention from a gate. Without it the operation would be an arbitrary weighted sum rather than an average, and the output could exceed the inputs.
    Take the first coordinate of each value vector: .
    Attention treats each coordinate the same way, so following one coordinate through is enough to see the mechanism.
    Form the weighted sum: .
    Each weight decides how much of its token contributes. A token with weight 0.5 supplies half its value; a token with weight 0.05 barely registers.
    Check the result against the inputs: lies between the smallest coordinate and the largest .
    A weighted average with weights that sum to 1 always lies inside the range of its inputs. That is the guarantee a convex combination gives, and it is why attention cannot manufacture a value that no token contained.
    Entrywise gate (Example 1)Attention (Example 2)
    Input entries(4, −2, 6)(1, 0, 2, −1)
    Multipliers(0.9, 0.7, 0.5)(0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05)
    Do multipliers sum to 1no — they sum to 2.1yes — they sum to 1.0 exactly
    Output(3.6, −1.4, 3.0)0.75 (for this coordinate)
    Total before → aftersum of absolute values 12 → 8the total is redistributed; every output sits inside the input range
    Can one entry rise while another fallsyes — a small entry with a gate near 1 can end up larger than a larger entry with a gate near 0, though both still shrankyes — but the sum is fixed, so a rise in one token's share is paid for by a fall in another's
    The distinction in one line: a gate scales each entry by its own dial and the total shrinks; attention shares out a fixed total of 1 and the total is conserved. Both sit in , so neither can amplify — but only attention is forced to pay for one entry's share by another's.
