    Extension · Sigmoids and gating 3/3

    What this implies for the taught paper's fusion — and the skip check

    WHAT

    This section taught two facts and then joined them. First, the logistic sigmoid is a function with range , saturating at both ends so that its derivative vanishes far from the middle. Second, a number in used as a multiplier is a gate: it attenuates and can never amplify. The final step is to apply both to the taught paper's fusion, where the two facts meet.

    Where the sigmoid appears in the paper

    First, the two objects being combined. The paper keeps two representations of each vertex. One is a rule-side embedding , learned from the logical rules that state how relations combine. The other is a structural embedding , learned from the shape of the graph itself. The fusion is the step that joins these two representations into one. Nothing in this card depends on the details of how either is learned; what matters is that comes out of a sigmoid and does not.

    The paper's structural encoder ends in a sigmoid: its structural embedding, written , is produced by applying entry by entry. Everything from the previous cards applies immediately. Each entry of lies strictly inside — never 0, never 1, for exactly the reason computed earlier ( is close to 1 but is not 1). This is a provable property of , not a tendency: whatever the input graph, the encoder's output is trapped in the open interval.

    That embedding is then used as a structural gate in the paper's fusion. The fusion multiplies entry by entry into the rule-side embedding , and then concatenates the product with the original (places the two vectors end to end, forming one longer vector). In symbols, the fused vector at a vertex is the concatenation of and itself, where is the entrywise product.

    The consequence, stated honestly

    Because every entry of is in , the product can only shrink the entries of , exactly as in the gating card. The paper's own words describe the structural signal as "amplified", and this needs reading with care: the multiplication cannot make any entry of larger than it started. What it can do is change the relative size of entries across vertices — a vertex whose structural gate is near 1 keeps its rule-embedding entry nearly intact, while a vertex whose gate is near 0 has that entry driven towards zero. So a vertex can end up standing out more compared with other vertices even though every vertex's entries were individually reduced.

    Two facts keep this honest. First, the ranking among vertices can change, because the gates differ per vertex, so "amplified" is a statement about relative position, not absolute magnitude. Second, and more important, the original is concatenated alongside the gated product rather than replaced by it. The unscaled rule embedding is still present in the fused representation, so nothing is destroyed: the model sees both the gated view and the untouched view, and can use whichever the task needs. The gate contributes a modulated copy, not the only copy.

    The one sentence to keep: the structural embedding is a sigmoid output, so it is a gate in ; multiplying by it can only shrink entries, which makes "amplified" a relative claim among vertices, and the concatenation of the unscaled original means no information is lost in the process.

    The section, in five claims

    • The logistic sigmoid is with range the open interval ; neither endpoint is ever produced.
    • The sigmoid saturates: its derivative peaks at when and falls towards 0 as grows, which is the vanishing-gradient problem in hidden layers.
    • Tanh and ReLU are the standard alternatives: has range and still saturates; ReLU has range , does not saturate for positive inputs, but is flat (derivative 0) for negative ones.
    • A gate is a value used as a multiplier; a gate in attenuates and never amplifies, so the total magnitude of a vector can only shrink under it.
    • Attention weights are also in but must sum to 1, so attention redistributes a fixed total while an entrywise gate scales entries independently and shrinks the total (attention and its sum-to-one rule were defined in card 2).
    The questions below are the check. The bar is not a score — it is that you did not have to think hard about any of them. If the fusion paragraph still reads as a surprise rather than the obvious consequence of a gate in , stay: the paper's fusion is explained in terms of exactly this, and the rest of the fusion cards assume it.
    EXAMPLE

    One worked pass over the paper's fusion. Take a rule-side embedding at a vertex, and let the structural gate at that same vertex be — three entries, each strictly inside as the encoder guarantees.

    Multiply entry by entry: , , . So .
    Each multiplier is below 1, so each result is closer to zero than its original: , , . No entry grew.

    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDThe paper's structural embedding is a sigmoid output, so every entry is in . What is the immediate effect of multiplying entry by entry into a rule embedding ?

    APPLYTwo vertices carry the same rule-embedding entry of . Their structural gates are and . What is the ratio of the larger gated entry to the smaller? ratio

    TRANSFERThe paper concatenates the gated product with the original rather than replacing with the product. Why does this matter?

    TRANSFERAttention weights and gate values both lie in . Why is attention able to shift emphasis between the items it attends to (words or word-pieces) while an elementwise gate can only remove it?

    You are ready for the paper's fusion. The structural encoder ends in a sigmoid, so its output is a gate in ; the fusion multiplies that gate into the rule embedding and keeps the unscaled copy alongside. Every later claim about the fusion can now be checked against one question: does it only shrink, or has the author smuggled in an amplification that a value in cannot supply?
    Extension · Ways to combine two signals 1/4

    The problem: two descriptions of the same object

    The taught paper holds two descriptions of every vertex — a one-number structural embedding and a many-number rule embedding — and has to combine them into one representation. This section lays out the four standard ways to do that (concatenation, weighted sum, elementwise gating, cross-attention), shows with worked arithmetic what each one gains and what each one loses, and then identifies exactly which one the paper uses: a broadcast gate followed by concatenation.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONFusion is any operation that takes two matrices describing the same set of objects and returns a single matrix describing those same objects. The two inputs are the signals (or streams); each has one row per object. The width of a signal is its number of columns — the number of numbers stored per object. Formally, fusion is a function that maps a first signal of width and a second of width to a combined signal of width . The widths and need not be equal, and the choice of is the whole subject of this section.You have two tables with the same rows, where each row is one object. The tables have different numbers of columns. Fusion glues them into one table that the rest of the network can read.

    Why anyone faces this problem. The taught paper describes every vertex of a graph twice. The first description gives one number per vertex, so that signal has width 1 — it is a single column. The second description gives many numbers per vertex (one per rule feature), so that signal has a wide shape, for example 200 columns. Both tables have the same rows, one per vertex, but they are not the same kind of table, and they are not the same width.

    This matters because of what comes next. A linear layer — the matrix multiply that does the actual learning — reads one matrix. It cannot accept two matrices and mix them entry by entry unless they have identical shapes. So the two descriptions must be merged before any downstream arithmetic sees them. Fusion is that bridge, and it is not a formality: the choice of decides how much the single-column signal is allowed to influence the result.

    The menu. Four mechanisms account for almost every fusion used in modern networks. They differ along two axes: whether they keep the two signals side by side or mix them into one number, and whether the mixing is fixed in advance or computed per object.

    MechanismEffect on shapesWhat it can expressWhat it cannotCost
    Concatenation and → ; both signals stacked side by side, unchangedA downstream layer may weight the two blocks independently — any coefficient on the first block, any on the secondNo interaction between the signals: a linear layer downstream reads each block separately, it cannot multiply one block by the otherThe downstream input grows to , so the next weight matrix gains columns of parameters
    Weighted sum (fixed weights)The narrower signal is broadcast across the wider one; the output keeps the wider width, One mixed number per column, produced cheaply, with no extra widthThe ratio between the two signals is fixed at design time; a downstream layer can rescale the mixed number but cannot pull the two parts apart againNo extra width; the two constant weights are two extra scalars
    Elementwise gating (Hadamard product, broadcast) → ; the single column is stretched across the row and multiplies entry by entryPer-object emphasis: each row is scaled by its own factor, so the same feature can be strong at one vertex and weak at anotherOne gate value per row, so all columns of a row share the same factor; and a gate in can only attenuate, never amplifySame width as the wider input, plus the cost of whatever produces the gate
    Cross-attention and → ; each entry of one signal is reweighted by its match with entries of the otherInput-dependent, normalised reweighting: emphasis is chosen per object and per feature, and the total is shared out rather than fixedNeeds projections on both sides to form the match scores, and the scores cost extra computation; because the weights are normalised, it reallocates a fixed total rather than scaling freelyExtra projection matrices plus the pairwise scores — much heavier than the other three
    The commonest mistake at this stage is to treat the four rows as interchangeable. They are not. Concatenation keeps both signals and hands the weighting decision to a later layer. A weighted sum merges them and fixes the weighting now. Gating modulates one signal by the other per object. Attention reallocates emphasis based on content. Each choice is a different claim about what the relationship between the two signals is, and picking the wrong one bakes that claim into the architecture. Card 2 prices the first two, card 3 the third.

    When fusion fails. Fusion cannot create information. If one of the two signals is uninformative for the task, no mechanism here will rescue it — a weighted sum will merely dilute the useful signal with noise, and a gate will multiply the other signal by noise. A fusion's job is to combine what is there, not to invent what is not.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a scale model you can count by eye. Three objects, described by a width-1 signal and a width-4 signal (four columns instead of the real two hundred, so the numbers stay readable).

    has shape : three rows, one column. has shape : the same three rows, four columns.
    Both tables describe the same three objects, so they share the number of rows. Only the widths differ — that mismatch is the entire problem fusion solves.
    Concatenate along the columns: the result has columns, so its shape is .
    Concatenation adds widths, not rows. The three objects are still three; each now carries five numbers instead of one plus four.
    The single column's share of the entries is , i.e. 20%.
    Every row has five numbers, of which exactly one came from . This fraction is the representation share, and the next example shows how small it becomes at the real width.

    Example 2 — the same arithmetic at the real widths. Now has width 1 and has width 200, as in the taught paper's setting (the rule embedding is wide; the structural embedding is a single column).

    fused width = 1 + 200 = 201 columns
    structural share = 1 / 201 = 0.004975 = 0.4975%
    rule share = 200 / 201 = 0.995025 = 99.5025%

    So under plain concatenation the single structural column supplies only about half of one percent of the fused representation — , which is slightly less than the one would guess from "one in two hundred", because the total is 201 columns, not 200. Compare that with 20% in the scale model: widening the rule embedding from 4 to 200 columns shrank the structural signal's share by a factor of about 40. This is the dilution the next card examines.

    This example covers concatenation only. It does not show what a weighted sum, a gate, or attention would produce from the same two signals; those are worked in the cards that follow.

    Extension · Ways to combine two signals 2/4

    Concatenation and weighted sums: what each loses

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA weighted-sum fusion picks two constants and , fixed when the model is designed, and combines a per-object scalar (the narrow signal, one number per row) with a per-object row (the wide signal) by broadcasting the scalar: the output at column is . The output has the wide signal's width . The constants and are the weights; a downstream linear layer may afterwards multiply the whole output by any constant it learns, but it receives only the mixture.Multiply each signal by a fixed number and add them. Since one signal is a single number per row, that number is spread across the row first, so the same contribution is added to every column.

    Why anyone wants a weighted sum. It is the cheapest possible fusion: no extra columns, two extra scalars, and one arithmetic operation. When the two signals are known in advance to be comparable — say, two measurements of the same quantity — a fixed blend is a reasonable prior. The trouble is exactly that word fixed.

    What concatenation loses: representation share. Concatenation preserves every value exactly, so it destroys no information. What it does not do is give the narrow signal a fair share of the representation. When a single column is joined to 200 columns, that column is 1 of 201 entries per row — under half a percent. The downstream weight matrix has one column of parameters for the structural signal against two hundred for the rule signal. Nothing forbids the layer from learning a large coefficient on that one column, but the architecture has offered it no head start and no interaction, and in a wide table a single coordinate is easy for training to neglect.

    What a fixed weighted sum loses: separability and the ratio. This one is sharper. Once has been formed, the two parts are added into one number and cannot be told apart again. Two different pairs can produce the same sum, and no downstream layer can recover which pair it was. Worse, the ratio between the structural contribution and the rule contribution is set by the constants alone. A downstream linear layer multiplies the mixed number by a single learned constant , which multiplies both contributions by — leaving their ratio exactly as it was.

    The misconception worth naming: people assume a weighted sum is more powerful than concatenation because "you can always concatenate and then learn the weights." That gets it backwards. Concatenation followed by a learned linear layer is strictly more general than a fixed weighted sum, because the learned coefficients are chosen per column and may include weighting one signal at zero. A fixed weighted sum is the special case in which that choice has already been made and frozen.

    When each fails. A weighted sum fails whenever the two signals should be weighted differently for different objects or different features — the ratio cannot depend on the input. Concatenation fails whenever the downstream layer is shallow, small, or under-trained, because in that case it will not discover the weighting that the narrow column needs; concatenation relies on something later doing the mixing.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the dilution, in three steps. Join a width-1 signal to a width-200 signal and ask how much of the result is structural.

    Add the widths: columns in the fused table.
    Concatenation adds widths because it places the blocks end to end; the rows are untouched.
    The structural column's share is .
    One number out of every 201 in a row. Dividing entries, not widths, is what makes this a share rather than a count.
    As a percentage that is , while the rule signal takes .
    Note it is a hair under half a percent, not exactly half: the denominator is 201, so the naive guess of "1 in 200" overshoots slightly. That difference is small here but the principle — the share is , not — is worth holding on to.

    Example 2 — a fixed weighted sum, and why training cannot rebalance it. Take a structural scalar , one rule entry , and fixed weights .

    fused entry = α·s + β·r = 0.5 × 0.8 + 0.5 × 4.0 = 0.4 + 2.0 = 2.4

    The structural part contributes and the rule part to the single number — the structural signal is of the mixed value. Now suppose training drives the downstream layer to multiply this number by .

    downstream output = 3 × 2.4 = 7.2 = (3 × 0.4) + (3 × 2.0) = 1.2 + 6.0

    The two contributions became and . Their ratio is , which is — exactly the we started with, because both were multiplied by the same . In terms of the original constants, the coefficients became and : still equal, still . Training can change the overall scale of the mixed number; it can never change the balance inside it.

    The merge is also irreversible. Choose a second pair with the same weights: and gives — the very same number as . Two different worlds, one observable value. A downstream layer handed cannot say which vertex it is looking at.

    Contrast with concatenation, where the two blocks stay in separate columns. There a downstream layer is free to place a coefficient of on the structural column and on a rule column — a ratio of , the opposite emphasis — and may choose a different ratio for every rule column. That freedom is exactly what the weighted sum gives up.
    This example uses one rule entry and one pair of fixed weights. It shows the frozen ratio and the irreversibility of the sum; it does not show how a per-object weighting would be produced, which is the subject of card 3.

    Where this is going: neither of the first two mechanisms lets the emphasis depend on the object. The third row of the menu does — a gate computes the emphasis per object. The next card works the broadcast case numerically, and states honestly what a gate can and cannot do.
    Extension · Ways to combine two signals 3/4

    Gating, and the broadcast trick

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA Hadamard product, written , combines two signals of the same shape by multiplying them entry by entry: . Broadcasting extends entrywise operations to different shapes by copying the smaller signal along the dimension where it is missing: a column of shape broadcast against a matrix of shape is first stretched to by repeating its single value across each row, and only then multiplied entry by entry. When the narrow signal is itself the output of a squashing function — a function that maps any input into a bounded interval, the sigmoid , which maps any real number into , being the standard example — it is called a gate, and the broadcast product is called gating.Gating multiplies two signals number by number. When one signal holds a single number per row, that number is copied across the row first, so it scales the entire row by the same factor.

    The vocabulary this card uses. A row of a signal is one object, and the paper's objects are the vertices of a graph — one row per vertex. The narrow signal stores one number per vertex. The wide signal's row at a vertex is that vertex's rule row: its rule features, one number per feature, where each feature is one learned dimension describing the logical rules attached to that vertex. The examples below use rule rows of three entries () so the arithmetic stays visible; the paper's rule rows are wide.

    Why anyone wants a gate. Cards 1 and 2 left one thing undone: neither concatenation nor a fixed weighted sum lets the emphasis between the two signals depend on the object. A gate does. Because the gate value can be computed from one of the signals itself, a vertex can carry a gate near 1 (its rule features come through nearly intact) while another vertex carries a gate near 0 (its rule features are pushed towards zero). The weighting becomes per-object, and it is learned, rather than fixed at design time.

    What broadcasting actually does. The narrow signal has one number per row. Broadcasting copies it across all columns, so it multiplies every entry of that row by the same factor. The result is a row that has been scaled — not a row whose columns have been readjusted relative to one another. It is worth being explicit about what this means: the gate cannot, for a single object, treat two features differently. One row, one factor.

    Honest limit: attenuation only. If every gate value lies strictly inside , then for each entry , with strict decrease whenever and . A gate in therefore can only shrink a magnitude; it can never enlarge one, and it cannot flip a sign. It can change the relative size of entries across rows — a row whose gate is near 1 keeps its entries while a row whose gate is near 0 loses them — but within one row every entry is scaled by the same positive factor, so their ordering is untouched.

    Why the gated result is concatenated with the ungated original. Because a gate can drive an entry towards zero, using the gated product alone would risk discarding the wide signal at any object whose gate is small. Concatenating the product with the untouched original keeps both views: the model sees a modulated copy and a full-strength copy, and can read whichever the task needs. The gate contributes an extra, context-weighted reading — it does not replace the signal it modulates.

    The contrast with attention. The table below sets gating beside cross-attention — a different mechanism for combining two signals, which this paper does not use, included here only because its multipliers also lie in and are easy to confuse with a gate. In cross-attention each entry of one signal is reweighted by how well it matches entries of the other: the mechanism computes a match score for every pair of entries, turns the scores into weights, and forms a weighted average of the values. Two consequences appear in the table. The weights are normalised — across the set they are matched to, they are positive and sum to 1, so the output is an average and cannot exceed its largest input. And because they sum to 1, one entry's larger weight must be paid for by another's smaller weight: attention reallocates a fixed total, while a gate scales each entry independently and the total falls.

    PropertyGating (broadcast Hadamard)Cross-attention
    Number of multipliersone per row (under broadcast) or one per entry (same-shape product)one per pair of matched entries
    Range of each multiplierwhatever the producing function gives — if a sigmoid produces it, and they are normalised: across the matched set they sum to 1
    Linked across the setno — gate values are independent of one anotheryes — the sum-to-one rule means one weight's rise is another's fall
    Effect on the total magnitudethe total shrinks whenever a gate is below 1the total is reallocated; a normalised average lies between the smallest and largest inputs
    Depends on the other signal's contentonly in that the gate may be computed from it; the multiplication itself is per-entryyes — the weights are the match scores between the two signals
    The wording to distrust is "the gate amplifies the important part." A value in cannot amplify anything. What a gate can do is change the ratio between objects: a row with a gate near 1 keeps its entries, a row with a gate near 0 loses them, so the first row stands out relative to the second. That is a relative claim among objects, and it is true; the absolute claim that an entry grew is false.

    When gating fails. Two failure modes follow from the definition. A gate cannot strengthen a signal that everything upstream has already suppressed. And a gate held near 0 blocks not only the forward value but also the backward gradient — the error signal that training sends back through the network to adjust the weights — because that signal is multiplied by the same small gate on its way back. A gate that shut a channel therefore also stops learning to reopen it. Gates earn their keep when they are allowed to sit away from the extremes.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a single gate value scaling a whole row. Let the broadcast gate at one vertex be and the rule row there be .

    Broadcast first: the single value is copied across the three columns, giving .
    This is the step that distinguishes gating from an entrywise product of equal shapes. Only after this copy do the shapes match and the multiplication become legal.
    Multiply entry by entry: , , , so the gated row is .
    The same factor touches every entry, so the whole row is scaled by 0.5 — not adjusted column by column.
    Check the magnitudes: , , . Every one halved, and no sign changed.
    A gate below 1 shrinks; it never enlarges and never flips a sign, because the multiplier is positive and less than 1. This is the attenuation fact seen on actual numbers.

    Example 2 — two vertices with different gates. Take the same rule row, , at a second vertex whose gate is .

    g = 0.9: (0.9 × 4, 0.9 × (−2), 0.9 × 8) = (3.6, −1.8, 7.2)
    g = 0.5: (0.5 × 4, 0.5 × (−2), 0.5 × 8) = (2.0, −1.0, 4.0)

    Look at the first column across the two vertices: against . Their ratio is , which is exactly the ratio of the gates . The gate has made one vertex's rule entry stand out against the other's by a factor of 1.8 — yet both gated entries are smaller than the original . That is the whole character of a gate: relative differences between objects change, absolute magnitudes only fall.

    Total magnitude tells the same story. The un-gated row has . At gate 0.5 the gated row's total is ; at gate 0.9 it is . Both fell, both stayed below 14 — a gate in removes energy, it does not move it.

    concat with the original: (2, −1, 4, 4, −2, 8)
    The last line is the fusion step. The gated copy and the untouched original are concatenated, so both views of the rule row survive. The first block is the modulated reading, the second the full-strength one — the model is not forced to choose between them.
    This example uses one row of width 3 and two gate values. It shows the broadcast, the attenuation, the relative-vs-absolute distinction, and the concatenation step; it does not show how the narrow signal's gate values are produced, it does not work through the attention comparison in the table, and it does not show a gate saturating near 0 and suppressing a gradient during training.

    Extension · Ways to combine two signals 4/4

    What the taught paper does — and the skip check

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONIn the taught paper, the fused representation over the vertices is . The structural embedding has shape — one number per vertex — and it is the output of a sigmoid, a squashing function that maps any input into the open interval , so each entry of lies strictly inside : it may be or , but never and never . The rule embedding has shape — one number per rule feature per vertex, where a rule feature is one learned dimension describing the logical rules attached to a vertex. The symbol is the elementwise product, applied after is broadcast across each row of ; the bar denotes concatenation along the column axis. The fused width is .Take the single structural number at a vertex — always between 0 and 1, since it comes out of a sigmoid — multiply it into every rule feature of that vertex, then place the result and the original rule features side by side. The structural value ends up shaping the rule features rather than sitting next to them as an extra column.

    This section built a menu of four ways to combine two signals of different widths, priced the first two, worked the third, and set attention beside it. The final step is to name the paper's own choice precisely, and to price exactly what it does and does not buy.

    The paper's fusion, stated exactly

    The paper's fusion broadcasts across , multiplies entry by entry, and then concatenates the product with the original rule embedding. Written out:

    The vertical bar denotes concatenation: the gated block is placed immediately before the untouched block . The gate is broadcast first — its single value per row is stretched across all columns — so the entrywise product is legal.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the structural embedding, shape — one number per vertex, produced by a squashing function whose output lies in
    the rule embedding, shape — many numbers per vertex, one per rule feature
    the elementwise (Hadamard) product, with broadcast across each row
    concatenation: the two blocks are joined along the column axis
    the width of the fused result — two blocks of width , so the structural embedding adds no column of its own

    The fused width is therefore : twice the rule width. The structural embedding does not appear as an extra column in the result — it enters only through the gate. This is worth noticing, because it is the opposite of plain concatenation, where the width-1 signal would have survived as its own extra column.

    What this buys, stated precisely

    A downstream linear layer with weight blocks and computes . Read the two terms: the layer receives two different linear readings of the same rule embedding — one taken from the gated copy, one from the untouched original — and it is free to weight the two readings differently. Within the gated reading, each vertex's row has been scaled by its own structural value.

    So the structural scalar acts as per-vertex context, not as a separate information channel. It does not carry new facts alongside the rule features; it changes how strongly each vertex's rule features come through one of the two readings. A vertex with a structural value near 1 contributes its rules nearly intact to the gated reading; a vertex near 0 contributes them heavily suppressed — while the unscaled copy keeps the full-strength version available in every case.

    The honest limit. Because the gate has one value per row, no two columns of the rule embedding can be gated differently for the same vertex. One vertex, one factor, applied to all of its rule entries. A full-width gate of shape could suppress some rule features and keep others for the same vertex; this fusion cannot. Whatever the structural signal needs to express, it must express it as a single per-vertex weight.

    The section, in five claims

    • Fusion combines two signals with the same rows into one; the four standard mechanisms are concatenation, weighted sum, elementwise gating, and cross-attention (which reweights one signal by how well it matches the other).
    • Plain concatenation preserves both signals but dilutes the narrow one: a width-1 column joined to width supplies a share of the entries — when .
    • A fixed weighted sum merges the two signals irreversibly and freezes their ratio; downstream scaling multiplies both contributions by the same constant, so it cannot change the balance.
    • Gating multiplies a narrow signal into a wide one by broadcasting: one gate value per row scales the whole row. A gate in can only attenuate, and concatenating the gated product with the ungated original prevents the shrinkage from destroying information.
    • The taught paper broadcasts a width-1 structural embedding into the rule embedding and concatenates the product with the original, giving a fused width of ; the structural value is a per-vertex context, and since it is one number per row it cannot gate columns differently.
    The questions below are the check. The bar is not a score — it is that you did not have to think hard about any of them. If the sentence "the fused width is twice the rule width" still reads as a surprise, or if you cannot say why the structural embedding adds no column of its own, stay: every later claim about the paper's fusion is read against exactly this shape.
    EXAMPLE

    One worked pass over the paper's fusion, at a small width. Take a rule row at one vertex ( here, instead of the real 200), and let the broadcast structural gate at that vertex be .

    Gate: broadcast across the three columns and multiply, giving .
    Each entry is scaled by the same per-vertex factor. Every magnitude fell — , , — since the gate is below 1.
    Concatenate the product with the original: the fused row is .
    The first three numbers are the gated reading, the last three the untouched rule row. Both readings are now present, which is what stops the gate from erasing the rule signal.
    Read off the width: the rule row had columns, the fused row has .
    The structural embedding contributed the gate but no column, so the width doubled rather than grew by one. At the real rule width of , the same rule gives a fused width of .

    Example 2 — a second vertex, with a small gate. Take the same rule row , but now at a vertex whose structural value is .

    X_s ⊙ R = (0.05 × 4, 0.05 × (−2), 0.05 × 8) = (0.2, −0.1, 0.4)
    fused row = (0.2, −0.1, 0.4, 4, −2, 8)

    Put the two vertices side by side. Corresponding rule features share the same original value, so the first columns of the two gated blocks are (from gate ) and (from gate ). Their ratio is , exactly the ratio of the structural values . A small structural value does not merely shrink the gated block — it shrinks it relative to other vertices, which is the per-vertex-context effect described above. And note once more that both gated blocks are smaller than the original : the gate removes magnitude, it does not move it.

    Compare the two blocks with the downstream layer's eye. At the first vertex the gated block is a mildly shrunk view of the rule row and the untouched block is the full view; at the second vertex the gated block is , heavily suppressed. In both rows a linear layer weighting the two blocks differently obtains a modulated reading and a plain one — the two readings the WHAT section described, now on concrete numbers.
    What these passes do not show: neither demonstrates how is produced, and neither exhibits the limitation on columns — at one could easily imagine gating the three columns separately. The point that a single per-row value cannot treat columns differently is a statement about width, not something a three-column row makes visible.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDIn the paper's fusion, how wide is the fused representation, and where does the structural signal enter?

    APPLYA rule embedding has 64 columns. After the paper's gate-and-concatenate fusion, how many columns does the fused representation have? columns

    You are ready for the paper's fusion. The structural embedding is a single number per vertex; the paper broadcasts it into the rule embedding, concatenates the product with the original, and hands the doubled-width result downstream. Every later question about the fusion can be checked against three facts: the fused width is , the gate carries one value per vertex and so cannot gate columns differently, and the untouched copy means nothing is destroyed when a gate is small.
    Extension · Evaluation protocols 1/5

    What an evaluation protocol is

    The same model, on the same graph, scores differently depending on three rules that are rarely stated together: which vertices may be learned from, which vertices are graded, and whether the graded vertices were already visible while the model trained. This section makes those rules explicit, contrasts the transductive and inductive regimes, explains what a protocol that mixes them can and cannot claim, and works through why a memorising model can look perfect under one discipline and worthless under another.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONAn evaluation protocol is the complete rulebook for one experiment. It fixes three things. First, the label regime: which vertices carry labels the model may learn from during training. Second, the scoring set: which vertices contribute to the number that gets reported. Third, the visibility rule: whether the scored vertices were already present in the graph — with their features (the attribute vector attached to each vertex) and their edges (their connections to other vertices) — while the model was training, even if their labels were withheld. Two experiments that agree on dataset, model and metric but disagree on any one of the three are not measuring the same quantity, so their numbers cannot be compared.A protocol is the rulebook for an experiment: what the model may look at while it learns, what gets graded at the end, and whether the graded items were already in front of the model while it learned.

    Why the split is not the whole story. You have already met the train/validation/test split. It assigns each example to one of three buckets, and it says the test bucket must guide nothing. That is one coordinate of a protocol, not the protocol. The split does not by itself say whether the vertices you will be scored on were physically in the graph during training. Two papers can run the identical split and still measure different things, because one removed the scoring vertices from the graph first and the other left them in place.

    How the three coordinates operate. Name them, because every results table silently commits to a value for each.

    1. Label regime — during training, whose labels the loss (the quantity training minimises) may use. In the example below, three vertices carry usable labels and one is held back for tuning.
    2. Scoring set — which vertices the reported metric averages over. Usually the test bucket. A validation score is also a number, but it is a tuning number, not a result.
    3. Visibility — whether the scored vertices existed in the graph, features and edges included, while the model trained. This is the coordinate readers forget, and the one that separates the transductive regime from the inductive regime.
    The most common misreading. "Test set" is often read as "data the model has never seen". Under a transductive protocol that reading is false: the scored vertices were in the graph the whole time, with features and edges fully visible. Only their labels were withheld. A reader who equates test with unseen will over-read every transductive number in the paper. Card 2 makes the distinction exact.

    When a protocol breaks. Two failure modes matter. (i) An unstated protocol cannot be compared: if a table reports two numbers obtained under different visibility rules without saying so, the gap between them may be entirely a change of rule rather than a change of method. (ii) A protocol can leak: if any label of a scored vertex reached the model during training, or reached the person choosing the settings, the reported number is inflated and no longer estimates performance on unseen data. Card 5 works through the arithmetic of one such leak.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a six-vertex graph, one protocol, filled in three steps. A graph has vertices v1 through v6 and edges v1–v2, v1–v3, v2–v3, v3–v4, v4–v5, v5–v6. It therefore has 6 vertices and 6 edges. The split is: v1, v2, v3 for training; v4 for validation; v5 and v6 for scoring.

    Label regime. v1, v2, v3 carry labels the loss may use — 3 vertices. v4's label is used to choose settings (tuning) and is never reported as a result. v5 and v6 contribute no training label at all. So 3 of the 6 vertices are learnable.
    The label regime counts labels the model may learn from, not labels that exist. A held-out validation label exists and is read by the person tuning, but it must not enter the training loss.
    Scoring set. v5 and v6 — 2 vertices. The reported number averages over exactly these two.
    Fixing the scoring set first is what keeps a number comparable with another paper's. If v4 were also scored, the reported figure would mix a tuning quantity with a result and mean neither.
    Visibility. Under a transductive protocol, v5 and v6 are present during training: their features and their edges (v4–v5 and v5–v6) are available to the model, and their labels are not. Under an inductive protocol, v5 and v6 are absent: they do not exist in the graph until scoring time.
    This is the coordinate that moves between protocols. The label regime and the scoring set above are identical in both; only this one changes, and it changes what the number means.

    Example 2 — the same graph under three protocols. In the table, labelled means the loss may use this vertex's label; present, unlabelled means the vertex and its edges are in the graph but its label is withheld; absent means the vertex is not in the graph at all during training.

    Protocolv1v2v3v4v5v6Scored
    Transductivelabelledlabelledlabelledlabelled (tuning)present, unlabelledpresent, unlabelledv5, v6
    Inductivelabelledlabelledlabelledlabelled (tuning)absentabsentv5, v6, introduced at scoring time
    Mixedlabelledlabelledlabelledlabelled (tuning)present, unlabelledabsentv5, v6

    Compare the rows. The label regime and the scoring set are the same in all three; only the visibility column moves. That is the entire content of the difference between protocols — one column, which decides what the reported number is a number of.

    Count the transductive row: 6 of 6 vertices are in the graph during training, and 4 of the 6 labels are usable, 3 for training plus 1 for tuning. Count the inductive row: 4 of 6 vertices are present at training time and 2 are absent; all 6 labels still exist eventually, but 2 of them appear only at scoring time. Same graph, same model, two different quantities.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich of these is a coordinate that a protocol fixes but a train/validation/test split, on its own, does not?

    APPLYA graph has 40 vertices: 24 are labelled for training, 6 are held for validation, and 10 are the scoring set. Under an inductive protocol, how many vertices are present in the graph while the model trains? vertices

    TRANSFERTwo papers report 85% on the same graph with the same model. Paper A withheld the scoring labels but left the scoring vertices in the graph; Paper B deleted them before training. What is the correct reading?

    Where this is going: the third coordinate — visibility — deserves its own card on each of its two values. Card 2 takes the transductive value; card 3 takes the inductive one.
    Extension · Evaluation protocols 2/5

    Transductive learning: the scored vertices are already there

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA transductive protocol is one in which the vertices that will be scored are present in the graph, with their features and their edges, for the whole of training. Their labels are withheld: the loss never sees them. The model therefore builds representations of the very vertices it will later be asked to label, and the task is to fill in blanks whose surrounding structure it has already been shown.In a transductive setup the scored vertices are already in the graph while the model trains. Their connections and features are fully visible; only their answers are hidden. The model labels the vertices it has been standing next to.

    Why this is legitimate, and when. Transductive evaluation is not a trick. When there is one fixed graph and the question is "label the vertices of this graph", the graph genuinely is known in advance: a citation network is published in full before anyone asks which papers belong to which field. Withholding only the labels is honest, because the model cannot copy an answer it never receives. This is the standard setting for citation and co-purchase benchmarks, where all the entities are collected first and classified afterwards.

    What it does not let you claim. The model that comes out of a transductive run is a labelling of this graph, not a function you can carry elsewhere. It was trained on this particular set of vertices, and nothing in the protocol required it to handle a vertex it has not seen. Two claims are therefore unsupported.

    • Generalisation to another graph. A model trained on graph G, with G's scoring vertices visible throughout, has learned about G. Its score on G says nothing about its score on a graph H.
    • Handling a graph that grows. If a new vertex arrives after training, the transductive model has no place to put it. Producing a label for it requires retraining, and retraining replaces the model that produced the earlier number.

    How message passing uses the visibility. A graph network labels a vertex by aggregating information from its neighbours. When the scored vertex is present, its neighbours include other scored vertices, and the aggregation performed during training already flows through them. Remove the scored vertices and the same aggregation sees a smaller neighbourhood. The protocol therefore changes the computation the model performs, not only the reporting.

    The misconception to kill. A reader who believes "test means unseen" will treat a transductive number as evidence of generalisation. It is not. The accurate sentence is: this model labels the vertices of this graph, which it saw unlabelled during training. Whether it works on a new graph is a different experiment — card 3's.

    When it fails. Three concrete cases. When the deployed graph is not the training graph — new users, new papers, a rebuilt graph. When the graph is a sample of a larger population you care about, and you quote the sample's score as the population's. And when a transductive number is placed beside an inductive number in one table without a note: the two are not on the same scale, and the gap may be entirely the protocol.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the six-vertex graph under the transductive rule. Recall the graph from card 1: vertices v1 to v6, edges v1–v2, v1–v3, v2–v3, v3–v4, v4–v5, v5–v6; training labels on v1, v2, v3; validation label on v4; scoring on v5 and v6.

    v5 has one edge, to v4, and v6 has one edge, to v5. Because both scored vertices are present, the model reads v5's features and uses the path v6 → v5 → v4 during training.
    The visibility rule is what permits this. The edge v5–v6 exists in the graph the model trains on, so two rounds of aggregation carry information from v6 to v4 and back.
    The loss may use the labels of v1, v2 and v3 only. The labels of v5 and v6 are withheld during training, so no update to the model's weights ever depends on them.
    This is the entire safeguard. The structure is visible and the answers are not, so the model cannot copy a label it never receives.
    At scoring time the model is asked for v5 and v6. It has already built representations for both, so it answers without any retraining.
    A transductive protocol does not re-run training between learning and scoring, because the vertices were there from the start. That is also why its number cannot be read as a claim about a vertex that was not there.

    Example 2 — the same graph after it grows. Suppose a seventh vertex, v7, is published a week later with an edge to v4. The trained transductive model was built for the six vertices it saw. v7 was never inside any aggregation, so it has no representation, and no neighbour of v7 has a message that was ever updated for it.

    To score v7 you add it to the graph and retrain. The new run sees 7 vertices instead of 6, and every vertex's representation may change.
    Retraining is not a formality here. Aggregation couples the vertices, so adding v7 changes what v4 aggregates, which changes v5's representation, and so on through the graph.
    The earlier reported number — over v5 and v6 in the six-vertex graph — now belongs to a model that no longer exists. It is not the score of the seven-vertex model, and it is not a bound on it either.
    This is the practical cost of the transductive rule. The number was a statement about one fixed graph; the graph changed, and the statement expired with it.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDIn a transductive protocol, what exactly is withheld from the model during training?

    APPLYA transductive experiment has 40 labelled training vertices and a scoring set of 10 vertices. How many vertices does the graph contain while the model trains? vertices

    TRANSFERA team reports 92% on a citation graph using a transductive model, then deploys it to classify newly published papers. What went wrong conceptually?

    Where this is going: the transductive number stops at the graph it was measured on. The claim a deployment needs — that unseen vertices are handled — is the inductive protocol, and it costs something.
    Extension · Evaluation protocols 3/5

    Inductive learning: the scored vertices do not exist yet

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONAn inductive protocol is one in which the vertices that will be scored are absent from the graph for the whole of training: they are not merely unlabelled, they are not there, and neither are their edges. At scoring time the model is presented with objects it has never encountered — often an entire graph it has never seen — and must produce labels for them. The quantity being learned is therefore a function from (features, neighbourhood) to label that does not depend on a fixed, known vertex set.In an inductive setup the scored objects do not exist during training. The model has to label things it has never met, using what it learned about the general relation between a vertex's features, its neighbours, and its label.

    Why deployment forces it. A model shipped to serve new records is asked about records that did not exist when it was trained. A recommendation model meets new users; a paper classifier meets new papers. There is no version of this in which the scored items were present during training, because they did not exist yet. Inductive evaluation is the closest honest approximation available on a fixed dataset: hold vertices out, remove them from the graph entirely, train, then introduce them for the first time at scoring.

    The honest trade-off. Inductive evaluation is harder, and the scores are typically lower, because the model cannot lean on representations of the specific vertices it is graded on. That is not a defect to be corrected; it is the price of a stronger claim. An inductive number supports the sentence "this model handles objects it has not seen", which a transductive number does not. Lower is not worse, and higher is not better, when the two numbers come from different protocols — they are readings from different instruments.

    How a model is built to pass it. Message passing labels a vertex by aggregating the features of its neighbours and combining them with its own features. Nothing in that computation refers to a vertex's identity, so it can be applied to a vertex introduced later, provided the model's parameters (the weights it learns) are shared across vertices rather than stored per vertex. A model that keeps a separate embedding (a learned vector) for each vertex cannot be used this way at all: a new vertex has no embedding to look up. This is why inductive capability is a property of the architecture, not a switch applied at the end.

    The misconception to kill. Inductive does not mean "the scoring graph is unrelated to training". It means the scored vertices were absent. The model still assumes the new vertices come from the same distribution as the training ones — the same kinds of features, the same kinds of neighbourhoods. If they do not, the inductive number is measured on a different problem, and the protocol's guarantee lapses.

    When it fails. (i) If the new objects are drawn from a different distribution — papers from an unrelated field, users from another country — the number describes a task the model did not train for, and performance will be worse than the number suggests. (ii) If the graph is fixed and you only ever care about it, inductive evaluation spends accuracy to answer a question nobody asked. (iii) If the split removes the scored vertices' features but leaves their connections dangling in the training graph, aggregation still traverses those connections, and the headline overstates what the model knows about genuinely new objects.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — two graphs, no overlap. A corpus supplies two citation graphs, G_A and G_B, 200 vertices each. The inductive experiment trains on G_A and scores on G_B.

    Training reads G_A's 200 vertices and their edges. G_B is not read at all — not its features, not its edges, not its labels. So the number of G_B vertices present during training is 0 of 200.
    This is the inductive rule taken literally. A transductive experiment on the same corpus would have shown G_B's structure during training; here it is withheld entirely.
    Scoring presents G_B for the first time. The model must label its 200 vertices using parameters learned on G_A.
    Nothing is retrained between training and scoring. The model is fixed and the scoring graph is new, which is the situation a deployed model is in.
    The two graphs together contain 400 distinct vertices, and the number of vertices shared between the training graph and the scoring graph is 0.
    Zero overlap is what makes the claim general. Had the graphs shared vertices, part of the scoring would have been on objects the model trained on, and part of the score would be a transductive measurement in disguise.

    Example 2 — labelling a vertex that has no stored embedding. Take one new vertex w, with features of its own and two neighbours, u1 and u2, that the model has already placed. A one-layer aggregator forms w's representation from its own features together with those of u1 and u2.

    Read w's own features and the neighbour representations of u1 and u2. There is no embedding table to consult for w.
    The model holds parameters, not per-vertex answers. That is what allows a vertex introduced after training to be processed at all.
    Combine them with the same weights used during training — the weights are shared across all vertices, so they apply to w unchanged.
    Sharing is what makes the function transferable. Had the model learned a distinct weight for each training vertex, none of those weights would apply to w.
    Output w's label from the combined representation. No retraining happened and no training vertex was revisited.
    This is the operation an inductive score measures over many new vertices. It is also why the same architecture can be scored transductively: leave the scoring vertices in the graph and the identical forward pass runs over a denser neighbourhood.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhat is the defining rule of an inductive protocol?

    APPLYAn inductive experiment trains on a graph with 320 vertices and scores on a second graph with 180 vertices. How many of the scored vertices were present in the graph during training? vertices

    TRANSFERA model scores 88% transductive and 74% inductive on the same data. A colleague says the model "lost 14 points" when it was made to generalise. What is wrong with that phrasing?

    Where this is going: a paper that wants a single headline can average the two regimes. Card 4 examines what that average does and does not mean — and why the same average can describe two very different models.
    Extension · Evaluation protocols 4/5

    Mixing the two regimes: what a "production" protocol averages

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA mixed protocol is one whose scoring set contains vertices from both regimes at once: some that were present, unlabelled, in the graph during training, and some that were absent during it. The reported number is a combination of the two regimes' scores — typically a weighted average, weighted by how many scored vertices came from each. A paper may call such a setting a production setting, meaning it approximates a deployed graph in which part of the data was already collected and part keeps arriving.A mixed protocol grades both kinds of vertex at once — the ones the model trained alongside, and the ones it never saw — and reports a single combined number.

    What the mixture is trying to model. A deployed graph is not purely one regime. When a system is switched on it already holds a backlog of vertices it trained alongside, and from that moment new vertices keep arriving. A benchmark that scores only the backlog understates the difficulty of the steady state; one that scores only the arrivals discards the part of the graph the system will actually be asked about most. Averaging the two is an attempt to report something closer to that steady state.

    The blended score is a weighted average of the two regime scores. The weights are the fractions of the scoring set that came from each regime, so they sum to 1.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the score on the transductive portion of the scoring set — vertices that were present but unlabelled during training
    the score on the inductive portion — vertices that were absent during training
    the fraction of scored vertices that belong to the transductive portion
    the fraction that belong to the inductive portion; it is

    When a mixture informs, and when it misleads. It informs when three conditions hold at once: both portions are scored on the same task with the same metric, the same model produced both numbers, and the weights are reported. Under those conditions the blend is a legitimate summary of one model on one benchmark, and it can be compared against another blend computed the same way. It misleads when the weights are omitted, when the two portions are drawn from different distributions so that the blend mixes two problems, or when the blend is quoted as though it were a single-regime score.

    One consequence to carry away. A blended headline hides which regime produced it. Two models can post the same blended score from very different profiles — one excellent on the backlog and poor on arrivals, the other ordinary on both. The recipe is legible only if the two component scores are printed beside the blend.

    When it fails. (i) An unpublished weight makes the blend unreproducible and uncomparable, because many different pairs of component scores give the same weighted sum. (ii) If one portion's vertices come from a different distribution than the other's, the blend is an average of two different problems, and no single model achieved it on one task. (iii) If the blend is placed against a single-regime number from another paper, the comparison is between different quantities, and any gap may be the protocol rather than the method.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — two regimes, equal weights. The transductive portion of a scoring set scores 80 and the inductive portion scores 60. Both are percentages, on the same task with the same metric, from the same model.

    equal weights: (80 + 60) / 2 = 70

    The blend is 70. Notice what that number is: no vertex received it. Each portion was summarised by its own average, and 70 is the average of those two averages. A reader who sees only 70 cannot tell whether it came from a model that is strong on the backlog, strong on arrivals, or middling on both.

    Example 2 — the same two component scores, a different mix. Suppose the scoring set is not half-and-half. Weight each component by the fraction of scored vertices from its regime.

    25% transductive, 75% inductive: 0.25 × 80 + 0.75 × 60 = 20 + 45 = 65
    75% transductive, 25% inductive: 0.75 × 80 + 0.25 × 60 = 60 + 15 = 75

    Identical component scores, blends of 65 and 75 — a 10-point spread produced entirely by the composition of the scoring set. This is why the weights belong to the result rather than to a footnote: two blended numbers cannot be compared unless both were weighted the same way.

    Example 3 — the same blend, three different models. Equal weights throughout; only the component scores change.

    (80 + 60) / 2 = 70 (85 + 55) / 2 = 70 (70 + 70) / 2 = 70

    Three different models, three different profiles, one headline. The first is strong on the backlog and weak on arrivals; the second is stronger on the backlog and weaker still on arrivals; the third is flat. Averaging has discarded the information that separates them — which is exactly the information a reader needs when deciding whether to deploy one.

    None of this makes a mixed protocol wrong. It answers a real and well-posed question — how does this model do on a benchmark shaped like deployment — provided the component scores and the weights are on the page. The mistake is not averaging; it is averaging silently.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDA mixed protocol reports one number over a scoring set containing both vertices that were present during training and vertices that were absent. What must accompany that number for it to be reproducible?

    APPLYA scoring set is 30% transductive vertices and 70% inductive vertices. The model scores 80 on the transductive portion and 60 on the inductive portion. What is the blended score, as a weighted average? score

    TRANSFERTwo papers report a blended 70 on a mixed benchmark. Paper A's components are 80 and 60; Paper B's are 70 and 70, both with equal weights. What can a reader conclude from the headline alone?

    Where this is going: the arithmetic of regimes explains why numbers move. Card 5 asks why one model can score 100 under one discipline and chance under another, and closes the section with a skip check.
    Extension · Evaluation protocols 5/5

    Why the same model scores differently — and a skip check for this section

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONLabel leakage is any route by which information about the label of a vertex in the scoring set reaches the model, or reaches the person choosing settings, before the final number is computed. The route may be direct — the label enters the loss (the quantity training minimises) — or indirect: a setting is chosen because it improved the score on the scoring set. In both cases the reported number is optimistically biased, because part of the scoring set has already been used to fit.Label leakage is any path by which the answers you are graded on reach you, or reach the person choosing your settings, before the grading happens.

    The question the section leaves open, answered by the mechanism. Transductive and inductive are rules, not properties of a model. Change the rule and the same trained network, with the same weights, produces a different number — because the set of vertices being scored has changed. The extreme case is a model that memorises, and its behaviour exposes the mechanism cleanly: a model that has absorbed its training vertices looks perfect when those vertices are scored, and worthless when genuinely new ones arrive.

    The indirect route is the one people miss. Reaching into the scoring results to pick the best configuration, then reporting that configuration's score, is leakage exactly as surely as feeding the labels into the loss. The defence is procedural rather than statistical: build the split and freeze it before any tuning begins, and make every later choice on validation data or a training-fold average, never on the scoring set.
    • State a protocol as three coordinates: the label regime, the scoring set, and whether the scored vertices were visible during training.
    • Identify a transductive protocol and say what it supports — a labelling of this graph — and what it does not — generalisation to an unseen graph.
    • Identify an inductive protocol, and explain why deployment requires it and why it costs accuracy.
    • Read a mixed or production score as a weighted average, and ask for its component scores and weights before believing the headline.
    • Recognise label leakage in both its forms: labels entering training, and results steering the choice of settings.
    • Explain why a memorising model can score at the top of one protocol and at chance under another.
    The questions below are the check. The bar is not a passing score — it is that you answered each one without hesitating. If the arithmetic of the memoriser in the example gave you pause, stay: it is the cleanest statement of why the protocol, not the model, decides the number.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a model that only memorises. Build a model with no learning at all: a lookup table. During training it stores, for each vertex, the label it was shown. Asked later about a vertex in its table, it returns the stored label. Asked about a vertex that is not in the table, it falls back to a fixed default — here class A. The training set has six vertices, two in each of three classes: v1 = A, v2 = A, v3 = B, v4 = B, v5 = C, v6 = C.

    Score the model on the six vertices it trained on, with the labels hidden at scoring time. It consults its table and returns each stored label, so it is correct on all six: 6/6 = 100%.
    The labels were withheld at scoring and the model produced them anyway, because it had absorbed them during training. A protocol that scores training vertices with their labels hidden measures memory, not prediction.
    Now score it on six genuinely new vertices, again two in each class. None of them is in the table, so the model answers A every time. It is right on the two A-vertices: 2/6 = 33.3%.
    Same model, same weights, different protocol. The drop is not a change in the model; it is a change in what is being asked.
    The gap between the two numbers is 100 − 33.3 = 66.7 percentage points, and 33.3% is what a three-class guesser that always answers one class achieves, since 1/3 = 33.3%.
    That last equality is the diagnosis. A model scoring at chance on new vertices has learned nothing that transfers, however high its score was on the vertices it was trained on.

    Example 2 — the same model, a hundred times larger. Training set of 300 vertices, 100 in each of three classes; scoring set of 300 new vertices, again 100 per class.

    on the 300 training vertices: 300 / 300 = 100%
    on the 300 new vertices, default A: 100 / 300 = 33.3%
    gap: 100 − 33.3 = 66.7 percentage points

    In this construction the gap is identical to the small case, which is the point: the failure is structural, not a small-sample accident. Making the dataset larger does not repair a protocol that scores vertices the model already memorised. What changes the number is changing the protocol, not changing the size.

    The practical rule that follows: construct the split first, then let nothing about the scoring set influence training or tuning. If any part of the scoring set — its labels, or your knowledge of them — reaches either the model or the choice of settings, the reported number belongs to the family above, and no amount of scale changes that.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhy can the same trained model score 100% under one protocol and about 33% under another?

    APPLYA model is correct on all 45 of the vertices it trained on, and on 15 of 45 new vertices drawn equally from three classes, where it always answers the same class. What is its score on the new vertices, in percent? percent

    TRANSFERA team tunes settings by repeatedly checking the test set, keeps the setting with the best test score, and reports that score. What is the status of the reported number?

    You are ready to read the protocols block of a results table. Every number now carries three questions — what the model may learn from, what is scored, and whether the scored vertices were present during training — and a blended number carries a fourth: in what proportion.
    Extension · Classification metrics 1/3

    Accuracy, and the baseline it must beat

    A paper reports one number for a node-classification task, and that number is only as meaningful as the metric behind it. This section builds accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from zero, works them on small confusion matrices by hand, and gives the rule for which one to report — and when accuracy misleads.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONAccuracy is the fraction of examples a classifier labels correctly: the number of correct predictions divided by the total number of predictions. If examples are classified and of them receive their true label, accuracy is , a number between and (usually reported as a percentage). Every example contributes to the count exactly once, so every example is worth the same.Accuracy is the share of examples the model got right — correct answers divided by all answers, and nothing more. It counts every example once, no matter which class that example belongs to.

    Why a bare accuracy is not a result. A figure like "91% correct" sounds like a verdict, but it is only interpretable next to the score of a classifier that has learned nothing. If a model that ignores its input entirely already reaches 91% on this test set, then 91% is the floor, not an achievement. The first job in reading any accuracy is to compute the baseline it has to beat.

    Baseline 1 — always predict the majority class. Count the labels in the test set and predict the most frequent one for every example. Its accuracy is exactly the frequency of that class, written . A model that reaches this score has demonstrated that it can count labels, and nothing else.

    Baseline 2 — predict at random, matching the class frequencies. Draw a label for each example with probability equal to how often that class occurs. These frequencies are the class priors . The chance of being right on any single example is — square each prior, then add — and averaging over examples gives the same value. If instead you draw all classes with equal probability, the expected accuracy is .

    A reported accuracy is uninterpretable until both baselines are on the table. Thirty percent looks weak on a ten-class benchmark where uniform guessing already scores 10%, and looks strong on a benchmark where a majority-class predictor scores 29%. The number is the same; the baselines are what differ.

    When accuracy fails. Accuracy fails in one specific situation: when the classes are unbalanced and the rare classes are the ones that matter. Because every example contributes equally to the count, a model that never predicts a rare class loses only the few rare examples, and the penalty is small. If 95% of a test set belongs to one class, predicting that class for everything scores 95% while being useless. Accuracy remains the right summary when the classes are roughly balanced and every kind of error costs the same.

    The misconception to kill now. The common belief is that a higher accuracy means a better model. It does not. Two models can report the same accuracy while one has learned nothing and the other has learned almost everything — card 1's second example builds exactly that pair. The accuracy number alone cannot tell them apart; only the baseline and a per-class view can.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a skewed three-class set. A test set of examples contains of class A, of class B and of class C. The priors are , , .

    Always predict A. This classifier is right on the examples of class A and wrong on the others, so its accuracy is .
    This is the majority-class baseline. It equals , the frequency of the most common class, and needs no computation beyond counting.
    Predict at random with the priors. On each example the chance of being right is .
    Squaring each prior and summing asks: what is the chance a random draw lands on the true class? Because class A is so common, even a random predictor scores well here.
    Guessing uniformly among the three classes gives .
    Uniform guessing ignores the priors, so on a skewed set it scores far below prior-guessing. The two random baselines are different numbers; quoting the wrong one changes the story.
    On this set a do-nothing classifier scores . A model reporting would be strictly worse than counting labels — yet reported on its own looks like a good score. The baseline is what turns the number into information.

    Example 2 — ten classes, 1000 examples. This is the shape the paper's benchmarks can take. Class A has examples; the other nine classes have each. Then , the number of classes is , and the priors are with for each of the nine others.

    Majority-class baseline. Predicting A always is right on of the examples, so accuracy is .
    The majority baseline equals . Any model must clear this before its accuracy means anything.
    Prior-guessing baseline. . Uniform guessing would give .
    The nine minority terms are each tiny, but they add up; the dominant term is the squared majority share. Guessing with priors beats uniform guessing precisely because the priors are skewed.
    Now take a model that is genuinely informative. Suppose it classifies all nine minority classes perfectly — correct — but gets only of the majority examples right. Its total correct is , so its accuracy is : identical to the do-nothing baseline.
    The arithmetic is the point. A model that has learned nine of the ten classes lands on exactly the same accuracy as one that learned none of them.
    The two models are not the same. The trivial model has recall on every minority class. The informative model has recall on all nine minorities and on the majority — it misses most of the common class. Averaging recall over the ten classes gives the balanced accuracy: for the trivial model against for the informative one.
    Averaging per-class recall weighs every class the same, so the nine rare classes count as much as the common one. Accuracy refuses to do that, which is exactly why it cannot separate these two models.
    Same accuracy, for both; balanced accuracy versus . A single accuracy figure cannot distinguish a model that learned nothing from one that learned nine of the ten classes. Closing that gap is what card 2's per-class metrics are for.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhy does an accuracy figure need a baseline before it can be interpreted?

    APPLYA five-class dataset has test examples: of class 1 and each of the other four. What accuracy does a classifier that always predicts class 1 achieve? accuracy

    TRANSFERA model reports accuracy on a test set in which of examples belong to one class. What is the most defensible reading?

    Where this is going: accuracy is one number, and its two baselines are enough to reveal the trap but not to fix it. Card 2 replaces the single number with a per-class view — precision, recall and F1 — which is what separates the two models of Example 2.
    Extension · Classification metrics 2/3

    Confusion, precision, recall and F1

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONGiven a classifier and a labelled test set, the confusion matrix is a table whose rows are the true classes and whose columns are the predicted classes; the entry in row , column counts the examples whose true class is and whose predicted class is . For one chosen class , write (true positives) for its examples predicted as , (false positives) for examples of other classes predicted as , and (false negatives) for examples of class predicted as something else. Then the precision of class is , its recall is , and its F1 is the harmonic mean of the two, .Precision asks: of the examples the model labelled class k, how many really were class k? Recall asks: of the examples that really were class k, how many did the model find? F1 is a single number that is large only when both are large.

    Why one accuracy number is not enough. Accuracy collapses the matrix to a single count: it says how many predictions were right, not where the wrong ones went. A model can reach a given accuracy by making its errors on one class, on another, or spread evenly, and those are different failures. The confusion matrix keeps the detail; precision, recall and F1 are three ways of summarising one class's row and column of it.

    QuantityFormulaThe question it answers
    Accuracycorrect / totalOf all examples, how many did the model get right?
    Precision (class k)When the model says class k, how often is it right?
    Recall (class k)When the truth is class k, how often does the model catch it?
    F1 (class k)Is the model good at both of the above at once?
    Precision divides by the number of times the model claimed class — everything the model put in that column. It drops whenever the model over-predicts a class.
    SymbolWhat it means
    examples that truly are class and were predicted as class — the hits
    examples of some other class predicted as class — the false alarms
    the share of the model's class- predictions that turned out correct
    Recall divides by the number of examples that truly are class — the whole row. It drops whenever the model misses instances of a class.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the same hits as in precision
    examples that truly are class but were predicted as something else — the misses
    the share of the true class- examples the model found
    F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, not their ordinary average. The harmonic mean is small whenever either term is small: precision with recall gives F1 , whereas the ordinary average would give . That is the whole reason F1 is used — it refuses to reward a model that is good at only one of the two.
    SymbolWhat it means
    precision of class , as above
    recall of class , as above
    one number that is large only when both precision and recall are large

    Macro-averaging versus micro-averaging. A confusion matrix with classes gives precisions, recalls and F1 values. To report one number you average, and there are two standard ways. Macro-averaging takes the plain, unweighted mean of the per-class values: every class counts equally, so a class with examples weighs as much as one with . Micro-averaging pools the counts first — add up all , all and all across the classes, then compute one precision and one recall from those totals. In single-label classification, where each example belongs to exactly one class, the pooled is the number of correct predictions and both pooled denominators are the number of examples, so micro-precision, micro-recall and micro-F1 all equal the accuracy. Macro and micro therefore agree only when the classes are balanced; on skewed data macro-F1 sits below accuracy.

    Two misconceptions. First, F1 is not a better accuracy. It ignores true negatives altogether — examples the model correctly leaves out of a class contribute to nothing — and its harmonic mean weights precision and recall equally, which is a choice rather than a law. F1 is the right instrument for a single class, often a rare one; it is the wrong instrument for an overall score on balanced data. Second, "the F1 of a multi-class model" is not a defined quantity: without saying macro or micro, the number could be either, and the two disagree by as much as the class imbalance.

    When these break. Precision is undefined for a class the model never predicts, because its denominator is zero; recall is undefined for a class that does not appear in the test set. Implementations return zero or a warning, and either way the value is a convention rather than a measurement.
