F1 is meaningful only for a single class or as an average with a stated rule, and it says nothing about the classes a model correctly ignores, so it cannot stand in for accuracy when false positives on the negative class matter.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — two classes, one matrix. A test set has cats and dogs. Of the cats the model calls cats and dogs; of the dogs it calls cats and dogs. Rows are truth, columns are prediction:

    predicted Catpredicted Dogtrue total
    true Cat35540
    true Dog154560
    pred total5050100
    Accuracy is the sum of the diagonal divided by the total: , so accuracy .
    The diagonal holds the correct predictions. Off-diagonal entries are errors, and accuracy ignores which off-diagonal they sit on.
    For Cat, , (dogs called cats) and (cats called dogs). Precision ; recall .
    Precision divides by the column total — everything predicted Cat. Recall divides by the row total — everything truly Cat. Swapping row and column is the most common error with this matrix.
    Cat F1 . For Dog, precision , recall and F1 . Macro-F1 .
    Macro-F1 is the plain mean of the two per-class values. With classes of a similar size it stays close to accuracy ( here) — the second example shows what happens when they are not.

    Example 2 — three classes of unequal size. Same layout, three classes A, B and C, with rows true and columns predicted:

    pred Apred Bpred Ctrue total
    true A508260
    true B1015530
    true C23510
    pred total622612100
    Accuracy is the diagonal over the total: , so accuracy .
    The three classes have , and examples — unequal, which is what makes the next steps differ from each other.
    Per-class precision and recall. A: precision , recall . B: precision , recall . C: precision , recall .
    Every precision divides by that class's column total (, , ); every recall divides by its row total (, , ). The rare class C has the lowest precision because a handful of its column's entries come from other classes.
    Per-class F1: A ; B ; C .
    The harmonic mean punishes the weaker of the two numbers, which is why class C's F1 () sits well below its recall ().
    Macro-F1 is their unweighted mean: . Micro-F1 pools the counts first: pooled , pooled and pooled each total over examples, so micro-precision micro-recall , and micro-F1 — the accuracy again.
    The two averaging rules disagree here: macro-F1 is , micro-F1 is , a gap of about 9.7 points. Macro counts the small class C as heavily as the large class A, so it falls; micro lets the large class dominate, so it reproduces accuracy.
    One model, one test set, and four numbers: accuracy , macro-F1 , micro-F1 , and a rare-class F1 of . Which of these is the score is exactly the question card 3 settles.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDFor a single class, what does recall measure?

    APPLYA three-class confusion matrix has rows (true) and columns (predicted): true X gives [40, 5, 5], true Y gives [4, 20, 6], true Z gives [1, 4, 15]. What is the recall of class Z? recall

    UNDERSTANDA model never predicts class D, although class D is present in the test set. What are class D's precision and recall?

    TRANSFERThe same model, on the same test set, reports micro-F1 and macro-F1 . What does the gap tell you?

    Where this is going: precision, recall and the two F1s give a per-class and a per-example view of the same confusion matrix. Card 3 turns these into a decision rule for which number to report — and closes the section with its skip check.
    Extension · Classification metrics 3/3

    Which metric to report, and the skip check

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONMetric choice is the decision of which single number to put in a results table, and it is fixed by two facts about the problem rather than by preference: whether the classes are balanced, and whether every kind of error costs the same. Accuracy is the share of examples labelled correctly, and it is the right report when the classes are balanced and all errors are equally costly. Macro-F1 is the unweighted mean of the per-class F1 scores; because every class counts equally it is the right report when the classes are unbalanced or the rare classes matter. Micro-F1 pools every class's counts before computing F1 and, for single-label classification, equals accuracy; it is the right report when the per-example count matters rather than the per-class balance.Pick the metric by the shape of the data and by the cost of mistakes. Accuracy when the classes are balanced and every error is equally bad; macro-F1 when the classes are unbalanced or the rare ones matter; micro-F1 when you care about counting examples rather than classes.
    SituationReportBecause
    Classes roughly balanced, all errors equally costlyAccuracyIt counts every example once, which is what you want when every example is worth the same
    Classes unbalanced, or the rare classes matterMacro-F1It weights every class equally, so a rare class's failures cannot be hidden by a common class's successes
    The per-example count is what mattersMicro-F1It pools all examples before computing, so each example counts once; for single-label data this is accuracy

    The honest consequence of choosing badly. Because accuracy lets a majority-class predictor score high, a paper can look strong by reporting accuracy on a skewed benchmark while beating nothing at all. The reported number is real; the claim it appears to support is not. The safeguard is mechanical: for every reported accuracy, ask what the majority-class and prior-guessing baselines score on the same split, and how many examples each class has.

    What the taught paper reports, and how to read it. The taught paper reports accuracy on its node-classification tasks. Accuracy is a fair summary only where the class distribution is close to uniform, so the reading depends on the dataset. On a benchmark with many classes, or with one dominant class, the same accuracy can be matched by predicting the majority label, and a high figure alone is then not evidence of skill. When you read the paper's tables, put each accuracy next to two things: the number of classes and the label distribution, and the baselines in the same table. If a dataset is known to be skewed, treat an accuracy column as a weak signal and look for a per-class figure; if the table reports accuracy only, no reader can tell from the table whether the rare classes were learned.

    • Define accuracy and compute the two baselines it must beat: the majority class () and prior-guessing ().
    • Build a confusion matrix and read a class's precision from its column and its recall from its row.
    • Compute F1 as the harmonic mean and say why the harmonic mean refuses to reward a model good at only one of the two.
    • Compute macro-F1 (unweighted mean of the per-class F1) and micro-F1 (pool the counts first), and explain why micro-F1 equals accuracy for single-label data.
    • State the decision rule: accuracy when balanced and errors equal, macro-F1 when unbalanced or rare classes matter, micro-F1 when the per-example count matters.
    • Say what choosing the wrong metric costs: a majority-class predictor can post a high accuracy, so an accuracy column on a skewed benchmark can make a weak model look strong.
    The questions below are the check for the whole section. The bar is not a passing score — it is that you answered each one without stopping to reconstruct anything. If the decision rule or the macro-versus-micro gap gave you pause, cards 2 and 3 are short and worth the re-read.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a 95% score that has learned nothing. A binary test set has negatives and positives. A model predicts negative for every example.

    Accuracy: the model is right on all negatives and wrong on the positives, so accuracy .
    This is the majority-class baseline exactly: the negative class is the majority at frequency .
    Positive class: , , and the model makes no positive predictions, so precision is undefined. Recall and F1 .
    F1 is the harmonic mean, and a zero recall forces it to zero no matter what precision would have been. A class the model never touches scores nothing here.
    Negative class: , (the positives called negative), . Precision , recall , and F1 .
    The model's only errors are on the rare class, so the common class looks almost perfect — which is precisely the distortion accuracy inherits.
    Macro-F1 is the mean of the two per-class values: .
    Macro-F1 gives the five positives the same weight as the ninety-five negatives, so the total failure on the rare class halves the score.
    Accuracy , macro-F1 . The accuracy figure is nearly perfect; the per-class figure shows not a single positive was found. Choosing the metric is choosing which of those two facts the reader sees.

    Example 2 — a model that is informative but still weak on the rare class. Same negatives and positives, but now the model calls examples positive: of the true positives and false alarms. So , , and .

    Accuracy: correct predictions are , so accuracy .
    Lower than Example 1's 0.95, so by accuracy alone this model looks worse — the comparison is misleading, and the next steps show why.
    Positive class: precision , recall , F1 .
    This model actually finds most positives (recall 0.80), unlike Example 1. But it raises many false alarms, so precision is low — the two directions disagree, and F1 records both.
    Negative class: precision , recall , F1 .
    Precision divides by the negative column's total and recall by its row total — the same row-and-column rule as card 2, applied to the other class.
    Macro-F1 .
    Example 1 scored 0.487 and this one 0.667, even though Example 1 had the higher accuracy (0.95 versus 0.88). Measured per class, the model that finds positives is clearly ahead.
    Accuracy ranks the two models one way ( before ); macro-F1 ranks them the other way ( before ). Neither ranking is wrong — they answer different questions, and the decision rule is what tells you which question this problem is asking.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhen should macro-F1 be reported in place of accuracy?

    APPLYA five-class dataset has test examples: of class 1 and each of the other four. What accuracy does a classifier that always predicts class 1 achieve? accuracy

    TRANSFERA paper reports only accuracy on a twelve-class node-classification benchmark. The figure is high. What is the strongest conclusion you can draw?

    APPLYWhich of these make a reported accuracy hard to interpret? Select all that apply. (select all that apply)

    You are ready to read the results table. Every accuracy in the taught paper now resolves into two questions — how many classes there are, and what a majority-class predictor scores on the same split — and every per-class figure into whether it was averaged macro or micro. The four numbers of card 2 and the rule of card 3 are the whole of it.
    Extension · Ablation studies 1/3

    What an ablation is for

    An ablation is the experiment a paper runs to support the sentence "this component is what makes the model better": remove the component, hold everything else fixed, and measure the difference. This section covers the logic of that contrast, the controls that make it valid, and how to read an ablation table — including the two failure shapes that make such a table look informative while proving nothing. The paper's experimental chapter runs ablations over a module, a tree count and a layer count, so a later chapter judges those tables by exactly these rules.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONAn ablation is a controlled experiment in which exactly one component of a system is removed — or replaced by a version that contributes nothing — while every other ingredient (the data, the split between training and test, the training budget, the tuning procedure) is held fixed. The measured change in the reported number is then attributed to that component.Take one piece out of the model, leave everything else exactly as it was, and see how much the result changes. If the result drops, that piece was doing work.

    Why a claim needs it. A paper states that a module improves the model. That is a statement about a cause. Causes are never visible in a single number: a high score shows that the whole system works and nothing more. A cause becomes visible only in a contrast — a run with the module and a run without it, identical in every other respect. An ablation is that contrast, written down and measured.

    The two ways to take the piece away. The component can be deleted, or it can be left in place with its contribution forced to nothing. The two are not interchangeable, and a paper that does not say which it used has left part of the result underspecified.

    MethodWhat you doWhen it is the right choice
    RemovalDelete the component and its connections. Where the component fed something downstream, add a bypass so the shapes still match.When the component can be deleted without changing what the rest of the network sees.
    Neutral replacementKeep the component's place in the network, but force its output to carry no information: a learned gate set to 1, a gate closed to a constant, a set of attention weights made uniform.When deleting the component would also disturb the architecture — its shapes, its parameter count, its layer structure — so a deletion would change more than one thing.

    When an ablation stops meaning anything. It fails as soon as more than one thing changes between the two runs. If the ablated version also gets a different learning rate, a different number of passes over the training data, or a different data split, then the score difference is a difference between two complete systems, and no part of it can be assigned to the piece you removed. It fails again when each arm is run only once, because a single run cannot separate a real effect from the run-to-run wobble; the next card makes that precise.

    The common misreading. Readers treat "without the module, the score fell" as proof that the module is clever. It is not proof of that. It shows only that removing this module hurts in this setup. A module that quietly adds parameters, a module that adds random noise during training, or a module that changes some other quantity as a side effect will all produce the same drop. The ablation localises where the effect lives, not why it lives there.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — the smallest useful ablation

    A model is assembled from three parts. A paper claims that part Z helps.

    Run the full model on a fixed test set. Reported accuracy: 82.5.
    This is the reference run. Its score is not interesting by itself; it is the number every later run is compared against.
    Remove Z, add a bypass so the downstream layer still receives correctly shaped input, change nothing else, and rerun on the same test set: 80.9.
    Only one thing changed. Adding the bypass is part of the removal, not a second change — it restores the interface the rest of the network already expected.
    Take the contrast: 82.5 - 80.9 = 1.6 points. That 1.6 is what this experiment attributes to Z.
    The subtraction is the ablation. Without it there are two numbers and no claim.
    What this example did not show. Nothing here says whether 1.6 is larger than the run-to-run wobble. Each arm was run once. With a single run per arm, an effect of 1.6 could be the luck of the seed. Putting a size on the noise is the job of the next card's example.

    Example 2 — removal versus neutral replacement

    The component in this second model is a learned gate that multiplies a feature vector, so the layer computes times the feature. During training, settles somewhere between 0 and 1.

    • Removal. Delete the multiplication. Now the layer produces a different output, the parameter count drops by the gate's weights, and the layer that consumed the gated features has to be rewired.
    • Neutral replacement. Keep the multiplication and force . The layer now outputs the unchanged feature vector — the gate contributes nothing — while the architecture, the shapes and the parameter count are untouched.
    • The neutral version changes exactly one thing: the gate's value. The removal version changes the gate and the architecture together.
    When a table entry reads "w/o gate", the honest question is which of the two was done. The neutral run answers "what is the gate worth, with everything else left as it is". The removal run answers a slightly muddier question — it is one step closer to changed the model than to switched off a mechanism.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich of these turns two experimental runs into an ablation?

    APPLYA full model reports 79.3. The same model with component W removed reports 78.1. By how many points does this ablation attribute the change to W? points

    TRANSFERA team reports "w/o attention: 80.2", but in that run they also halved the learning rate to keep training stable. How should the number be read?

    Where this is going: an ablation is only as good as the quantities it holds fixed. The next card states those controls, and supplies the missing piece this card deliberately left out — a size for the run-to-run noise.
    Extension · Ablation studies 2/3

    What makes an ablation valid

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA valid ablation is one whose two arms differ in a single factor and in no others, and whose reported effect is judged against the experiment's own run-to-run variation rather than against zero. "Everything else unchanged" is not a slogan; it is a list of quantities that must be identical across the arms: the data, the split, the training budget, the tuning procedure, the number of runs, and the evaluation protocol.A trustworthy ablation keeps every knob except one fixed, then asks whether the change is bigger than the wobble you get by rerunning the very same experiment.

    Why the controls carry the whole weight. The ablation's claim is "this difference is due to that component". That claim is only as strong as its weakest shared control. A single mismatched setting makes the difference unassignable — and the mismatch is usually invisible in the paper's headline table, so a reader has to know what to look for.

    • Data and splits. Same dataset version, same training/test partition, same preprocessing, same seed for the split.
    • Budget. Same number of passes over the training data, same stopping rule, same maximum training time.
    • Tuning. The same search procedure over the same grid for both arms. If the component brings hyperparameters of its own, those are the values allowed to differ — but each arm must get the same tuning budget, or one arm is quietly favoured.
    • Runs. The same number of independent runs per arm, each with its own seed. Five to ten is the usual range, and the reason is not decoration: you cannot judge an effect without an estimate of the wobble.
    • Evaluation. Same metric, same averaging over runs, same test set.

    Compare the effect against the wobble, not against zero. Train the same configuration twice with two seeds and the score moves. That movement is the experiment's own noise floor, and it is the yardstick. An effect smaller than the noise floor is not evidence of anything, even though it is not zero: a rise of 0.3 points in a setup whose runs scatter by a point is a rise you would have seen from the seed alone.

    Switching a component off is not the same as retraining without it. In one design you take the fully trained model, disable the component, and re-evaluate; the other weights stay exactly as they were. In the other design you build the model without the component and train it from scratch. The first isolates the component's contribution given the rest of the trained model. The second lets the rest of the model adapt to the component's absence, which is the more honest question about the design, and also the design in which a single mismatched setting can contaminate the answer. Papers usually mean the second. Which one was done has to be stated, because the two can disagree.

    Two readings people get wrong. First: "the ablation lowered the score, so the module matters." A lowering inside the noise band is fully consistent with the module doing nothing. Second: "we retrained from scratch without it, so the ablation is clean." Retraining does not make it clean — holding the other settings fixed does. If the retrained arm also used a different budget or a different search, the cleanliness is gone.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a 0.4-point gain against a 0.9-point spread

    A paper claims that component C helps. Both arms are run five times, with five seeds, and everything except C is identical.

    Run (seed)Without CWith C
    171.873.0
    272.672.2
    373.074.6
    473.473.4
    574.273.8
    Mean without C: (71.8 + 72.6 + 73.0 + 73.4 + 74.2) / 5 = 365.0 / 5 = 73.0.
    The mean is the arm's headline number, and it is the only quantity the two arms get compared on.
    Mean with C: (73.0 + 72.2 + 74.6 + 73.4 + 73.8) / 5 = 367.0 / 5 = 73.4.
    Same five-run recipe, one component different.
    Effect: 73.4 - 73.0 = 0.4 points.
    This is the number the paper would print. On its own it looks like a gain.
    Spread: within each arm, a run sits about 0.9 points from that arm's own mean — the standard deviation is 0.89 on both sides.
    This is the wobble, measured from the arm's own five runs rather than asserted from anywhere else.
    The effect (0.4) is smaller than half the wobble (0.9). Two arms whose true performance is identical would produce a difference of 0.4 fairly often. At this point nothing has been demonstrated.

    Example 2 — turning the spread into an interval

    Two means are being compared, so the noise that matters is the standard error of their difference, not the spread of one run.

    The standard error of a difference between two independent means, when both arms have runs with the same spread . It is the square root of the sum of the two arms' variances; the square root is why the two arms' errors do not add directly.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the run-to-run spread (standard deviation) inside one arm
    the number of runs (seeds) in one arm
    the typical size of the difference you would see between two arms that are actually identical
    Standard error of one arm's mean: 0.89 / √5 = 0.89 / 2.24 = 0.40 points.
    Dividing the run-to-run spread by the square root of the number of runs gives the typical distance between an arm's mean and its true value.
    Standard error of the difference: 0.40 × √2 = 0.40 × 1.41 = 0.57 points.
    Each independent arm carries its own error, and the errors combine in quadrature — hence the factor √2.
    Effect as a multiple of the noise: 0.4 / 0.57 ≈ 0.7 standard errors.
    A common convention: an effect below about 2 standard errors is not treated as established.
    Rough 95% interval: effect ± 2 standard errors = 0.4 ± 1.13, that is from -0.73 to 1.53 points.
    The interval is the effect's uncertainty. Its job is to list the true effects the data are compatible with.
    The interval runs from a loss of 0.73 to a gain of 1.53, so it contains zero. The experiment cannot tell "C helps by 0.4" apart from "C does nothing". A formal two-sample interval with eight degrees of freedom gives about -0.90 to 1.70 — the same conclusion. Pairing the arms by seed does not rescue it either: the per-run differences are 1.2, -0.4, 1.6, 0.0, -0.4, whose mean is 0.4 and whose standard error is 0.42, so the paired effect is about 0.95 standard errors — still inside the noise.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDAn effect is said to be "inside the noise" when…

    APPLYTwo arms of five runs each show a difference of 0.6 points, and the standard error of that difference is 0.4 points. What is the lower end of the rough 95% interval, effect minus 2 standard errors? points

    TRANSFERA reviewer re-runs your ablation with new seeds, and the sign of a small delta flips from +0.3 to -0.2. What does this tell you?

    TRANSFERFour teams remove the same module. Which removal is a valid ablation?

    Where this is going: with the controls and the noise in place, the remaining skill is reading a whole ablation table at once — its rows, its columns, and the pattern of differences. The next card does that and closes the section.
    Extension · Ablation studies 3/3

    Reading an ablation table, and the skip check

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONAn ablation table is a grid whose rows are variants of one model — the full model, plus one variant per removed or neutralised component — and whose columns are the datasets or settings the model is evaluated on. Each cell holds a score. The quantity a reader studies is the delta: the difference between a variant's cell and the full model's cell in the same column. The object of study is the pattern of deltas down a column and across a row, not any single cell.Rows are models, columns are datasets, cells are scores. Subtract the full-model row from each other row and read the pattern of differences, not one number.

    Why the pattern and not the number. A single delta is one sample of a noisy quantity, so it carries little on its own. The same comparison repeated across several datasets and several variants produces a shape: does the gap to the full model keep the same sign and roughly the same size everywhere, or does it appear in one column and vanish — or reverse — in the others? A consistent sign across independent datasets is far harder to produce by noise than any single cell. That is the signal an ablation table is built to expose.

    1. Find the full-model row. It is the reference; every delta is measured against the cell above or below it in the same column.
    2. In each column, take variant score minus full-model score, and keep the sign.
    3. Read each variant across the columns: is the gap consistent in sign, and roughly stable in size?
    4. Read the variants against each other: which one produces the largest gaps? That is the component the data says carries the most weight.
    5. Compare the gaps with the run-to-run spread the paper reports. If it reports none, treat gaps of a fraction of a point with suspicion.

    Failure pattern 1 — every delta is inside the noise

    If every variant's gap is small and its sign wanders from column to column, the table is consistent with all the variants being equal to the full model. The components may each do nothing. This does not prove they do nothing — the experiment may be too small to detect an effect — but the table supplies no evidence that they help.

    Failure pattern 2 — one knob varies while others move too

    Suppose the rows are labelled by one hyperparameter, but each row also differs in how many layers it has and how long it trains. Then a gap between two rows is a gap between two complete systems, and no part of it can be assigned to the labelled knob. The table looks like an ablation because of its shape, but the single-difference condition is violated, and the pattern is uninterpretable however consistent it looks.

    A sweep is not an ablation

    A sweep (a hyperparameter scan) evaluates one model while varying one of its hyperparameters — the number of trees, the number of layers, a learning rate — usually to find the value that scores best. A sweep and an ablation share the phrase "vary one thing" but not its meaning. In an ablation the varied thing is a component whose causal role is the question, and the answer is a difference in scores. In a sweep the varied thing is a setting whose best value you are selecting, and the answer is a chosen value. Running a sweep and then reporting only the winning setting is model selection, not an ablation — and it hides the curve, which is the most informative part. A sweep turns into an ablation only when you fix the selection (say, at the value chosen for the full model) and then ask what happens when one component is taken away.

    • Explain what an ablation is for: it turns "this component improves the model" into a controlled contrast in which one thing changes.
    • Name the controls a valid ablation needs — same data, split, budget, tuning and number of runs — and say why the effect is judged against run-to-run variation rather than against zero.
    • Read an ablation table by its pattern of deltas, and recognise the two failure shapes: all deltas inside the noise, and one labelled knob with several others also moving.
    • Say what a sweep is, and why printing one chosen setting from it is not an ablation.
    The questions below are the check. The bar is not "mostly right" — it is that none of them made you think hard. If any one of them felt like a guess, the earlier cards hold the pieces.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — reading a small table

    Three datasets, four variants. The first row is the reference.

    VariantSet ASet BSet C
    Full model82.478.674.1
    Full minus M81.177.973.6
    Full minus N82.278.473.9
    Full minus M and N80.977.673.4
    Row "Full minus M": deltas are 81.1 - 82.4 = -1.3, 77.9 - 78.6 = -0.7, 73.6 - 74.1 = -0.5.
    Same column each time, so the dataset is held constant and only the variant changes.
    Row "Full minus N": deltas are 82.2 - 82.4 = -0.2, 78.4 - 78.6 = -0.2, 73.9 - 74.1 = -0.2.
    Uniform to a tenth of a point, and small. Without a reported noise band this is indistinguishable from zero.
    Row "Full minus M and N": deltas are 80.9 - 82.4 = -1.5, 77.6 - 78.6 = -1.0, 73.4 - 74.1 = -0.7.
    Close to the two single removals added together (-1.5 vs -1.5, -1.0 vs -0.9, -0.7 vs -0.7). Near-additivity suggests the two components are doing largely separate jobs here.
    Read the shape. Removing M costs 1.3, 0.7 and 0.5 points: largest on Set A, still present on all three, same sign everywhere — hard to explain by noise. Removing N costs 0.2 points on every set, uniform and tiny. The pattern says M matters and N is unproven, and it says this from all three columns at once, which is exactly what no single cell could do.

    Example 2 — the two failure shapes

    • All inside the noise. A variant scores 80.1, 80.3, 79.9, 80.2 against a full model of 80.0 on four settings. The deltas are +0.1, +0.3, -0.1, +0.2: the sign flips, and no gap exceeds a fraction of a point. Nothing here supports the component doing work.
    • Too many knobs. Rows are labelled "1, 2, 4, 8 layers", but the 8-layer row also trains four times as long and uses a larger learning rate. The score rises from 78.0 to 81.0 across the rows. The labelled knob moved, and two others moved with it — the +3.0 cannot be assigned to depth.

    Example 3 — what a sweep produces, and what it does not

    A team sweeps the number of trees and records: 1 tree gives 76.0, 2 gives 78.2, 4 gives 79.9, 8 gives 80.6, 16 gives 80.8, 32 gives 80.8. The curve rises and then flattens; the team reports 16 trees.

    This answers "which value scores best". It does not answer "does the tree count matter as a design choice" — that would require comparing the full model at its chosen count against a variant with that design decision neutralised, everything else equal. The flattened tail (80.8 at both 16 and 32) is the kind of shape a sweep is for; it is not a delta against a reference, so it is not an ablation.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDIn an ablation table, what is the delta of a variant in a given column?

    APPLYA variant reports 77.4 on Set B, while the full model reports 78.1 on Set B. What is the variant's delta? points

    TRANSFERAn ablation table shows every variant's deltas ranging from -0.1 to +0.2, with signs flipping across columns, and the paper reports no spread. What is the honest reading?

    TRANSFERA paper sweeps the number of trees from 1 to 32, finds that 16 scores best, and prints only "16 trees: 80.8". Why is this not an ablation of the tree count?

    Where this is going: the paper's experimental chapter presents ablations over a module, a tree count and a layer count, and a later chapter judges them. You now have the three criteria that judgement uses — one factor changed, effect measured against the spread, and the pattern of deltas read across datasets rather than one cell at a time. If you skipped this section, those three sentences are the summary to keep.
    Extension · Average ranks and significance 1/3

    Why average ranks, not average scores

    The paper's headline comparison is a single average rank per method, computed over ten datasets. This section builds that number from zero: why raw scores from different datasets cannot be averaged, how a rank is computed and how tied scores are handled, and what the resulting number does and does not prove about a difference between two methods.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONSuppose methods are compared on datasets, where a dataset is one benchmark on which every method is run once and produces one score, with higher scores meaning better. Within a single dataset the rank of a method is its position after sorting the methods from the best score to the worst: the best score receives rank , the next rank , and the worst of the methods receives rank . A method's average rank over the datasets is , where is its rank on dataset . Lower means the method finished ahead more often.On each dataset, write down which method came first, second, third. Average those finishing positions across the datasets. First place counts as 1, so the smallest average is the best method.

    Two scores that are equal on a dataset produce a tie. The convention for handling ties is the subject of card 2, and none of the examples in this card contains one — everything below assumes the methods' scores on each dataset are distinct.

    Why the obvious summary does not work. The natural way to summarise a comparison is the mean score: add up a method's scores and divide by the number of datasets. That fails for a reason that has nothing to do with randomness. The datasets do not share a unit. One reports accuracy on a 0–100 scale; the next reports F1 or AUC on a 0–1 scale; another reports a correlation. Adding those numbers produces a quantity measured in nothing at all, and the datasets that happen to use the wider numeric scale dominate the sum purely because their digits are larger.

    What ranking removes. Replace each score by its position among the methods on that dataset. Every dataset, whatever its unit and range, now speaks the same language: 1 for the best, 2 for the next, and so on. The magnitudes are gone, and with them the unit problem — and every dataset now contributes to the average with the same weight, whether it was scored on a 0–1 scale or a 0–100 one. What is left is a single number per method that can legitimately be placed beside the others.

    Two consequences worth stating up front. First, lower is better: rank 1 is the best position, so the method with the smaller average rank finished ahead more often. Second, the average rank and the average score can disagree, and when they do it is not a paradox — they answer different questions. The average score asks who accumulated the largest numbers; the average rank asks who was ahead more often. A common misbelief is that the two summaries must agree, so that a disagreement signals an arithmetic slip; they measure different things and are free to differ, and the disagreement is itself information about the method. The examples below construct a case in which one method has the higher average score and the worse average rank, and show why.

    When this is the wrong tool. Ranking is not free. It throws away the margin: a method that wins by 10 points and one that wins by 0.1 point both receive rank 1, so if the size of the gap is the scientific question, the rank cannot answer it. It also assumes the datasets measure comparable tasks — ranking methods across benchmarks that test unrelated things is no more meaningful than averaging across them, only less visibly so. And with only two methods a rank can be 1 or 2 and nothing else, which carries almost no information. Card 3 gathers the limits in full; for now, note that the average rank is a summary with a price.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — a two-dataset warm-up. Two methods, A and B, are compared on two datasets. D1 reports AUC, a quality score that runs from 0 to 1. D2 reports accuracy, a percentage that runs from 0 to 100.

    DatasetMetric (scale)Method AMethod B
    D1AUC (0–1)0.800.72
    D2accuracy (0–100)6188

    The raw scores. Average them and A gets while B gets .

    A: (0.80 + 61) ÷ 2 = 30.90
    B: (0.72 + 88) ÷ 2 = 44.36

    Neither number has a unit or a meaning: 30.90 is the sum of an AUC value and an accuracy percentage, halved. Nothing in the study was measured on that scale. The comparison is being decided by the fact that accuracy happens to sit on a wider numeric range, so the accuracy dataset is worth about a hundred times as much to the sum as the AUC dataset.

    The ranks. On D1, A is ahead (), so A takes rank 1 and B rank 2. On D2, B is ahead (), so B takes rank 1 and A rank 2.

    • A's ranks are 1 and 2 — sum 3, so A's average rank is .
    • B's ranks are 2 and 1 — sum 3, so B's average rank is also 1.5.
    The two datasets disagree, and the ranks say so plainly: one win each, an average rank of 1.5 for both. The raw scores also disagreed — but for the wrong reason, since their split was produced by the choice of numeric scale rather than by which method actually finished ahead.

    Example 2 — a higher mean score with a worse average rank. Now four datasets, deliberately scored on different scales, and two methods A and B. F1 and AUC are quality scores running from 0 to 1; accuracy is a percentage running from 0 to 100. Higher is better on every dataset.

    DatasetMetric (scale)Method AMethod B
    D1accuracy (0–100)9590
    D2F1 (0–1)0.7400.750
    D3AUC (0–1)0.6400.650
    D4accuracy (0–100)4142

    Step 1 — the average scores.

    A: 95 + 0.740 + 0.640 + 41 = 137.380 → 137.380 ÷ 4 = 34.345
    B: 90 + 0.750 + 0.650 + 42 = 133.400 → 133.400 ÷ 4 = 33.350

    A's average score is the higher, by . Look at where that lead comes from. On the two 0–100 datasets A is ahead by and behind by , a net in the sum, which is in the average. On the two 0–1 datasets A is behind by and behind by — a net in the sum, which is in the average. So the two 0–1 datasets, where B is genuinely the better method, move the average score by half a hundredth; the wide-scaled pair moves it by a full point. The wide-scaled datasets decide the number on their own.

    Step 2 — the ranks. Sort the two methods on each dataset and record the positions.

    Datasetrank of Arank of B
    D1 (accuracy)12
    D2 (F1)21
    D3 (AUC)21
    D4 (accuracy)21
    D1: A is ahead (), so A gets rank 1 and B rank 2.
    Rank 1 is the best position, not the largest number. The sorting uses the scores; the number written down is the position.
    D2: B is ahead (), so B gets 1 and A gets 2.
    The gap is only 0.010, but a rank records who finished ahead, not by how much — so a 0.010 win counts exactly as much here as the 5-point win on D1.
    D3: B is ahead () and D4: B is ahead (), so B gets rank 1 on both.
    D3 and D4 are again narrow, and B again takes the top position. B is ahead on three of the four datasets, each time by a small margin.
    Sum each method's ranks and divide by the number of datasets: and .
    Dividing by turns a sum of positions into an average position. A smaller average rank is better, so B is ahead.
    The reversal, and the check that goes with it. A has the higher average score, 34.345 against 33.350, and the worse average rank, 1.75 against 1.25. Both statements are correct, and they answer different questions: the score says who accumulated the largest numbers, the rank says who finished ahead more often. The ranks also satisfy a bookkeeping check. Each dataset holds two methods, so its two ranks sum to ; over four datasets the ranks of A and B must therefore total , and indeed . Card 2 turns that check into a general rule you can apply to any table.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhy is the mean of the raw scores across datasets not a usable summary of a comparison?

    APPLYThree datasets compare methods P and Q. D1 gives P = 88, Q = 91; D2 gives P = 0.70, Q = 0.65; D3 gives P = 55, Q = 54. Higher is better on all three. What is P's average rank? average rank

    TRANSFERA method turns out to have the highest mean raw score in the table and the worst average rank. What is the best reading?

    UNDERSTANDWhich question can an average rank not answer?

    Where this is going: card 2 makes the arithmetic exact — the ranking rule, the tied-rank convention, and the invariant that lets you check a table by hand.
    Extension · Average ranks and significance 2/3

    The arithmetic of an average rank, and the ties

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONFix one dataset containing methods, each with a score, higher meaning better. The rank of a method is its position after sorting the methods from the best score to the worst: rank for the best score, rank for the worst. When two or more methods have equal scores they are tied, and under the standard convention each tied method receives the mean of the ranks that it and its tied partners jointly occupy: a tie for second and third place gives each of the two methods . With datasets, a method's average rank is , where is its rank on dataset . Lower is better.A rank is a finishing position, 1 for the best. If two methods tie at second and third, each gets 2.5 — the average of the two positions they share — rather than an arbitrary 2 or 3. Average those positions over the datasets.

    One invariant that lets you check a table by hand. Within a single dataset holding methods, the positions are all consumed — the methods are being ordered, so every position from first to last is used exactly once between them. Their sum is therefore , whatever the scores were. A tie does not change the total: a tie between second and third place still consumes positions 2 and 3 between the two tied methods. Across datasets, the ranks of all the methods together must sum to . This is a checkable invariant: total every rank you assigned and compare. A mismatch means a tie was handled away from the convention, or a rank was misread.

    The average rank of one method. Each is that method's finishing position on dataset ; dividing by the number of datasets makes the result comparable across methods however many experiments were run.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the average rank — the single number reported per method; smaller is better
    the number of datasets, that is, the number of experiments being pooled
    the method's rank on the -th dataset: an integer from to , or a half-integer such as when tied
    add the method's ranks over all the datasets

    Why the tied ranks are averaged. The convention is chosen precisely so the invariant survives. Three methods with scores , , occupy positions 1, 2 and 3. Giving the two tied methods the mean of the positions they share, each, produces ranks , which still sum to . Awarding both the lower position gives , summing to . Awarding both the higher position gives , summing to . Neither arbitrary choice keeps the total fixed, and each silently biases every average rank computed from the table: one flatters the tied methods, the other penalises them. Averaging the shared positions is what makes the bookkeeping exact rather than conventional.

    The two mistakes that actually happen. First, direction: rank 1 is the best position, so a smaller average rank wins — readers who carry over a habit of higher-is-better invert every conclusion in the table. Second, silent ties: if scores are rounded before ranking, methods that differ in the third decimal become tied, which drags both towards the middle and can reorder the average ranks. Rank the raw scores, not a rounded printout of them.

    When the arithmetic stops discriminating. The ranks on one dataset can only take the values , so an average rank lives between and , and the same value means different things in different studies: an average rank of sits between first and second place in a comparison of three methods, but is near the very top in a comparison of thirty. Average ranks from comparisons with different numbers of methods are not on a common scale. And when most datasets are ties, the ranks pour into the middle and every method's average rank drifts towards — the method that wins and the method that loses can end up with almost the same number. Ties do not distort the total, but they thin out the differences the total is meant to express.

    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — three methods, four datasets, one tie. Methods M1, M2 and M3 are compared on four datasets; higher is better.

    DatasetM1M2M3
    D10.910.880.88
    D20.750.800.70
    D30.600.650.62
    D40.500.520.55
    D1: M1 is best at 0.91 and takes rank 1. M2 and M3 tie at 0.88 and jointly occupy positions 2 and 3, so each takes the mean .
    This is the tied-rank convention. It is also why this row still sums to 6: the tied pair consumes two positions between them, so nothing is skipped.
    D2: the scores 0.80, 0.75, 0.70 are distinct, so M2 = 1, M1 = 2, M3 = 3.
    With no ties the ranks are the positions after sorting, and they sum to 6 — the value the invariant predicts for three methods.
    D3: 0.65, 0.62, 0.60 give M2 = 1, M3 = 2, M1 = 3.
    M1 is last here. A method that leads on one dataset can trail on another, and the average rank pools both facts rather than choosing between them.
    D4: 0.55, 0.52, 0.50 give M3 = 1, M2 = 2, M1 = 3.
    M3 climbs from last to first across the four datasets. The per-dataset table shows that movement; the average rank will compress it into one number.
    DatasetM1M2M3row total
    D112.52.56
    D22136
    D33126
    D43216
    M1: 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 9 → 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25
    M2: 2.5 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6.5 → 6.5 ÷ 4 = 1.625
    M3: 2.5 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 8.5 → 8.5 ÷ 4 = 2.125
    Read the result, then check it. M2 has the smallest average rank (1.625), ahead of M3 (2.125) and M1 (2.25) — smaller is better, because smaller means finishing nearer the top more often. Every row of the rank table totals 6, as it must for three methods since . The three averages come from sums , and the invariant predicts . The table is consistent.

    Example 2 — the tie convention, with the alternatives written out. Take D1 from the table above: scores 0.91, 0.88, 0.88, one method clear at the top and two tied below it.

    Tie ruleranks givenrow total
    Mean of the shared positions (standard)1, 2.5, 2.56
    Both take the lower position1, 2, 25
    Both take the higher position1, 3, 37
    All three tied (a different dataset)2, 2, 26

    Only the standard convention keeps the row total at 6. The other two choices break the invariant, and each biases the averages in a direction: awarding the lower position flatters the tied methods, awarding the higher position penalises them. In the last row all three methods tie, so each takes the mean of positions 1, 2 and 3, which is ; the total is still 6.

    The invariant is a diagnostic, not a formality. Because one dataset's ranks always use up the whole set of positions , a wrong total points straight at a mistake. In a comparison of methods over datasets, the sum of every rank in your table must equal . If it does not, look at the ties first — an inconsistent tie rule is the usual cause.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDThree methods score 0.91, 0.88 and 0.88 on one dataset. Why do the tied pair receive 2.5 each rather than 2 each?

    APPLYA method's ranks across four datasets are 3, 1.5, 2 and 4. What is its average rank? average rank

    TRANSFERYou total every rank in a table of 5 methods across 3 datasets and get 44. What do you conclude?

    TRANSFERFour methods are compared and every dataset is a four-way tie. What average rank does every method get?

    UNDERSTANDA reader looks at a table of average ranks and concludes that the method with the largest average rank is the strongest, since it accumulated the most. What is the error?

    APPLYThree methods score 0.91, 0.877 and 0.876 on one dataset, and the table rounds every score to two decimals before ranking. How does that change this dataset's ranks?

    Where this is going: card 3 states what the number hides, and what a claim of significance would still require.
    Extension · Average ranks and significance 3/3

    Skip check: what an average rank hides

    WHAT

    A comparison across datasets is turned into one number per method. This card asks what that number can support and collects its limits. If you can do all of the following unaided, skip ahead — nothing later depends on a step you cannot take.

    • Say why raw scores from different datasets cannot be averaged, and what ranking puts in their place.
    • Compute a method's average rank from a table of per-dataset scores, remembering that rank 1 is the best position.
    • Apply the tied-ranks convention — the mean of the shared positions — and check a table with the invariant that each dataset's ranks sum to k(k+1)/2.
    • State what an average rank discards, and what its range depends on.
    • Explain why a difference between two average ranks needs a paired test across datasets, and why a count of dataset wins is not one.

    What an average rank hides

    The margin is discarded. A method that wins a dataset by 10 points and one that wins it by 0.1 point both receive rank 1. If the question is by how much, the average rank cannot answer it, and a method with a small average rank may owe it to many trivial leads rather than to a few decisive ones. The per-dataset scores belong beside the ranks whenever the size of the gap could matter.

    The range depends on how many methods were compared. Ranks on one dataset run from 1 to , so the average rank is confined to . The same value, say 1.5, is a middling position in a comparison of three methods but a near-top result in a comparison of thirty. Average ranks from studies with different numbers of competitors are not on a common scale, and a gap of 0.2 in one study does not mean the same as a gap of 0.2 in another with a different roster. The number of datasets does not change the range, but it does change the resolution — an average over ten datasets with no ties is a multiple of one tenth, and a tie can make the step finer still, since an even number of tied positions averages to a half-integer — and, as the next paragraph shows, it changes what significance is reachable at all.

    A mean says nothing about the spread. An average rank summarises the datasets with one number and hides how the ranks were distributed. A method ranked 1 on five datasets and 4 on the other five has average rank 2.5; a method ranked 2.5 on every dataset also has average rank 2.5. The first is a specialist that wins half the time and finishes badly the other half; the second is consistently middling and never wins. These are different claims about the method, and the mean alone cannot tell them apart — the per-dataset ranks, or a spread around the mean, have to be reported too.

    A difference in means is not yet a result. Two average ranks will usually differ in the decimal places — and even when they agree exactly, as in Example 1, that equality can hide opposite behaviours — so the real question is whether the observed difference is larger than what the datasets could produce by chance. Because the same datasets are used for every method, the comparison is paired: what matters is the set of per-dataset differences between the two methods, dataset by dataset, rather than two independent samples. A paired test — the sign test, which counts only which method won each dataset; the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which also weighs the size of each difference; or the Friedman test, the analogue of the signed-rank test when more than two methods are compared — is what turns "these numbers are not equal" into "this difference is hard to explain by luck".

    The number of datasets caps how small a p-value you can reach. A paired test that uses only the signs and sizes of the per-dataset differences — assuming nothing about how those differences are distributed — works from those differences, and with datasets there are only possible sign patterns. The smallest two-sided p-value the exact sign test can produce is , reached only when every dataset points the same way. With ten datasets that floor is ; with five datasets it is , which is above the conventional 0.05, so a five-dataset study cannot reach significance this way even with a clean sweep. More datasets do not merely add evidence — they lower the floor.

    A count of wins is not a significance test. "Our method wins on 8 of 10 datasets" is a description of the sample — a tally of signs — not a comparison against a chance model. It carries no p-value, no null hypothesis and no stated error rate. Turn it into the simplest possible test and the gap appears: under the null that the two methods are interchangeable, each dataset's winner is a fair coin, so the count of wins is binomial with ten trials and probability one half. That leaves equally likely win patterns, of which 45 give exactly eight wins, 10 give exactly nine, and 1 gives all ten. Eight wins then give a two-sided p-value of , which is not significant at 0.05. Nine wins give , and only a clean ten gives . The headline count sounds decisive and, on its own, is not.

    The over-claim this section exists to prevent. A table of average ranks makes two things look proved that are not proved. That the method with the smallest average rank is significantly the best does not follow from the table; it requires a paired test over the per-dataset differences. That winning a majority of datasets demonstrates superiority does not follow either; a count of wins describes the sample, and 8 wins out of 10 corresponds to p ≈ 0.11 under the simplest test.
    The questions below are the check. Five correct answers is not the bar — the bar is that none of them required real thought. If the tied-rank convention, the invariant, or the difference between a count and a test made you pause, stay with this section.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — one average rank, two different methods. Ten datasets, and four methods in total. The table lists the ranks of two of them, S and T, and omits the other two for clarity. In a four-method comparison rank 4 is last, and rank 2.5 is the mean of the two tied middle positions 2 and 3. On each dataset one of the omitted methods is tied with T at those same positions and takes rank 2.5 as well, while the other takes the single remaining position — rank 4 where S is first, rank 1 where S is last. Either way the four ranks total . Each cell below gives a method's rank on one dataset.

    Methodits ranks, dataset by datasetsumaverage rank
    S1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4252.5
    T2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 2.5, 2.5252.5
    S: 5 × 1 + 5 × 4 = 5 + 20 = 25 → 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5
    T: 10 × 2.5 = 25 → 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5

    Identical average ranks, opposite behaviours. S finishes either first or last and nothing in between: it wins half the datasets outright and trails on the other half. T never wins a dataset and never finishes last; it sits consistently in the middle. A reader told only "both average rank 2.5" would conclude the two methods are indistinguishable, which is the opposite of what the per-dataset rows show. This is the ordinary weakness of every mean, made sharp here because ranks are already a coarse summary. The example also shows only part of the picture: the ranks record who finished where, not by how much, so on the five datasets where S is ranked 1 its winning margin could have been 10 points or 0.01 — both give rank 1 — and the size of the gaps is not visible in the table.

    Example 2 — a count of wins turned into a test. Suppose two methods are compared on ten paired datasets and one of them is ahead on 8 of them. Under the null that the methods are interchangeable, each dataset's winner is a fair coin, so the number of wins is binomial with ten trials and probability one half. There are equally likely win patterns, of which give exactly eight wins, give nine, and gives all ten. Summing those far-tail terms and doubling for the two-sided test gives the p-values below.

    datasets won (of 10)two-sided p-valuebelow 0.05?
    8≈ 0.109no
    9≈ 0.021yes
    10≈ 0.002yes
    8 wins: 2 × (45 + 10 + 1) ÷ 1024 = 112 ÷ 1024 ≈ 0.109
    9 wins: 2 × (10 + 1) ÷ 1024 = 22 ÷ 1024 ≈ 0.021
    10 wins: 2 ÷ 1024 = 1 ÷ 512 ≈ 0.002

    Two things follow. First, "we won 8 of 10" sounds decisive and is not: under the simplest paired test it corresponds to , well above the usual 0.05 bar — eight wins out of ten is an ordinary coin-tossing outcome. Second, the number of datasets sets a floor. With ten datasets the smallest two-sided p-value any sign-based test can reach is , obtained only by a clean sweep; with five datasets the floor is , already above 0.05, so a five-dataset study cannot reach significance this way however complete its victory.

    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDA report states that a method "wins on 9 of the 12 datasets". What does this sentence establish on its own?

    APPLYAn exact sign test compares two methods across 8 paired datasets. What is the smallest two-sided p-value it can return? two-sided p-value

    TRANSFERTwo methods both have average rank 2.5 over six datasets. Method P is ranked 1 on three datasets and 4 on the other three; method Q is ranked 2.5 on all six. Which reading is supported?

    UNDERSTANDWhich of these can an average rank not tell you?

    TRANSFEROne paper reports a method's average rank as 1.5 from a comparison of 3 methods. Another paper reports 1.5 for a different method from a comparison of 30 methods. What follows?

    Where this is going: with the concept, the arithmetic and the limits in hand, a table of average ranks can be read for exactly what it says — and any claim that the best method is significantly the best can be checked against the paired test it requires, rather than assumed from the size of the number.
    Extension · Hyperparameters and reproduction 1/5

    What it means to reproduce a result

    A method section is a recipe, and a recipe you cannot cook from is not a recipe. This section separates the three things people mean by "reproduction", lists the items an independent implementer needs before their result is even determined, and shows how to read a hyperparameter table as a description of the model rather than a report of a result. It is the vocabulary for judging what a paper's own tables do and do not let a reader rebuild.
    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA reproduction of a reported result is an attempt to obtain a result consistent with it. The three levels differ in how much of the original pipeline is reused. At level 1 (rerun) the authors' released code and data are executed as they are, so nothing is re-derived. At level 2 (reimplementation) the method is rebuilt from the paper's description alone, so the description is the only input. At level 3 (independent confirmation) a different implementation — other code, often other splits or hardware — checks whether the paper's conclusion still holds: whether the method lands on the same side of the comparison the paper draws, such as beating a named baseline, rather than whether it prints the same decimal.Reproducing a result is not one action. The weak version runs someone else's code; the strong version rebuilds the method from the description and still gets the same answer to the question the paper asked.

    Why this distinction decides what you can do with a paper. A reader rarely has the authors' machine, their exact library versions, or their patience. What a reader wants to know is whether the claim holds up when the details not written down are filled in differently. So the level that matters for reading a paper is level 3, and the level a method section alone can reach is level 2 — nothing beyond it.

    LevelWhat is reusedWhat it establishes
    1 — RerunThe authors' code, data and settingsThat the released artefacts still produce the released number on a comparable machine
    2 — ReimplementationOnly the paper's descriptionThat the description is complete enough to rebuild the method
    3 — Independent confirmationAn independent implementation; often different code, splits or hardwareThat the paper's conclusion survives a different implementation

    A method section alone can reach level 2, and only as far as it is complete: every choice the implementer must make has to be stated, or the implementer supplies their own value and the rebuilt method is no longer the paper's method. Level 1 is out of reach without released code, data and environment. Level 3 is the standard that matters for a reader, because it is the only level at which a defect in one implementation — a leaked test set, a lucky seed — cannot silently carry the result along with it.

    The misconception to drop first. Because a paper says its code is released, it is tempting to treat the result as reproducible. Released code makes level 1 possible and says nothing about level 2 or level 3. A rerun reproduces the artefact: if the code contains a mistake, the rerun reproduces the mistake too, in exactly the same way, and the number comes out identical. Identical output from identical code is evidence about the code, not about the claim.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — three readers and one paper. A paper reports that its method beats a baseline on a benchmark. Three readers approach it, and all three end up agreeing with the paper.

    • Reader A downloads the released code and data and runs it. The score matches the paper's. Reader A has done level 1.
    • Reader B reads only the method section, writes their own training loop, and lands within a fraction of a point of the paper — same conclusion. Reader B has done level 2.
    • Reader C writes their own loop, draws their own random split, and still finds the method ahead of the baseline, though by a smaller margin. Reader C has done level 3.

    The three outcomes look similar and mean very different things. A's result is guaranteed by construction: run the same code and of course it returns the same number. B's result shows that the description is concrete enough to rebuild. Only C's speaks to whether the claim is a property of the method rather than of one particular pipeline.

    Example 2 — a rerun that reproduces nothing. Suppose the authors' code standardises every feature using the mean and standard deviation of the whole dataset, and only afterwards splits it into train and test. The released code reruns perfectly and returns the published number. Reader C's own pipeline, written without that step because the method section never mentions it, standardises using only the training split.

    The two runs now differ — not because either is broken, but because the original quietly let test-set statistics reach the training process. Level 1 succeeded while level 3 failed, and the failure is the informative one: the published number depended on a step the method section never disclosed. This is the pattern to anticipate, and the next card turns it into a checklist.

    Notice what neither example shows: level 1 says nothing about whether the method is right, and level 2 says nothing about whether a hidden step mattered. Only the independent comparison can fail in a way that teaches you something.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich level of reproduction does a method section by itself make possible?

    APPLYA colleague runs the authors' released repository unchanged and obtains the paper's published number. Which level has been performed, and what has been established?

    TRANSFERA method section is complete enough that two independent teams reimplement it and reach the same conclusion, but one team's score is a point lower than published. Is the result reproduced?

    Where this is going: level 2 is the level a method section owes you, so the next card lists exactly what that section must contain — and what breaks, silently, when each item is missing.
    Extension · Hyperparameters and reproduction 2/5

    What a method section owes the reader

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA method section is complete for reproduction when it specifies every choice an independent implementer must fix before their result is determined. Six groups of choices matter: the architecture and the shape of every tensor it transforms; every hyperparameter (a value set before training rather than learned during it) together with the rule that produced it; the search space and budget, if any settings were searched; the data split protocol and the seeds (the integers that fix the random state); the preprocessing, including the procedure that built any constructed structure such as a graph or an invented feature; and the computing environment, at least in outline.For someone to rebuild your method they need the six things that decide the answer: the model's shape, every knob and how you picked it, how hard you searched, how you split the data and fixed randomness, what you did to the inputs beforehand, and roughly what machine you ran on.

    Why a checklist rather than a general plea for detail. Omissions are silent: a missing item does not announce itself, and the implementer fills the gap with their own choice without noticing that they have. The result is a rebuild that is not the paper's method, and a disagreement that cannot be traced to its cause. Naming the six items turns a vague failure into a specific one, and a specific one can be fixed.

    ItemWhat it must stateWhat breaks if it is missing
    Architecture and shapesNumber of layers, hidden widths, and the input and output dimensions of every tensor the method transformsThe parameter count is unknown, so the model's size — and any comparison against a baseline at a matched size — cannot be judged
    Every hyperparameter and how it was chosenLearning rate, batch size, dropout, weight decay, optimiser, early-stopping rule, and the rule that produced each valueA default cannot be told from a tuned value, so the share of the result attributable to the method rather than to the search is unknown
    Search space and budgetWhich settings were searched, over what range, how many trials, and on which data the trials were scoredA number produced by a long search is not comparable to one produced by a short search; without the budget the reported value has no scale
    Split protocol and seedsHow train, validation and test were formed; the seeds used; whether the same splits were given to every methodIf one method saw a friendlier split, the comparison measures the split rather than the method
    Preprocessing and constructed structureEvery transform applied to inputs, and the procedure that built any graph or feature the authors inventedA transform can leak test information into training; an undescribed construction cannot be rebuilt at all
    Computing environmentHardware, library versions, numerical precisionIndependent attempts fail for reasons unrelated to the method, and a rerun cannot distinguish a real effect from an environment difference
    The misconception that costs the most. A method section that names every hyperparameter feels complete, because hyperparameters are what people check first. The items that most often decide whether a result survives independent work are the ones that are not numbers at all: the split protocol, the preprocessing, and the search budget. A paper can list twenty hyperparameters to five decimal places and still be unrebuildable.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — one missing line, unusable method. A method learns on a graph it builds from the data. The authors state that they construct a nearest-neighbour graph. The method section does not say how many neighbours each node takes, which distance produces the neighbour ranking, or whether the graph is rebuilt inside each cross-validation fold or fixed once for all folds.

    An implementer supplies a neighbour count. A graph with few neighbours is sparse; one with many is dense, and the message-passing step behaves differently on each. The reported number now belongs to a graph the paper never described.
    The neighbour count changes which nodes exchange information, so it changes the model's input rather than only its training.
    The implementer also supplies a distance. Two reasonable choices can rank neighbours differently for the same nodes, giving a different graph again.
    The construction of the structure is part of the method; leaving it implicit hands the definition of the data to the implementer.
    Finally the implementer guesses whether the graph is fixed once or rebuilt per fold. If the graph was built once over all data and then reused inside folds, information from validation examples has already shaped the graph.
    This is the same leakage mechanism as Example 2 of the previous card, reached through a constructed structure rather than a standardisation step.

    Three unstated choices, each individually small, and the rebuild is no longer the paper's method. None of the three is a hyperparameter in the usual sense; all three sit in the preprocessing and constructed structure row of the table.

    Example 2 — the budget is part of the result. A reported value that came from a search is a different kind of number from one that came from a single run, and the difference is countable.

    Multiply the choices: 3 learning rates × 2 batch sizes × 4 layer counts = 24 candidate settings.
    Every combination is one point in the search space, so the product counts the points.
    Each candidate is scored by 5-fold cross-validation, so the search trains 24 × 5 = 120 models.
    Cross-validation repeats each setting once per fold, so the cost of one candidate is the number of folds.
    The published model is then trained once more on the full training split, so the total is 120 + 1 runs, not 120.
    The search only scores candidates; the reported score comes from a separate final fitting step, and leaving it out understates the cost.
    A checklist is a diagnostic, not a demand that every paper be self-contained down to the last decimal. Its use is to name which omission you are looking at, so that "this did not reproduce" can be reported as a specific missing fact rather than a vague failure.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDA paper lists every hyperparameter to several decimal places. Which item can still be missing and still prevent a rebuild?

    APPLYA search crosses 5 learning rates with 3 batch sizes and 2 weight-decay values, and scores each candidate with 5-fold cross-validation. How many training runs does the search cost? training runs

    TRANSFERTwo papers report the same method with the same chosen hyperparameters. Paper A selected them with a 10-trial search; Paper B with a 500-trial search. Both print the best value found. What should a reader suspect?

    Where this is going: the split protocol and the seeds in that checklist are the reason a single number is not a result. The next card makes that precise with arithmetic.
    Extension · Hyperparameters and reproduction 3/5

    Why one run is not a result

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA run is one complete training of a model from an initialised state to a final score. A seed is the integer that fixes the random state at the start of a run, and therefore fixes the initial weights, the order in which data is drawn, and — if the split is generated randomly — the split itself. Because these draws differ between seeds, a run's score is a random variable: repeating the run with a different seed gives a different number. Reporting a result therefore means reporting a summary of several runs: a mean, together with the spread of the runs around that mean.One training run is one draw from a lottery you cannot see, and the seed decides which draw you get. A single number says which ticket came up, not how the lottery behaves — so a result is a mean over several runs plus how much those runs disagreed.

    Why a single run is not a result. Three things move when the seed changes. The initial weights start the model in a different place, so it settles in a different minimum. The order in which training examples arrive changes the update path. And if the train and test split is drawn randomly, the split itself changes. Each source nudges the final score, and their combined effect is measurable — which is why a one-decimal difference between two methods can be entirely seed noise.

    How the spread is measured. Run the same code with several seeds and collect the scores. The mean says where the runs sit; the sample standard deviation says how far a typical run falls from that mean. If the gap between your method and the baseline is smaller than the spread, the gap may be a seed rather than an effect.

    The sample standard deviation over runs with scores and mean . The sum adds the squared distances of each run from the mean; dividing by averages those squared distances over the runs; the square root returns the answer to the units of the scores.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the score of the -th run; the index runs from 1 to
    the mean of the scores
    the number of runs; the divisor is used so the spread is not underestimated by measuring distances from a mean that was fitted to the same runs
    the sample standard deviation — the typical distance of a run from the average run
    Two misconceptions to separate. The first is that a small standard deviation means the result is correct; it means the runs agreed with one another, which a systematically broken pipeline also does. The second is that the standard deviation over seeds is a confidence interval for the gap to the baseline: it describes spread within your own runs, and the gap between two methods also carries the baseline's own seed spread.
    EXAMPLE

    Example 1 — five runs and their average. Five seeds give accuracies 82.5, 84.0, 81.5, 83.5 and 83.5. The mean is the sum divided by the count.

    82.5 + 84.0 = 166.5
    166.5 + 81.5 = 248.0
    248.0 + 83.5 = 331.5 ; 331.5 + 83.5 = 415.0
    mean = 415.0 / 5 = 83.0

    Example 2 — the spread of those same five runs. Now measure how far each run falls from the mean of 83.0.

    Subtract the mean from each score: −0.5, +1.0, −1.5, +0.5, +0.5.
    The distance of each run from the average is the raw material of the spread.
    Square each distance: 0.25, 1.00, 2.25, 0.25, 0.25, which sum to 0.25 + 1.00 + 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 4.00.
    Squaring makes every distance count positively; without it the negative and positive distances would cancel and the spread would look like zero.
    Divide by n − 1 = 4: 4.00 / 4 = 1.00. That is the sample variance.
    Dividing by n − 1 rather than n corrects the downward pull you get from measuring distances to a mean that was fitted to the same five numbers.
    Take the square root: √1.00 = 1.00. The sample standard deviation is 1.0 accuracy points.
    The square root undoes the squaring, returning the spread to accuracy points rather than squared accuracy points.

    How large must an effect be to be visible? The spread of a single run is points. The spread of the mean of five runs is smaller, because averaging cancels part of the noise: it is the standard error, . Comparing two methods each averaged over five seeds, the gap between the two means has a standard error of about . A gap of twice that, roughly 1.3 accuracy points, is where the difference starts to sit outside the seed noise. A gap of half a point, on five seeds, is not something these runs can resolve.

    Look at the range of the five runs: the best is 84.0 and the worst is 81.5, a spread of 2.5 points. If the authors kept only the best of five and reported 84.0, the reported number would sit 1.0 point above the mean — the same size as the standard deviation. Selecting the best run is not a neutral choice; it shifts the reported number by an amount comparable to the run-to-run noise it was meant to summarise.

    What "mean and standard deviation over five seeds" does and does not establish. It does show that the score moves under seed change and give a rough scale for how much, which is enough to stop a reader treating a one-decimal difference as real. It does not establish that five seeds represent the distribution, because the standard deviation is itself estimated from only five numbers and is therefore a rough quantity. It is not a confidence interval or a significance test. And it does not constrain the gap to a baseline, which was also run over seeds of its own.

    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhy does changing the seed change the final score?

    APPLYFive seeds give 61.0, 63.0, 62.0, 64.0 and 60.0. Compute the sample standard deviation. accuracy points

    TRANSFERMethod A reports 84.0 from a single run chosen as its best over several. Method B reports 83.0 as the mean over ten seeds. Which statement is best supported?

    Where this is going: a hyperparameter table is the other half of a method section, and it can be read as a description of the model itself. The next card does that arithmetic.
    Extension · Hyperparameters and reproduction 4/5

    Reading a hyperparameter table as a description of the model

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA hyperparameter is a value fixed before training and not updated by it, in contrast to a parameter, which the training algorithm fits. A hyperparameter table lists the values used for one experiment. Architecture hyperparameters — the number of layers, the width (the number of units in a hidden layer) of each, and the input and output dimensions — do not only tune the model: they determine its parameter count, the total number of fitted values, and therefore its size and its cost.Hyperparameters are the knobs you set; parameters are what training sets. Some knobs — how many layers, how wide each layer is, how large the input is — decide how big the model is, and that size can be computed straight from the table.

    Why a reader should do this arithmetic. Two models reported under the same hyperparameter table are not necessarily two models of the same size. A larger model has more parameters, which usually costs more to train and can change how much of a difference is attributable to the method rather than to capacity. Reading the counts price both claims, and it also lets a reader tell whether a baseline was given the same budget.

    When the arithmetic works, and when it does not. The formula below describes a plain fully connected stack, in which every input is connected to every hidden unit. It fails as a description of a model with shared weights — a convolution reuses one filter across positions, so its count does not follow the layer-count-and-width rule — and it fails for any layer whose size depends on the input at run time. Reading a parameter count off a table is valid only when the table names a layer type whose count you can compute.

    The parameter count of a single-hidden-layer network: input dimension , hidden width , output dimension . The network builds hidden units from inputs — that is weights plus biases — then outputs from those hidden units: weights plus biases.
    SymbolWhat it means
    input dimension — how many numbers describe one example
    hidden width — how many units the hidden layer has
    output dimension — how many numbers the model produces
    the parameter count — the total number of fitted values
    EXAMPLE
