    Next: the step the paper calls a proof — that this encoder is invariant to column permutations. It is short, and reading it shows exactly how much (and how little) a proof of this kind establishes.
    5.7 · Invariance proof

    The column-permutation proof: what two lines actually establish

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA proof of invariance shows that a function's output does not change when its input is relabelled in a way that does not change the underlying object. Here the claim is that for any permutation of the hyperedge index set, — the structural embedding is unchanged when the columns of the incidence matrix are reordered.Shuffling the order of the relations in the file must not change any vertex's structural number. The paper proves this in two lines, and both lines are worth understanding — along with what they leave out.

    The proof, as the paper gives it. Let be a permutation of the column indices. Then:

    1. The sum is unchanged. . The reasoning is that addition does not care about order: adding a set of numbers in a different sequence gives the same total. What was column in the original is column in the permuted matrix, and the sum runs over all columns either way.
    2. The transformation is unaffected. is applied vertex-wise — that is, row by row. A column permutation reorders entries within each row, and never looks across a row: it receives a single scalar per vertex and returns a single scalar. So the same input produces the same output.
    3. Therefore the composition is invariant. is identical for and .
    Why the proof is short: the encoder is trivial. is a scalar sigmoid, and a scalar function cannot see column order even in principle. The interesting content is not the proof's technique but its premise — that this encoder was chosen to be a function of the degree alone, and a degree is a symmetric function of a row, hence automatically permutation-invariant. The proof is short because the design pre-committed to invariance.

    Which raises the question a reader should ask: if invariance was guaranteed, is the proof doing any work? It is doing two things. It confirms that no implementation detail (an index-based lookup, a per-column weight) has crept in and broken the property — which does happen in practice and is worth asserting. And it makes the paper's claim explicit and checkable, which is better than leaving invariance as an unstated hope.

    What the proof does not establish, stated plainly, because a proof's boundary is as informative as its content: it says nothing about whether the degree is a good structural summary, nothing about invariance to row permutations (which holds, by the same elementwise argument, and just permutes the output rows), and nothing about any encoder other than this one.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — permute the columns and watch nothing happen. Reuse the four-person graph's incidence matrix, with rows for vertices 1–4 and columns for edges , , .

    Swap columns 1 and 3, so the column order becomes . The matrix's rows are now , , , .
    This is what a program reading the hyperedge list in a different order produces. Nothing about the hypergraph has changed; only the file's layout has.
    Row sums: ; ; ; . Identical to the unpermuted rows .
    This is the first line of the proof, executed. The row sum is the same number however the columns are arranged, because it is a sum over the same multiset.
    Apply to each: the same four outputs in the same order.
    The second line of the proof. Since acts on each row's total independently, and the totals are unchanged, the outputs are unchanged — including their order, because row permutation was not involved.
    A sharper observation about the choice of aggregation. Over a 0/1 row, the three symmetric aggregations behave very differently. The sum gives the degree — informative. The mean gives the degree divided by , the number of hyperedges — a constant multiple of the degree, hence informative in exactly the same way. The max gives 1 for every vertex that belongs to at least one hyperedge, and 0 otherwise — which collapses almost the entire graph to a single value. Of the three standard symmetric functions, only two carry structural information at all, and one is degenerate. That is the real reason the paper's encoder looks the way it does, and the proof does not mention it.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich fact alone makes the sum invariant to column permutation?

    APPLYA vertex's row of the incidence matrix holds 30 entries, of which are 1. What does the mean aggregation return, as an expression in ? Answer with the arithmetic for and 30 columns, to four decimals. mean value

    5.8 · Figure 2

    Figure 2: how a tree's questions become a vector

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONFigure 2 is the pipeline diagram of the Task-Driven Rule Encoder. It has three panels: pre-training, which trains a boosted tree ensemble on a task; a content mapping and a position mapping, which turn each tree's inner nodes into numbers; and a final panel showing the resulting per-vertex vectors assembled across trees.Left: train some trees. Middle: turn each tree into a list of questions, and give each question a value and a weight. Right: line up the answers into a vector per vertex.

    The one thing to see before reading the details. In the middle panel, the shapes matter: the rounded rectangles with letters — A, B, C, in orange, green and blue — are leaf nodes, and the dashed purple ellipses are inner nodes. The legend in the bottom-right corner says exactly this. The paper's entire rule encoding is built on the inner nodes; the leaves are shown only to explain what the tree was trained to predict. If you take one thing from this figure, take that distinction, because every symbol in Equations (4)-(8) refers to inner nodes.

    Original Figure 2 (Feng et al., TPAMI 2026). Left: the boosted ensemble is pre-trained on a task. Middle: content mapping μc marks each inner node, position mapping μp weights it by depth. Right: the per-tree rows are assembled into the knowledge-embedded features.
    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — the left panel. A feature matrix enters a box labelled Gradient Boosting Decision Tree, and out comes Task — drawn as four coloured circles.

    • This is the pre-training stage: the ensemble is fitted to a task in the ordinary way, and its predictions are the coloured circles.
    • The task's classes are drawn in orange, green and blue; the same three colours label the leaves of the trees in the middle panel. So the middle panel's trees are the trained ensemble from the left, redrawn to expose their internal questions.
    • Note what the arrows out of the pretraining box do not carry: the predictions go to the Task output and are then dropped. Everything routed to the right comes from the trees' internal structure. The paper does not use the ensemble's forecasts at all — the point made in Equation (2)'s card, now visible in the diagram.

    Walk 2 — the middle panel, top: content mapping. Two trees are drawn, and , each annotated with the same three colours.

    Count the inner nodes of : a root asking and one child asking — two questions.
    The number of questions is the length of that tree's contribution to the embedding, per Equation (7). It is not the number of leaves and not the depth — it is the count of inner nodes.
    Count the inner nodes of : a root asking , with children asking and — three questions.
    So the two trees contribute 2 and 3 entries respectively, and the concatenation in Equation (8) produces a row of entries for this two-tree ensemble.
    Each dashed ellipse is one slot in the vector. For a given vertex, each slot holds a number derived from whether that vertex's features satisfy the question there.
    This is the content mapping : it records whether the vertex satisfies the rule. The direction is inverted — 0 for satisfied, 1 for not — and Equation (5) pins that down.

    Walk 3 — the middle panel, bottom: position mapping. A decaying curve labelled is plotted against Depth of Node in the Decision Tree, with three reference circles marked , , .

    The curve is the whole idea of position weighting, drawn. Because depth appears in the denominator, the weight falls as depth grows — steeply at first, then flattening. The paper's argument is that boosted trees select the most task-relevant features first, so a question near the root is more informative than one deep in the tree. The curve therefore encodes an assumption about how boosting works, not a mathematical necessity: if the ensemble had been grown breadth-first or randomly, the same curve would be unjustified.

    Walk 4 — the right panel. The assembled vectors are drawn as two stacked layers of purple matrices, labelled 1st Layer and 2nd Layer, with dashed lines connecting them.

    • This is Equation (8)'s concatenation, drawn as a vertical assembly: each tree's contribution becomes one block, and the blocks stack into one row per vertex.
    • The dashed connecting lines suggest the concatenation is a rearrangement rather than a computation — the blocks are not mixed, they are laid end to end.
    • The label Knowledge-Embedded Features is the same label that appears on the purple block in Figure 1, which is how the two figures join up: Figure 1's lower path is exactly this figure's output.

    Next: Section IV-B-2, the encoder this figure describes — what it takes as input, what it produces, and why the paper chose boosted trees as its rule source rather than any other model.
    5.9 · TDR-Encoder

    The Task-Driven Rule Encoder: harvesting a tree ensemble as a questionnaire

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThe Task-Driven Rule Encoder is a function mapping a feature matrix and a pre-trained boosted ensemble to a rule embedding , composed of two mappings — a content mapping and a position mapping — applied to the inner nodes of every tree.Train a team of small trees on the task. Then, for every question those trees learned to ask, record two things about each vertex: whether it satisfies the question, and how important the question is. Line up all the answers into a row.

    Why trees, and why boosted trees specifically. The paper names its reason in one word: interpretability. A tree's inner nodes are explicit predicates on individual features — "", "" — so they can be read, enumerated and counted. No other standard model offers learned structure in a form that can be written down as a list, which is what makes the ledger construction possible at all. A neural network fitted to the same features would have no inner nodes to enumerate.

    The pipeline, in the paper's own terms. First the ensemble is pre-trained on a predefined task, producing a fitted model . Then each vertex's feature vector is run against the inner nodes, and two mappings are composed into a per-tree encoding ; finally the per-tree encodings for all trees are concatenated into the vertex's row . The whole thing is computed once, before the hypergraph network is trained on it.

    One detail that the equations settle and the prose leaves ambiguous. Equation (5) evaluates for an inner node using the vertex's features directly — there is no condition that lie on the path the vertex would take through the tree. So the encoder does not record the tree's decision path. It evaluates every question in the tree against the vertex, independently. The vector is a questionnaire, not a trail of breadcrumbs, and this is worth being clear about because the two would behave very differently: a questionnaire asks about branches the vertex would never have reached.

    What the encoder is a function of. Given the fitted ensemble, each entry of depends only on 's feature vector — not on the hypergraph, not on other vertices, and not on 's position in the graph. Two vertices anywhere in the dataset with identical features receive identical rule embeddings. So the rule encoder and the structural encoder are genuinely orthogonal in their inputs: one reads the feature matrix, the other the incidence matrix, and neither can see what the other sees.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — the questionnaire on two vertices. Take the small ensemble from Figure 2: tree asks then ; tree asks , then and . That is five questions in total, so and every vertex's row has five entries.

    VertexSatisfied questions row
    P357all five
    Q019 and
    R000none
    Look at vertex P. It satisfies every question, and its content row is all zeros. That is not a bug — it is what the encoding means: a 0 records that a rule covers this vertex, and a vertex covered by everything contributes nothing. is a failure ledger: it records, weighted by importance, what the rules did not explain about you. This is the single most important thing to understand before Equation (9), because it explains why the Hadamard product there behaves the way it does.

    Walk 2 — the two encoders describe different things. Compare P with a vertex S that has the same features as P but sits in 20 hyperedges rather than 2. Their rule rows are identical — the rule encoder cannot see the graph. Their structural values differ — the structural encoder cannot see the features. The fusion in Equation (9) is the only place the two descriptions meet.

    EXERCISES

    Next: Equations (4) and (5) — the content mapping, formalised, with the failure-ledger convention pinned down and worked through on real feature values.
    5.10 · Equations (4)–(5)

    Equations (4) and (5): the rule content mapping

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONEquation (4) declares two mappings over the inner nodes of a tree: a content mapping and a position mapping . Equation (5) defines the first: if the feature vector satisfies the rule attached to node , and otherwise.For each question a tree asks, look at the vertex's features and write down one bit: 0 if the question is satisfied, 1 if it is not.
    Equation (5) is a predicate test, and its output is a single bit. The domain in Equation (4) is worth reading: takes a feature vector and a node, so it is defined for any pair of those — not only for nodes that the vector could reach during a traversal.
    SymbolWhat it means
    a vertex's feature vector, of length
    an inner node of some tree — that is, one question
    the rule attached to : a threshold test on one feature, or a boolean check, as the paper puts it
    the set of inner nodes of the tree; the paper also calls these chance nodes
    one bit: 0 when the rule covers , 1 when it does not
    The direction is inverted, and it is the single most error-prone convention in the paper. A satisfied rule yields 0. A reader who assumes 1 means "yes" will invert the meaning of every rule embedding while still getting the arithmetic right — the worst kind of error, because it produces no symptom. Section IV-B-2 gives no reason for the choice; what the choice achieves is a ledger of what the rules failed to explain, which is developed below.

    What the 0/1 bit is, in words. A 0 says "this rule already accounts for you" and a 1 says "this rule has nothing to say about you — other rules must". So a vertex's bit-vector is not a description of the vertex; it is a list of where the ensemble's explanations leave off. Two vertices with identical bit-vectors are indistinguishable to the rule encoder regardless of their actual features, provided only that every question happens to agree about them.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — every question against every vertex. Using the five questions of the paper's Figure 2 ensemble, compute for three vertices.

    Vertex for
    P357
    Q019
    R000
    Take R, with every feature zero. The first question is : is false, so the rule is not satisfied and the entry is 1. Repeating for all five gives an all-ones vector.
    An all-ones vector means no rule in the ensemble covers this vertex — it sits entirely outside what the ensemble learned about the feature space. That is a meaningful state, not a degenerate one.
    Take Q, with , , . Check each: fails (1); fails (1); holds (0); fails (1); holds (0).
    The fourth and fifth entries are the instructive ones. satisfies but fails — the same feature, two thresholds, opposite verdicts. This is why a single feature can occupy several coordinates of the embedding and why they are not redundant.
    Take P, with , , . Every question is satisfied, so the vector is all zeros.
    P is fully explained by the ensemble, and its rule embedding is therefore zero. Hold this case — it is the one that makes Equation (9)'s behaviour comprehensible.
    The all-zeros row has a consequence that propagates through the whole method. For vertex P, the rule embedding is ; the structure-aware embedding of Equation (9) is ; and the fused feature is . A vertex that the ensemble explains completely receives an all-zero feature vector and enters the network indistinguishable from a vertex whose every slot is zero for other reasons. With a real ensemble of hundreds of questions this is essentially unreachable — the odds that a vertex satisfies every one of hundreds of thresholds are negligible — but for small ensembles it is a real failure mode, and it follows directly from choosing 0 to mean "covered".

    Next: Equation (6), the other half of the rule encoding — the mapping that turns each question's depth into an importance weight.
    5.11 · Equation (6)

    Equation (6): the rule position mapping, and how gentle it turns out to be

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONEquation (6) defines the position mapping: , where is the depth of node in its tree — the root having depth 0 — and are hyperparameters. The mapping is decreasing in depth, so questions nearer a tree's root receive larger weights.A question's importance is its height in the tree: the root is worth the most, and the deeper a question sits, the less it counts. Two numbers, α and β, control how fast that fall-off happens.
    A rectangular hyperbola in the depth. Because β is added to the depth before dividing, the curve's steepness is set by how large β is relative to the depths the tree actually reaches — and the paper's chosen range for β makes the curve far flatter than the formula's shape suggests at first glance.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the depth of node ; the root is 0 and depth increases downwards
    a scale factor — it multiplies every weight, so it changes the overall magnitude but not the ratios between depths
    a shift — it controls how quickly the weight decays with depth, and stops the expression from dividing by zero at the root
    the weight later multiplied into that node's content bit in Equation (7)

    The paper does state where these values come from, and it is worth reading carefully. Section V-A-4 says the coefficients are "determined through grid search within the range , and the optimal pair is selected according to validation performance". So three facts are on the record: the search is a five-by-five grid, it is done on the validation split rather than the test split, and the selected pair differs by dataset. And Table IV does report the chosen pair for every dataset: the values it lists run across the whole range, from 6 to 10. So the procedure, the search space and the outcome are all on the record — which is better practice than many papers manage.

    And now the consequence, which is easy to miss and changes how you read the method. With , the decay is slow. Take , inside the searched range: the root weighs and a node at depth 7 weighs — a factor of only across the entire tree. My first pass at this card used and produced a factor of ; that is arithmetically correct for those values but lies outside the paper's range and badly overstates the effect. Within the range actually used, the depth weighting is close to uniform: a question seven levels deep still carries nearly half the weight of the root question.

    What that does to the paper's stated motivation. Section IV-B-2 motivates the weighting by arguing that boosted trees select task-relevant features early, so root questions matter more. The formula expresses that idea, but the chosen hyperparameters make it a mild preference rather than a strong one. That is not a defect — a gentle weighting may be exactly what validation selected — but it does mean the phrase "positional importance" should be read as a soft ordering, not as a hierarchy in which deep questions are negligible. The paper's own numbers put the two ends within a factor of about two.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — the weight table, inside the paper's range. Evaluate at depths 0 through 6 under four of the twenty-five searchable pairs.

    Depth
    0 (root)1.0000.6001.6671.000
    10.8570.5451.4290.909
    20.7500.5001.2500.833
    30.6670.4621.1110.769
    50.5450.4000.9090.667
    70.4620.3530.7690.588
    Compare the columns at the root: versus . Changing from 6 to 10 lowers every weight, because the denominator grew.
    shifts the curve down as well as flattening it. Reaching for a larger makes deep questions matter more relative to the root, but it also makes every weight smaller in absolute terms.
    Compare the columns row by row: every entry in the column is exactly times the entry.
    is a pure scale, as claimed. It cannot reorder the weights, so it cannot change which question dominates — only how large the whole rule contribution is compared with whatever else reaches the network.
    Now measure the decay over a realistic tree. With , the ratio of the root's weight to a depth-7 node's is .
    This single ratio is the honest measure of how much the paper's mechanism actually does. Compare it with the ratio implied by the shape of the curve at small — with it would be eightfold — and you can see that the searched range, not the functional form, is what determines the strength of the effect.
    The transferable lesson. Whenever a formula's behaviour is controlled by a hyperparameter, the formula alone tells you nothing about how strong the effect is in practice — you have to look up the value. And when the paper reports a range rather than a value, the gentlest and harshest behaviours inside that range are both consistent with everything stated. That is a real limit on what the method section alone can establish, and it is the sort of gap Chapter 7 collects.

    Next: Equation (7), where the content bit and the position weight are multiplied together to form one tree's contribution.
    5.12 · Equation (7)

    Equation (7): one tree's contribution, as a failure profile

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONEquation (7) composes the two mappings into a per-tree encoding: over the inner nodes . Its output dimension equals the number of inner nodes in that tree.Multiply each question's importance weight by its 0/1 answer, and line the products up into a vector — one entry per question in that tree.
    A product of two scalars per node. Because is 0 or 1, each entry is either exactly or exactly the node's weight — there are no intermediate values.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the -th tree of the pre-trained ensemble
    its set of inner nodes — its questions
    the node's depth weight from Equation (6): larger near the root
    the 0/1 content bit from Equation (5): 0 when the rule covers , 1 when it does not

    The product is a mask, and this is the cleanest way to see what the vector is. Since is 0 or 1, the multiplication does one of two things to each weight: it keeps it, or it deletes it. So the per-tree vector's nonzero entries are exactly the depth weights of the questions this vertex fails. Another way to say the same thing: the vector is a failure profile — a list of which questions failed, each valued at the importance of the question.

    Three consequences follow immediately, and all three are checkable. First, a vertex that satisfies every question in a tree gets an all-zero block — the all-zeros case from Equation (5), now visible at the level of one tree. Second, the norm of the block measures how badly the tree explains the vertex: , so failing a root question costs far more than failing a deep one. Third, two vertices that fail the same set of questions receive identical vectors, however different their feature values are. The encoding keeps only the pattern of pass and fail, not the margin by which a threshold was passed.

    That third point is a real limit and worth stating plainly. A vertex with and one with both satisfy and contribute the identical entry. All the information about how far past the threshold a value lies is discarded. This is inherent to a threshold-based rule encoding — the same property that makes the encoding interpretable and cheap also makes it coarse.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — the profile for four vertices. Take tree with questions (depth 0) and (depth 1), and weights , inside the paper's searched range, so .

    VertexFails
    P35nothing
    Q05the depth-1 question
    R30the root
    S00both
    Read the norm of each row. P: . Q: . R: . S: .
    The norm orders the vertices by how poorly the tree explains them, and it does so with the depth weighting built in: R, which fails only the root, scores higher than Q, which fails only a deeper question.
    Now find a vertex that would tie with R. Any vertex satisfying but failing gets the same vector .
    This is the coarseness in action. A vertex with and one with are indistinguishable to this block — and would remain indistinguishable no matter how many vertices the dataset contains.
    Finally, check the structure of the values: every entry is either or one of the two weights.
    With the weights for depths 0 through 4 run , so a block has only five possible nonzero values. The embedding is not continuous in the depth — it takes a handful of distinct magnitudes. That is a strong limitation on how much a downstream linear layer can differentiate, and it follows from the formula rather than from any implementation choice.
    Notice what the walk reveals about the whole design. The rule embedding's information per vertex is: which of questions failed. That is at most bits, and after the depth weighting it is a vector whose entries come from a small set of magnitudes. Whether that is enough to improve node classification is an empirical question — and it is the question the paper's ablation is meant to answer, by comparing a model with this encoding against one without.

    Next: Equation (8), which assembles the per-tree blocks into one row per vertex — and this is where the embedding's width, and its main practical cost, become explicit.
    5.13 · Equation (8)

    Equation (8): assembling every tree into one row

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONEquation (8) concatenates the per-tree encodings into a single row per vertex: , where denotes concatenation and is vertex 's features. The resulting width is , the total number of questions across the whole ensemble.Run the vertex's features through every tree's questionnaire, and stack all the answers end to end into one long row.
    Concatenation, not a sum. The blocks are laid end to end and stay distinguishable, so a downstream layer can in principle weight the questions of one tree differently from those of another — an option that summing would have destroyed.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the number of trees in the pre-trained ensemble
    the -th tree's block, from Equation (7)
    concatenation: the widths add, nothing is combined
    the total width — the sum of inner-node counts over all trees, not a hyperparameter the user sets directly

    The width is not a free parameter, and that is the important structural fact here. is determined by two things the experimenter chooses — the number of trees and their depth — and nothing else. Table IV reports those two per dataset. So the embedding's width is a consequence of the ensemble configuration rather than a dimension anyone picked, and a reader who wants to know how wide the model is must multiply out the table rather than look it up.

    ConfigurationTreesMax depthInner nodes per tree upper boundFused width
    Heloc, Tencent2037140280
    Amazon-P, ModelNet40190371,3302,660
    Amazon-C1904152,8505,700
    Github150712719,05038,100
    Read the last row of that table carefully. The rows are the paper's own Table IV configurations, not invented ones. A full binary tree of depth 7 has inner nodes, and Github is configured with 150 trees at maximum depth 7 — so up to rule slots per vertex, and a fused vector up to entries wide. Every other dataset stays under three thousand. This is arithmetic the paper leaves to the reader, and it is the single largest cost in the method.
    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — the two-tree ensemble, assembled. Use the paper's Figure 2 trees: has questions (depth 0) and (depth 1); has (depth 0), (depth 1) and (depth 1). With the weights are for and for .

    Vertex (T₁) (T₂)Width
    P 5
    Q 5
    R 5
    Check the width: , and every row has five entries.
    The widths add because concatenation is the operation. A sum would have produced a width of 3 — the length of the longer block — and would have merged T₂'s third question with nothing.
    Confirm that each row is exactly its two blocks, in order, with no mixing.
    This is what preserves the block structure. Had the paper summed the blocks instead, the first entry of would have been either way — but the second — from T₁ and from T₂ — would have collapsed to a single , and no later layer could have recovered the fact that two different trees both failed.
    Note that Q and R have different rows even though both fail the same number of questions in some sense — Q fails two, R fails five.
    And more importantly the pattern differs, not just the count. Two vertices with the same number of failures but at different depths would also differ, because depth is baked into the magnitudes. The encoding is of patterns, not counts.
    One efficiency observation, since it explains the table above. Most vertices in this walk have rows that are mostly zero — P's is entirely zero, Q's has two nonzeros out of five. In a real ensemble the same holds: a vertex fails only those questions its features fall outside, and for a tree ensemble fitted to real data that is a minority of the questions. So the rule embedding is sparse, which is why the width of tens of thousands is not as ruinous as it first appears. The paper does not say whether it exploits this; a dense implementation of per vertex on 37,700 vertices would need on the order of a billion floating-point entries at the largest settings.

    Next: Equation (9), where the two knowledge embeddings finally meet. It is the paper's central mechanism, and reading it is easier now than it would have been at any earlier point.
    5.14 · Equation (9)

    Equation (9): the fusion, and exactly what the Hadamard product buys

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONEquation (9) defines the fusion in two steps: first the structure-aware embedding , formed by the expanded Hadamard product in which the single column is broadcast across all columns of ; then the knowledge-embedded feature .Multiply every vertex's row of rule values by that vertex's single structural number, then place the scaled row and the original row side by side.
    The paper writes the two symbols with a diacritic to keep them apart — the input rule embedding and the output structure-aware one. (Their text extraction loses the accent, so a reader working from plain text will see the same letter twice; the figure and the original PDF distinguish them.)
    SymbolWhat it means
    the structural embedding from Equation (3) — one number per vertex
    the rule embedding from Equation (8) — numbers per vertex
    the Hadamard product, expanded: the one-column operand is broadcast across every column of the other
    the structure-aware embedding — the scaled copy, same width as
    concatenation, giving a vector twice as wide
    the knowledge-embedded feature that replaces the raw features at the network's input

    Why the paper says plain concatenation would fail. Its stated reason is the dimension disparity: has one column and has , so concatenating them directly would give a vector of entries in which a single structural number has to compete with hundreds of rule entries. The paper's word for the consequence is underfitting — the network can too easily ignore the one entry that carries structure.

    What the operation actually does, stated precisely. Because has a single column, the broadcast means every entry of a vertex's row is multiplied by the same scalar: for every . So the Hadamard step is a per-vertex rescaling of the entire rule row, not a column-by-column selection. Two consequences follow, and both are worth carrying.

    • It cannot make the columns of differ from one another. One scalar multiplies the whole row, so the relative sizes of a vertex's rule entries are untouched. The structural number cannot say "this rule matters more to me than that one" — only "all of my rule values count for more, or less".
    • It cannot amplify. comes out of a sigmoid, so every entry lies strictly in , and a per-row factor below 1 shrinks the row. High-degree vertices are shrunk less than low-degree ones — a reweighting, which is what the design needs, but not the increase the paper's wording suggests.
    And here is what the concatenation buys, which is more than it looks. Let the network's first linear layer be , split into its top and bottom halves . Applying it to gives — two different linear readings of the same rule row, mixed by the vertex's structural scalar. So the structure does not enter as an extra piece of information; it enters as a per-vertex weight deciding how much of the first reading to blend into the second. That is a meaningful mechanism, and it is a more precise description of the fusion than "integrating two types of knowledge".
    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — the arithmetic, on two vertices. Let , with rule rows and — deliberately identical, so that only the structural number differs.

    Give A degree 4 and B degree 1, and take from the structural encoder's card. Then and .
    The two vertices have the same rules and different structure — exactly the case the fusion exists to handle.
    Scale: and .
    Both rows shrank, and A's shrank less. Note the ratio within each row is still 2:4 — the scaling preserved it, as the first bullet above says.
    Concatenate: and .
    The last two entries are identical because the original rows were. The two vertices differ only in the first two entries.
    Apply one output dimension with and . Then the pre-activation is , giving for A and for B.
    This is the two-readings picture made concrete. The first reading picks out the first rule entry (value 2) and is weighted by the structural scalar; the second picks out the second entry (value 4) unweighted. The structural number moves the result by 0.27 — a small but real effect, and its size is set entirely by , which is learned.
    A check worth running on the design. Suppose the Hadamard step were removed and — the same row placed twice. Then the same computation gives v">, which is one linear reading, not two. So the scaling is not decoration: without it the concatenation would be exactly redundant, and the network would gain nothing from the doubled width. The Hadamard product is what makes the second half of differ from the first — and by how much is the structural signal.

    Next: Equation (10), the two-line definition of RD-HGNN and DD-HGNN — after which the method chapter is essentially complete, with only the two variants' justification and the laboratories remaining.
    5.15 · Equation (10)

    Equation (10): the two models, and a confound worth noticing

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONEquation (10) defines the paper's two models in two lines: for RD-HGNN, and for DD-HGNN. Both receive the incidence matrix and run the same network layer, Equation (1); they differ only in what arrives as the feature matrix.RD feeds the network the rule embedding alone. DD feeds it the fused vector — rule embedding plus structure. Same network, different input.
    Read the two lines against each other and the difference is exactly one term: , the fusion, which is what brings — the structural embedding — into the picture.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the rule embedding , from the boosted ensemble and the features
    the structural embedding — written here as a function of because the paper passes the whole dataset; what it actually reads is
    the fusion function — MDK-Fusion, Equation (9)
    the incidence matrix, supplied to the network in both models
    the network: Equation (1) applied as many times as there are layers

    The naming, decoded. Rule-Driven means the model's input is the rules and nothing else. Dual-Driven means both kinds of knowledge drive it. And because the fusion is Equation (9), DD's input is , while RD's is just .

    Here is a confound the two-line form makes visible, and it matters for reading the ablation. RD's network input has columns; DD's has . So switching from RD to DD changes two things at once — it adds the structural knowledge and it doubles the width of the first weight matrix. If DD beats RD, part of the gain may come from the extra capacity rather than from the structural information. A clean ablation would compare DD against a model with the same input and no structural content — for instance , whose degeneracy the previous card established — or against a version where the broadcast scalar is a learned per-vertex parameter rather than a degree-derived one. The paper runs neither comparison. This does not invalidate its result; it bounds what the result can be said to show.

    One more thing worth being precise about: RD is not structure-free. Both models pass to the network, so in RD the structure still enters — through the smoothing, exactly as in every prior hypergraph network. What RD omits is the structure as an explicit feature. The word "Rule-Driven" therefore means "rules are the only embedded knowledge", not "the model ignores the graph". A reader who takes it the second way will misread the whole ablation.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — trace what each model's network actually sees. Use the two-tree ensemble from Figure 2, so , and a vertex with rule row and structural value .

    RD-HGNN inputDD-HGNN inputWidth

So the width alone cannot explain DD's advantage in full — but the comparison needed to establish that is a model with the same width and a non-redundant, non-structural second block, which the paper does not run.
    What Chapter 6 will therefore be able to say, and what it will not. The DD-versus-RD gap is evidence that the combination helps, given the architecture. It is not clean evidence that structural knowledge is what helps, because width and content moved together. Whether that gap is larger on datasets with bigger hyperedges — which is the paper's own prediction — is a separate and more informative check, and it is the one to look for in the results tables.

    Next: the paper's own discussion of which model to choose — Section IV-D-2, where it states a prediction about when each variant should win, and which dataset property it expects to drive the difference.
    5.16 · Section IV-D-2

    RD or DD: the paper's prediction, and how to test it

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThe paper makes a conditional recommendation: RD-HGNN is "suitable for scenarios where vertex features dominate and structural information is relatively sparse", while DD-HGNN "is more appropriate for hypergraphs with rich high-order connectivity". It then cites an experimental observation in support: on datasets with higher average hyperedge degree, DD-HGNN's improvement over RD-HGNN is "more stable".One model is for data where the features carry the signal; the other is for data where the connections do. The paper says the difference shows up mainly on datasets with big group relations.

    This is a testable claim, and it is worth stating exactly what would confirm it. The claim has three parts, each checkable separately: (i) the per-dataset gap between DD and RD should be larger where the average hyperedge degree is larger; (ii) the gap should be positive on those datasets — DD should not lose; (iii) the phrase "more stable" should mean something specific, such as a smaller spread across the five random seeds the paper reports, or a consistently positive sign across the datasets in that group.

    Part of the claimWhat would confirm itWhat would weaken it
    Larger gap where relations are biggerA positive association between average edge degree and the DD − RD difference across the ten datasetsA flat or negative association — the grouping would then be arbitrary
    DD wins on structure-rich dataAll six hypergraph datasets show DD ≥ RDAny dataset where the ordering reverses
    "More stable"A smaller seed-to-seed spread for DD on those datasets than for RDNo reported spread, which is what the paper's tables do in fact provide — so this part is untestable from the paper alone
    The word "stable" is doing a lot of work in the original sentence and carries no measurable content. Stability is not printed anywhere. If the authors meant "the improvement is consistently positive", they could have said so; if they meant "the variance across seeds is smaller", that number exists in their runs but is not reported. Read charitably, the sentence is an informal way of saying "the pattern holds across those datasets" — and that reading is checkable, because it reduces to the sign of a difference on each row.

    The practical recommendations that follow. The paper suggests RD for "credit scoring or recommendation with sparse relations" and DD for "scientific collaboration networks, brain connectivity analysis, or 3D object recognition". These map onto specific datasets in its own table: Heloc is the credit data, and DBLP-Conf, CA-Cora, CC-Cora and ModelNet40 are the collaboration, co-citation and 3D ones. So the recommendations are not general claims about domains; they are claims about those rows, dressed as guidance.

    A useful habit when a paper offers deployment guidance. Turn each recommendation into the row it was derived from. "Use DD for scientific collaboration networks" is really "use DD on DBLP-Conf", which is one dataset with one hyperedge construction and one set of hyperparameters. The generalisation to the domain is the authors' extrapolation, not their evidence — and it is worth knowing which of the two you are reading.
    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — how to test the prediction with the numbers the paper actually gives. Suppose — for illustration only, since the real tables are Chapter 6's business — that the DD − RD gap is , and points on three datasets whose average edge degrees are 982.2, 4.5 and 2.0 respectively.

    Rank the ten datasets by average edge degree and rank them by DD − RD gap. If the prediction holds, the two orderings should agree in direction.
    This is a rank correlation, and it is a weak test by design — it needs only the ordering to line up, not the magnitudes. A weak test is the right one here, because with ten points and one random seed the magnitudes are unlikely to be informative.
    Check the sign separately. The prediction is not merely that the gap grows — it is that DD wins on structure-rich data.
    Growing but negative would satisfy a correlation and contradict the claim. Whenever a paper predicts a pattern, check that you are testing the pattern and not just a proxy for it.
    Finally, ask what would falsify it. If DD and RD were within noise on every dataset, or if the largest gaps fell on the four plain-graph datasets, the grouping would be unsupported.
    Having a falsification condition in mind before looking at the table is what stops the eye from finding a story in whatever pattern happens to be there. Ten datasets offer plenty of accidental patterns.
    This is the exercise Chapter 6 performs on the real numbers. The preparatory work is done here: you know which quantity to extract (the DD − RD gap per dataset), which axis to sort by (average edge degree from Table I), and what would count as a refutation.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhich dataset property does the paper expect to determine whether DD beats RD?

    APPLYIn the illustrative numbers above, what is the gap on the dataset with average edge degree 4.5? points

    TRANSFERThe paper recommends DD for "scientific collaboration networks". What is the status of that recommendation?

    Next: the paper's positioning against its nearest predecessor, BGNN — the one comparison in the method chapter that is about the literature rather than about equations.
    5.17 · Section IV-D-1

    The line against BGNN: what is taken from the trees

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThe paper positions itself against BGNN, a prior method that combines boosted trees with graph neural networks. Its stated distinction is that BGNN "employ[s] GBDT as a preprocessing module that transforms heterogeneous tabular node features into representations subsequently refined by GNNs", whereas this paper encodes both rule content and rule position explicitly and fuses them with hypergraph structural knowledge through MDK-Fusion.Both methods put a tree ensemble in front of a graph network. The difference the paper claims is what each one takes out of the trees.

    The distinction, stated at its sharpest. A fitted boosted ensemble offers two quite different things. It offers an output: run a vertex's features through it and get a prediction, or a leaf index, or some function of the leaves. And it offers a structure: a set of questions, arranged by depth, which describe the feature space the ensemble learned to carve up. BGNN, on the paper's account, takes the first. This paper takes the second.

    Taking the ensemble's outputTaking the ensemble's questions
    What is usedThe fitted model as a function: features in, a representation outThe inner nodes and their depths
    What it depends onThe ensemble's accuracy — a better ensemble gives a better representationThe questions only; the ensemble's accuracy is irrelevant
    InterpretabilityNone — the output is a vectorFull — each coordinate is a readable predicate
    LengthChosen by the designerForced by the ensemble: one coordinate per question
    Fails whenThe ensemble is poorly fitted, or its output is low-dimensionalThe ensemble asks few questions, or the same question repeatedly
    A caveat about verifying this, stated honestly. The characterisation above is the taught paper's summary of BGNN. To check it properly you have to read BGNN, and this site has not — so treat the table as a description of the contrast the paper draws, not as an independently verified account of what BGNN does. If the distinction turns out to be thinner than the paper suggests, the novelty claim narrows accordingly. Whenever a paper's novelty rests on a contrast with one specific predecessor, that predecessor is the first thing worth reading yourself.

    Why the distinction, if it holds, is substantive. The two choices differ in what they inherit from the tree ensemble. Taking the output means inheriting its errors: if the ensemble is wrong about a vertex, its representation is wrong in an unreadable way. Taking the questions means inheriting its vocabulary: even a poorly fitted ensemble's questions are legible predicates, and a vertex's answers to them are facts about the vertex rather than predictions about it. This also explains why this paper can discard the ensemble's accuracy entirely, as earlier cards noted.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — the two extractions, from one fitted ensemble. Take the two-tree ensemble of Figure 2 and a vertex with features , , .

    • Output extraction. Run the vertex down both trees. In it takes the branch → false, then → false, landing in some leaf; in it takes → true, then one of the two depth-1 questions. The extraction is the leaf indices, or the leaves' values, as a short vector — length two here, one entry per tree, regardless of tree size.
    • Question extraction. Evaluate all five inner-node predicates against the vertex: . Length five, one entry per question.
    Compare the two vectors' dependence on the ensemble's correctness. The leaf vector changes if the ensemble is refitted with a different random seed, because different trees mean different leaves. The question vector also changes — but locally: only the coordinates whose predicates moved change, and each coordinate still says something legible about the vertex. That locality is the practical difference between the two designs, and it is why the paper's embedding can be audited by a human while an output-based embedding cannot.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhat does the paper say distinguishes its use of GBDT from BGNN's?

    APPLYUnder output-based extraction with 2 trees, the representation has 2 entries. Under question-based extraction with the same two trees, how many entries does it have? entries

    TRANSFERA paper's novelty rests on a contrast with one specific predecessor. What is the first thing to do?

    Laboratory 1 · Equation (1)

    Laboratory: run the smoothing layer yourself

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThis laboratory evaluates one application of the propagation operator from Equation (1) — — on a four-vertex hypergraph whose hyperedges you control. The weight matrix and the parameter matrix are set to the identity and the nonlinearity is omitted, so that the arithmetic of the propagation is visible without a learned transform obscuring it.Slide the four values, press the button, and watch one layer of neighbourhood averaging happen — including what it does to the spread of the values.

    What to look for while you play. Three things, in this order. First, watch a single vertex's value after one step and check it against the walkthrough you read in Equation (1)'s card. Second, watch the range — the gap between the largest and smallest value — because that is the quantity that measures how much the layer has smoothed. Third, press the button repeatedly and watch the range shrink towards zero: that is over-smoothing, and you are causing it one application at a time.

    Two deliberate omissions, so you do not misread the numbers. means every hyperedge is weighted equally — in a trained model these weights are learnable. and omitted means no learned mixing happens between feature channels; with the real the output is a learned linear combination, and with the sigmoid applied to values like these every entry would saturate to nearly , erasing the differences you are about to watch.

    Hypergraph smoothing sandbox — Equation (1)
    Vertices v1–v4 with hyperedges e1={1,2}, e2={2,3}, e3={2,4} — a star with v2 at its centre. Optionally add e4={1,2,3}, which makes vertex 2 a hub in a group of three.

    Task 1 — reproduce the card's walkthrough. Leave all four sliders at their defaults and the extra hyperedge off, then press Apply one layer once.

    Read the vertex degrees shown under the sliders: they should be (1, 3, 1, 1), because vertex 2 belongs to all three hyperedges and the others to one each.
    If the degrees do not match, something has been changed — check the checkbox first. Getting the degrees right before stepping is what makes the next number interpretable.
    Read the four values after the step. They should be close to , , , — matching the walkthrough in Equation (1)'s card to three decimals.
    This is the check that the arithmetic in the card was not a special case. If your numbers match, the card's five moves — damp, collect, average, distribute, damp — are the actual computation.
    Read the range. It should have fallen from to about .
    This is the number to remember. One layer contracts the spread by roughly a quarter. That single ratio is the whole of over-smoothing: apply the layer times and the range is roughly for some .

    Task 2 — cause over-smoothing. Press Apply one layer five more times, watching the range after each press.

    Record the range after steps 2, 3 and 4, and compute the ratio between consecutive ranges.
    The ratio should be roughly constant, which is what makes the contraction geometric rather than accidental. A constant ratio is the signature of a linear operator being raised to a power.
    Keep pressing until the range is below about 1, then stop and look at the four values.
    They will all be close to the graph's weighted average. The information has not been destroyed by an error — it has been averaged away by exactly the operation the method is built on.
    Press Reset and try again with the slider values replaced by — the same multiset in a different arrangement. Compare eight steps of each.
    Both converge to the same constant, because the limit depends on the weights each vertex carries in the stationary distribution, not on the initial arrangement. Whenever a process forgets its input, the input cannot have been what the process was for.

    Task 3 — give the hub a group to belong to. Tick add hyperedge e4 = {1,2,3} and press Apply one layer from the defaults.

    Check what changed before pressing: vertex degrees are now (2, 4, 2, 1) and hyperedge degrees are (2, 2, 2, 3).
    Adding one relation changed three vertices' degrees and added a relation of size three. Everything downstream of the incidence matrix is now different — which is the point of the exercise.
    Press once and compare the output with the three-hyperedge case.
    The values differ in every coordinate. A single hyperedge changed the entire layer's output, which is what makes the construction of hyperedges — the of Chapter 2's discussion — a modelling decision rather than a preprocessing detail.

    Laboratory 2 · Equations (4)–(9)

    Laboratory: turn a tree ensemble into a vector

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThis laboratory runs Equations (4) through (9) on the two-tree ensemble of Figure 2. It computes the content bits by testing every inner-node predicate against the vertex's features, the position weights from each node's depth, the per-tree block as their product, the concatenated row , and finally the fused vector with fixed at for display.Slide three feature values and two weighting knobs, and watch each question in a two-tree ensemble turn into a number — then watch those numbers become the vector the network actually receives.

    What to look for. Three things. First, that a satisfied question contributes zero — the inverted convention from Equation (5), which is the single easiest thing to get backwards. Second, that the nonzero entries are exactly the depth weights of the questions that failed, so the vector's magnitudes come from a small set rather than a continuum. Third, that the fused vector is always twice as wide as , and that its first half is the second half scaled by the same number for a given vertex.

    is held fixed here. A real vertex's structural value comes from its degree through Equation (3), which needs the hypergraph — this laboratory isolates the rule side, so the structural factor is pinned at one value to keep the arithmetic visible. The scaling behaviour is what matters: multiply any entry of the first half by and you recover the corresponding entry of the second half.

    6.0 · Experimental settings

    What the experiments actually are

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONThe paper evaluates two models — RD-HGNN and DD-HGNN — on ten datasets under two evaluation settings, against five baselines drawn from three methodological families, with each configuration run five times under different random seeds and reported as a mean with a standard deviation.Ten datasets, five competing methods, two ways of testing, five runs each. That is the whole experimental design in one sentence.
    ComponentWhat the paper usesWhere it is documented
    DatasetsFour plain graphs (Cora, Github, Amazon-P, Amazon-C) and six hypergraphs (CA-Cora, CC-Cora, DBLP-Conf, Tencent, ModelNet40, Heloc)Table I
    BaselinesMLP and GBDT (feature-only), GCN and HGNN (structure-oriented), TLF (trees plus a network)Table I's setup plus Tables V and VI
    SettingsTransductive and production — the latter combining transductive and inductive predictionsTables II and III for the splits
    ModelsRD-HGNN and DD-HGNN, plus the structural ablation implied by their differenceTables V–X
    RunsFive random seeds per configuration; results reported as mean and standard deviationStated once, in Section V-A

    The three families of baseline are the part worth noticing, because they determine what the results can show. Two baselines see only features, so they answer "is a graph or hypergraph model needed at all?". Two see only structure, so they answer "does adding knowledge beat the standard structural approach?". One combines trees with a neural network, so it answers the sharpest question: "does this paper's particular way of combining them beat the nearest predecessor?". Each family carries a different burden, and the results should be read family by family rather than as one undifferentiated table of numbers.

    The presence of a feature-only baseline is a design decision worth crediting. On most of these datasets, a gradient-boosted tree ensemble over the raw features is a strong competitor — that is the whole motivation for the paper's rule encoder. Reporting GBDT's numbers on the same splits means a reader can see whether the graph machinery earns its keep at all, rather than only whether it beats other graph methods. Many graph papers omit this comparison.

    Two things the setup paragraph does not state, both of which matter for interpretation. First, how many hyperparameters were tuned per model, and whether the baselines received the same tuning effort as the proposed models — an untuned baseline flatters any proposal. Second, what the "predefined task" of the tree pre-training is, which the method chapter also leaves open. Neither is a fatal omission, but together they bound how much weight the numbers can carry.

    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — count the comparisons before reading any numbers. With two proposed models, three families of baseline and two settings, the number of distinct claims the experiments could support is larger than it first appears.

    Within the transductive setting: DD against HGNN (the standard structural baseline), DD against GBDT (the standard feature baseline), and DD against RD (the ablation).
    Three different questions. The first asks whether knowledge embedding beats conventional hypergraph convolution; the second asks whether it beats ignoring the graph entirely; the third asks what the structural encoder contributes.
    Repeat all three in the production setting, where the inductive vertices make the task harder.
    A method that helps transductively may do nothing inductively, because the test vertices were visible during training in the first case and not in the second. Reporting both is what lets a reader separate the two.
    Now note which of these six comparisons the abstract's headline numbers could be quoting — and that the abstract names none of them.
    This is the question Chapter 3 raised and could not settle. With the design now in hand, you can at least enumerate the candidates, and Chapter 6 will recompute them from the tables until one matches.
    A habit that pays off immediately here. Before reading a results table, write down the comparisons you intend to check. Otherwise the eye lands on whichever number is largest and the reading becomes confirmation rather than evaluation. The six comparisons above are the checklist for this paper, and every remaining card in this chapter refers back to them.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhy does the paper include MLP and GBDT as baselines when both ignore the graph entirely?

    APPLYThe paper reports five random seeds per configuration. If a table column has three hypothetical methods, how many trained runs back that column (ignoring any tuning runs)?

    Next: the baselines themselves, taken one at a time — what each does, and what beating it would and would not demonstrate.
    6.1 · Table I

    Table I: the ten exam papers

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONA dataset-statistics table reports, for each benchmark, the descriptors that determine how hard learning on it is: the number of vertices |V|, the number of edges or hyperedges |E|, the feature dimension, the average edge degree (how many vertices one relation touches on average), the average vertex degree (how many relations one vertex touches on average), and the number of classes.Table I is the roster of exam papers: it says how big each of the ten datasets is, before any model is trained on them.

    Every results table later in this paper reports scores on exactly these ten datasets, so Table I is the first thing to read if you want to know what the experiments are actually made of. Ten rows split into two families: four ordinary graphs (Cora, Github, Amazon-P, Amazon-C), where each relation joins exactly two vertices, and six true hypergraphs (CA-Cora, DBLP-Conf, CC-Cora, Tencent, ModelNet40, Heloc), where one relation may join any number.

    Before reading a single number, separate the two degree columns — they point in opposite directions and are the most common source of confusion in this table. Average edge degree = how many vertices one relation involves (it is always exactly 2 for the four ordinary graphs; for a hypergraph it can be large). Average vertex degree = how many relations one vertex belongs to.

    Original Table I (Feng et al., TPAMI 2026). The first four rows are graph datasets; the last six are hypergraphs.
    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — read one row, cell by cell. Take the Cora row. 2,708 papers (vertices). 7,440 citation relations (edges). 1,433 words (features — every paper is represented as a bag of words). Average edge degree 2, because a citation is always between two papers. Average vertex degree 3.9, meaning the average paper is cited by or cites about four others. 7 classes, the number of topics to be predicted. That row is the complete CV of one task: a 7-way classification problem with 2,708 samples.

    Walk 2 — two rows side by side, to see graph versus hypergraph. Cora and CA-Cora are the same corpus drawn two ways. As an ordinary graph: 7,440 pairwise edges, average edge degree 2. As a hypergraph: 970 hyperedges, average edge degree 4.5. Far fewer relations carry the same crowd structure, because each hyperedge can embrace several papers at once.

    Take the extreme row, DBLP-Conf: only 20 hyperedges, embracing 4,057 authors, with average edge degree 982.2 and average vertex degree 4.8.
    Twenty relations is startlingly few — this is the row that shows what a hyperedge buys you.
    Multiply: 20 × 982.2 = 19,644. That is the total number of author-slots across all hyperedges — one author who sits in three hyperedges is counted three times.
    Edge degree is a per-relation count, so multiplying it by the number of relations converts it into the total number of memberships.
    Divide that total back over the 4,057 distinct authors: 19,644 ÷ 4,057 = 4.84, which rounds to the 4.8 printed in the vertex-degree column.
    The two columns now agree. This is the check to run whenever a table reports both degrees: (average edge degree) × |E| should reconstruct (average vertex degree) × |V|.
    But that check is conditional, and this very table shows why. The identity holds only when both columns count the same thing. Github obeys it: 2 × 144,501 ÷ 37,700 = 7.67, matching the printed 7.7. Amazon-P instead obeys the other convention, |E| ÷ |V| = 238,163 ÷ 7,650 = 31.13, matching its printed 31.1. And Cora obeys neither — 2|E|/|V| gives 5.49 and |E|/|V| gives 2.75, while the table prints 3.9. So Table I mixes degree conventions across rows. Keep that in your pocket: the point of this walk was not that the table is tidy, but that you can now tell a tidy row from an untidy one.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTAND"Average edge degree" and "average vertex degree" — what does each count?

    APPLYHow many of Table I's ten datasets are true hypergraphs? datasets

    TRANSFERModelNet40 is a collection of 3D shapes. Why does this paper use it as a hypergraph?

    How this paper uses it: every later table — V, VI, VII — reports scores on these ten rows, and the four/six split is the paper's own axis of comparison: the authors claim the method helps most on the six true hypergraphs and merely matches strong baselines on the four ordinary graphs. Next: card 90p turns the degree check into a drill.
    6.1 · Practice

    Practice: read a dataset table without being fooled

    Practice set for card 90 — the number of items here is whatever it takes to cover this topic, not a fixed quota.
    WHAT

    This set drills one skill: reading a dataset-statistics table and knowing, cell by cell, whether the numbers in it are consistent. It is a separate card because three exercises cannot cover it — the topic has one central trap and four distinct ways of falling into it.

    Keep these four results from card 90 in hand; every item below uses one of them.

    • Edge degree counts vertices per relation; vertex degree counts relations per vertex. In the four ordinary graphs edge degree is exactly 2 by definition.
    • For a hypergraph, multiplying edge degree by |E| gives the total number of memberships (an author in three hyperedges counts three times).
    • Dividing that total by |V| must reproduce the printed vertex degree: (edge degree × |E|) ÷ |V| ≈ vertex degree.
    • That check is conditional: it fails if the two columns were computed under different conventions. Cora is the worked counter-example.
    If any of the four is not yet solid, go back to card 90 before starting. The exercises below will not re-explain them.
    EXAMPLE

    One fully worked prototype, so you know the shape of every item below. Take the Github row: |V| = 37,700 papers, |E| = 144,501 edges, printed average vertex degree 7.7.

    Github is an ordinary graph, so every relation joins exactly two vertices and the average edge degree is 2.
    Identify the family first — it fixes one of the two columns outright.
    Total memberships = 2 × 144,501 = 289,002.
    Each edge contributes two endpoints, so multiplying by 2 converts edges into endpoint-slots.
    Spread over the vertices: 289,002 ÷ 37,700 = 7.666…, which rounds to 7.67.
    This is the predicted vertex degree under the standard convention.
    Compare with the table: 7.7 printed, 7.67 predicted — a match to the printed precision. Github is a consistent row.
    Notice what a match does not mean: it does not certify the other nine rows. Each row has to be checked on its own.
    EXERCISES

    UNDERSTANDWhy is the average edge degree exactly 2 in all four ordinary-graph rows?

    UNDERSTANDIn a hypergraph row, what does the |E| column count?

    APPLYGithub: compute 2|E| ÷ |V| = (2 × 144,501) ÷ 37,700. Give two decimals. dimensionless

    APPLYAmazon-P: compute |E| ÷ |V| = 238,163 ÷ 7,650. Give two decimals. dimensionless

    APPLYDBLP-Conf: how many total memberships do its hyperedges contain? Compute (average edge degree) × |E| = 982.2 × 20. memberships

    APPLYCora prints average vertex degree 3.9. Which convention reproduces that number?

    TRANSFERA new dataset is described as an ordinary graph with |V| = 1,000, |E| = 5,000 and average vertex degree 10. Is that description internally consistent?

    TRANSFERModelNet40's hypergraph was built by linking each point to its k nearest neighbours. If the authors rebuilt it with a much larger k, which columns of Table I would change?

    Where this leads: the Cora row is not a curiosity — it is one of the ten findings the critique chapter audits, where several rows of Table I turn out to mix conventions. Having done this set, you can check that claim yourself instead of taking it on trust.
    6.3 · Table IV

    Table IV: the hyperparameters, and the model size they imply

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONTable IV lists, for each of the ten datasets, the six settings that determine the model's configuration: the learning rate, the number of trees in the pre-trained ensemble, the dimension of the hidden layer, each tree's maximum depth, and the two position-mapping coefficients and .Six numbers per dataset. Read together they describe not just a training recipe but the size of the model — which is what this card works out.

    The two columns that determine the rule embedding's width. The number of trees and the maximum depth are the inputs to the arithmetic from Equation (8)'s card: a full binary tree of depth contains inner nodes, so the rule embedding's width is at most (trees inner nodes per tree). Everything else in the table affects training; these two affect what the model is.

    ConfigurationTreesMax depthInner nodes per tree upper boundFused width

The bound is an upper limit because trees are often grown shallower than the maximum depth allowed; the paper does not report realised depths, so the true widths lie between this bound and roughly times the depth actually reached.
    SymbolWhat it means
    the number of trees, the table's second column
    the maximum depth, the table's fifth column

    Look at where the largest configuration lands. Github — a plain graph dataset with 37,700 vertices — is given 150 trees at depth 7, an order of magnitude heavier than any other setting. The configuration is largest exactly where, according to the results tables, the method gains least. That is not an error, and it may simply be what validation selected; but it is the kind of fact that makes you want to see the per-dataset tuning curves, which the paper does not show.
    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — read the table as a model description. Take Cora: learning rate , trees, hidden dimension , maximum depth , , .

    Compute the rule embedding's width bound: a depth-4 full binary tree has inner nodes, so questions per vertex, and the fused vector is at most entries wide.
    Compare that with the raw feature dimension: Cora has 1,433 features. So the knowledge embedding is of the same order of magnitude as the original features — neither negligible nor dominant.
    Now check the , pair against the search range: and , both inside .
    The pair is at a corner of the grid — the largest and the smallest available. From Equation (6)'s card, gives the sharpest decay the grid allows, so Cora receives the strongest position weighting in the whole table.
    Note that the hidden dimension is for every one of the ten datasets.
    One width for datasets spanning 2,708 to 37,700 vertices. A single fixed capacity across a fourteen-fold range of scale is a deliberate simplification, and it is the sort of setting you would expect a reviewer to ask about — a larger dataset might benefit from a wider layer, and a small one might overfit a wide one.
    What the table documents and what it does not. Documented: every setting it names, per dataset, and the / search range in the text. Not documented: the search space for the learning rate, the tree count or the depth; how many seeds the search was run with; the training time or memory; and whether the baseline methods received comparable tuning effort. The last omission is the one that matters most for interpreting the results — an untuned baseline makes any proposal look better, and no column of this table reveals how much care each column of Table V received.

    6.4 · Table V

    Table V: the main results, recomputed cell by cell

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONTable V reports vertex-classification accuracy under the transductive setting for seven methods across ten datasets, each cell being the mean over five random seeds with the standard deviation alongside. The final row gives each method's average rank across the ten datasets, where a method's rank on a dataset is its position among the seven, and ties are broken by assigning the best of the tied positions.Seven methods, ten datasets, one accuracy each. The bottom row turns those seventy numbers into one rank per method — and that row is the one this card is about.

    The columns, named once. MLP and GBDT see only vertex features. GCN and HGNN see the structure — a graph convolution and a hypergraph convolution respectively. TLF combines boosted trees with a network, and is the nearest relative of this paper's own rule encoder. RD-HGNN and DD-HGNN are the paper's two models. Bold marks the best entry in each row; on four of the ten rows the bold entry is a baseline rather than a proposed model.

    Original Table V (Feng et al., TPAMI 2026): accuracies under the transductive setting, mean ± standard deviation over five seeds, with the average-rank row beneath.
    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — the average-rank row, reproduced from the cells above it. This is the paper's own headline statistic, so it is worth computing rather than reading. Rank the seven methods on each dataset, keeping ties, then average each method's ten ranks.

    MethodRank recomputed hereRank printed in Table VMatch?
    MLP6.005.8differs by 0.2
    GCN3.903.9exact
    GBDT5.305.1differs by 0.2
    HGNN3.403.3differs by 0.1
    TLF6.206.1differs by 0.1
    RD-HGNN1.701.7exact
    DD-HGNN1.501.5exact
    The discrepancies are not errors in the table — they are a tie convention. Two rows contain ties: on Tencent, MLP, GBDT and TLF all score 92.85; on Heloc, MLP, GBDT and HGNN all score 71.61. Averaging the tied positions gives each of them a middling rank; assigning the best of the tied positions gives each of them a lower number.
    Recomputing under the best-of-ties convention reproduces the printed row exactly for all seven methods. The table is internally consistent; it simply does not state which convention it uses.
    Because RD and DD are never tied with anything on any of the ten datasets, their ranks are unaffected by the convention: RD sums to 17 and DD to 15, giving 1.70 and 1.50.
    This is the important consequence. The two numbers the paper cares about most are convention-independent — so they can be verified without resolving the ambiguity.
    Now compare with what the paper's own text says: "our methods, RD-HGNN and DD-HGNN, demonstrated exceptional performance with average rankings of 1.9 and 1.7".
    Neither 1.9 nor 1.7 reproduces under any tie convention — and as just established, no convention could affect them, because these two methods never tie. The table prints 1.7/1.5; the text quotes 1.9/1.7. The text's numbers read like the table's row shifted along by one method.

    Walk 2 — the two average gains the text quotes. Section V-B says the methods beat GBDT and HGNN "with average gains of 5.86 and 2.28, respectively". Computing from the cells:

    ComparisonRecomputed from Table VQuoted in the textGap
    DD-HGNN mean − GBDT mean5.860.20
    DD-HGNN mean − HGNN mean2.280.16
    DD-HGNN mean − RD-HGNN meannot quoted—
    Both quoted gains come out roughly 0.2 too high, and the discrepancy is systematic rather than random — which usually means a different column of numbers is being used rather than a slip of arithmetic. One plausible source is a slightly different value in one or two cells; the table region is small and densely set. The honest position is: from the cells as printed, the gains are 5.66 and 2.12, not 5.86 and 2.28. If your reading of a cell differs from this card's, the arithmetic can be redone in a minute — which is precisely why the site gives you the cells and not just the conclusion.
    The third row of that table is worth a moment. DD's mean exceeds RD's by 0.046 of a percentage point — a difference far inside any of the reported standard deviations — yet DD's average rank is better, 1.50 against 1.70. The two statistics disagree because a rank discards the margin: winning by 0.01 and by 10 both count as winning. This is the single cleanest illustration of why a paper reports both, and of why a rank can look decisive where the underlying gap is not.

    6.5 · Table VI

    Table VI: the production setting, and what the delta columns are actually measuring

    WHAT
    DEFINITIONTable VI repeats the comparison under the production setting. Each dataset occupies three rows — Production, Transductive and Inductive — and four methods are reported (GBDT, HGNN, RD-HGNN, DD-HGNN) together with two difference columns, and . The footer row is labelled "Avg. Rank/Avg." and carries average ranks for the four methods and average differences for the two delta columns.Same ten datasets, but now each is tested three ways: the combined production task, its transductive part, and its inductive part. Two extra columns report how much better the proposed models are than the two baselines.

    The three settings per dataset, and how they relate. The production setting combines the two test sets, so its score is the headline. The transductive and inductive rows split that test set: transductive vertices were visible during training with their labels withheld, inductive ones were not present at all. A reader should therefore read the production row as a blend and the other two as its ingredients — and should not expect the production row to equal either one of them.

    Original Table VI (Feng et al., TPAMI 2026): three settings per dataset, four methods, and two difference columns.
    EXAMPLE

    Walk 1 — the delta columns, and which model they use. This is the part a reader cannot guess, so it has to be worked out. Take the Cora Production row: GBDT , HGNN , RD-HGNN , DD-HGNN , with printed deltas and .

    Test DD against the baselines: and . Neither matches the printed deltas.
    So the DD column is not the source, despite it being one of the paper's own models.
    Test RD: and . Both match exactly.
    So the deltas are computed from RD-HGNN on this row — which is also the bolded entry, since RD edges out DD on Cora.
    Now try a hypergraph dataset where DD wins. CA-Cora Production: GBDT , HGNN , RD , DD , printed .
    DD − GBDT exactly, while RD − GBDT . Here the deltas are computed from DD. So the column is not tied to one model.
    Check the rule on all thirty rows: the deltas equal (the better of RD and DD) minus the baseline.
    It holds on twenty-nine of the thirty rows, to within the rounding of the printed cells. The delta columns therefore report the proposed method's best available number against each baseline, switching model from row to row without saying so — which is a legitimate way to present results, but it means the deltas are not measuring one model's performance and cannot be averaged as if they were.

    Walk 2 — the one row that does not reconcile. Github, Production: GBDT , HGNN , RD , DD . The printed is .

    CandidateComputationValue
    RD against HGNN
    DD against HGNN (the better of the two here)
    Printed in Table VI—
    This is the paper's cleanest numerical anomaly, and it is a sign error rather than a rounding error. Both of the proposed models lose to the plain HGNN baseline on this row, by 0.12 and 0.09 points — small, but negative. Printing removes the sign. The dedicated transductive and inductive rows for the same dataset behave differently ( and ), so the anomaly is confined to this one cell. Nothing about the paper's overall conclusion turns on it — but its position matters: it sits in the column that summarises how much better the proposed models are, and it converts a loss into a draw.

    Walk 3 — the footer row. The footer is labelled "Avg. Rank/Avg." and reads , , , for the four methods and , for the two delta columns.

That is a presentational choice worth knowing about, because a reader skimming the bottom row will read six numbers as one family. And the two averages are not mutually consistent either: the reproduces as the Production-row mean against HGNN using RD, while the reproduces under no aggregation tried here — the same computation gives .
